ISO/IEC 27001:2022

Information security management system

ISMS-GDE-01 guide Download .docx Markdown

Guide: the 93 Annex A controls and where the kit covers each

A reading aid that lists every Annex A control number of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 with a short theme in plain words and the kit documents that implement it, for use when building the Statement of Applicability and the control tracker.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.3. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. How to use this guide

Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 lists 93 reference controls in four groups: organisational (5.1 to 5.37), people (6.1 to 6.8), physical (7.1 to 7.14) and technological (8.1 to 8.34). The standard requires you to compare the controls you chose from your risk treatment with this list, confirm that nothing necessary was missed, and record in a Statement of Applicability which controls apply, why, and whether they are implemented.

The tables below give each control number a theme written in this kit's own words. The themes are a memory aid, not the standard's titles; when you need the authoritative text, read the standard itself. The third column names the kit documents that implement the control. Where several documents are listed, the first is the primary one and the others supply records or related rules.

Use the tables in three places:

  1. ISMS-REG-01 Statement of Applicability. The control numbers and themes are prefilled there. For each row decide Applicable Yes or No, write a justification in one or two sentences, set the implementation status, and copy the kit IDs you actually use into the implementing documents column.
  2. ISMS-REG-02 Control implementation tracker. The same 93 rows carry the owner, the evidence, the test method and the last test result for each applicable control. ISMS-PRO-04 explains how controls are tested.
  3. Gap analysis in step 3 of PB-02. Walk the tables with the people who run each area and mark what exists, what exists informally and what does not exist.

Three rules save time at audit. First, a control marked Not applicable needs a justification that an auditor can accept: either no risk in GOV-REG-05 needs it and no requirement in ISMS-REG-03 demands it, or the activity it governs does not happen at all in the scope (for example in-house development where no software is developed). "We use the cloud" is not by itself a justification for excluding the physical controls; it moves most of them to the provider and leaves offices, home working and devices with you. Second, every applicable control needs an owner and evidence that it operates, not only a document. Third, the justification should name the risk or requirement it satisfies, so that when the risk changes the Statement of Applicability can be re-checked.

The 2022 edition also attaches attributes to each control (control type, security property, cybersecurity concept, operational capability, security domain). The kit does not reproduce them. If you want to filter controls by, for example, detective versus preventive, add an attribute column to ISMS-REG-01 and populate it from your own copy of the standard.

6. Controls that most often need attention

Experience of first certifications points to the same handful of controls where a document exists but the evidence does not. Check these first:

  • 5.9 and 7.10. The asset inventory is often a spreadsheet nobody reconciles. GOV-PRO-16 sets a quarterly reconciliation; keep the dated export.
  • 5.18. Access reviews are promised quarterly and performed once. GOV-REG-12 should show four dated entries per system per year, each with the account list that was reviewed.
  • 5.22. Supplier reviews stop after onboarding. GOV-REG-07 needs a review date within twelve months for every Tier 1 supplier.
  • 6.3. Training records show attendance but not currency. GOV-REG-09 should let you compute, for any date, who is overdue.
  • 8.8. Severity windows are written but not measured. GOV-REG-14 should produce the closure measure in ISMS-PRO-04 without manual work.
  • 8.13. Backups run; restores are never tested. GOV-REG-15 needs a test per critical system per quarter with the time taken.
  • 8.15 and 8.16. Logs exist; nobody looks at them. GOV-PRO-14 defines a review cadence; keep the review notes and the alert tickets.
  • 8.32. Emergency changes bypass the record. GOV-REG-11 should hold every production change, including the emergency ones with their retrospective approval.

7. Where the kit leaves decisions to you

The kit cannot decide applicability for you. Controls 7.1 to 7.14 depend on whether you have offices, server rooms or only laptops and a provider; GOV-PRO-17 explains what remains for a cloud only organisation. Controls 8.4, 8.25 to 8.31 and 8.33 apply only where software is developed or materially configured in house. Control 8.30 applies only where development is outsourced. Control 5.23 applies to almost everyone. Record every decision, and its reason, in ISMS-REG-01.

Guide: mandatory documented information and records for ISO/IEC 27001:2022

Lists the documents and records that ISO/IEC 27001:2022 explicitly requires, the kit item that satisfies each, and the further documents that are not required by name but that auditors expect and that make the system run.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 4.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 5.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 7.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 7.5; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 8.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 8.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 8.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 10.2. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Two kinds of documented information

The standard uses one term, documented information, for two things that behave differently. Documents say what you intend to do: the scope, the policy, the risk method, the objectives. They are approved, versioned and reviewed. Records show what you did: an audit report, a risk assessment result, a management review minute, a training record. They are created by running a process and are not edited afterwards. GOV-PRO-01 controls both.

The standard names a short list of items that must exist. Everything else is at your discretion, with one condition: you must keep whatever documented information you yourself decide is needed for the management system to work. In practice, an auditor who finds a process running well without a procedure will accept it; an auditor who finds a process running inconsistently will ask for the procedure that should have prevented it. The discretionary table in section 4 lists what experience says is worth having.

Clause What must exist, in plain words Kit item

6.2 The information security objectives, kept as documented information ISMS-PLN-01, GOV-REG-21
7.5.1 The documented information required by the standard plus what the organisation determines necessary This guide, GOV-REG-01
8.1 Documented information to the extent needed to have confidence that operational processes ran as planned ISMS-PRO-03 and the process documents it lists

Annex A adds its own documentation expectations where a control is applicable, for example topic specific policies (5.1), rules for acceptable use (5.10), supplier agreements (5.20), incident records (5.26 and 5.28), legal requirements (5.31), operating procedures (5.37), confidentiality agreements (6.6), logs (8.15), change records (8.32) and secure development rules (8.25 to 8.28). ISMS-GDE-01 maps each of these to the kit document that provides it.

4. Discretionary documents and why they earn their place

Kit item Why it is worth having
ISMS-PRO-01 and ISMS-REG-03 Clause 4.1 and 4.2 require you to determine issues and interested parties; they do not require a document. Without one, every audit begins with the same hour of questions and no two answers match.
GOV-POL-01 Roles and authorities must be assigned and communicated (5.3). A governance document with a roles table and committee charter is the fastest proof.
ISMS-PLN-02 Clause 7.4 asks you to determine what, when, with whom and how to communicate. A one page plan answers all four at once.
GOV-PRO-01 and GOV-REG-01 Clause 7.5 requires control of documented information; a procedure plus a master list is how organisations of every size do it.
ISMS-PRO-04 Clause 9.1 requires you to determine what to monitor and measure, by what methods and when. Writing it down is the only way to get the same measure twice.
GOV-PRO-02 Clause 9.2 requires an audit programme and audits; a procedure sets independence, grading and reporting rules that stay stable when auditors change.
GOV-PRO-03 Clause 9.3 lists mandatory inputs and outputs; a procedure with an agenda stops them being forgotten.
GOV-PRO-04 Clause 10.2 requires reaction, evaluation, action and review; a procedure sets root cause methods and closure authority.
ISMS-REG-02 Not required by name, but the simplest way to show the 6.1.3 and 9.1 evidence per control.
GOV-CHK-03 A readiness checklist four weeks before an external audit is the cheapest insurance against a stage 1 surprise.
Topic policies (GOV-POL-02, GOV-POL-04, GOV-POL-05, GOV-POL-06) Annex A 5.1 expects topic specific policies where the risks need them; these four cover the topics every organisation has.
Operational procedures (GOV-PRO-06 to GOV-PRO-27) Each implements a group of Annex A controls; they are discretionary only in the sense that you could run the control without writing it down.

5. What auditors look for in each item

  • A control block on every document (identifier, owner, approver, version, dates) and a revision history that matches GOV-REG-01.
  • Approval evidence for the policy, the scope and the risk method: a signature, an approval record or a minute.
  • Dates that make sense. The risk assessment precedes the Statement of Applicability, which precedes the treatment plan; the internal audit and the management review both precede the stage 2 audit.
  • Records that are not editable after the fact, or that carry a change history if they are.
  • Consistency. The scope in ISMS-STM-01, the asset list in GOV-REG-10, the systems in GOV-REG-24 and the risks in GOV-REG-05 describe the same organisation. A system that appears in one and not the others is the first question an auditor asks.
  • Currency. Every document within its review date; every register with entries from the current period.

6. Building your master list

Create GOV-REG-01 before anything else and add every item in sections 2 to 4 as a row with status Draft. As each document is approved, change the status and record the version and location. The master list is then both your project plan and your proof of clause 7.5. ISMS-REG-05 holds the implementation tasks that produce each item; PB-02 gives the order.

Guide: the certification journey from decision to recertification

Walks through every stage of an ISO/IEC 27001 certification, from the business case to the three year recertification, with what each stage demands, the findings that most often derail it, and how to choose a certification body.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 4.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 10.2. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. What certification is and is not

Certification is an independent, accredited body's confirmation that your management system conforms to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and is operating. It is not a statement that you are secure, that no incident will happen, or that every control works perfectly. It says that you have a system that identifies risk, treats it, checks itself and improves. A certificate lasts three years, with surveillance audits in between, and the scope wording on it is the only thing a customer can rely on.

The journey below assumes you are implementing with this kit. PB-02 gives the twelve implementation steps; this guide covers what happens around them and after them.

2. Stage by stage

2.1 Decision and business case

Someone has to decide that certification is worth the cost, and that decision has to be made by the people who will fund it. Write the case in one page: which customers or markets require it, what it costs (certification body fees, internal time, tooling, possibly external support), what it saves (shorter security questionnaires, fewer bespoke audits, lower insurance friction), and the earliest realistic date. Get the Chief Executive Officer to sign GOV-STM-01 at this point, not at the end. A certificate pursued without that signature stalls at the first budget conversation.

2.2 Scope

Decide what the certificate will cover. A narrow scope (one product, one location) is quicker to certify and harder to sell; a wide scope is the reverse. The wording goes into ISMS-STM-01 and later onto the certificate. Two tests: would a customer reading the certificate conclude that the service they buy is covered, and can you honestly include every system that touches that service? Scopes that exclude the support team, the identity provider or the build pipeline do not survive a careful customer or a careful auditor.

2.3 Gap analysis

Compare what exists with clauses 4 to 10 and with the Annex A tables in ISMS-GDE-01. Record three states: exists and evidenced, exists informally, does not exist. GOV-REG-28 is built for this. The output is the task list in ISMS-REG-05 with owners and weeks. Resist the urge to write policies before the gap analysis is finished; the gap analysis tells you which policies you actually need.

2.4 Risk assessment

Run GOV-PRO-05 across the scope. The method must be written before the first assessment, and the first assessment must be complete before the Statement of Applicability. Auditors read risk registers closely: they expect risks that reflect your business (your data, your providers, your people), not a generic list, and they expect the treatment column to point to real controls and real tasks.

2.5 Statement of Applicability

Complete ISMS-REG-01. Every one of the 93 controls gets a decision and a reason. The Statement of Applicability is the document most referenced during stage 2, because the auditor uses it as the sampling frame. Its version number appears in your scope wording and in the audit report; change control it strictly.

2.6 Implementation

Work through ISMS-REG-05. Policies and procedures are approved under GOV-PRO-01, controls are implemented and evidenced in ISMS-REG-02, registers start to fill. The common mistake is to treat this as a writing exercise. A procedure that has never been followed is worth nothing at audit; a control that has been operating for three months with records is worth everything.

2.7 Operating evidence

Certification bodies expect to see the management system operating, not only designed. Plan for at least three months of operation before stage 2, during which the following have all happened at least once: an access review, a vulnerability cycle with closures, a change through change management, a backup restore test, an incident or an incident exercise, awareness training with records, a supplier review, a risk review, a quarterly performance report under ISMS-PRO-04, and a steering committee meeting with minutes. Some bodies accept less for a very small organisation; none accept zero.

2.8 Internal audit

Clause 9.2 requires an internal audit covering the whole system before certification. Use GOV-PRO-02 and the checklist ISMS-REG-04. The auditor must be independent of the areas audited; in a small organisation that usually means an external person or a trained colleague from an unrelated function. The audit must produce findings. An internal audit report with no findings is itself a finding, because no first implementation is clean. Record the corrective actions in GOV-REG-03 and close or at least plan every one before stage 2.

2.9 Management review

Clause 9.3 requires a management review with the inputs listed in GOV-PRO-03, minuted with GOV-TPL-03. It must happen after the internal audit and before stage 2, because audit results are a mandatory input. Keep it real: a review in which leadership only receives information, and decides nothing, reads as a formality. Decisions about resources, objectives and improvements are what the auditor looks for in the minutes.

2.10 Stage 1 audit

The certification body's auditor reviews your documented information and your readiness, usually over one or two days and often remotely. They check the scope, the policy, the risk method and results, the Statement of Applicability, the audit and review evidence, and whether the system has operated long enough. Stage 1 produces a list of concerns, any of which could become a nonconformity at stage 2 if not addressed. Run GOV-CHK-03 four weeks before stage 1 and fix what it shows.

2.11 Stage 2 audit

The auditor tests whether the system operates as documented. Expect interviews with the Chief Executive Officer, the Information Security Manager, system owners, developers, support staff and people in the business who have no security role, sampling of records from every register, inspection of configurations, and a walk through of offices or a review of the provider's assurance where you have none. Findings are graded, usually as major nonconformity (a requirement is missing or systematically not met), minor nonconformity (an isolated lapse), observation, and opportunity for improvement. A major blocks the certificate until closed and verified; minors need an accepted corrective action plan. The certificate is issued after the body's independent review of the audit report, typically four to eight weeks after stage 2.

2.12 Surveillance

In each of the two years after certification the body audits a sample of the system, always including the clauses on leadership, risk, internal audit, management review and corrective action, plus a rotation through Annex A so that every applicable control is seen within the three year cycle. The evidence they want is continuity: the registers kept filling, the audits and reviews happened on schedule, actions closed, changes were controlled. Surveillance is where organisations that treated certification as a project rather than an operating system lose their certificate.

2.13 Recertification

Before the certificate expires the body performs a full audit comparable to stage 2, reviews the three years of performance, and issues a new certificate for a further three years. Scope changes, mergers and major incidents in the cycle are examined closely. Start preparing six months ahead; use the same readiness checklist.

3. Typical findings and how to avoid them

Finding Why it happens How the kit prevents it
Scope statement does not match the systems actually in use Scope written early and never updated ISMS-STM-01 section 8 triggers and the thirty day update rule
Risk assessment is generic or has no link to treatments Template risks copied in GOV-PRO-05 scenario method; GOV-REG-05 treatment and SoA reference columns
Statement of Applicability out of date or without justifications Treated as a one off deliverable ISMS-REG-01 last reviewed column; ISMS-PRO-01 step 4.7(e)
Objectives not measurable Written as aspirations ISMS-PLN-01 rule 3.2
Competence records missing for key roles Training tracked, competence not ISMS-PRO-02 matrix and assessment
Access reviews not performed or not evidenced Promised quarterly, done once GOV-PRO-10; GOV-REG-12 dated entries
Supplier reviews absent after onboarding No renewal diary GOV-REG-07 next review column; ISMS-PRO-04 measure
Internal audit not independent or not covering all clauses One person does everything GOV-PRO-02 independence rule; ISMS-PLN-03 coverage rule
Management review missing mandatory inputs Agenda improvised GOV-TPL-03 one heading per input
Corrective actions without root cause or effectiveness check Fix and close GOV-PRO-04; GOV-TPL-02 verification section
Backups never restored Backup success assumed GOV-PRO-12 quarterly test; GOV-REG-15
Incident procedure untested No incidents, no exercise GOV-PRO-07 exercise cadence; GOV-REG-16
Logs collected, never reviewed No review cadence GOV-PRO-14 review step and records
Documents without approval evidence or past review date Document control informal GOV-PRO-01; GOV-REG-01

4. Choosing a certification body

  • Accreditation. Use a body accredited by the national accreditation body for ISO/IEC 27001 certification. An unaccredited certificate is not recognised by informed customers and some tenders reject it outright.
  • Sector and size fit. Ask which clients of your size and sector they certify. A body used to large enterprises may bring expectations and day rates that do not fit a forty person company.
  • Auditor continuity and competence. Ask whether the same lead auditor will perform stage 1, stage 2 and surveillance where possible, and what the auditor's background is in your technology. Technical scopes need auditors who can read a cloud configuration.
  • Audit days and cost. The number of audit days is calculated from headcount and complexity by the accreditation rules, so quotes should be similar; large differences deserve a question. Ask for the full three year cost, including surveillance and travel.
  • Scheduling. Lead times of two to four months for stage 1 are normal. Book when your internal audit is scheduled, not when it is finished.
  • Language and location. Confirm that audits can be conducted in the languages your staff work in, and remotely where your scope allows.
  • Report quality. Ask for a sample report. A report with specific, evidence based findings is worth more to you than a tick list.
  • Integrated audits. If you plan ISO/IEC 27701 or other standards, a body that can audit them together saves days every year.

5. Keeping the certificate

After certification, the management system is a calendar. The recurring events that surveillance auditors check are: quarterly access reviews, quarterly performance reports, at least annual risk review, at least annual internal audit covering the programme in ISMS-PLN-03, at least annual management review, annual awareness refresher, annual supplier reviews, annual policy reviews, and corrective actions closed with effectiveness verified. Put every one in a shared calendar with an owner, and let GOV-REG-21 show whether each happened. A system that runs on the calendar passes surveillance without a project.

Information security objectives and plan

The rules for setting measurable information security objectives, the objectives for the current period with their measures, owners and actions, and how progress is measured and reported.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 5.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.1; SOC 2 CC3.1. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This plan turns the commitments in GOV-POL-03 into a small number of measurable objectives for the period, each with an owner, actions, resources and a date, so that leadership can see whether the management system is improving the outcomes it exists for.

2. Scope

The plan covers the whole scope in ISMS-STM-01. It is set for one financial year and tracked in GOV-REG-21.

3. Rules for setting objectives

3.1 Each objective is consistent with GOV-POL-03 and traceable to at least one of: a risk in GOV-REG-05, a requirement in ISMS-REG-03, a legal or contractual obligation in GOV-REG-04, or a result reported under ISMS-PRO-04.

3.2 Each objective is measurable. Before it is approved, the measure, the formula, the target, the frequency and the data source are written against it. An objective that cannot be measured is rewritten until it can be.

3.3 Each objective has an owner role, a list of actions, the resources needed, and a completion date within the period.

3.4 The steering committee approves the objectives in the month after the management review, and the Information Security Manager records them in GOV-REG-21 and communicates them under ISMS-PLN-02 to the roles that contribute to them.

3.5 Progress is reviewed quarterly by the steering committee. Each objective carries a status of Green (on target), Amber (behind but recoverable within the period) or Red (target will be missed without intervention). An objective that is Red at two consecutive reviews is raised as a nonconformity under GOV-PRO-04.

3.6 An objective may be changed during the period only by the steering committee, with the reason recorded in GOV-REG-22.

3.7 The plan holds between six and ten objectives. More than ten dilutes attention; fewer than six usually means a risk area has been left without a target.

4. Objectives for [Year]

The objectives below are examples of the form a complete objective takes. Replace them with [Organisation]'s own, keeping the same structure.

No. Objective Measure and target Owner Reviewed
1 Close critical vulnerabilities inside the agreed window Critical findings in GOV-REG-14 fixed within 7 days, divided by all critical findings closed in the quarter: 95 percent or more Head of Engineering Monthly
2 Complete every access review on time Reviews recorded in GOV-REG-12 within 10 working days of quarter end, divided by reviews due: 100 percent Information Security Manager Quarterly
3 Make every joiner competent before they handle customer data New starters with induction recorded in GOV-REG-09 within 10 working days of start, divided by all starters: 98 percent or more Head of People Quarterly
4 Prove that critical systems can be restored Restore tests in GOV-REG-15 that met the recovery time objective, divided by tests performed: 100 percent, at least one test per critical system per quarter Head of Engineering Quarterly
5 Reduce susceptibility to phishing Click rate in simulations 5 percent or lower and report rate 50 percent or higher by the final simulation of the year Information Security Manager Per simulation
6 Contain serious incidents quickly Severity 1 and 2 incidents in GOV-REG-08 contained within 4 hours of detection, divided by all such incidents: 90 percent or more Incident Lead Quarterly
7 Keep supplier assurance current Tier 1 suppliers in GOV-REG-07 with a review dated within the last 12 months, divided by all Tier 1 suppliers: 100 percent Head of Operations Quarterly
8 Close audit findings before they age Corrective actions in GOV-REG-03 closed by their due date, divided by actions due in the quarter: 90 percent or more Information Security Manager Quarterly

5. Actions and resources

No. Planned actions Resources Evidence of completion
1 Enrol every production asset in scanning; agree the patch window with product owners; add an exception route under GOV-PRO-24 Scanning licence, [Number] engineer days per month GOV-REG-14 trend report
2 Publish the review calendar; pre-build account exports for each system; assign a deputy reviewer per system [Number] hours per system per quarter GOV-REG-12 entries with evidence links
3 Add the security induction to the starter workflow; block system access until the induction record exists Learning content, people team time GOV-REG-09 and GOV-CHK-01 records
4 Define the critical system list with the business impact analysis; schedule tests; record results and gaps Test environment, [Number] engineer days per quarter GOV-REG-15 entries
5 Run a simulation each quarter with a different lure; brief managers on results; target repeat clickers with coaching Simulation service, awareness time Simulation reports, GOV-REG-09
6 Run two incident exercises in the year; publish the on-call rota; pre-approve containment actions for common scenarios Exercise time, on-call budget GOV-REG-08 timestamps, GOV-REG-16
7 Tier every supplier; collect assurance evidence; diarise renewals ninety days ahead Procurement and security time GOV-REG-07 review dates
8 Review open actions fortnightly; escalate items older than sixty days to the steering committee Information Security Manager time GOV-REG-03 closure dates

6. Measurement and reporting

6.1 Owners extract the measure for each objective from the named register by the fifth working day after each period, using the formula written in GOV-REG-21.

6.2 The Information Security Manager compiles the values into the quarterly performance report produced under ISMS-PRO-04, assigns the Green, Amber or Red status, and adds one sentence of commentary and one sentence on the next action for every objective not Green.

6.3 The steering committee reviews the report each quarter. The year end values and the status of every objective are an input to the management review under GOV-PRO-03, which decides the objectives for the next period.

7. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-21 Security objectives and measures tracker: the approved objectives, the latest values and the status history.
  • Quarterly performance reports under ISMS-PRO-04.
  • Steering committee minutes approving the objectives and recording quarterly reviews.
  • GOV-REG-22 entries where objectives were changed or carried over.

8. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this plan annually after the management review, and within thirty days of a change to GOV-POL-03, a change of scope, or a severity 1 incident that shows an objective was missing.

Communication plan

Who communicates what about information security and privacy, to whom, when and through which channel, inside and outside [Organisation], and how those communications are approved and recorded.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 7.4; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 6.4.4; SOC 2 CC2.2; SOC 2 CC2.3. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This plan fixes the routine communications that keep the management system working: staff hear about the rules and the results, leadership hears about performance and risk, and customers, regulators, suppliers and auditors hear what they are entitled to hear, on time and from an authorised voice.

2. Scope

It covers planned communications about the management system inside the scope of ISMS-STM-01 and to the interested parties in ISMS-REG-03. Communications during an incident or a personal data breach follow GOV-PRO-07 and PIMS-PRO-04; section 6 explains how this plan hands over to them.

3. Principles

3.1 Every communication in the tables below has one named sending role. Nobody else sends it, and a deputy is named for each when the role holder is absent.

3.2 External statements about [Organisation]'s security or privacy posture, including answers to customer questionnaires, are approved by the Information Security Manager before they leave, and by the Chief Executive Officer when they commit [Organisation] to a new obligation.

3.3 No communication claims a certification, an audit result or a level of compliance that a current certificate or report does not support. Safe wording is "operates an information security management system aligned with" until a certificate exists, and "certified to" with the scope wording from ISMS-STM-01 afterwards.

3.4 Communications about individuals (disciplinary matters, personal data breaches affecting named people) go only to the roles with a need to know.

3.5 A record is kept of what was sent, when, to whom and by whom. For internal broadcast items the record is the message in the channel; for external items it is a copy filed with the customer, supplier or regulator record.

4. Internal communications

What When With whom How and by whom
New or changed policy or procedure On approval, within five working days All staff, or the roles the document applies to Announcement in the staff channel by the Information Security Manager; acknowledgement collected in GOV-REG-23
Security objectives and quarterly performance Within ten working days of quarter end All staff (summary); steering committee (full report) Summary posted by the Information Security Manager; full report presented at the steering committee
Awareness messages and training invitations Monthly message; induction and annual refresher per GOV-PRO-08 All staff Staff channel and learning platform, sent by the Information Security Manager
How to report a security event or a privacy concern At induction, and repeated quarterly All staff Poster or pinned message with the reporting channel, maintained by the Information Security Manager
Risk register changes and new high or critical risks At each steering committee, and immediately for a new critical risk Steering committee, affected risk owners Agenda item presented by the Information Security Manager; critical risk by direct message the same day
Access review requests Start of each quarter System Owners and line managers Ticket raised by the Information Security Manager with the due date from GOV-PRO-10
Changes that affect security (new system, new supplier, architecture change) Before the change is approved Information Security Manager, Privacy Officer where personal data is involved Change request GOV-TPL-08 routed by the change requester
Internal audit schedule and results Schedule at the start of the cycle; results within ten working days of the closing meeting Auditees, process owners, steering committee Audit plan ISMS-PLN-03 and audit report GOV-TPL-01 sent by the Internal Auditor
Management review outcomes and decisions Within ten working days of the review Steering committee, owners of actions Minutes GOV-TPL-03 and action tracker GOV-REG-22 circulated by the Information Security Manager
Phishing simulation results Within five working days of each simulation All staff (aggregate); line managers (their team) Aggregate message by the Information Security Manager; individual coaching by the line manager
Continuity exercise schedule and lessons Before each exercise; lessons within ten working days after Participants, steering committee Invitation and lessons note by the Head of Operations, recorded in GOV-REG-16

5. External communications

What When With whom How and by whom
Security questionnaire and due diligence responses Within the customer's deadline, normally ten working days Customers and prospects Written response approved by the Information Security Manager, sent by the account owner, copy filed
Certificate status and scope On request, and within ten working days of a change Customers Copy of the certificate and the scope wording from ISMS-STM-01, sent by the account owner
Changes to sub-processors or hosting locations Before the change, with the notice period in the contract Customers who are controllers Written notice by the Privacy Officer under PIMS-PRO-05
Security requirements and policy changes affecting suppliers At onboarding and within thirty days of a change Suppliers in GOV-REG-07 Contract schedule or written notice by the Head of Operations under GOV-PRO-06
Incidents at a supplier or affecting a supplier As set in the contract, normally within 24 hours of confirmation The supplier's named contact By the Incident Lead under GOV-PRO-07
Breach notifications Within the legal deadline from awareness Supervisory authority; affected individuals where required By the Privacy Officer under PIMS-PRO-04 using GDPR-TPL-10
Changes to scope, ownership, locations or a major incident Within thirty days, or as the certification agreement requires Certification body Written notice by the Information Security Manager
Vulnerability reports received from outside Acknowledgement within five working days; outcome when fixed The reporter By the Information Security Manager under GOV-PRO-27
Privacy notice and cookie notice Published at all times; updated before a change in processing takes effect Website visitors, customers, staff, applicants Published by the Privacy Officer using GDPR-TPL-01 to GDPR-TPL-04
Contact with authorities and specialist groups As required, and at least one check of contact details each year Regulators, law enforcement, sector security forums By the Information Security Manager or Privacy Officer, contact list kept with GOV-PRO-25
Insurer notifications Within the policy's notification period Cyber insurer By the Chief Executive Officer or delegate, with the Incident Lead

6. Incident and breach communications

6.1 When an incident is declared under GOV-PRO-07, the Incident Lead owns all communications about it until closure. The tables above do not apply to incident updates; the incident procedure's roles, approval rules and templates (GOV-TPL-05, GOV-TPL-11) do.

6.2 Any external statement about an incident, including to customers, media or on a public status page, is approved by the Chief Executive Officer. Statements describe confirmed facts, the actions taken and the next update time; they do not speculate on cause or attribution.

6.3 Where an incident involves personal data, the Privacy Officer runs the breach assessment and notifications under PIMS-PRO-04 in parallel, and the two leads agree a single message to any party that both must inform.

7. Approval and records

7.1 The steering committee approves this plan and any change to it.

7.2 The Information Security Manager keeps a communications log for external items: date, recipient, subject, approver and file location. Internal broadcast items are evidenced by the message itself in the channel.

7.3 Contact details for every external party in section 5 are checked once a year and after any change of counterpart, and the check is recorded in ISMS-REG-03.

8. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this plan annually, after any incident where a communication was late or sent by the wrong role, and within thirty days of a change to ISMS-REG-03 that adds or removes an external party.

Annual internal audit plan

The schedule of internal audits for one year of the audit cycle, giving for each audit the scope area, the clauses and controls covered, the auditor, the auditee, the timing and the method, together with the coverage rule that proves every clause and every applicable control is audited within the cycle and the statement of auditor independence.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.2.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.2.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.35; SOC 2 CC4.1. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This plan turns the audit programme in GOV-PRO-02 into a dated schedule for year [Number] of the [Number]-year cycle. It tells auditees when to expect an audit and what will be examined, tells auditors what they are responsible for, and gives the Chief Executive Officer and the external auditor a single page that shows the whole management system is independently checked.

2. Scope and criteria

The plan covers the management system described in ISMS-STM-01. The criteria for every audit are the clause 4 to 10 requirements of ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the Annex A controls declared applicable in ISMS-REG-01, the SOC 2 criteria tagged to those controls in GOV-REG-27 where a SOC 2 report is in scope, and the policies, procedures and registers of [Organisation] as listed in GOV-REG-01. Where ISO/IEC 27701 has been adopted, the privacy extensions audited in each area are those tagged in the Statement of Applicability.

3. The cycle and this year's position

The audit cycle is [Number] years, matching the certification cycle. Year 1 of the cycle, and the year before a first certification audit, covers every clause and every applicable control. In later years the clause 4 to 10 requirements are audited every year, controls that meet any of the annual triggers in section 4 are audited every year, and the remaining controls are spread across the cycle so that none goes unaudited for more than [Number] years.

This plan is for year [Number]. The programme in section 6 is written for a year in which everything is covered; when a later year rotates controls, the rows are kept and the clauses and controls column is reduced, with the reconciliation in section 4 proving that nothing falls out of the cycle.

4. Coverage rule

4.1 Every clause 4 to 10 requirement is audited every year. Audits IA-01 and IA-10 carry this coverage between them.

4.2 Every control marked Applicable in ISMS-REG-01 is audited at least once within the cycle, and every control that meets one of the following triggers is audited every year: it treats a risk rated High or Critical in GOV-REG-05; a major nonconformity against it is open or was closed within the last twelve months; an incident in GOV-REG-08 involved it within the last twelve months; or the system or process it protects changed significantly during the year.

4.3 At the end of each year the Information Security Manager reconciles the Criteria column of every audit marked Reported or Closed in GOV-REG-02 against the applicable controls in ISMS-REG-01 and against clauses 4.1 to 10.2. Any item not covered is scheduled in the first quarter of the next year's plan. No clause and no applicable control may remain unaudited when the cycle ends.

4.4 A control added to ISMS-REG-01 during the year, or changed from Not applicable to Applicable, is added to the next audit whose scope area fits, and in any case audited within twelve months of the change.

4.5 Coverage is recorded in GOV-REG-02, not in this plan. This plan states the intention; the register proves the outcome.

5. Independence statement

5.1 No auditor audits work they performed, managed or designed, or an area where they hold a control owner role in ISMS-REG-02. The Internal Auditor does not report to the Information Security Manager for the purpose of audit work and is not directed by the auditee on what to examine.

5.2 The Information Security Manager owns the management system and therefore does not audit any clause 4 to 10 requirement, nor any control whose owner column in ISMS-REG-02 names that role.

5.3 The Internal Auditor performs or witnesses control tests under ISMS-PRO-04 during the year. Audit IA-10, which examines performance evaluation and improvement, is therefore assigned to a second auditor: a trained person from a department outside the security function, or an external auditor engaged for the purpose.

5.4 Where no independent internal person is available for an area, the Information Security Manager engages an external auditor before the audit's planned quarter and records the arrangement in GOV-REG-02.

5.5 Independence is confirmed in writing for each audit in the Notes column of GOV-REG-02 before fieldwork begins, naming the auditor role and the reason the auditor is independent of the area.

Role May not audit
Information Security Manager Any clause 4 to 10 requirement; any control owned by that role; incident management; supplier security; awareness and training
Internal Auditor Controls the Internal Auditor tested under ISMS-PRO-04 in the same year; the internal audit process itself; measurement and reporting under clause 9.1
Head of Engineering and System Owners Any technological control they operate; change, development and configuration records they approved
Privacy Officer Personal data safeguards and breach handling where the Privacy Officer runs the process

6. Programme by quarter

Each audit is identified as IA-[Year]-[Number]. Timing is given in weeks of the quarter so that the plan can be re-dated each year without rewriting; the agreed dates are entered in GOV-REG-02 when the audit plan is issued. Method follows GOV-PRO-02 step 4.6: document review, interview, observation and sampling of records chosen by the auditor from the full population.

Quarter 1

IA-[Year]-02 Governance, policy, legal and compliance controls Annex A 5.1 to 5.8 and 5.31 to 5.37 Internal Auditor; auditees Information Security Manager and Privacy Officer Weeks 7 to 8; document review; sampling of GOV-REG-04 obligations, GOV-REG-23 acknowledgements and project gate records under PB-07; interviews with two line managers

Quarter 2

Audit Scope area Clauses and controls Auditor and auditee Timing and method

7. Timetable for each audit

Point What happens Source
Ten working days before fieldwork The auditor issues the audit plan with scope, criteria, interviewees, records required and the ISMS-REG-04 rows in play GOV-PRO-02 step 4.4
Three working days after the plan The auditee confirms availability and names deputies GOV-PRO-02 step 4.4
Day one Opening meeting, then fieldwork of one to three days depending on the scope area GOV-PRO-02 step 4.5
Last day of fieldwork Closing meeting; every finding presented in four parts and the facts confirmed GOV-PRO-02 step 4.8

Ten working days after the report, five for a major nonconformity Auditee returns GOV-TPL-02 with root cause and plan; logged in GOV-REG-03 GOV-PRO-02 step 4.10
Within ninety days of the report Major nonconformities re-audited GOV-PRO-02 step 4.11

8. Resources

The programme needs about [Number] auditor days for the year: two days of preparation and fieldwork and one day of reporting for each audit, plus [Number] days for follow-up. Auditees should expect to give two to four hours per audit for interviews and evidence. The Internal Auditor must meet the competence requirements in GOV-PRO-02 step 4.3 before leading an audit; where the second auditor for IA-10 is external, the engagement is approved by the Chief Executive Officer in the first quarter so that availability is secured.

9. Changes to the plan

An audit may be moved within its quarter by agreement between the auditor and the auditee, recorded in GOV-REG-02. Moving an audit to a later quarter needs the written approval of the Chief Executive Officer under GOV-PRO-02 section 6, and no audit may be moved out of the year. A new system, supplier, site or incident of severity 1 or 2 during the year triggers a review of whether an additional audit is needed; the Information Security Manager proposes it to the steering committee within one month of the trigger.

10. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-02 Audit programme and findings: one row per audit in this plan, with dates, independence note, status and finding counts.
  • The audit plan issued for each audit and the completed ISMS-REG-04 checklist.
  • Audit reports on GOV-TPL-01 and the corrective actions in GOV-REG-03.
  • The year-end coverage reconciliation described in section 4.3, filed with the plan for the following year.

11. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager drafts the plan for the following year in the last quarter, using the coverage reconciliation, the risk register, the incident register and the findings of the current year to set which controls need annual attention. The Chief Executive Officer approves it before the year begins. The plan is also reviewed when the scope changes, when a framework is added or withdrawn, and after any external audit finding about internal audit.

Context of the organisation and interested parties procedure

How [Organisation] identifies the internal and external issues that affect its security and privacy outcomes, the parties with an interest in those outcomes and their requirements, and how the results shape the scope, risks and objectives of the management system.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 4.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 4.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 4.3; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.2.1; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.2.2; SOC 2 CC3.1. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure gives [Organisation] a repeatable way to understand the conditions it operates in, who depends on its security and privacy performance, and what those parties require, so that the scope, the risk assessment and the objectives rest on recorded facts rather than assumptions.

2. Scope

It applies to the whole management system described in ISMS-STM-01, every function and location within it, and the privacy extension where [Organisation] operates one. It runs at least once a year and after any trigger event in step 4.1.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Chief Executive Officer Sponsors the analysis, confirms the issues that matter at leadership level, approves the output through the steering committee.
Information Security Manager Runs the analysis, keeps ISMS-REG-03 current, carries the results into the scope, the risk register and the objectives.
Privacy Officer Contributes data protection obligations and the expectations of supervisory authorities and data subjects.
Heads of function Contribute the issues and parties for their area, own the requirements assigned to them, confirm the register reflects their contracts and regulators.
Internal Auditor Checks each year that the register is current and that its results trace into the risk register and the objectives.

4. Procedure

4.1 Timing. The Information Security Manager schedules the context review once a year, in the quarter before the management review, and within thirty days of any of these events: a new market or jurisdiction, a new service or product, an acquisition or divestment, a change of principal supplier, a change in applicable law, a severity 1 or 2 incident, a customer gained or lost that changes the risk profile, or a change of ownership or leadership.

4.2 Preparation. Five working days before the workshop the Information Security Manager circulates the current ISMS-REG-03, the previous issues analysis, a summary of GOV-REG-05 and GOV-REG-04, incident and audit trends for the period, and the security questionnaires and contract clauses received from customers since the last review.

4.3 Internal issues. In a workshop of at most two hours the participants answer the questions in table 1 for each category. Each issue is recorded as one sentence that states the condition and whether it helps or hinders a security or privacy outcome, with the function that owns it. An issue that cannot be stated as a condition with an effect is not recorded.

Table 1. Internal issue categories

Category Questions to answer
Governance and strategy Growth plans, funding, planned products, appetite for risk, leadership changes
People and culture Headcount change, skills gaps, turnover, reliance on contractors, remote working pattern
Technology and architecture Legacy components, provider dependence, technical debt, planned migrations
Processes and maturity Which processes are documented and followed, where work is informal
Information and assets New data categories, volume growth, where restricted information concentrates
Resources Budget, tooling and time available for security and privacy work
Past performance Incident, audit, nonconformity and measurement trends in the period

4.4 External issues. The participants repeat the method with table 2. Each issue is recorded with the source it was learned from, so that it can be re-checked at the next review.

Table 2. External issue categories

Category Questions to answer
Legal and regulatory Laws, regulators and sector rules in each jurisdiction served; changes expected within eighteen months
Customers and market Security demands in contracts and tenders, certifications competitors hold, customer concentration
Threat environment Threat types seen against the sector, findings from GOV-PRO-27, fraud patterns seen by support and finance
Suppliers and technology Provider concentration, announced provider changes, end of support dates in GOV-REG-24
Economic and financial Pricing pressure, insurance availability and conditions, currency and payment exposure
Social and environmental Public expectations on privacy, physical hazards at each location, travel or access restrictions

4.5 Interested parties. The participants confirm the list of interested parties using the categories in table 3, adding and removing parties as the business has changed. For each party the register records the relationship and why the party cares about [Organisation]'s performance.

Table 3. Interested party categories

Party category Typical requirements
Customers and their own customers Confidentiality, availability targets, breach notification, certifications, right to audit, data location
Regulators and supervisory authorities Compliance with law, timely notifications, cooperation with enquiries
Staff and contractors Clear rules, usable controls, protection of their own personal data, fair monitoring
Owners, board and investors Risk within appetite, protection of value, honest reporting
Suppliers and partners Clear obligations, agreed interfaces, controlled access to systems
Data subjects Lawful and transparent handling, rights answered on time
Certification bodies and auditors Access to evidence, conformity with the standard, notice of major changes
Insurers Control baselines named in policy conditions, incident notification within policy terms

4.6 Requirements. For each party the Information Security Manager records every requirement in ISMS-REG-03 as one row: the party, the requirement in plain words, its type (Legal, Contractual, Voluntary commitment or Expectation), the source, the owner, how it is addressed and its priority. Whether the requirement is met through the management system is recorded explicitly; a requirement handled outside it names the function that handles it.

4.7 Using the results. Within twenty working days of the workshop the Information Security Manager: (a) updates ISMS-STM-01 if an issue or requirement changes the boundary; (b) raises or updates a risk in GOV-REG-05, using GOV-PRO-05, for every issue that hinders an outcome; (c) adds or updates obligations in GOV-REG-04 for every legal or contractual requirement; (d) proposes objectives for ISMS-PLN-01 where a requirement needs a measurable commitment; (e) checks ISMS-REG-01 for any control whose applicability justification depends on an issue or requirement that has changed.

4.8 Approval. The steering committee reviews the issues analysis and ISMS-REG-03 at its next meeting and records acceptance in its minutes. Where participants disagree about whether a requirement applies, the committee decides and the decision is minuted.

4.9 Reporting. A summary of the changes in context since the last review is a mandatory input to the management review under GOV-PRO-03.

5. Records and evidence

  • ISMS-REG-03 Interested parties and requirements register, with a last reviewed date on every row.
  • The completed issues analysis (tables 1 and 2), dated and controlled under GOV-PRO-01.
  • The workshop attendance list and the preparation pack.
  • Steering committee minutes recording acceptance.
  • Entries in GOV-REG-05, GOV-REG-04 and ISMS-PLN-01 that cite the review date as their source.

6. Exceptions

The workshop may be replaced by a desk review by the Information Security Manager only when none of the events in step 4.1 occurred in the period and the previous review was workshop based. The substitution is recorded in ISMS-REG-03 and may not be used in two consecutive years.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually and after any audit finding against clauses 4.1 to 4.3. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Competence and awareness procedure

How [Organisation] decides what competence each security role needs, checks whether the people in those roles have it, closes gaps, keeps the records, and makes every person aware of what the management system expects of them.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 7.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 7.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.3; SOC 2 CC1.4. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure makes sure that the people who operate, administer, develop, audit and lead within the management system are able to do so, and that everyone else knows the rules that apply to them and why they matter. Awareness content and delivery are described in GOV-PRO-08; this procedure defines the competence requirements, the assessment and the records.

2. Scope

It applies to employees, contractors and temporary workers who hold any role in the competence matrix in step 4.1, and to all staff for the awareness requirements in step 4.6. Supplier personnel who administer in-scope systems are covered through the equivalence rule in step 4.7.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Information Security Manager Owns the competence matrix, approves training plans for security roles, keeps GOV-REG-09 complete.
Line manager Maps each person to the roles they hold, assesses them against the matrix on appointment and annually, agrees gap closing actions.
Head of People Runs induction scheduling, keeps employment records that show competence evidence, confirms contractor equivalence.
Individual Completes assigned training by the due date and tells the line manager of any gap in knowledge needed for the role.
Internal Auditor Samples competence records each audit cycle and confirms their own independence and competence before each audit.

4. Procedure

4.1 Competence matrix. The Information Security Manager maintains the matrix below. A person who holds more than one role meets the requirements of each.

Role Competence required Evidence accepted Refresh
Information Security Manager Working knowledge of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clauses 4 to 10 and Annex A, risk assessment, audit practice, incident command, [Organisation]'s technology Recognised security management certification, or three years of relevant experience plus an implementer course; annual continuing education record Annual
Privacy Officer Data protection law in the jurisdictions served, impact assessment, rights handling, breach assessment Recognised privacy qualification or two years of relevant experience; annual legal update Annual
System Owner The system's purpose, data classification, access model, dependencies and the procedures that apply to it Role induction completed; one access review performed under supervision On appointment and at role change
Administrator with privileged access Secure configuration, logging, patching, incident escalation for the platforms administered Platform training or a task demonstrated under supervision; GOV-CHK-02 walkthrough signed off Annual
Developer The secure coding rules in GOV-PRO-15, threat modelling basics, secrets handling, dependency hygiene Secure coding course completed; participation in peer review Annual
Internal Auditor Audit technique, the requirements of the standard, independence rules, report writing Internal auditor course; one full audit shadowed before leading one Every two years
Incident Lead GOV-PRO-07, evidence preservation, communication rules, decision making under time pressure Participation in an exercise or a real incident review within the last twelve months Annual
Line manager Joiner, mover and leaver duties, policy enforcement, how to report concerns Manager briefing completed Annual
All staff The policies that apply to them, how to report an event, consequences of breaches Induction within ten working days of start and annual refresher Annual

4.2 Assessment. On appointment and once a year the line manager compares the person with the row for each role held, records whether each element of competence is met, and lists gaps. The assessment is dated and kept with the training record.

4.3 Gap closing. For each gap the line manager and the Information Security Manager choose one or more actions: a course, mentoring or supervised practice, a temporary external specialist, or recruitment. Each action has a due date. A gap in a role with privileged access or incident authority is closed within ninety days; until then the person acts under the supervision of someone who meets the requirement.

4.4 Verification of effectiveness. After the action is complete the line manager confirms competence by one of: a test result, a task observed and signed off, an audit or review result, or the quality of work produced over the following quarter. The method and result are recorded; an action without a recorded verification is not counted as closed.

4.5 Records. The Head of People records every assessment, course, certificate, supervised task and verification in GOV-REG-09, with the session record GOV-TPL-10 where a session was delivered. Records are kept for the period of engagement plus [Number] years.

4.6 Awareness. Every person in scope knows the information security policy GOV-POL-03, how their work contributes to the objectives in ISMS-PLN-01, the benefit of following the controls that apply to them, how to report an event under GOV-PRO-07, and the consequences of not following the rules under GOV-PRO-18. Awareness is delivered under GOV-PRO-08 and acknowledged in GOV-REG-23.

4.7 Contractors and supplier personnel. Before access is granted, the engaging manager obtains evidence that the person meets the matrix row for the role, or that the supplier applies an equivalent requirement under the contract managed through GOV-PRO-06. The evidence or the contract reference is recorded in GOV-REG-09.

4.8 Auditor competence and independence. Before each internal audit the Information Security Manager confirms that the auditor meets the matrix row, has no responsibility for the area audited in the preceding twelve months, and has reviewed the current audit plan. Where no independent internal person exists for an area, an external auditor is engaged and the same evidence is obtained.

4.9 Review of the matrix. The Information Security Manager reviews the matrix annually and within thirty days of a new system, a new role, a change in law that affects the Privacy Officer, or an incident or audit finding that points to a competence gap.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-09 Training and awareness register: assessments, courses, verifications and due dates for every person in scope.
  • GOV-TPL-10 Awareness session record and acknowledgement for each delivered session.
  • GOV-REG-23 Policy acknowledgement register.
  • The dated competence matrix and the annual review note.
  • Auditor independence confirmations filed with each audit under GOV-PRO-02.

6. Exceptions

A person may be appointed to a role before meeting the matrix row only with the written agreement of the Information Security Manager, a named supervisor who meets the row, and a closing date within ninety days recorded in GOV-REG-09. No exception applies to the Internal Auditor independence rule.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually and after any audit finding against clauses 7.2 or 7.3. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Operational planning and control procedure

How the processes that deliver the management system's controls are planned, given operating criteria, implemented from the risk treatment plan, kept under control when they change, and governed when another organisation performs them.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 8.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.3; SOC 2 CC5.1; SOC 2 CC5.3. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure connects the plans of the management system (the risk treatment plan, the objectives, the policies) to day to day operation. It defines which processes exist, what each must achieve, how a control agreed in the Statement of Applicability becomes something that actually runs, how planned and unplanned changes are handled, and how processes performed by suppliers stay under [Organisation]'s control.

2. Scope

It applies to every operational process that implements a control in ISMS-REG-01 or an action in GOV-REG-05, whether performed by staff, contractors or an external provider, across the whole scope in ISMS-STM-01.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Information Security Manager Keeps the process inventory in step 4.1, tracks implementation of treatments, chairs the monthly operations review.
Process owner Named for each process in the inventory; runs the process to its criteria, keeps its records, reports its measures.
System Owner Confirms that controls on their system are implemented and operating; approves changes to it under GOV-PRO-09.
Head of Operations Governs processes performed by suppliers under GOV-PRO-06 and GOV-PRO-26.
Steering committee Approves planned changes to the management system and accepts residual risk after unplanned changes.

4. Procedure

4.1 Process inventory. The Information Security Manager maintains the inventory below. Every process has a governing document, operating criteria (the measurable conditions that show it is working) and the records that prove it ran.

Process Governing document Operating criteria Records
Risk assessment and treatment GOV-PRO-05 Full assessment annually and on triggers; every risk above appetite has a treatment with owner and date GOV-REG-05, GOV-REG-06
Access management GOV-PRO-10 Joiner access within one working day of approval; leaver removal within one working day; quarterly reviews on every in-scope system GOV-REG-12, GOV-REG-13
Change management GOV-PRO-09 No production change without approval, test evidence and rollback plan; emergency changes reviewed within five working days GOV-REG-11
Vulnerability and patch management GOV-PRO-11 Findings fixed within the severity window; exceptions approved under GOV-PRO-24 GOV-REG-14
Backup and restore GOV-PRO-12 Backups complete to schedule; restore test per critical system each quarter GOV-REG-15
Logging and monitoring GOV-PRO-14 Required events logged on every in-scope system; alerts triaged within the set time; logs retained for the set period Alert tickets, log retention evidence
Incident management GOV-PRO-07 Response within the severity time; review within ten working days GOV-REG-08, GOV-TPL-11
Supplier management GOV-PRO-06 Every supplier tiered; due diligence before use; annual review of Tier 1 GOV-REG-07
Secure development GOV-PRO-15 Peer review and security tests before release; no secrets in code; environments separated Release approvals, pipeline results
Awareness and competence GOV-PRO-08, ISMS-PRO-02 Induction within ten working days; annual refresher; competence assessed annually GOV-REG-09, GOV-REG-23
Business continuity GOV-PRO-13 Business impact analysis current; plans exercised to the cadence set GOV-REG-16
Asset management GOV-PRO-16 Every asset has an owner and a classification; inventory reconciled quarterly GOV-REG-10, GOV-REG-24

4.2 Setting criteria. When a process is created or its governing document changes, the process owner proposes the operating criteria and the Information Security Manager confirms that each criterion can be measured from the process's own records. Criteria that cannot be measured are rewritten before the document is approved under GOV-PRO-01.

4.3 Implementing treatments. Each treatment action in GOV-REG-05, and each control marked Planned or Partial in ISMS-REG-01, is given a task with an owner and a due date in ISMS-REG-02. The owner implements it, attaches evidence that it operates (configuration export, record sample, screenshot showing account and date), and the Information Security Manager updates the status in ISMS-REG-01 and ISMS-REG-02. A control is not marked Implemented until evidence of operation exists.

4.4 Planned changes to the management system. A change to scope, policy, process, organisation structure or principal technology that affects how a control operates is proposed in writing with its purpose, the controls affected, the resources needed, and the responsibilities that move. The Information Security Manager assesses the effect on GOV-REG-05 and ISMS-REG-01; the steering committee approves; the affected documents are updated under GOV-PRO-01 before the change takes effect. Technical changes to systems follow GOV-PRO-09 in addition.

4.5 Unintended changes. When a change has happened without this review (for example a provider alters a service, a team adopts a new tool, a control stops operating), the person who notices reports it as an event under GOV-PRO-07. The Information Security Manager reviews the consequences within five working days, records any new or changed risk in GOV-REG-05, and raises a nonconformity under GOV-PRO-04 if a control failed.

4.6 Externally provided processes. Where a supplier performs a process in the inventory, or part of one, the Head of Operations records it in GOV-REG-07 with the process name, the contract clause that requires the operating criteria, the evidence the supplier must provide and how often, and the person who reviews that evidence. Cloud services are governed under GOV-PRO-26 and the shared responsibility split in ISMS-STM-01. A supplier's failure to meet a criterion is handled as a nonconformity against the supplier under GOV-PRO-06.

4.7 Documented information from operation. Each process keeps the records named in the inventory for the retention period in the retention schedule, in a form that shows who did what and when. Records are controlled under GOV-PRO-01.

4.8 Monthly operations review. The Information Security Manager meets the process owners each month, checks each process against its criteria using the latest records, lists breaches of criteria, and agrees corrections. Breaches that repeat for two months, or that affect a critical system, go to GOV-PRO-04. The review note is filed and feeds the quarterly report under ISMS-PRO-04.

5. Records and evidence

  • The process inventory in step 4.1, dated at each revision.
  • ISMS-REG-02 Control implementation tracker: implementation tasks, evidence and status for every applicable control.
  • ISMS-REG-01 Statement of Applicability with implementation status.
  • Change proposals and steering committee approvals for planned changes.
  • Monthly operations review notes.
  • GOV-REG-07 entries for processes performed by suppliers, with the evidence received.

6. Exceptions

A treatment or control may operate without the evidence in step 4.3 for at most thirty days after implementation while the first records accumulate. No process may operate without a named owner.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually and after any audit finding against clause 8.1 or 6.3. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation procedure

What [Organisation] measures about its controls and its management system, how and how often the data is collected, who analyses it, how control effectiveness is tested, and how results reach the steering committee and the management review.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.36; SOC 2 CC4.1; SOC 2 CC4.2. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure produces the evidence that the management system works: a fixed set of measures with formulas and targets, a test of every applicable control at least once a year, and a quarterly report that tells leadership where performance is below target and what is being done about it.

2. Scope

It applies to every process in the inventory of ISMS-PRO-03, every applicable control in ISMS-REG-01, and every objective in ISMS-PLN-01, across the scope in ISMS-STM-01.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Information Security Manager Owns the measurement set, compiles the quarterly report, plans control testing, presents results.
Process owner Extracts the measures for their process by the due date, explains variances, proposes actions.
System Owner Provides configuration and record extracts for control tests on their system.
Internal Auditor Performs or witnesses the tests marked for independent testing; may not test a control they operate.
Steering committee Reviews the quarterly report, decides on actions for Red items, confirms targets for the next year.

4. Procedure

4.1 Measurement set. The measures below are collected for every period. Each is defined by a formula, a target, a frequency and the register it is drawn from, so that two people would compute the same value.

Measure Formula Target Frequency and source
Critical vulnerability closure Critical findings fixed within 7 days divided by critical findings closed in the period 95 percent or more Monthly, GOV-REG-14
Patch currency In-scope hosts patched within their cycle divided by in-scope hosts 98 percent or more Monthly, GOV-REG-24 and GOV-REG-14
Access review completion Reviews completed within 10 working days of quarter end divided by reviews due 100 percent Quarterly, GOV-REG-12
Leaver access removal Leavers with all access removed within one working day divided by leavers 98 percent or more Monthly, GOV-CHK-01 records and GOV-REG-12
Training currency Staff with induction and a refresher within the last 12 months divided by headcount 98 percent or more Quarterly, GOV-REG-09
Phishing susceptibility Recipients who clicked divided by recipients, and recipients who reported divided by recipients 5 percent or lower; 50 percent or higher Per simulation, simulation report
Incident containment time Median hours from detection to containment for severity 1 and 2 incidents 4 hours or less Quarterly, GOV-REG-08
Restore test success Restore tests that met the recovery time objective divided by tests performed 100 percent Quarterly, GOV-REG-15
Change success Changes completed without rollback or incident divided by changes completed 97 percent or more Monthly, GOV-REG-11
Corrective action timeliness Actions closed by their due date divided by actions due in the period 90 percent or more Quarterly, GOV-REG-03
Risk treatment progress Treatment actions completed by their due date divided by actions due in the period 85 percent or more Quarterly, GOV-REG-05
Supplier review currency Tier 1 suppliers reviewed within the last 12 months divided by Tier 1 suppliers 100 percent Quarterly, GOV-REG-07

4.2 Data collection. By the fifth working day after each period the process owner extracts the value from the named register, keeps the extract (export or filtered view with its date), and enters the value and the extract location in GOV-REG-21. A value that cannot be computed because the register is incomplete is recorded as missing, not estimated.

4.3 Control effectiveness testing. At the start of each year the Information Security Manager plans a test of every control marked Implemented in ISMS-REG-01 and records the plan in ISMS-REG-02: the test method, the sample, the tester and the quarter. Methods are inspection of configuration, sampling of records, re-performance of the control, interview, and observation. Controls that protect restricted information or privileged access are tested by someone who does not operate them. The tester records the result as Pass or Fail with the evidence reference and the date. A Fail is raised under GOV-PRO-04 within five working days.

4.4 Sampling rule. For a control that runs daily or more often, the tester examines at least 25 instances spread across the year; weekly, at least 10; monthly, at least 3; quarterly or less often, every instance. A single exception in the sample is a Fail unless the process owner shows it was detected and corrected by the process itself at the time.

4.5 Analysis. The Information Security Manager compares each value with its target and with the previous four periods, assigns Green (at or better than target), Amber (within 10 percent of target or a single miss after four Greens) or Red (below that), and writes one sentence of cause and one of action for every Amber and Red. Trends matter as much as single values: three consecutive periods moving away from target is reported as Amber even if still above target.

4.6 Quarterly report. Within fifteen working days of quarter end the Information Security Manager issues the quarterly performance report containing: the measurement table with status, the objectives from ISMS-PLN-01 with status, control test results from ISMS-REG-02 (tests planned, performed, passed, failed), open nonconformities from GOV-REG-03 by age, and the actions proposed. The steering committee reviews it at its next meeting and the decisions are minuted.

4.7 Annual evaluation. The year's four reports, the full year control test results and the trend of every measure are an input to the management review under GOV-PRO-03. The review confirms or changes the measures and targets for the next year, and the Information Security Manager updates this procedure and GOV-REG-21 within thirty days.

4.8 Data quality. Every reported value can be traced to a dated extract. If a formula or source changes, the change is recorded in GOV-REG-21 and values before the change are not compared with values after it without a note.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-21 Security objectives and measures tracker: values, extracts and status for every measure and objective.
  • ISMS-REG-02 Control implementation tracker: the test plan and the result of every control test.
  • Quarterly performance reports and the steering committee minutes that reviewed them.
  • Dated extracts from the source registers.
  • Nonconformities raised in GOV-REG-03 from failed tests or Red measures.

6. Exceptions

A measure may be suspended for at most two periods when its source register is being rebuilt, with the reason recorded in GOV-REG-21 and reported in the quarterly report. No control marked Implemented may go untested for more than twelve months.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually after the management review, and within thirty days of a change to ISMS-PLN-01 or to the process inventory in ISMS-PRO-03. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.
