ISMS scope statement

Defines the boundary of the information security management system, the organisation, locations, services, systems, interfaces and exclusions it covers, and how that boundary is changed.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 4.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 4.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 4.2. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Statement of scope

The information security management system (ISMS) of [Organisation] covers the people, processes, information and technology used to design, deliver, operate and support [Service or product description] for its customers from the locations listed in section 2, together with the corporate functions named there. The boundary was set after the context analysis recorded in ISMS-REG-03 and takes account of the internal and external issues, the interested parties and the dependencies described below.

The scope wording used on certificates and in public statements is:

The information security management system supporting the design, development, operation and support of [Service or product description] for customers, delivered from [Location] and the hosted infrastructure described in the Statement of Applicability version [Number].

2. Organisation and locations

Location Function performed In scope
[Head office city] Leadership, engineering, operations, customer support, finance, people Yes
[Second office city] [Function] [Yes or No]
Home working locations of staff Engineering, operations and support work performed under GOV-POL-05 Yes, for the staff and managed devices covered by that policy
[Provider hosting region] Hosting of production and non-production environments Yes, within the shared responsibility split in section 5

Employees, contractors and temporary workers who perform work within the functions above are inside the scope for the duration of their engagement.

3. Services and products

Service or product Description Service Owner
[Service name] [One sentence on what it does and for whom] [Role]
Customer support Handling of support requests and the customer information they contain [Role]
Internal corporate systems Identity, email, collaboration, finance and people systems that hold [Organisation] information [Role]

4. Information, systems and networks

Element What is included
Information Customer data processed by the services above; personal data of staff, candidates and customer contacts; source code, configuration, credentials and keys; commercial and financial records; the records of this ISMS.
Systems Production and non-production environments of [Service name]; the source code repository and build pipeline; the identity provider; the device management platform; the ticketing and documentation systems; end user devices issued to staff.
Networks The office network at [Location]; the virtual networks in the hosting account or accounts; the remote access path used by administrators; the managed device fleet. Home networks are outside the scope except for the controls placed on the device under GOV-POL-05.
Registers of record GOV-REG-10 lists each information asset in scope with its owner and classification. GOV-REG-24 lists hardware and software, including end of support dates.

5. Interfaces and dependencies

[Organisation] relies on external providers for parts of the environment. The split of responsibility is recorded here and in GOV-PRO-26, and the providers themselves are listed in GOV-REG-07.

Dependency Provider responsibility [Organisation] responsibility
Cloud hosting Physical security of data centres, hypervisor, physical network, availability of the platform services used Account configuration, identity and access, encryption settings, logging, backups, network rules, workload patching
Identity and productivity suite Service availability, security of the platform itself Tenant configuration, user lifecycle, multi-factor enforcement, data sharing settings
Payment, email and analytics processors Security of their own service as contracted Choice of provider, contract terms, data minimisation, monitoring under GOV-PRO-06
Outsourced development or support, where used Delivery to the contract and to the security clauses in it Oversight, access provisioning, code review and acceptance

Interfaces between in-scope and out-of-scope elements, for example an integration from [Service name] to a customer's own system, are listed in GOV-REG-25 with their classification and protection.

6. Exclusions and justification

Excluded element Justification Remaining interface
[Business unit or product not covered] Separately managed, separate systems, no access to in-scope information Shared identity provider; the shared tenant controls stay in scope
Physical security of provider data centres Operated by the provider and covered by its own assurance reports, which are reviewed under GOV-PRO-06 Assurance report review recorded in GOV-REG-07
Personal devices not enrolled in device management Not permitted to reach in-scope systems under GOV-POL-02 Technical block enforced by the identity provider

An exclusion is permitted only where it does not reduce [Organisation]'s ability to protect in-scope information or to meet a requirement recorded in ISMS-REG-03. Each exclusion is re-examined during the annual risk assessment.

7. Requirements considered

The scope reflects the requirements of the interested parties recorded in ISMS-REG-03, the legal and contractual obligations in GOV-REG-04, and the issues identified through ISMS-PRO-01. Where a customer contract requires a particular system or location to sit within a certified scope, that requirement is recorded against the contract in GOV-REG-04 and reflected here.

8. Changes to the scope

8.1 Any role may propose a scope change. The proposal names the element to add or remove, the reason, the affected interested parties and the expected effect on risk.

8.2 The Information Security Manager assesses the proposal against the risk register (GOV-REG-05) and the Statement of Applicability (ISMS-REG-01) and presents it to the steering committee defined in GOV-POL-01.

8.3 The Chief Executive Officer approves the change. The Information Security Manager then updates this statement, GOV-REG-10, the risk assessment and ISMS-REG-01 within thirty days, and notifies the certification body where a certificate is held.

8.4 The following events require a scope review within thirty days: a new product or service, a new office or hosting region, an acquisition or divestment, a new category of customer data, a change of principal provider, or a contract that requires a change of scope.

ISO/IEC 27701

Privacy information management, the PIMS extension

PIMS-GDE-01 guide Download .docx Markdown

Guide: ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A (controller) and Annex B (processor) controls and where the kit covers each

A reading aid that lists every control in Annex A and Annex B of ISO/IEC 27701 with a short theme in plain words and the kit documents that implement it, and explains how the clause 5 and clause 6 extensions change an existing ISMS, for use when extending the Statement of Applicability.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.4.1.3. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. How to use this guide

ISO/IEC 27701 does not stand alone. It extends an information security management system built on ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27002 so that it also manages personal data, and it calls the result a privacy information management system. The 2019 edition has four working parts. Clause 5 adds privacy requirements to each ISO/IEC 27001 clause, mostly by saying that wherever the security standard says information security, you read information security and privacy, and by requiring you to decide whether you act as a controller, a processor, or both. Clause 6 adds privacy guidance to the ISO/IEC 27002 controls, for example on training, classification, backups, logs, test data, suppliers and incidents. Clause 7 gives guidance for controllers and clause 8 for processors. Annex A lists the controller controls and Annex B the processor controls; these two annexes are normative, which means your Statement of Applicability must cover them in the same way it covers the ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A controls.

Which annex applies depends on the role decision under PIMS-PRO-01. A pure controller applies Annex A; a pure processor applies Annex B; an organisation that is both, which is most product companies, applies both, and the justification column of ISMS-REG-01 says for which processing activities each applies.

The tables below give each control number a theme written in this kit's own words. The themes are a memory aid, not the standard's titles; read the standard itself for the requirement. The third column names the kit documents that implement the control, the first being the primary one. Use the tables in three places:

  1. ISMS-REG-01 Statement of Applicability. Add the Annex A and Annex B rows under the ISO/IEC 27001 rows, decide Applicable Yes or No for each, justify, set the implementation status, and copy the kit IDs you actually use.
  2. ISMS-REG-02 Control implementation tracker. Add the same rows with owner, evidence, test method and the effectiveness grade from PIMS-PRO-07.
  3. Gap analysis in step 5 of PB-05. Walk the tables with the Processing Owners and mark what exists, what exists informally and what does not exist.

5. Editions and numbering

This guide uses the numbering of the 2019 edition of ISO/IEC 27701, in which the standard is an extension to ISO/IEC 27001:2013 and ISO/IEC 27002:2013 and the controller and processor controls sit in Annex A and Annex B as listed above. A later edition restructures the standard so that it can be certified on its own and renumbers its clauses and annexes; the themes above survive the restructuring, the numbers do not. Before building your Statement of Applicability, confirm with your certification body which edition it audits against, add a column to ISMS-REG-01 for that edition's numbering, and map each theme row once. The kit document IDs do not change; only the control reference in the first column does. Keep the mapping with GOV-REG-01 as an external document reference so that the next auditor can follow it.

Privacy information management policy

The top-level commitment that extends the information security management system to the protection of personal data, the principles every processing activity must satisfy, and the roles that make them happen.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.3.2; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.2.1; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 6.2.1.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 5.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.34; GDPR Article 5; GDPR Article 24. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This policy extends [Organisation]'s information security management system into a privacy information management system. It states the principles that every processing of personal data must satisfy, names the roles accountable for them, and commits [Organisation] to the procedures and records that prove the principles are applied.

2. Scope

It applies to all personal data that [Organisation] processes within the scope in ISMS-STM-01, whether as a controller, a processor, or both, in every system, service, office and supplier arrangement, and to every employee, contractor and supplier who handles that data. Personal data means any information relating to an identified or identifiable individual, including identifiers, online identifiers and data that becomes identifying when combined.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Chief Executive Officer Approves this policy, provides the Privacy Officer with resources and direct access, and accepts residual privacy risk rated high.
Privacy Officer Owns this policy and the privacy procedures, advises on obligations, monitors compliance, runs assessments, handles requests and breaches, and is the contact point for individuals and the supervisory authority. Reports to the Chief Executive Officer and is not instructed on how to perform these tasks.
Information Security Manager Integrates privacy requirements into the risk method, the Statement of Applicability, the audit programme and the management review.
Processing Owner The manager accountable for a processing activity in PIMS-REG-01. Keeps its entry current, applies this policy to it and answers for it in assessments and audits.
System Owner Implements the technical measures a processing activity needs in the system that supports it, including retention, access and rights support.
Head of Engineering Applies PIMS-PRO-06 to every product and feature that processes personal data.
Human Resources Applies this policy to employee and applicant data and runs privacy training through GOV-PRO-08.
All staff and contractors Handle personal data only for the recorded purpose, report suspected breaches and requests from individuals immediately, and complete privacy training.

4. Policy statements

4.1 Lawfulness, fairness and transparency. Every processing activity has a lawful basis recorded in PIMS-REG-01 before it starts, and the individuals concerned are told about it through a notice managed under PIMS-PRO-05. No personal data is processed in a way the individuals would not reasonably expect from that notice.

4.2 Purpose limitation. Personal data is collected for the specific purposes recorded in PIMS-REG-01 and is not used for a new purpose unless the Privacy Officer confirms in writing that the new purpose is compatible or that a new lawful basis and notice are in place.

4.3 Minimisation. Each processing activity collects and keeps only the data fields the recorded purpose needs. The Processing Owner confirms this at the privacy by design review in PIMS-PRO-06 and at every inventory review.

4.4 Accuracy. Personal data is kept accurate and up to date in proportion to the harm an error could cause. Individuals can correct their data through PIMS-PRO-03, and corrections reach every system and recipient that holds the data.

4.5 Storage limitation. Personal data is kept no longer than the period in PIMS-REG-07, set under PIMS-POL-02, and is then deleted, anonymised or returned, including copies in backups and logs within their own cycle.

4.6 Integrity and confidentiality. Personal data is protected by the controls in the Statement of Applicability ISMS-REG-01, selected through GOV-PRO-05 with the harm to individuals treated as an impact in its own right. Access is granted under GOV-PRO-10 on a need to know basis only.

4.7 Accountability. [Organisation] can show that each statement in this policy is met, through the registers in section 5, the assessments in PIMS-REG-08 and the monitoring report produced quarterly under PIMS-PRO-07.

4.8 Roles decided first. Before any new processing activity, contract or supplier arrangement starts, the Privacy Officer records under PIMS-PRO-01 whether [Organisation] acts as controller, joint controller or processor, because the obligations differ.

4.9 Privacy risk and impact assessment. Every new or changed processing activity is screened under PIMS-PRO-02 before design approval, and a data protection impact assessment is completed and approved before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals begins.

4.10 Rights of individuals. Requests from individuals are handled under PIMS-PRO-03 within one month of receipt, free of charge, with every request and its outcome recorded in PIMS-REG-02.

4.11 Breaches. A suspected personal data breach is reported immediately through the incident channel in GOV-PRO-07 and assessed under PIMS-PRO-04, with the supervisory authority notified within 72 hours of awareness where the risk to individuals requires it and the controller notified without undue delay where [Organisation] is a processor.

4.12 Processors and sharing. Personal data is shared with a processor only under written terms that meet GDPR Article 28, based on PIMS-TPL-02, after approval under GOV-PRO-06, and the processor is listed in PIMS-REG-06.

4.13 International transfers. Personal data leaves the region in which [Organisation] is established only under a mechanism approved in PIMS-POL-03 and recorded in PIMS-REG-05.

4.14 Privacy by design and by default. Every product, feature, system and procurement that processes personal data passes the review in PIMS-PRO-06, and the default configuration offered to individuals is the most privacy-protective option available.

4.15 Training. Every person completes privacy training at induction and annually under GOV-PRO-08, with role-based content for people who design systems, handle requests or respond to incidents, recorded in GDPR-REG-05.

4.16 One management system. Privacy controls are selected, implemented, audited and reviewed through the same processes as security controls: GOV-PRO-05 for risk, ISMS-REG-01 for applicability of the ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A and Annex B controls, GOV-PRO-02 for internal audit and GOV-PRO-03 for management review. The Privacy Officer attends every management review.

4.17 Consequences. A breach of this policy is handled under the disciplinary process in GOV-PRO-18, and for a supplier under the contract.

5. Records and evidence

  • PIMS-REG-01 Personal data processing inventory, with roles, purposes, bases and retention.
  • PIMS-REG-02 Data subject request register and PIMS-REG-03 Personal data breach register.
  • PIMS-REG-04 Consent record register, PIMS-REG-05 International transfer register and PIMS-REG-06 Processor and sub-processor register.
  • PIMS-REG-07 Retention schedule with check results and PIMS-REG-08 DPIA register.
  • ISMS-REG-01 Statement of Applicability showing the Annex A and Annex B controls that apply.
  • Quarterly privacy monitoring reports under PIMS-PRO-07 and GOV-REG-23 acknowledgements of this policy.

6. Exceptions

No exception to statements 4.1 to 4.7 is possible, because they restate legal obligations. An exception to any other statement is requested under GOV-PRO-24 with the Privacy Officer's written assessment of the effect on individuals and is approved by the Chief Executive Officer.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this policy annually, after a personal data breach notified to a supervisory authority, after a change in applicable privacy law recorded in GOV-REG-04, after a change in [Organisation]'s role under PIMS-PRO-01, and after an audit finding against it. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01 and are communicated under ISMS-PLN-02.

Data retention and disposal policy

The rules that decide how long each category of information is kept, what starts the clock, how it is disposed of, how legal holds suspend disposal, and how backups and logs are treated, with the schedule itself held in PIMS-REG-07.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.4.7; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.4.8; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.4.5; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.4.7; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.4.8; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.4.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.33; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.10; GDPR Article 5. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This policy keeps information for as long as it is needed and no longer. Over-retention increases the harm of every breach, makes requests from individuals harder to answer and breaks the storage limitation principle; under-retention loses records that the law, a contract or a dispute requires.

2. Scope

It applies to all information that [Organisation] holds, in every system, backup, archive, log, mailbox, device, paper file and supplier service, with particular rules for personal data. Where [Organisation] is a processor, the client's instructions and the agreement take precedence over the schedule, and the policy governs what happens at the end of the service.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Privacy Officer Owns this policy and PIMS-REG-07, approves every period and its justification, imposes and lifts legal holds with the legal adviser.
Processing Owner Proposes the period and trigger for each category they own and confirms the quarterly check.
System Owner Configures retention and deletion in their system, runs manual disposal where configuration is impossible, and records the result.
Information Security Manager Sets the retention of security logs and backups under GOV-PRO-14 and GOV-PRO-12 and supplies the disposal methods for media under GOV-PRO-16.
Legal adviser Confirms statutory periods and limitation periods recorded in GOV-REG-04.

4. Policy statements

4.1 The schedule. Every category of information is listed in PIMS-REG-07 with its systems, its retention period, the trigger that starts the period, the reason for the period, the disposal method and the owner. A category not in the schedule is added within thirty days of being found, and until then is treated as held for the default in 4.3.

4.2 Justified periods. Each period is justified by one of: a statutory retention requirement, a contractual requirement, the limitation period for legal claims, or a documented operational need, in that order of preference. The justification names the source in GOV-REG-04 where it is legal or contractual. "We might need it" is not a justification.

4.3 Default period. Personal data with no entry in the schedule is deleted [Number] months after the purpose for which it was collected ends, and at most twelve months after.

4.4 Triggers. Periods run from a defined event (end of contract, last activity, decision date, end of employment, financial year end, closure of a case, creation of the record), never from an undefined "when no longer needed". The trigger is recorded in the system where possible.

4.5 Configured disposal. Where a system can enforce retention, the System Owner configures it and records where. Where it cannot, the System Owner runs a disposal at least quarterly and records the run. The Privacy Officer samples each category at least annually and records Pass, Fail or To confirm in PIMS-REG-07.

4.6 Disposal methods. Personal data is disposed of by secure deletion, by irreversible anonymisation, or by return to the controller or individual. Paper is cross-cut shredded or placed in confidential waste. Media and devices are wiped or destroyed under GOV-PRO-16 and recorded in GOV-REG-20. Deleting a reference, a link or an index entry while the data remains is not disposal.

4.7 Anonymisation. Data counts as disposed of by anonymisation only when no party, using means reasonably likely to be used, can re-identify the individuals, and the Privacy Officer has recorded the assessment. Pseudonymised data remains personal data and stays in the schedule.

4.8 Copies and derived data. Disposal covers every copy: primary stores, replicas, exports, reports, caches, temporary files, search indexes, analytics data sets, test environments and data held by processors. The Processing Owner lists the locations from GOV-REG-25 and PIMS-REG-06 and confirms each.

4.9 Backups. Backups are kept for the period set under GOV-PRO-12 and recorded in PIMS-REG-07, so that data deleted from a primary system leaves the backups within that period without a separate deletion. Data restored from backup during recovery that had been deleted from the primary system is deleted again within five working days of the restore.

4.10 Logs. Logs are kept for the period set under GOV-PRO-14 and recorded in PIMS-REG-07. Logs are personal data where they identify an individual and are disposed of on the same terms; they are not kept longer than the security purpose needs because they might one day be useful.

4.11 Legal hold. When litigation, an investigation, an authority enquiry or a complaint is reasonably anticipated, the Privacy Officer or the legal adviser issues a written legal hold naming the categories, systems, individuals and custodians affected. Disposal of the named information is suspended, custodians are instructed in writing, configured deletion is paused for the affected data, and the hold is reviewed every ninety days and lifted in writing. Legal holds are listed in PIMS-REG-07.

4.12 End of a processor service. When [Organisation] stops acting as processor for a client, it returns or deletes the client's personal data as the agreement based on PIMS-TPL-02 requires, within the time it states, and provides written confirmation of deletion. When a supplier stops processing for [Organisation], the supplier owner obtains the same confirmation under GOV-PRO-06 and records it in PIMS-REG-06.

4.13 Requests and breaches. Erasure requests under PIMS-PRO-03 override the schedule unless an exemption applies. Records of requests, breaches, assessments and consents are themselves in the schedule, because they prove compliance.

4.14 Schedule examples. The following rows illustrate the form of PIMS-REG-07. Every period is an example for [Organisation] to replace from its own obligations in GOV-REG-04; none is a legal statement.

Category Trigger Period Disposal
Customer account and contract data End of contract [Number] years, set by the limitation period Secure deletion, anonymised aggregates may remain
Prospect and marketing contacts Last meaningful interaction [Number] months Secure deletion and suppression entry kept
Support tickets and chat transcripts Ticket closure [Number] years Secure deletion
Employee records End of employment [Number] years, set by employment and tax law Secure deletion, paper shredded
Unsuccessful applicant data Recruitment decision [Number] months Secure deletion
Payroll and tax records End of the tax year As set by tax law in GOV-REG-04 Secure deletion
Building access and visitor logs Entry date [Number] months Secure deletion
Security logs Event date Period set under GOV-PRO-14 Automatic expiry
Backups Backup creation Period set under GOV-PRO-12 Automatic expiry
Data subject request records Request closure [Number] years Secure deletion
Personal data breach records Breach closure [Number] years Secure deletion
Consent records Withdrawal or end of processing Period set by the limitation period Secure deletion
Impact assessments and processing inventory Processing ceases Life of the processing plus [Number] years Archive then secure deletion

5. Records and evidence

  • PIMS-REG-07 Retention schedule: every category with its period, trigger, configuration, check results and legal holds.
  • Configuration exports showing retention settings in each system.
  • Disposal run records and GOV-REG-20 Media and equipment disposal log.
  • Deletion confirmations from processors and to clients.
  • Legal hold notices, custodian instructions and lift notices.

6. Exceptions

An extension beyond the schedule for a named data set is approved by the Privacy Officer for a stated reason and a stated end date of no more than twelve months, recorded in PIMS-REG-07, and reviewed at the end date. A legal hold is not an exception; it is a suspension under 4.11.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this policy and the schedule annually, after a change in statutory periods in GOV-REG-04, after a new system or processor starts holding personal data, and after a breach or request that revealed over-retention. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

International transfer policy

The rules under which personal data may leave the region in which [Organisation] is established, the transfer mechanisms in plain words, the assessment required before a transfer relies on contractual safeguards, and the register that records every transfer.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.5.1; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.5.2; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.5.3; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 8.5.1; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.5.1; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.5.2; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.5.3; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.5.1; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.5.2; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.5.4; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.5.5; GDPR Article 44; GDPR Article 45; GDPR Article 46; GDPR Article 47; GDPR Article 49. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This policy keeps the protection that individuals have at home attached to their data when it goes abroad. A transfer without a recognised mechanism is unlawful regardless of how secure the recipient is, and a mechanism applied without assessing the destination can be unlawful too.

2. Scope

It applies to every movement of personal data from [Organisation] to a recipient in another country or international organisation, including hosting, backup and support arrangements, remote access by a supplier or employee from abroad, sub-processors of processors, group companies, clients, authorities and any onward transfer by a recipient. It applies whether [Organisation] is controller or processor. The region of establishment is [Region], as recorded in GOV-REG-04.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Privacy Officer Approves every transfer mechanism, runs or reviews transfer impact assessments, keeps PIMS-REG-05 and monitors changes in law.
Processing Owner Identifies transfers in their processing activities and keeps the PIMS-REG-01 transfer column current.
Supplier owner Establishes the processing locations of each supplier and its sub-processors before contract.
Legal adviser Confirms the mechanism, the clause version and the derogation reasoning.
System Owner Configures hosting regions and support access under GOV-PRO-26 and provides the evidence.

4. Policy statements

4.1 What counts as a transfer. Personal data is transferred when it is sent to, stored in, or made accessible from another country, including remote viewing by a support engineer, replication to a backup region, and processing by a sub-processor abroad. Transit through another country with no access and no storage is not a transfer. The Privacy Officer decides doubtful cases.

4.2 No transfer without a recorded mechanism. Personal data leaves the region of establishment only after the Privacy Officer has approved a mechanism in 4.3 and recorded the transfer in PIMS-REG-05 with the importer, the destination, the data, the mechanism and its reference. A transfer found without an entry is stopped or regularised within ten working days and recorded as a nonconformity under GOV-PRO-04.

4.3 Mechanisms in plain words. The Privacy Officer selects the first of these that applies:

Mechanism What it means When [Organisation] uses it
Adequacy The relevant authority has formally recognised the destination as giving protection equivalent to home law, so the data may flow as if it stayed in the region Any destination on the current adequacy list recorded in GOV-REG-04; the entry is reviewed if the recognition is withdrawn
Standard contractual clauses Contract wording approved by the authority that binds the importer to protections; the right module is chosen for the roles of the parties and the wording is not altered except to add protections The usual mechanism for suppliers, sub-processors and clients outside adequate destinations; always with a transfer impact assessment
Binding corporate rules Group-wide rules approved by an authority that bind every group company to the same protections Transfers between group companies where such rules have been approved
Approved codes or certifications A code of conduct or certification approved by an authority, with binding commitments by the importer Where the importer holds one and the Privacy Officer has verified it
Derogations Narrow exceptions for occasional transfers: the individual's explicit informed consent, a contract with or in the interest of the individual, important public interest, legal claims, or the individual's vital interests Last resort, for a specific non-repetitive transfer, never for routine processing, and only with the legal adviser's written confirmation

4.4 Transfer impact assessment. Before a transfer relies on standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules or a code or certification, the Privacy Officer completes GDPR-TPL-08: the data and the individuals; the importer and its role; the law and practice of the destination, including access by public authorities and the remedies available to individuals; the importer's own experience of such access; and the supplementary measures that close any gap, such as encryption with keys held only in the region of establishment, pseudonymisation before export, split processing, or contractual commitments to challenge and notify access requests. The assessment is approved before the first transfer, referenced in PIMS-REG-05, and repeated every [Number] months and whenever the destination's law, the importer or the data changes.

4.5 Supplementary measures. Where the assessment finds that the destination's law undermines the clauses and no supplementary measure closes the gap, the transfer does not take place. Measures are implemented and evidenced before the transfer starts, not promised.

4.6 Suppliers and sub-processors. The supplier owner establishes under GOV-PRO-06, before contract, every country in which the supplier and its sub-processors store, process, back up or access the data, records them in PIMS-REG-06 and GOV-REG-07, and obtains notice of any change. Hosting regions are chosen under GOV-PRO-26 to avoid transfers where a regional option exists at reasonable cost.

4.7 Onward transfers. An importer may pass personal data to another country only under a mechanism that gives equivalent protection and that is recorded in the contract. Sub-processor chains are followed to the last link.

4.8 Transfers where [Organisation] is a processor. [Organisation] transfers a client's personal data only on the client's documented instruction, under the mechanism the client has approved, and notifies the client of every country involved and every change. A request from a client to transfer without a lawful mechanism is declined and recorded.

4.9 Working from abroad. An employee or contractor accessing personal data from outside the region of establishment is a transfer; approval under GOV-POL-05 includes the Privacy Officer's confirmation of the mechanism and the device and network controls that apply.

4.10 Requests from foreign authorities. A legally binding request from a public authority outside the region for personal data is handled under GOV-PRO-25 by the Privacy Officer and the legal adviser: its validity is checked, the minimum data is disclosed, the controller is told where [Organisation] is a processor and the law allows, and individuals are told where the law allows. Each request and response is recorded in PIMS-REG-05 as a disclosure.

4.11 Individuals informed. Every notice under PIMS-PRO-05 states that data is transferred, where, under which mechanism, and how the individual can see the safeguards.

4.12 Records. PIMS-REG-05 records every transfer and every disclosure to a foreign authority; PIMS-REG-01 and GDPR-REG-02 cross-reference it. Signed clauses, assessments and approvals are kept for the life of the transfer plus the period in PIMS-REG-07.

4.13 Change in law. When an adequacy recognition is withdrawn, a clause set is replaced, or a court decision changes the assessment of a destination, the Privacy Officer reviews every affected PIMS-REG-05 entry within thirty days and reports to the next management review.

5. Records and evidence

  • PIMS-REG-05 International transfer register with the mechanism, reference and assessment for every transfer.
  • Completed GDPR-TPL-08 transfer impact assessments and their reviews.
  • Signed standard contractual clauses or other instruments, with the version and the module used.
  • PIMS-REG-06 and GOV-REG-07 location entries for suppliers and sub-processors.
  • GOV-PRO-26 region evidence and GOV-POL-05 approvals for working abroad.

6. Exceptions

A derogation under 4.3 is the only exception and is used as that row describes. No transfer proceeds on the basis that a mechanism will be put in place later.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this policy annually, after any change in transfer law or adequacy recognitions recorded in GOV-REG-04, after a request from a foreign authority, and after an audit finding. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Determining controller and processor roles

The test applied to every processing activity and every counterparty to decide whether [Organisation] acts as controller, joint controller or processor, how the decision is recorded, and what obligations follow from it.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.2.1; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.2.6; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.2.7; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 8.2.1; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.2.7; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.2.1; GDPR Article 4; GDPR Article 26; GDPR Article 28. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This procedure makes the role decision explicit and recorded, because the role decides which obligations apply: a controller answers to individuals and the supervisory authority for the whole processing, a processor answers to the controller for following instructions, and joint controllers must agree who does what. Getting the role wrong leaves obligations unowned.

2. Scope

It applies to every processing activity in PIMS-REG-01, every supplier that receives personal data, every client contract under which [Organisation] receives personal data, every group company arrangement and every data sharing agreement, from the first proposal until the processing ends.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Privacy Officer Runs the test, records the decision and its reasoning, decides disputed cases with the legal adviser, and re-assesses on change.
Processing Owner Supplies the facts about who decided the processing, its purpose and its means, and applies the resulting obligations.
Supplier owner Raises the test for every new supplier under GOV-PRO-06 before personal data is shared.
Sales or account lead Raises the test for every client contract that involves personal data before signature.
Legal adviser Confirms contract wording matches the decided role.

4. Procedure

4.1 Trigger. The Processing Owner, supplier owner or account lead asks the Privacy Officer for a role decision when a processing activity is proposed, when a supplier or client arrangement involving personal data is proposed, when the purpose or the parties of an existing activity change, and at the annual review of PIMS-REG-01. No personal data flows under a new arrangement until the decision is recorded.

4.2 Facts gathered. The requester provides, in writing: the parties involved, who initiated the processing, what each party gets out of it, which party chose the data items, the individuals concerned, the retention period and the recipients, which party could stop the processing, and whether any party may use the data for anything of its own.

4.3 The decision test. The Privacy Officer answers five questions for each party.

Question Points to controller Points to processor
Why does the processing happen? The party decided it should happen for its own ends The party does it only because another party engaged it
Who decides the purpose? The party sets or shares the purpose The purpose is set entirely by the other party
Who decides the essential means? The party decides which data, which individuals, how long and who receives The party decides only technical or organisational detail within instructions
Does the party gain beyond a fee? Yes, a commercial, legal or operational benefit of its own No, it is paid for the service and nothing more
Could the party use the data for anything else? Yes, or it already does No, contract and practice forbid it

Three or more answers in the controller column make the party a controller. A party that decides the purpose is always a controller, however the other answers fall. A party that processes only within another party's documented instructions, decides nothing essential and gains nothing beyond its fee is a processor.

4.4 Joint controllership. Where two or more parties are controllers of the same processing, the Privacy Officer asks whether they decided the purposes and means together, including the case where each party's decision depends on the other's so that the processing could not happen without both. If so they are joint controllers and an arrangement is required. If each party pursues its own purpose with its own means on the same data, they are independent controllers and a data sharing agreement is used instead.

4.5 Recurring cases. The Privacy Officer applies the test, not a label, but records the usual outcome for recurring patterns in a short table kept with this procedure: cloud hosting and software providers acting on instruction (processor); payroll providers and benefits administrators (usually processor); professional advisers, auditors and regulators using data for their own professional duties (controller); payment and banking services (usually controller); staff augmentation working under [Organisation]'s direction (part of [Organisation], not a separate party); a group company providing a shared service to other group companies (processor for that service); a client that sends personal data for [Organisation] to deliver a service (client is controller, [Organisation] is processor); a client that buys data [Organisation] collected for its own purposes (both controllers). A pattern never overrides facts that point the other way.

4.6 Documenting the decision. The Privacy Officer records in PIMS-REG-01 the role for each processing activity and, in a note on the row, the reasoning in no more than three sentences and the date. For a supplier the role is also recorded in PIMS-REG-06 and the processor terms flag in GOV-REG-07. For a client contract the role is recorded in the contract summary held by the account lead and in PIMS-REG-01.

4.7 Consequences for [Organisation] as controller. The Processing Owner applies the full set: a lawful basis and a notice (PIMS-PRO-05), inventory entry (PIMS-REG-01), impact assessment screening (PIMS-PRO-02), rights handling (PIMS-PRO-03), breach notification to the authority and individuals (PIMS-PRO-04), processor terms with every processor (PIMS-TPL-02), transfer mechanisms (PIMS-POL-03) and retention (PIMS-POL-02).

4.8 Consequences for [Organisation] as processor. The Processing Owner applies: processing only on the controller's documented instructions and flagging any instruction that appears unlawful; confidentiality commitments from staff; the security measures in the agreement; no sub-processor without the controller's authorisation and no change without notice (PIMS-REG-06); assistance with rights requests, security, breaches and assessments; notification of breaches to the controller without undue delay (PIMS-PRO-04); deletion or return at the end of the service; processor records in PIMS-REG-01; and making information available for the controller's audits. [Organisation] does not use the data for its own purposes, including product improvement, analytics or marketing, unless the agreement allows it and [Organisation] becomes a controller for that use.

4.9 Consequences for joint controllers. The Privacy Officer agrees a written arrangement with the other controllers that allocates the notice, the rights handling, the breach notification, the contact point for individuals and the record keeping, and makes the essence of the arrangement available to individuals through the notice. Each controller remains answerable to individuals regardless of the allocation.

4.10 Contract alignment. The legal adviser confirms before signature that the contract wording matches the decided role: processor terms based on PIMS-TPL-02 for a processor, a joint controller arrangement for joint controllers, a data sharing agreement for independent controllers. A contract that labels a party a processor while the facts make it a controller is corrected, not signed.

4.11 Disputed cases. Where the counterparty disagrees with the role decision, the Privacy Officer records both positions and the reasons, and the legal adviser decides. Until the dispute is settled, [Organisation] applies the controller obligations, which are the wider set.

4.12 Re-assessment. The decision is re-assessed when the purpose, the parties, the data items or the benefit to any party changes, when a processor starts using data for its own ends, and at the annual inventory review under GDPR-PRO-01. A changed decision is recorded with the date and triggers a contract review within thirty days.

5. Records and evidence

  • PIMS-REG-01 Personal data processing inventory: the role column and the reasoning note on each row.
  • PIMS-REG-06 Processor and sub-processor register and GOV-REG-07 Supplier register entries.
  • Signed processor terms, joint controller arrangements and data sharing agreements.
  • The recurring-case table kept with this procedure, with the date of its last review.

6. Exceptions

No exception applies. A processing activity without a recorded role is not started, and an existing one found without a role is assessed within five working days of discovery.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this procedure annually, after guidance from a supervisory authority or a court decision that changes how roles are assessed, and after any dispute under step 4.11. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Privacy risk and data protection impact assessment procedure

How every new or changed processing activity is screened for privacy risk, when a full data protection impact assessment is required, how risks to individuals are scored and treated, who approves the residual risk, and when the supervisory authority is consulted first.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.2.5; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.4.1.2; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.2.5; GDPR Article 35; GDPR Article 36. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This procedure finds the harm a processing activity could do to the individuals concerned before the activity starts, reduces that harm by design, and records the decision so that [Organisation] can show it considered the risk. It also satisfies the legal duty to assess, and where necessary consult the authority about, processing likely to result in a high risk.

2. Scope

It applies to every new processing activity, every significant change to an existing one (new purpose, new data items, new individuals, new technology, new recipient, new country), every system or feature that handles personal data, and every procurement of a service that will process personal data. It applies whether [Organisation] is controller or processor; as a processor [Organisation] assists the controller's assessment rather than approving its own.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Processing Owner Completes the screening, drafts the assessment with the project team, implements the measures and owns the residual risk at low or medium.
Privacy Officer Decides whether a full assessment is required, advises throughout, challenges the risk scoring, records the outcome in PIMS-REG-08 and prepares any consultation with the authority.
Information Security Manager Supplies the security measures and links the privacy risks to GOV-REG-05.
Head of Engineering or System Owner Confirms that technical measures are built and tested before go-live.
Chief Executive Officer Approves residual risk rated high and decides whether to proceed to prior consultation.

4. Procedure

4.1 Screening at concept stage. Before design approval, the Processing Owner completes section 1 of PIMS-TPL-01, answering each screening trigger Yes or No with one line of justification, and sends it to the Privacy Officer. The triggers are:

  1. evaluation or scoring of individuals, including profiling and prediction of behaviour, location, health, interests or reliability;
  2. decisions made about individuals by automated means that have legal or similarly significant effects;
  3. systematic monitoring of individuals, including monitoring of a publicly accessible area, employee monitoring and tracking of location or online behaviour;
  4. special categories of data, criminal offence data or data of a highly personal nature such as financial detail or private communications;
  5. processing on a large scale, judged by the number of individuals, the volume and range of data, the duration and the geographical extent;
  6. matching or combining data sets from different sources or collected for different purposes;
  7. data about individuals who may be vulnerable or have little choice, including children, patients, employees and applicants;
  8. use of new or innovative technology, including machine learning, biometrics, connected devices and AI features;
  9. processing that could deny individuals a service, a contract, a benefit or access, or could lead to discrimination, exclusion or physical harm;
  10. data obtained without the individuals' direct involvement where a notice is impractical;
  11. transfer of personal data outside the region where [Organisation] is established;
  12. any processing type that the supervisory authority has listed as requiring an assessment, as recorded in GOV-REG-04.

4.2 Screening decision. Within five working days the Privacy Officer records the outcome in PIMS-REG-08. A full assessment is required when two or more triggers apply, when trigger 2, 4 or 12 applies on its own, or when the Privacy Officer judges any single trigger to carry a high risk. A decision that no assessment is required is recorded with reasons, and the processing still passes the privacy by design review in PIMS-PRO-06.

4.3 Stage gates. A required assessment advances through four gates, each recorded in PIMS-REG-08: gate 1, description and necessity complete before build starts; gate 2, risks scored and measures agreed before the go-live gate in PB-07; gate 3, residual risk approved before any personal data is processed in production; gate 4, review at the interval in step 4.11. A project does not pass a gate on a promise; a measure not yet built is a To confirm item with an owner and a due date.

4.4 Description of the processing. The Processing Owner completes section 2 of PIMS-TPL-01: nature (how data is collected, used, stored, shared and deleted, with a data flow referenced in GOV-REG-25 or GDPR-REG-02), scope (data items, special categories, volume, individuals, retention, geography), context (relationship with the individuals, their expectations, prior concerns, technology novelty) and purposes (the benefit to [Organisation], to the individuals and to others).

4.5 Necessity and proportionality. The Processing Owner and the Privacy Officer record in section 3 why the purpose cannot be achieved with less data or less intrusion, the lawful basis, how each principle in PIMS-POL-01 is met, the alternatives considered and rejected, how individuals are informed and how they exercise rights, the processors involved and the transfer mechanism.

4.6 Consultation. The Privacy Officer decides who is consulted and records it in section 4: the Information Security Manager always; the individuals or their representatives, through user research, a survey, a works council or a client advisory group, unless the Privacy Officer records why that is not practicable; processors, for the measures they operate; and the legal adviser where the lawful basis or a transfer is in question. Views received, and whether they changed the design, are recorded.

4.7 Identifying risks to individuals. The project team lists risks from the individual's point of view, not the organisation's: loss of control over their data, unauthorised disclosure, re-identification, inaccurate data leading to a wrong decision, discrimination, financial loss, identity theft, reputational damage, physical danger, loss of a service, distress, and inability to exercise rights. Each risk names its source (an event, an actor or a design weakness).

4.8 Scoring. Each risk is scored on the 1 to 5 likelihood scale in GOV-PRO-05 and on a severity scale for individuals: 1 negligible (inconvenience, easily overcome); 2 limited (annoyance, minor cost, short-lived); 3 significant (real difficulty, financial loss, distress, recoverable with effort); 4 severe (lasting harm, serious financial or psychological consequence, hard to recover from); 5 critical (danger to life, irreversible harm, loss of liberty). Score is likelihood multiplied by severity, banded as in GOV-PRO-05: 1 to 4 low, 5 to 9 medium, 10 to 15 high, 16 to 25 critical.

4.9 Measures and residual risk. For every risk at medium or above the team records the measures that remove the source, reduce likelihood or reduce severity (less data, pseudonymisation, encryption, access limits, shorter retention, transparency, human review, opt-out, contractual terms), the owner and the date. The risk is re-scored after the measures. Every measure becomes a backlog item or a contract clause, and every medium or higher residual risk also appears in GOV-REG-05 with a cross-reference to the assessment.

4.10 Approval of residual risk. Residual low or medium is approved by the Processing Owner with the Privacy Officer's written agreement. Residual high is approved only by the Chief Executive Officer after written advice from the Privacy Officer, and is reviewed every six months. Residual critical is not approved; the processing is redesigned or abandoned. The approval, the approver and the date are recorded in section 7 of PIMS-TPL-01 and in PIMS-REG-08.

4.11 Prior consultation with the supervisory authority. Where a residual high risk cannot be reduced further, the Privacy Officer prepares a consultation containing the assessment, the roles of the parties, the purposes, the measures and the Privacy Officer's contact details, and submits it to the authority. The processing does not start until the authority responds or the period set by law expires without a response. The Chief Executive Officer decides whether to consult or to abandon the processing.

4.12 Review. The Processing Owner reviews a completed assessment annually where residual risk is high, every two years otherwise, and immediately when a change in step 2 occurs, a breach affects the processing, a complaint is received about it, or the law or authority guidance changes. The review outcome is recorded even when nothing changes.

4.13 Processor assistance. Where [Organisation] is a processor, the Processing Owner supplies the controller, within the time in the agreement, with the description of the processing, the security measures and the sub-processors involved, and implements the measures the controller's assessment requires.

5. Records and evidence

  • PIMS-REG-08 DPIA register: every screening outcome and every assessment with its gate dates, residual rating, approver and next review.
  • Completed PIMS-TPL-01 documents, stored with the project record and retained for the life of the processing plus the period in PIMS-REG-07.
  • GOV-REG-05 entries for medium and higher residual risks; backlog items and contract clauses for measures.
  • Consultation records and any correspondence with the supervisory authority.

6. Exceptions

An activity may start before gate 3 only in a declared Severity 1 or 2 incident under GOV-PRO-07 where the processing is needed to contain harm, and then only with the Privacy Officer's recorded agreement; the assessment is completed within ten working days afterwards. No other exception applies.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this procedure annually, after any prior consultation, after new authority guidance on assessments, and after an audit finding. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

8. Related documents

  • PIMS-TPL-01 Data protection impact assessment template
  • PIMS-REG-08 DPIA register
  • PIMS-POL-01 Privacy information management policy
  • PIMS-PRO-06 Privacy by design and by default procedure
  • GOV-PRO-05 Risk assessment and treatment methodology
  • GOV-REG-05 Information security risk register
  • GOV-REG-25 Data flow and interface inventory
  • GDPR-REG-02 Data flow and transfer map
  • PB-07 Playbook: the go-live security and privacy gate for a software project
  • AI-PRO-01 AI risk assessment procedure

Data subject rights handling procedure

How a request from an individual about their personal data is received, verified, logged, answered within one month and recorded, right by right, including when a request may be refused and what [Organisation] does when it is a processor.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.3.1; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.3.6; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.3.9; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 8.3.1; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.5; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.6; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.7; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.8; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.9; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.10; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.3.1; GDPR Article 12; GDPR Article 15; GDPR Article 16; GDPR Article 17; GDPR Article 18; GDPR Article 20; GDPR Article 21; GDPR Article 22. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This procedure gets every request from an individual answered correctly and on time, by named people following the same steps, so that individuals get what the law gives them and [Organisation] can prove it.

2. Scope

It applies to every request, however phrased and through whatever channel, in which an individual asks about or wants something done with personal data that [Organisation] holds about them as a controller: access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection, review of an automated decision and withdrawal of consent. It also sets what [Organisation] does with a request it receives as a processor.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
All staff Recognise a request in any form, forward it to the privacy mailbox the same working day, and never answer it themselves.
Request handler A person trained for the role and named by the Privacy Officer. Logs, verifies, coordinates, drafts and sends the response, and keeps PIMS-REG-02 current.
Privacy Officer Decides extensions, refusals, fees, complex scope questions and disputes; reviews every refusal before it is sent.
System Owner Searches their system, extracts, corrects, restricts or deletes within the time the handler sets, and confirms in writing.
Processor Assists within the time in its agreement and does not answer the individual directly.

4. Procedure

4.1 Intake. Requests arrive through the privacy mailbox and web form published in the notice, by post, through customer support, through account managers, through Human Resources, or verbally to any employee. Every channel counts. A request made verbally is written down by the person who received it, with the date, and confirmed back to the individual. A request does not have to cite the law or use any particular words.

4.2 Logging. The request handler records the request in PIMS-REG-02 within one working day of receipt: date received, channel, requester type, the rights exercised, and the clock start. The one month period runs from the day of receipt and ends on the same date of the following month, or the last day of that month if there is no such date.

4.3 Identity verification. The handler confirms identity in proportion to the sensitivity of the data. Where the individual writes from the contact details held on their account, or is signed in to their account, no further proof is requested. Otherwise the handler asks, within three working days and using the GDPR-TPL-05 verification letter, for the minimum extra information that confirms identity, and records in PIMS-REG-02 the date it arrives; the period then runs from that date. Identity documents received are deleted once checked. A request made by a representative is honoured only with written authority from the individual.

4.4 Acknowledgement and scope. Within three working days of logging, the handler sends the GDPR-TPL-05 acknowledgement with the expected response date. Where the request is broad, the handler may ask the individual to clarify what they want, without stopping the clock; if no answer arrives within ten working days the handler responds to the request as reasonably understood.

4.5 Extension. Where the request is complex or the individual has made several, the Privacy Officer may extend the period by up to two further months. The extension and its reasons are sent to the individual before the first month ends, using the GDPR-TPL-05 extension letter, and are recorded in PIMS-REG-02.

4.6 Locating the data. The handler identifies every system and processor that may hold the individual's data from PIMS-REG-01 and PIMS-REG-06, instructs each System Owner and processor in writing with a deadline of no more than ten working days, and records the confirmations. Searches cover primary systems, support tools, email and messaging where the individual is a subject, derived data, and backups where restorable within the period.

4.7 Handling each right.

Right What the handler does
Access Collates the data, removes or redacts other people's data and material covered by an exemption, and provides a copy together with the purposes, categories, recipients, retention, source, the existence of automated decision making and its logic, the right to complain and the other rights. Delivered securely in a commonly used electronic format, or through the account portal where one exists.
Rectification Checks the correction against evidence where accuracy matters, applies it in every system within five working days, tells every recipient the data was shared with, and confirms to the individual. Disputed accuracy is recorded alongside the data until resolved.
Erasure Confirms a ground applies (purpose ended, consent withdrawn, objection upheld, unlawful processing, legal obligation, child's data from an online service), checks no exemption applies (legal obligation to retain, legal claims, freedom of expression, public interest), then deletes or anonymises across primary systems, derived data and processors under PIMS-POL-02, records that backup copies expire within their cycle, informs recipients, and confirms to the individual.
Restriction Marks the data so that it is stored but not otherwise processed, in every system, for as long as the ground applies (accuracy contested, processing unlawful but erasure declined, data needed for legal claims, objection pending), tells recipients, and informs the individual before lifting the restriction.
Portability Where the data was provided by the individual and processed by automated means on the basis of consent or contract, exports it in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format, and transmits it directly to another controller where technically feasible and requested.
Objection For direct marketing, stops the processing without exception and records the suppression. For processing based on legitimate interests or public task, stops unless the Privacy Officer records compelling grounds that override the individual's interests, using GDPR-TPL-07, and tells the individual the outcome with reasons.
Automated decisions Where a decision with legal or similarly significant effect was made solely by automated means, arranges a review of the decision by a competent person, explains the logic and the main factors in plain words, lets the individual put their point of view, and records the reviewed decision.
Withdrawal of consent Actions the withdrawal under PIMS-PRO-05 step 4.5 and confirms it, without affecting processing that took place before.

4.8 Refusal and limitation. A request is refused or limited only on a ground the Privacy Officer confirms in writing: the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive, in particular because it repeats a recent request; the data is covered by an exemption in the law recorded in GOV-REG-04; or disclosure would adversely affect the rights of another person. The refusal letter in GDPR-TPL-05 states the reasons, the right to complain to the supervisory authority and the right to seek a judicial remedy, and is sent within the period. A partial refusal still answers the rest of the request.

4.9 Fees. Responses are free. A reasonable fee covering administrative cost is charged only for further copies or for a request the Privacy Officer has recorded as manifestly unfounded or excessive, and the individual is told the fee before work continues.

4.10 Response. The handler sends the response using the GDPR-TPL-05 response letter through a channel that matches the sensitivity of the content: the account portal, encrypted file transfer or password-protected archive with the password sent separately. Paper responses go by tracked post. The response is written in plain language and, where the individual is a child, in language a child can understand.

4.11 Requests received as a processor. Where the request concerns data [Organisation] processes for a client, the handler forwards it to the client within two working days, tells the individual that it has been passed to the controller, takes no other action unless the client instructs it, and records it in PIMS-REG-02 with the client named. Assistance requested by the client is provided within the time in the agreement.

4.12 Closure and records. The handler records in PIMS-REG-02 the outcome, the date closed and whether the deadline was met, and files the correspondence and the search confirmations with the request. Request records are retained for the period in PIMS-REG-07. A complaint about the handling is recorded and reviewed by the Privacy Officer within five working days.

4.13 Monitoring. The Privacy Officer reports the number of requests, the proportion answered on time, extensions, refusals and complaints quarterly under PIMS-PRO-07. Two late responses in a quarter raise a corrective action in GOV-REG-03.

5. Records and evidence

  • PIMS-REG-02 Data subject request register: every request with dates, rights, handler, outcome and timeliness.
  • The correspondence for each request, including GDPR-TPL-05 letters sent and identity verification records.
  • Written confirmations from System Owners and processors for each search, correction, restriction or deletion.
  • Privacy Officer decisions on extensions, refusals, fees and objections, with reasons.

6. Exceptions

Where a search cannot be completed within the extended period because data is held in an archive that cannot be restored in time, the handler provides everything found, states what remains outstanding and when it will follow, and the Privacy Officer records the case. No other exception applies.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this procedure annually, after any complaint to a supervisory authority about request handling, after a change in law or authority guidance on rights, and after a new system or processor changes where personal data is held. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

8. Related documents

  • GDPR-TPL-05 Data subject request response letters
  • PIMS-REG-02 Data subject request register
  • PIMS-REG-01 Personal data processing inventory
  • PIMS-REG-06 Processor and sub-processor register
  • PIMS-PRO-05 Consent and privacy notice management procedure
  • PIMS-POL-02 Data retention and disposal policy
  • GDPR-TPL-07 Legitimate interests assessment template
  • PIMS-PRO-07 Privacy control effectiveness monitoring procedure

Personal data breach assessment and notification procedure

What happens from the moment an incident is found to involve personal data: the 72 hour clock, the assessment of risk to individuals, the decision whether to notify the supervisory authority and the individuals, the processor duty to tell the controller, and the record kept whether or not anyone is notified.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 clause 6.13.1.1; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 6.13.1.5; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.2.5; GDPR Article 33; GDPR Article 34. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This procedure turns an incident involving personal data into a documented assessment and, where required, a notification made within the legal deadline, so that individuals can protect themselves, the authority is told what the law requires, and [Organisation] can show its reasoning afterwards.

2. Scope

It applies to every breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to, personal data that [Organisation] holds as controller or processor, including breaches at a processor or sub-processor. It runs alongside GOV-PRO-07, which handles the technical response; this procedure handles the assessment, the notification decisions and the privacy record.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Incident Lead Informs the Privacy Officer the moment personal data is suspected to be involved and records the time of awareness.
Privacy Officer Runs this procedure, assesses the risk to individuals, drafts notifications, keeps PIMS-REG-03 and is the contact point for the authority.
Legal adviser Confirms the notification duties in each jurisdiction and reviews the wording of notifications.
Chief Executive Officer Approves notification to individuals and any public statement; is informed of every notification to an authority before it is sent.
Processing Owner and System Owners Supply the facts about the data, the individuals and the systems, within the times below.
Communications lead Prepares the channels for notifying individuals and handles enquiries, under GOV-PRO-07.

4. Procedure

4.1 Trigger and time of awareness. GOV-PRO-07 step 4.4 triggers this procedure. The Incident Lead records the time at which [Organisation] became aware, meaning the time at which a person in [Organisation] had a reasonable degree of certainty that a breach of personal data had occurred, not the time the investigation finished. For a breach reported by a processor, awareness is the time the processor's report is received. The 72 hour clock runs from this time, including outside working hours.

4.2 Register entry. Within two hours of the trigger the Privacy Officer opens an entry in PIMS-REG-03 with the GOV-REG-08 reference, the time of awareness and the 72 hour deadline, and sets the status to Under assessment.

4.3 Facts within 24 hours. The Privacy Officer obtains from the Incident Lead and the Processing Owner, within 24 hours of awareness: what happened and how; whether the breach affects confidentiality, integrity, availability or several; the categories and approximate number of individuals and of records; whether special categories, financial data, credentials or children's data are involved; whether the data was encrypted or pseudonymised and whether the keys are safe; who received or could access the data and whether it has been recovered; whether the breach is ongoing; and which processing activities in PIMS-REG-01 are affected. Facts not yet known are recorded as unknown with the time they are expected.

4.4 Role check. For each affected data set the Privacy Officer confirms from PIMS-REG-01 whether [Organisation] is controller or processor. A single incident can put [Organisation] in both roles for different data; each role follows its own path below.

4.5 Processor path. Where [Organisation] is a processor, the Privacy Officer notifies each affected controller without undue delay and in any case within the time in the agreement, or within 24 hours of awareness where no time is agreed, using the contact in PIMS-REG-06 or the contract. The notification gives the facts known, states what is still being established, and promises updates at the agreed cadence. [Organisation] does not notify the authority or the individuals for the controller's data unless the controller instructs it in writing, and gives the controller the assistance it needs to meet its own deadline.

4.6 Risk assessment to individuals. Where [Organisation] is a controller, the Privacy Officer assesses the risk to the individuals using the likelihood and severity scales in PIMS-PRO-02 step 4.8, considering: the type of breach; the nature, sensitivity and volume of the data; how easily individuals can be identified; the severity of the consequences (identity theft, fraud, financial loss, discrimination, reputational damage, physical harm, distress, loss of control); whether the individuals are vulnerable; the number affected; the nature of the recipient, if known; and the measures already in place, such as encryption with uncompromised keys, or taken since, such as recovery of the data before it was read. The outcome is one of three: risk unlikely, risk likely, high risk likely.

4.7 Decision table. The Privacy Officer applies the table within 48 hours of awareness and records the decision, the reasoning and the legal adviser's confirmation in PIMS-REG-03.

Outcome Supervisory authority Individuals Record
Risk to individuals unlikely Not notified; reasoning recorded Not notified PIMS-REG-03 entry with facts, effects, measures and the reasons for not notifying
Risk likely Notified within 72 hours of awareness Not required; may be informed where it helps them PIMS-REG-03 entry plus the notification and any authority correspondence
High risk likely Notified within 72 hours of awareness Notified without undue delay, unless an exemption in step 4.9 applies PIMS-REG-03 entry plus both notifications, the exemption reasoning if used, and enquiries received

4.8 Notification to the authority. The Privacy Officer completes GDPR-TPL-10 with the nature of the breach, the categories and approximate numbers of individuals and records, the contact point, the likely consequences and the measures taken or proposed, informs the Chief Executive Officer, and submits it through the authority's published channel within 72 hours of awareness. Where the facts are incomplete, the notification is made in phases: the initial notification within 72 hours with what is known, and further information as soon as it is available. A notification made after 72 hours states the reasons for the delay. Where individuals in more than one jurisdiction are affected, the legal adviser identifies the lead authority and any further authorities from GOV-REG-04.

4.9 Notification to individuals. Where high risk is likely, the Privacy Officer drafts a notice in plain language stating what happened, the contact point, the likely consequences, the measures [Organisation] has taken and the steps individuals can take to protect themselves. The Chief Executive Officer approves it and the communications lead sends it directly to each individual by the most reliable channel available. Direct notification may be replaced by a public communication only where the Privacy Officer records that one of these applies: the data was made unintelligible to any unauthorised person, for example by encryption with keys not compromised; measures taken since mean the high risk is no longer likely to materialise; or individual contact would involve disproportionate effort. The authority may require notification even where [Organisation] decided against it.

4.10 Other notifications. The Privacy Officer and legal adviser check GOV-REG-07 for clients with contractual notification rights, GOV-REG-04 for other regulators and sector obligations, the insurance policy for its notification time, and decide with the Incident Lead whether law enforcement is informed. Each is recorded in PIMS-REG-03.

4.11 Record keeping. Every breach, notified or not, is recorded in PIMS-REG-03 with the facts, the effects, the measures taken, the assessment outcome and the reasoning behind each decision. The record is retained for the period in PIMS-REG-07 and is available to the authority on request.

4.12 Review and corrective action. The post-incident review under GOV-PRO-07, using GOV-TPL-11, includes the Privacy Officer and covers whether the time of awareness was set correctly, whether the deadlines were met and whether the notifications were adequate. Corrective actions go to GOV-REG-03; the affected risks in GOV-REG-05 and any assessment in PIMS-REG-08 are updated within thirty days.

4.13 Timeline summary. From awareness: register entry within 2 hours; facts within 24 hours; processor notification to controller within the agreed time or 24 hours; decision within 48 hours; authority notification within 72 hours; individuals without undue delay once high risk is established; post-incident review within ten working days of closure.

5. Records and evidence

  • PIMS-REG-03 Personal data breach register: one entry per breach with the times, the assessment, the decisions and their reasoning.
  • GOV-REG-08 Incident register entry and GOV-TPL-05 incident report for the technical response.
  • Completed GDPR-TPL-10 forms, authority acknowledgements and correspondence.
  • Notices sent to individuals and controllers, with the approval record and the distribution evidence.
  • GOV-TPL-11 post-incident review and GOV-REG-03 corrective actions.

6. Exceptions

No exception applies to the deadlines. Where a deadline is missed, the reasons are recorded in PIMS-REG-03 and in the notification itself, and the miss is reported at the next management review.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this procedure annually, after every breach notified to an authority, after an annual breach exercise run with GOV-PRO-13, and after a change in notification law or authority guidance. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

8. Related documents

  • GOV-PRO-07 Information security incident management procedure
  • GOV-REG-08 Incident register
  • GOV-TPL-05 Incident report form
  • GOV-TPL-11 Post-incident review template
  • GDPR-TPL-10 Personal data breach notification form
  • PIMS-REG-03 Personal data breach register
  • PIMS-REG-01 Personal data processing inventory
  • PIMS-REG-06 Processor and sub-processor register
  • PIMS-TPL-02 Data processing agreement template
  • ISMS-PLN-02 Communication plan
