Consent and privacy notice management procedure

When consent is the right basis, what makes it valid, how it is captured, recorded and withdrawn, what every privacy notice must contain and when it must be shown, and how notices are changed under control.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.2.3; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.2.4; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.3.2; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.3.3; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.3.4; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.2.3; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.2.4; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.2; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.3; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.4; GDPR Article 7; GDPR Article 12; GDPR Article 13; GDPR Article 14. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This procedure makes consent provable and notices accurate. A consent that cannot be shown to have been given freely, specifically and knowingly is no basis at all, and a notice that does not match what actually happens to the data is a transparency failure that every other control inherits.

2. Scope

It applies to every processing activity in PIMS-REG-01 where [Organisation] is a controller, to every point at which personal data is collected from or about an individual, to every privacy notice, cookie notice and consent form published by [Organisation], and to the systems that record consent and withdrawal.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Privacy Officer Decides the lawful basis, approves every consent capture and notice, owns the notice versions and runs the annual check.
Processing Owner Proposes the basis, designs the capture point with the product team, keeps the PIMS-REG-04 entry current and actions withdrawals.
Head of Engineering or System Owner Builds the capture, the record, the withdrawal mechanism and the suppression, and provides the sample exports for checks.
Legal adviser Reviews notices and consent wording before first publication and after a material change.
Marketing lead Applies the marketing rules in this procedure and the suppression list.

4. Procedure

4.1 Choosing the basis. For each purpose the Processing Owner proposes a lawful basis and the Privacy Officer confirms it in PIMS-REG-01. Consent is used only where the individual has a genuine choice and can refuse or withdraw without detriment. It is not used for processing needed to deliver a contract, to meet a legal obligation, or that [Organisation] would carry out regardless of the answer. For employees and applicants consent is used only for genuinely optional matters, such as a voluntary benefit, because the imbalance of power makes other consent unreliable. Where legitimate interests are proposed, GDPR-TPL-07 is completed first.

4.2 Conditions for valid consent. A consent capture approved under this procedure meets all of these: the request is separate from other terms and written in plain language; the purpose is specific, and each distinct purpose has its own choice; the individual is told who is asking, what data, for what purpose, that they can withdraw at any time and how, and what happens if they refuse; consent is given by a clear affirmative act, never by a pre-ticked box, silence, inactivity or continued use; refusing has no effect on the service beyond the part that depends on the consent; and withdrawing is as easy as giving. For special categories the consent is explicit: a statement or a ticked statement that names the category and the purpose. For children below the age set in GOV-REG-04 for the jurisdiction, consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility, verified in proportion to the risk.

4.3 Designing a capture point. Before a capture point goes live the Processing Owner records it in PIMS-REG-04 with the purpose, the audience, the mechanism, the notice version shown, the consent wording version, where the records are stored and the withdrawal method, and obtains the Privacy Officer's approval. Forms are based on GDPR-TPL-06. Cookie and tracker consent follows GDPR-TPL-04 and the inventory in GDPR-REG-04, with non-essential trackers blocked until consent is given.

4.4 Recording consent. The system records, for each consent: who gave it, when, through which capture point, the version of the notice and of the wording shown, which purposes were accepted and which refused, and the evidence of the affirmative act. Records are kept in the system of record for the life of the processing plus the period in PIMS-REG-07, protected against alteration, and exportable for a request under PIMS-PRO-03 or an authority enquiry. A consent whose record cannot be produced is treated as not given.

4.5 Withdrawal. Withdrawal is available through at least the channel through which consent was given, and always through the privacy mailbox. The Processing Owner actions a withdrawal within two working days, and for marketing within 72 hours: processing for that purpose stops, the suppression is applied so that the individual is not re-added by a later import, processors are instructed within the same time, and the data is deleted under PIMS-POL-02 unless another recorded basis applies to it. The withdrawal is recorded with the date and confirmed to the individual. Processing that took place before withdrawal remains lawful.

4.6 Refreshing consent. The Processing Owner reviews each capture point every twelve months and records it in PIMS-REG-04. Consent is obtained again when the purpose, the data or the recipients change materially, when the wording that was shown would no longer meet step 4.2, and for marketing where there has been no contact for [Number] months.

4.7 Notice content. Every notice covers, for data collected from the individual: the identity and contact details of [Organisation] and of the Privacy Officer; each purpose and its lawful basis; the legitimate interests relied on; the recipients and categories of recipients; transfers outside the region and the safeguard used; the retention period or the criteria that set it; the rights, including withdrawal of consent and the right to complain to the supervisory authority; whether providing the data is a legal or contractual requirement and what happens if it is not provided; and the existence, logic and significance of any automated decision making. For data not collected from the individual the notice also states the categories of data and their source. The templates GDPR-TPL-01, GDPR-TPL-02, GDPR-TPL-03 and GDPR-TPL-04 contain these elements.

4.8 Notice timing. A notice is provided at the point of collection where data comes from the individual, with a layered summary at the form and the full notice one step away. Where data comes from elsewhere, the notice is provided within one month, or at the first communication with the individual, or before the first disclosure to another recipient, whichever is earliest, unless the Privacy Officer records that the individual already has the information or that providing it is impossible or would involve disproportionate effort, in which case the information is published instead.

4.9 Notice form. Notices are written in plain language, structured under headings that match the content list, readable on a small screen, available in the languages [Organisation] serves its individuals in, and in language a child can understand where children are the audience. Each notice shows its version and effective date, and every previous version is retained.

4.10 Notice change control. A change to a notice is drafted by the Privacy Officer from a change in PIMS-REG-01, PIMS-REG-05 or PIMS-REG-06, reviewed by the legal adviser, approved by the Privacy Officer and published under GOV-PRO-01 with a new version number. A change that adds a purpose, a recipient, a transfer or a longer retention is communicated to the affected individuals before it takes effect, through the channel in ISMS-PLN-02, and consent is obtained again where the change affects a consented purpose. Notice versions are listed in GOV-REG-01.

4.11 Annual check. Once a year the Privacy Officer compares every published notice against PIMS-REG-01, PIMS-REG-05, PIMS-REG-06 and GDPR-REG-04, samples consent records from each capture point, tests a withdrawal end to end, and records the results in PIMS-REG-04. A notice that does not match the registers is corrected within thirty days and the gap is recorded in GOV-REG-03.

5. Records and evidence

  • PIMS-REG-04 Consent record register: every capture point with its versions, record location, checks and status.
  • Consent records in the systems of record, exportable per individual.
  • Published notices with version history and approval records in GOV-REG-01.
  • GDPR-REG-04 Cookie and tracker inventory and the consent configuration of the website.
  • Withdrawal confirmations and suppression list exports.

6. Exceptions

A capture point may go live with a notice summary rather than the full notice only where the full notice is reachable from it in one step. No exception applies to the conditions in step 4.2.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this procedure annually, after a complaint about consent or transparency, after authority guidance on consent or cookies, and after a new product or channel starts collecting personal data. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Privacy by design and by default procedure

The checklist that every product, feature, system and procurement involving personal data passes through the development and purchasing lifecycle, so that minimisation, protective defaults, access limits, retention, transparency, security and rights support are built in rather than added later.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.4.1; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.4.2; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.4.3; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.4.4; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.4.5; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.4.6; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.4.9; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 8.4.1; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.4.1; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.4.2; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.4.4; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.4.1; GDPR Article 25. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This procedure puts privacy decisions at the points where they are cheap: in the backlog, the design review, the supplier selection and the go-live gate. It turns the principles in PIMS-POL-01 into checks with evidence, and makes the most protective setting the one an individual gets without doing anything.

2. Scope

It applies to every new product, feature, system, integration, report, internal tool and AI feature that processes personal data, to every significant change to one, and to every procurement of a service that will process personal data, whether [Organisation] is controller or processor. It works alongside GOV-PRO-15 for development, GOV-PRO-06 for suppliers, GOV-PRO-09 for changes and PB-07 for the go-live gate.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Product Owner or Processing Owner Raises the privacy requirements at the start, completes the checklist with the team and owns the evidence.
Head of Engineering and System Owner Design and build to the checklist, verify defaults by test, and keep test environments free of production personal data.
Privacy Officer Reviews the checklist at each gate, decides To confirm items, screens for an impact assessment under PIMS-PRO-02 and records the review.
Supplier owner Applies the procurement path for a service that processes personal data.
Information Security Manager Confirms the security checks against the Statement of Applicability.

4. Procedure

4.1 Entry points. The procedure starts when: a product or feature involving personal data enters the backlog; a change request under GOV-TPL-08 answers Yes to personal data processing changed; a supplier is proposed under GOV-PRO-06 for a service that processes personal data; an AI feature or tool is proposed under AI-POL-02; or an existing system is found processing personal data without a record. The Product Owner opens a privacy review record with the project reference and the PIMS-REG-01 processing ID, new or existing.

4.2 Privacy requirements. At the same time as the security requirements in GOV-PRO-15 step 4.1, the Product Owner writes privacy requirements as backlog items with acceptance criteria: which data items are needed and why, the retention period and deletion mechanism, which settings are on by default, how individuals are informed, how each right is supported, and who may access what. The Privacy Officer screens the processing under PIMS-PRO-02 step 4.1 at this point.

4.3 The checklist. The team completes the checklist below at design and again before go-live, attaching evidence for each check. Each check is Verified, To confirm (with owner and date), Not implemented or Not applicable (with reason).

Area Checks Evidence
Minimisation Each data item is traced to a purpose; optional fields are marked optional; free text fields are limited where structured data suffices; identifiers are pseudonymised where the purpose allows; data is aggregated or anonymised for analytics. Data dictionary with purpose per field; schema review record
Defaults The most protective option is active without user action; optional sharing, profiling, marketing and public visibility are off until the individual turns them on; location, contacts and device permissions are requested only when needed and explained; settings are reversible. Screenshots of a fresh account; configuration export; test case results
Access Access to personal data is by role and least privilege under GOV-PRO-10; administrative access to personal data is logged; support staff see only what the case needs; bulk export is restricted and logged. Role matrix; log sample; GOV-REG-12 review
Retention Retention and deletion are configured per PIMS-REG-07; deletion covers derived data, caches, search indexes and processor copies; temporary files and exports are removed on a schedule; backups expire within their cycle. Configuration export; deletion test result; PIMS-REG-07 row
Transparency The notice covers the processing and is shown at collection; in-product explanations exist where data use would surprise; changes to the notice are versioned under PIMS-PRO-05. Notice version reference; screenshots of the collection point
Security Data is encrypted in transit and at rest under GOV-PRO-20; environments are separated and test environments hold no production personal data; secrets are managed under GOV-PRO-15; logging under GOV-PRO-14 does not capture personal data it does not need; transfers use an approved channel under GOV-PRO-23. ISMS-REG-01 references; configuration evidence; test data confirmation
Rights support The system can find all data about one individual, export it in a machine-readable format, correct it, delete it, restrict it and suppress marketing, each within the times in PIMS-PRO-03; automated decisions can be reviewed by a person. Demonstration record of each function; PIMS-PRO-03 reference
Accuracy Data is validated at entry; individuals can correct their own data; stale data is flagged or expired; sources of data not from the individual are recorded. Validation rules; correction flow test

4.4 Registers updated. Before gate 2 of PIMS-PRO-02, or before go-live where no assessment is required, the Product Owner updates PIMS-REG-01 (purpose, basis, data, retention, recipients), GOV-REG-25 and GDPR-REG-02 (flows and interfaces), PIMS-REG-06 (processors) and PIMS-REG-05 (transfers), and records any new risk in GOV-REG-05.

4.5 Test data. Development, test and staging environments use synthetic or irreversibly masked data. A request to use production personal data outside production is an exception under GOV-PRO-24, approved by the Privacy Officer only with the same controls as production and a deletion date of no more than thirty days.

4.6 Procurement path. For a supplier service, the supplier owner applies the checklist to the service as offered, using GDPR-TPL-09 and the supplier's documentation and configuration options as evidence, records the result in the supplier assessment under GOV-PRO-06, and the Privacy Officer confirms processor terms based on PIMS-TPL-02 and a transfer mechanism under PIMS-POL-03 before any personal data is sent.

4.7 Default verification. Before go-live the System Owner creates a fresh account or tenant, records every privacy-relevant setting at its default, and attaches the record. A default that exposes data or enables optional processing without an affirmative act is a blocker at the gate in PB-07.

4.8 Go-live gate. The Privacy Officer reviews the completed checklist and the register updates at the gate in PB-07. Any Not implemented check in Minimisation, Defaults, Retention or Rights support stops production use of personal data until fixed; a To confirm item needs an owner and a date within thirty days; the review and its outcome are recorded on the privacy review record.

4.9 Operation and change. The checklist is repeated for a significant change under GOV-PRO-09 and at the assessment review in PIMS-PRO-02. New data items added through configuration, integrations or forms without a review are treated as a nonconformity under GOV-PRO-04.

4.10 Decommissioning. When a system or feature is retired, the System Owner exports what the schedule requires, deletes the rest under PIMS-POL-02, obtains deletion confirmation from processors, and the Product Owner sets the PIMS-REG-01 status to Ceased with the date.

5. Records and evidence

  • The privacy review record for each project with the completed checklist, its evidence and the Privacy Officer's gate reviews.
  • Updated rows in PIMS-REG-01, PIMS-REG-05, PIMS-REG-06, PIMS-REG-07, GOV-REG-25 and GDPR-REG-02.
  • Default verification records and test data confirmations.
  • GOV-REG-29 go-live checklist entries and GOV-TPL-12 verdict notes for the privacy area.

6. Exceptions

A check may be marked Not applicable only with a reason the Privacy Officer accepts. Production personal data in a non-production environment is permitted only under step 4.5. No other exception applies.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this procedure annually, after a breach or complaint traced to a design decision, after a change in the development lifecycle under GOV-PRO-15, and after authority guidance on privacy by design. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Privacy control effectiveness monitoring procedure

The measures that show whether the privacy controls work, how they are collected and graded each quarter, the structure of the quarterly privacy report, and how the results reach the management review and the corrective action process.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.7.1; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.7.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.1; GDPR Article 24. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This procedure replaces the feeling that privacy is under control with numbers that are collected the same way every quarter, graded against targets, and acted on. It gives the management review the privacy performance input it needs and gives the Privacy Officer early warning before a missed deadline becomes a regulatory matter.

2. Scope

It applies to every privacy procedure and register in the kit, to the ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A and Annex B controls marked applicable in ISMS-REG-01, and to the processing activities in PIMS-REG-01. It extends ISMS-PRO-04, which covers security measurement, and uses the same reporting cycle.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Privacy Officer Owns the measure set, collects or receives the values, grades effectiveness, writes the quarterly report and presents it.
Processing Owners and System Owners Provide register exports and configuration evidence by the fifth working day after quarter end.
Information Security Manager Supplies security measures that bear on privacy and records control test results in ISMS-REG-02.
Internal Auditor Uses the reports to focus the audit programme and tests a sample of reported values.
Chief Executive Officer Receives the report, decides on resources and accepts or rejects proposed actions at the management review.

4. Procedure

4.1 The measure set. The Privacy Officer maintains the measures below in GOV-REG-21 with their targets. Each has a defined formula, a named source register and a frequency, so that two people computing it get the same number.

Measure How it is calculated Source Target
Requests answered on time Requests closed within the deadline divided by requests closed in the quarter PIMS-REG-02 100 percent
Median days to close a request Median of days from receipt to closure PIMS-REG-02 [Number] days or fewer
Requests refused or extended Count of refusals and extensions, each with a recorded reason PIMS-REG-02 Every one has a Privacy Officer decision
Breaches assessed within 48 hours Breaches with a decision within 48 hours of awareness divided by breaches in the quarter PIMS-REG-03 100 percent
Authority notifications within 72 hours Notifications sent within 72 hours divided by notifications required PIMS-REG-03 100 percent
Breaches per quarter and trend Count by nature and root cause against the previous four quarters PIMS-REG-03, GOV-REG-08 Downward or stable trend
Privacy training completion People with current training divided by people in scope GDPR-REG-05, GOV-REG-09 95 percent or more
Assessments completed before go-live Processing activities that started with an approved assessment or a recorded screening divided by activities that started PIMS-REG-08, PIMS-REG-01 100 percent
Assessment reviews overdue Count of assessments past their next review date PIMS-REG-08 Zero
Processors with signed terms Processors with terms signed divided by processors active PIMS-REG-06 100 percent
Transfers with a current assessment Transfers relying on contractual safeguards with an assessment within its review period divided by such transfers PIMS-REG-05 100 percent
Retention checks passed Categories checked with result Pass divided by categories checked PIMS-REG-07 95 percent or more, no Fail older than one quarter
Consent withdrawals actioned in time Withdrawals actioned within the time in PIMS-PRO-05 divided by withdrawals received PIMS-REG-04, system exports 100 percent
Notices reviewed in the last twelve months Published notices with a recorded review within twelve months divided by notices published PIMS-REG-04, GOV-REG-01 100 percent
Inventory rows reviewed in the last twelve months PIMS-REG-01 rows with a review date within twelve months divided by active rows PIMS-REG-01 100 percent
Privacy corrective actions overdue Open GOV-REG-03 actions with a privacy source past their due date GOV-REG-03 Zero

4.2 Collection. By the fifth working day after each quarter end, owners send the register exports and evidence named in the source column. The Privacy Officer computes each value, records it in GOV-REG-21 with the date and the export used, and files the exports under the evidence rules in PB-09 so that the Internal Auditor can recompute any value.

4.3 Sampling. Each quarter the Privacy Officer samples, in addition to the measures: five closed requests from PIMS-REG-02 for correctness of the response; every breach entry for the quality of the risk assessment; three processing activities from PIMS-REG-01 for a match between the notice, the inventory row and the system; and one withdrawal tested end to end. Sample results are recorded with the report.

4.4 Control effectiveness grades. For each applicable Annex A and Annex B control in ISMS-REG-01, the Privacy Officer records in ISMS-REG-02 a grade from the measures and samples that bear on it: Effective, the measures are at target and the sample found no exception; Largely effective, one measure is below target or one sample exception was found, with an action open; Partly effective, two or more measures are below target, a sample found a repeated exception, or any statutory deadline was missed; Not effective, the control is not operating or the exceptions are systemic. Partly effective and Not effective raise a corrective action in GOV-REG-03 within ten working days.

4.5 The quarterly privacy report. The Privacy Officer issues the report by the fifteenth working day after quarter end, with these sections: 1 Overall grade and the three things management must know; 2 Measures against targets with the trend over four quarters; 3 Breaches and incidents involving personal data, notifications made and lessons; 4 Requests from individuals, complaints and authority contact; 5 Assessments completed, overdue and the significant changes in processing; 6 Processors, sub-processor changes and transfers; 7 Training and awareness; 8 Audit findings, corrective actions and their status; 9 Risks changed in GOV-REG-05 and decisions required from management. The overall grade uses the scale in step 4.4 applied to the programme as a whole.

4.6 Distribution and action. The report goes to the Chief Executive Officer, the Information Security Manager and the steering committee under GOV-POL-01, and forms the privacy input to the management review under GOV-PRO-03, where decisions on resources and improvements are minuted in GOV-TPL-03 and tracked in GOV-REG-22.

4.7 Annual consolidation. The fourth quarter report includes the year's trend for every measure, the effectiveness grade for every applicable control, the outcome of the annual notice check under PIMS-PRO-05 and the annual retention sampling under PIMS-POL-02, and proposes targets for the following year for approval at the management review.

4.8 Changing the measure set. A measure is added, changed or retired by the Privacy Officer with the Information Security Manager's agreement, recorded in GOV-REG-21 with the reason, and never within a quarter already being reported, so that trends stay comparable.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-21 Security objectives and measures tracker: the privacy measures, their targets and each quarter's values.
  • Quarterly privacy reports with the register exports and sample records behind them.
  • ISMS-REG-02 Control implementation tracker: effectiveness grades for Annex A and Annex B controls.
  • GOV-REG-03 Corrective action log entries raised from the grades.
  • GOV-TPL-03 Management review minutes recording the privacy input and decisions.

6. Exceptions

A measure whose source register holds no items in the quarter is reported as Not applicable for that quarter with the reason, not as 100 percent. No other exception applies.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this procedure annually at the fourth quarter consolidation, after a management review that changed the measure set, and after an audit finding about performance evaluation. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

  • GOV-PRO-04 Nonconformity and corrective action procedure

Describe what will actually happen to the data. Reference a data flow in GOV-REG-25 or GDPR-REG-02 rather than drawing a new one here.

Aspect Description

Data processing agreement template

Plain-English processing terms, with placeholders, covering every element a contract between a controller and a processor must contain, for [Organisation] to use when it engages a processor or when it acts as a processor for a client, together with the three annexes that describe the processing, the security measures and the approved sub-processors.

Serves: GDPR Article 28; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.2.6; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 8.2.1; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.2.6; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.2.1; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.5.6; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.5.7. Owner: Privacy Officer.

Guidance notes are in italics. This template is a starting point for the legal adviser, not legal advice; the legal adviser confirms the wording against the law of each jurisdiction in GOV-REG-04 before signature. Use it in two directions: as the terms [Organisation] requires from a processor it engages, and as the terms [Organisation] offers when it is the processor. The word Controller below means the party that decides the purposes and means under PIMS-PRO-01, and Processor means the party that processes on the Controller's instructions. Where standard contractual clauses are needed for an international transfer under PIMS-POL-03, they are attached as a further annex and take precedence over any conflicting term here.

1. Parties and roles

Field Entry
Controller [Organisation name], [registered address], [registration number]
Processor [Organisation name], [registered address], [registration number]
Main agreement The service contract these terms attach to, with its date. [Reference], [Date]
Effective date [Date]
Controller's privacy contact [Role], [contact channel]
Processor's privacy contact [Role], [contact channel]

1.1 These terms form part of the main agreement and apply whenever the Processor processes personal data on behalf of the Controller in performing it. If these terms conflict with the main agreement on the processing of personal data, these terms prevail.

1.2 The parties agree that, for the processing described in Annex 1, the Controller determines the purposes and means and the Processor acts only on the Controller's behalf. Each party remains responsible for its own compliance with the law that applies to it.

2. Definitions

2.1 Personal data, processing, data subject, personal data breach, supervisory authority and special categories have the meanings given to them in the data protection law that applies to the Controller, named in Annex 1.

2.2 Sub-processor means any third party engaged by the Processor to process personal data under these terms. Instructions means the Controller's written instructions, including the main agreement, Annex 1 and any later instruction given through the contact in section 1.

3. Subject matter, duration, nature and purpose

3.1 The subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of the processing, the types of personal data and the categories of data subjects are set out in Annex 1. The Processor processes personal data only to the extent and for the duration needed to provide the services.

3.2 The processing lasts for the term of the main agreement and for the deletion or return period in section 13 after it ends.

4. Instructions

4.1 The Processor processes personal data only on the Controller's documented instructions, including with regard to transfers to another country, unless the law that applies to the Processor requires otherwise. In that case the Processor tells the Controller of the legal requirement before processing, unless that law prohibits the notice on important grounds of public interest.

4.2 The Processor tells the Controller without delay if, in its opinion, an instruction infringes data protection law. The Processor may suspend the instruction concerned until the Controller confirms or withdraws it.

4.3 The Processor does not process personal data for its own purposes, including product improvement, analytics, marketing, profiling or the training of any model, unless Annex 1 expressly allows a specific use and the Controller has confirmed the lawful basis for it.

4.4 Instructions are given by the Controller's privacy contact or a person the Controller names in writing. The Processor may ask for an instruction to be confirmed in writing before acting.

5. Confidentiality

5.1 The Processor allows access to personal data only to people who need it to provide the services, who are bound by a written confidentiality obligation or a statutory duty of confidentiality, and who have received training in the protection of personal data.

5.2 The Processor keeps a record of the people and roles authorised to access the Controller's personal data and makes it available to the Controller on request.

6. Security

6.1 The Processor implements and maintains the technical and organisational measures in Annex 2, and any further measures needed to provide a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, the cost of implementation, and the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing and the risks to individuals.

6.2 The Processor may update the measures in Annex 2 provided the level of protection does not fall below what Annex 2 provides, and gives the Controller notice of material changes.

6.3 The Processor assists the Controller in meeting the Controller's own security obligations, taking into account the nature of the processing and the information available to the Processor.

7. Sub-processors

7.1 The Processor engages a sub-processor only with the Controller's authorisation. The parties choose one of the following: [Specific authorisation: each sub-processor is approved in writing before engagement] or [General authorisation: the sub-processors in Annex 3 are approved, and the Processor gives the Controller at least [Number] days' written notice of any addition or replacement, during which the Controller may object on reasonable grounds relating to data protection].

7.2 Where the Controller objects under a general authorisation and the parties cannot resolve the objection within [Number] days, the Controller may terminate the affected services without penalty.

7.3 The Processor imposes on every sub-processor, by written contract, data protection obligations no less protective than these terms, in particular the security measures in Annex 2. The Processor remains fully liable to the Controller for the sub-processor's performance.

7.4 The Processor keeps Annex 3 current, including the location of each sub-processor's processing, and provides it to the Controller on request.

8. Assistance with the rights of individuals

8.1 The Processor assists the Controller, by appropriate technical and organisational measures and so far as possible, in responding to requests from individuals to exercise their rights, including access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection and the review of automated decisions.

8.2 The Processor forwards to the Controller, within [Number] working days of receipt, any request from an individual that concerns the Controller's personal data, and does not respond to the individual except to say the request has been passed to the Controller, unless the Controller instructs otherwise.

8.3 The Processor provides the assistance in section 8.1 within [Number] working days of the Controller's request, or sooner where the Controller's legal deadline requires it.

9. Assistance with assessments and consultation

9.1 The Processor assists the Controller with data protection impact assessments and with any prior consultation with a supervisory authority, by providing the information about the processing, the security measures and the sub-processors that the Controller reasonably requests, within [Number] working days.

10. Personal data breach

10.1 The Processor notifies the Controller without undue delay, and in any case within [Number] hours, after becoming aware of a personal data breach affecting the Controller's personal data, through the Controller's privacy contact.

10.2 The notification describes, so far as known, the nature of the breach, the categories and approximate numbers of individuals and records concerned, the likely consequences, the measures taken or proposed, and a contact point. Information not available at first is provided in phases without undue delay.

10.3 The Processor cooperates with the Controller's investigation, preserves evidence, takes the containment measures the Controller reasonably instructs, and does not notify a supervisory authority, individuals or the public about the Controller's data unless the Controller instructs it in writing or the law requires the Processor to do so.

11. International transfers

11.1 The Processor does not transfer personal data to, or allow access from, a country outside [Region] except as set out in Annex 1 or Annex 3, or on the Controller's documented instruction, and only under a transfer mechanism that satisfies the applicable law.

11.2 Where a transfer relies on standard contractual clauses or similar safeguards, the parties execute them as an annex to these terms and the Processor cooperates with any transfer impact assessment the Controller performs.

11.3 The Processor tells the Controller of any legally binding request for the Controller's personal data from a public authority, before disclosure where the law allows, discloses only the minimum the request lawfully requires, and records every such request and disclosure.

12. Audits and information

12.1 The Processor makes available to the Controller all information necessary to demonstrate compliance with these terms, including relevant certifications and independent assurance reports where they exist.

12.2 The Processor allows and contributes to audits and inspections conducted by the Controller or an auditor mandated by the Controller, no more than once in any twelve months unless a breach or a supervisory authority requires otherwise, on at least [Number] days' notice, during business hours, under reasonable confidentiality terms and without unreasonable disruption to the Processor's operations. The Controller may rely on an independent assurance report in place of an on-site audit where the report covers the services and the period.

12.3 The Processor informs the Controller immediately if an audit reveals that an instruction or a part of the services infringes data protection law.

13. Deletion or return

13.1 At the end of the services, or earlier on the Controller's instruction, the Processor, at the Controller's choice, deletes or returns all personal data to the Controller in a commonly used format, and deletes existing copies, within [Number] days, unless the law that applies to the Processor requires storage of the personal data. In that case the Processor tells the Controller what is retained, under which law and for how long, and continues to protect it under these terms.

13.2 The Processor provides written confirmation of deletion, including deletion by sub-processors, and confirms that backup copies expire within [Number] days under the Processor's normal backup cycle and are not restored to production.

14. Records and demonstration of compliance

14.1 The Processor keeps a record of the categories of processing carried out on behalf of the Controller containing the information the law requires, and makes it available to the supervisory authority on request.

14.2 Each party keeps these terms, the annexes and the records they generate for the term of the main agreement and the period required by its retention schedule.

15. Liability and indemnity

15.1 Placeholder for the legal adviser. State how liability for breaches of these terms relates to the liability provisions of the main agreement, whether any cap applies to data protection claims, and the indemnity, if any, that each party gives the other for regulatory fines and third party claims arising from its own breach. [Liability and indemnity wording]

16. Term, termination and precedence

16.1 These terms start on the effective date and continue until the Processor has deleted or returned all personal data under section 13.

16.2 Either party may terminate the affected services if the other party is in material breach of these terms and does not remedy it within [Number] days of written notice.

16.3 Changes to these terms are made in writing and signed by both parties. The parties review these terms when the law, the services, the data or the sub-processors change, and at least every [Number] months.

Annex 2: Technical and organisational security measures

Describe the measures in place, not aspirations. Where the Processor holds a certification or an assurance report, reference it and still describe the measures. Suggested headings:

Area Measures
Governance and policies Security management system, policies, roles, risk assessment.
Personnel Screening, confidentiality, training, disciplinary process.
Access control Identity management, least privilege, multi-factor authentication, privileged access, periodic review, logging of access to personal data.
Encryption In transit, at rest, key management, who holds the keys.
Pseudonymisation and minimisation Where applied.
Physical security Data centre and office controls, or reliance on a hosting provider's controls.
Operations Change management, vulnerability and patch management, malware protection, logging and monitoring, time synchronisation.
Availability and resilience Backups, restore testing, redundancy, continuity plans, recovery objectives.
Environment separation Production separated from test; no production personal data in test.
Incident management Detection, response, breach notification path and timing.
Supplier management How sub-processors are assessed and contracted.
Data deletion Deletion and return process, media disposal, backup expiry.
Assurance Internal audits, penetration tests, certifications, independent reports, with dates.

Personal data processing inventory

One row per processing activity, recording what personal data is processed, why, on what basis, who receives it, where it goes and how long it is kept. This is the record of processing that the organisation keeps as a controller, and the operational source for notices, assessments and requests.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.2.8; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.2.8; GDPR Article 30.

Columns:

  • Processing ID: Permanent identifier for the activity.
  • Activity
  • Role
  • Purpose
  • Lawful basis
  • Special category: Health
  • Data subjects
  • Data categories
  • Recipients: Internal functions and third parties
  • Transfers outside region: Countries outside the home jurisdiction
  • Safeguard: Mechanism for any transfer
  • Retention: Period and trigger
  • Owner (role)
  • DPIA reference: PIMS-REG-08 row
  • Last review
  • Notes
PIMS-REG-02 register Download .xlsx

Data subject request register

One row per request from an individual to exercise a right over their personal data. Records the clock, the identity check, the outcome and the proof, so that the one-month deadline is met and the handling can be shown.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.3; GDPR Article 12.

Columns:

  • Request ID
  • Received: Starts the one-month clock.
  • Requester
  • Right requested
  • Identity verified
  • Due: One month from receipt
  • Extension taken
  • Outcome
  • Refusal basis: Required when the outcome is a refusal or a partial fulfilment.
  • Closed
  • Owner (role)
  • Evidence reference
  • Status
  • Notes

One row per personal data breach, whether or not it was notifiable. Records the awareness time that starts the seventy-two hour clock, the assessment of risk to individuals, and the notification decisions, so that accountability can be shown even when no notification was required.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27701 clause 6.13.1.5; GDPR Article 33; GDPR Article 34.

Columns:

  • Breach ID
  • Detected
  • Awareness time: Starts the seventy-two hour clock for the authority.

  • Data categories
  • Risk to individuals
  • Authority notified
  • Authority notified at
  • Individuals notified
  • Containment
  • Corrective action: GOV-REG-03 reference.

AICPA Trust Services Criteria: Security, Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, Privacy

SOC-GDE-01 guide Download .docx Markdown

Guide: SOC 2 in plain words

What a SOC 2 report is and is not, the difference between Type 1 and Type 2, the five categories, how criteria, controls and tests relate, and the parts of the process that surprise organisations the first time, written for a reader who has to run one.

Serves: SOC 2 CC1.1; SOC 2 CC2.3; SOC 2 CC4.1; SOC 2 CC9.2. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. What a SOC 2 report is

A SOC 2 report is an independent auditor's opinion on whether a service organisation's controls are suitably designed, and for a Type 2 report whether they operated effectively over a period, to meet a published set of criteria called the Trust Services Criteria. The criteria are issued by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants. The opinion is signed by a licensed public accounting firm, not by a certification body, and it is addressed to the organisation's customers and their auditors, who use it to decide how much they can rely on the organisation's controls without testing them themselves.

Three things follow from that. SOC 2 is an attestation, not a certification: there is no certificate, no register of certified organisations and no "SOC 2 compliant" status in law. The report is the deliverable, and it is a restricted-use document shared with customers under a non-disclosure agreement, not published. And the controls are the organisation's own: the criteria say what outcome must be achieved; [Organisation] decides how, writes its controls down in SOC-REG-01, and the auditor tests those.

2. Type 1 and Type 2

A Type 1 report gives an opinion on the design of controls at a single date: were the controls in place and capable of meeting the criteria on that day. A Type 2 report gives an opinion on design and on operating effectiveness across a period, usually between three and twelve months, by testing samples of the controls' records from inside that period.

Customers almost always want a Type 2. A Type 1 is still useful as a milestone: it proves the control set is complete and designed well before the clock starts, and it gives sales teams something to show while the first period runs. PB-03 treats the Type 1 as the day 90 outcome and the Type 2 as what follows the observation period. An organisation that skips the Type 1 saves money and loses an early warning.

3. The five categories

The criteria are grouped into five categories. Security is mandatory and is made up of the common criteria, CC1 to CC9, which cover the control environment, communication, risk assessment, monitoring, control activities, logical and physical access, system operations, change management and risk mitigation including vendors. The other four are added when a service makes commitments in that area.

Category Criteria Add it when
Security (common criteria) CC1.1 to CC9.2 Always. Every SOC 2 report includes it.
Availability A1.1 to A1.3 Contracts promise uptime, recovery times or capacity.
Processing integrity PI1.1 to PI1.5 The service transforms, calculates or delivers data and customers rely on the result being complete and accurate.
Confidentiality C1.1, C1.2 Customers give the organisation information they require to be protected and destroyed on terms.
Privacy P1.1 to P8.1 The organisation collects or processes personal information under its own privacy commitments, usually as a controller.

Choose categories by the commitments [Organisation] has actually made in contracts and service descriptions, not by ambition. Every added category adds controls, evidence and testing. A processor that handles personal data on customers' instructions usually covers that through Confidentiality and the security criteria, with privacy law met through the PIMS and GDPR documents in this kit, rather than adding the Privacy category.

4. Criteria, controls and tests

The three words are used loosely and the confusion costs time.

  • A criterion is an outcome the auditor must conclude on, for example that access is removed when no longer needed (CC6.2 in theme). The criteria are fixed and the same for every organisation.
  • A control is something [Organisation] does, written as an object and a state that can be checked: "quarterly access reviews completed and signed off for every in-scope system". One criterion usually needs several controls, and one control often serves several criteria. The controls live in SOC-REG-01.
  • A test is what the auditor does to a control: inspects a sample of access reviews, re-performs a calculation, observes a process, asks a person. The organisation's own version of the tests, run during the period, is SOC-PRO-01.

The auditor's report lists the controls and the tests side by side with the results. If a control is written vaguely ("access is managed appropriately") there is nothing to test, and the auditor will either rewrite it with you or report it as not testable.

5. Points of focus

Each criterion comes with points of focus: considerations that illustrate what the criterion is getting at. They are not requirements and the auditor does not issue an opinion on each one. Use them in two ways. When writing controls, read the points of focus for a criterion and check that the control set covers the themes they raise; a theme with no control is a gap to explain. When a point of focus does not apply (a cloud-only organisation and physical data centres, for example), say so in SOC-REG-01 so the auditor does not ask.

6. The audit period

For a Type 2, evidence must come from inside the period. A control that started operating in month four of a twelve month period is reported as operating for nine months, and the auditor's opinion will say so. A control that has no records for a month, because the person who ran it was on leave and nobody covered, is a gap in that month whether or not anything went wrong.

Periods run consecutively: the next report's period starts the day after the previous one ended, so that a customer reading two reports sees no uncovered time. Between the period end and the report's issue, and between reports, customers may ask for a bridge letter, a short statement from management that nothing material has changed. SOC-PRO-02 explains the same letter from the other side, when [Organisation] receives one from a supplier.

Most organisations choose a first period of three to six months to get a report into customers' hands, then move to twelve month periods aligned to the financial year.

7. Sampling

The auditor does not test every occurrence of a control. For each control they define the population, every occurrence in the period, and select a sample whose size depends on how often the control runs. Monthly controls might see three items tested, weekly five, daily twenty or more; the auditor's own table governs, and SOC-PRO-01 section 4.4 gives [Organisation]'s internal equivalent.

Two practical consequences. The auditor chooses the items, not the organisation, so there is no value in preparing beautiful examples; prepare complete populations as system exports instead. And a population must be complete: if the leaver list from the people system shows fourteen leavers and the identity provider shows sixteen accounts disabled, the auditor will ask about the two, and the answer had better be in a record.

8. Exceptions

An exception is a tested item that did not meet the control: a leaver whose access was removed in nine days instead of five, a change ticket with no approval. The auditor reports every exception with management's response. One isolated exception with a documented cause and a fix rarely affects the opinion. A pattern of exceptions in one control may lead the auditor to conclude the control did not operate effectively, which appears in the opinion as a qualification: the opinion holds except for that control and the criteria it serves. Customers read qualifications closely.

Handle an exception the way SOC-PRO-01 section 4.8 describes: classify it, find the cause, fix it, and show the fix operating. An exception found by [Organisation] in its own testing and corrected before the auditor arrives is reported as a corrected deviation; the same exception found first by the auditor is a surprise. Both are better than a hidden one, which becomes a question of integrity rather than of control.

9. The report's sections

A SOC 2 report has a fixed shape, and knowing it helps both in writing [Organisation]'s own and in reading a supplier's.

Section Written by Contains
Independent auditor's report The auditor The opinion, the scope, the period, the categories, the responsibilities of each party, any qualifications.
Management's assertion [Organisation] A signed statement that the description is fair and the controls were designed and operated effectively.
System description [Organisation] What the service is, its components, boundaries, commitments, changes and incidents in the period, subservice organisations and complementary user entity controls. SOC-TPL-01 is the template.
Criteria, controls, tests and results The auditor, from [Organisation]'s control list One row per control: the criteria it serves, the control text, the auditor's test, the result including exceptions.
Other information [Organisation] Anything management wants to add, such as responses to exceptions or future plans. The auditor does not opine on it.

Readers go to the opinion first, then the exceptions, then the complementary user entity controls. Write the description knowing that.

10. Complementary user entity controls

Some criteria can only be met if the customer does its part: manages its own users in the service, keeps its own credentials secret, reviews the reports the service sends. The description lists these as complementary user entity controls. They are honest statements of shared responsibility, not disclaimers, and the auditor will check that each one is genuinely needed for a criterion.

The same mechanism applies in reverse. Every supplier report [Organisation] relies on lists user entity controls that [Organisation] must operate. SOC-PRO-02 section 4.6 maps each of them to a control in SOC-REG-01, because a supplier's assurance does not hold if the organisation ignores its side.

11. Subservice organisations

A subservice organisation is a supplier whose controls are necessary for [Organisation] to meet a criterion: typically the hosting provider, sometimes the identity provider, payment processor or managed security service. The description must name them and say how they are treated.

Under the carve-out method, the default, the supplier's controls are excluded from [Organisation]'s report. The description names the supplier, the services used, the criteria that depend on them, and the complementary subservice organisation controls that [Organisation] assumes the supplier operates. [Organisation] then monitors the supplier by reviewing its own SOC report under SOC-PRO-02. Under the inclusive method the supplier's controls are tested inside [Organisation]'s report, which needs the supplier's agreement, participation and its own management assertion; it is rare outside closely held group companies.

A supplier that is merely a vendor, whose failure would not by itself cause a criterion to fail, is handled under GOV-PRO-06 and CC9.2 and does not need to be in the description.

12. Who the auditor is

The opinion must be signed by a licensed public accounting firm that is independent of [Organisation] and subject to peer review of its attestation practice. The same firm cannot design the controls and then audit them; a firm that offers both services separates the teams and will say so in its engagement letter. A readiness consultant who helps write controls is not the auditor, and the auditor will test what the consultant wrote exactly as hard as anything else.

When choosing, ask: how many SOC 2 examinations the firm issued in the last year for organisations of [Organisation]'s size and technology; who will do the fieldwork and how senior they are; the firm's sample size table; whether evidence is collected through a portal or by request list; how exceptions are communicated and when; the timeline from period end to issued report; and the total cost for the readiness review, the Type 1 and the Type 2. Price varies with the number of categories, systems, locations and controls, and with how organised the evidence is. A tidy evidence folder built as PB-09 describes is the single largest cost reducer.

13. Common misunderstandings

Belief What is true
"We are SOC 2 certified." There is no certification. [Organisation] has a SOC 2 report for a period, with an opinion that may be qualified. Say "we have a SOC 2 Type 2 report covering [period]".
"The auditor will tell us what controls to have." The auditor tests the controls [Organisation] wrote. Readiness help is separate from the audit.
"Policies are evidence." A policy proves a rule exists. Only records prove the rule was followed.
"We can fix it before the audit." For a Type 2, a control fixed in month ten operated for two months. The period is the period.
"One exception fails the report." One isolated, explained, corrected exception rarely affects the opinion. A pattern does.
"Our hosting provider's report covers us." It covers the provider's controls. [Organisation]'s own access, change, incident and vendor controls are still tested, and the provider's user entity controls become [Organisation]'s controls.
"Privacy category means GDPR." The Privacy criteria are a separate set of commitments. GDPR obligations are met through PIMS-POL-01, GDPR-POL-01 and their procedures whether or not the Privacy category is in scope.
"A screenshot is enough." A screenshot that shows account, environment and date may be. A system export of the whole population is always better.

14. Where to go next

Read PB-03 for the ninety day plan to the start of the observation period. Use SOC-REG-01 to write the control matrix, SOC-REG-03 to measure readiness, SOC-REG-02 to schedule the recurring evidence, SOC-TPL-01 to draft the description, SOC-PRO-01 to test the controls before the auditor does, SOC-PRO-02 for supplier reports, and SOC-GDE-02 for what the auditor will ask for and where in the kit each answer lives. SOC-GDE-03 maps every criterion to the kit documents that serve it.

Guide: the auditor's request list and how to answer it from the kit

The evidence requests a SOC 2 auditor typically issues, grouped by the team that produces each one, with the kit register or document that holds the answer and the form the answer should take.

Serves: SOC 2 CC4.1; SOC 2 CC2.1; SOC 2 CC6.1; SOC 2 CC7.2; SOC 2 CC8.1; SOC 2 CC9.2. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. How the request list works

A few weeks before fieldwork the auditor sends a request list: one line per item of evidence, each tied to one or more controls in SOC-REG-01, with a due date. The list is long, the dates are short, and the items land on five or six different teams. Organisations that struggle are not short of controls; they are short of a person who knows which team holds each answer and what form it should take.

This guide groups the typical requests by the owner who produces them. For each request it names the criteria, the kit register or document that holds the answer, and how to deliver it. Read it with PB-09, which sets the evidence rules that apply to every item: dated system exports over screenshots, complete populations over examples, file names that say what the file proves, and a To confirm status for anything not yet seen.

Four rules apply to every request.

  1. Deliver populations, not examples. The auditor samples; [Organisation] supplies the whole list with identifiers and dates and lets the auditor choose.
  2. Deliver evidence from inside the period. A record dated after the period end proves nothing about the period, however good it is.
  3. Deliver the system of record's own export. A spreadsheet typed from memory is not evidence of anything except memory.
  4. Deliver through one channel, with one person tracking status per item. The Information Security Manager owns the list; the teams below own the items.

8. Requests that catch organisations out

  • The population reconciliation. The auditor compares the people system's leavers to the identity provider's disabled accounts, and change tickets to deployments. Reconcile both yourself before fieldwork and have an explanation for every difference.
  • The quarter with no access review. A review done in month four and month nine is two reviews, not four. SOC-REG-02 exists so that this is seen in month five, not at the audit.
  • The policy acknowledged before it was approved. Acknowledgement exports must name the version, and the version's approval date must precede the acknowledgement.
  • The restore test that restored nothing. A backup job success export is not a restore test. GOV-REG-15 needs a restored item, a verification and a date.
  • The vendor report nobody read. Having a subservice organisation's SOC report on file is not CC9.2 evidence; the SOC-PRO-02 review record is.
  • The incident with no post-incident review. GOV-TPL-11 within the window in GOV-PRO-07, or the control did not operate for that incident.
  • The screenshot with no date or account. Retake it as PB-09 section 5 describes.
  • The control owner who is also the tester. SOC-PRO-01 section 4 requires independence; the auditor will ask who performed each internal test.

9. Preparing in advance

Everything in sections 2 to 7 can be produced on the day the control runs, which is what SOC-REG-02 schedules. An organisation that files the quarterly access review export on the day the review closes, the monthly vulnerability scan on the day it completes, and the change ticket export at month end, answers the request list in a week. An organisation that starts collecting when the list arrives answers it in two months and loses items to section 8. Use SOC-REG-03 to check readiness before the period starts, and keep the owner column of SOC-REG-01 current so that every request has a name on it before the auditor asks.

Guide: Trust Services Criteria mapped to kit documents

Every Trust Services Criterion with its theme in plain words and the kit policies, procedures, templates and registers that implement and evidence it, so that a control matrix, a gap assessment or an auditor's question can be answered from one table.

Serves: SOC 2 CC1.1; SOC 2 CC6.1; SOC 2 CC7.1; SOC 2 CC8.1; SOC 2 A1.1; SOC 2 C1.1; SOC 2 PI1.1; SOC 2 P1.1. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. How to read this map

Each table lists the criteria of one category. The theme column is a reminder in plain words of what the criterion is about; it is not the criterion's text, which belongs to its publisher and should be read in the original when writing controls. The documents column names the kit policies, procedures, guides and templates that implement the theme. The registers column names the registers and records that evidence it. Where this kit has no dedicated document, the entry says which general document carries the theme.

Use the map in three places: when filling the Kit documents column of SOC-REG-01, when answering a request from SOC-GDE-02, and when running the gap assessment in PB-03. The kit does not replace the criteria; an organisation writing controls reads the criteria and their points of focus for itself.

15. Where the kit is thin

Three themes are carried by general documents rather than dedicated ones, and an organisation may want to add its own. Fraud risk (CC3.3) is a scenario class inside GOV-PRO-05 and a segregation rule inside GOV-PRO-10; an organisation handling payments should add explicit fraud scenarios to GOV-REG-05. Anomaly analysis (CC7.2) rests on GOV-PRO-14's alert triage; a larger operation will want a written triage runbook. Processing specifications (PI1.1) are required by SOC-POL-01 but have no template in the kit; the output and input catalogues in SOC-PRO-03 and SOC-PRO-04 give the headings.

SOC-POL-01 policy Download .docx Markdown

Processing integrity policy

The rules that keep [Organisation]'s processing complete, accurate, timely and authorised, from the moment an input arrives to the moment an output is delivered and the data is stored, and the records that prove it.

Serves: SOC 2 PI1.1; SOC 2 PI1.2; SOC 2 PI1.3; SOC 2 PI1.4; SOC 2 PI1.5. Owner: Head of Engineering.

1. Purpose

Processing integrity means that [Organisation]'s systems do what they promise: inputs are accepted only when complete, accurate and authorised; processing follows the written specification; outputs reach the right people complete, correct and on time; and stored data is not silently altered or lost. This policy sets the rules the processing integrity criteria are tested against.

2. Scope

Every service [Organisation] provides whose processing integrity category is in the report scope, the systems inside the boundary in SOC-TPL-01, the interfaces that feed them, the outputs they deliver and the data stores that hold inputs, items in processing and outputs. It applies to automated processing and to the manual steps staff perform within it.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Head of Engineering Owns the policy, approves processing specifications, resources the controls.
System Owner Writes and maintains the processing specification for each service, operates the controls in SOC-PRO-03 and SOC-PRO-04, investigates failures.
Product or service manager Agrees processing commitments with customers and keeps them consistent with the specification.
Operations team Monitors jobs, performs reconciliations, handles rejected items and corrections.
Information Security Manager Tests the controls under SOC-PRO-01 and reports results.

4. Policy statements

4.1 Specification. Every in-scope service has a written processing specification, approved by the Head of Engineering, that defines its inputs, validation rules, processing logic in plain words, outputs, recipients, timing commitments and the data retained. The specification is controlled under GOV-PRO-01 and changes only through GOV-PRO-09.

4.2 Commitments match the specification. Processing commitments made to customers in contracts, service descriptions and the system description in SOC-TPL-01 are derived from the specification. The product or service manager reviews them against it at least annually and at every specification change, and records the review.

4.3 Inputs. A system accepts an input only after validating it against the specification's rules for format, range, referential integrity, completeness, duplication and authorisation. A rejected input is held in a quarantine with its reason, reported to the submitter within [Number] hours, and never silently discarded or silently corrected. SOC-PRO-03 governs.

4.4 Manual inputs. A manual input that changes customer data or a financial value is entered by one person and verified by a second before it takes effect, or is covered by a system check that the System Owner has documented as equivalent.

4.5 Processing. Every processing job records its start, end, items in, items out, items rejected and errors in a log kept under GOV-PRO-14. A job that fails, or whose counts fall outside the specification's tolerance, raises an alert to the operations team within [Number] minutes and is not marked complete until resolved.

4.6 Reconciliation. The operations team reconciles inputs received to items processed and outputs produced at least daily for each in-scope service, investigates every difference the same working day, and records the result with a preparer and a separate reviewer.

4.7 Outputs. Outputs are delivered complete, accurate and within the time the specification states, to the recipients and by the channel it names, over encrypted transport under GOV-PRO-23. A missed or incomplete delivery is detected by the system, not by the recipient, and is treated as an incident under GOV-PRO-07 when a customer commitment is missed. SOC-PRO-04 governs.

4.8 Corrections. An output found to be wrong is corrected by reissue with a version marker. The original is retained, the recipient is told what changed and why, and the cause is entered in the processing error log, with a corrective action under GOV-PRO-04 where the cause is systemic.

4.9 Storage. Inputs, items in processing and outputs are stored with controls that prevent and detect unauthorised alteration: access restriction under GOV-PRO-10, integrity checks under SOC-PRO-04 and backups under GOV-PRO-12. They are kept for the period in PIMS-REG-07 and are recoverable to the state at any processing step the specification requires.

4.10 Segregation of duties. No single person may both submit an input and approve it, both develop processing logic and deploy it to production, or both perform a reconciliation and resolve its differences without a second person's record. Where headcount makes this impossible, the compensating review is recorded in GOV-REG-06.

4.11 Errors and incidents. Processing errors are logged with cause, items affected, correction and date. An error that affects a customer commitment, more than [Number] items, or any financial value is an incident under GOV-PRO-07.

4.12 Measures. The System Owner reports monthly: inputs rejected by reason, reconciliation differences and time to resolve, outputs delivered late, corrections issued, and open processing errors. Targets are held in GOV-REG-21 and reviewed at management review under GOV-PRO-03.

5. Records and evidence

  • Approved processing specifications per service, with their change history in GOV-REG-11.
  • Input rejection and quarantine records with submitter notifications.
  • Job logs and alerts under GOV-PRO-14.
  • Daily reconciliation records with preparer and reviewer, and difference investigations.
  • Output delivery logs, acknowledgements and reissue records.
  • The processing error log and the monthly measures report.
  • SOC-PRO-01 workpapers for the processing integrity controls in SOC-REG-01.

6. Exceptions

A service may deviate from a statement only under GOV-PRO-24, with a compensating control approved by the Head of Engineering and a duration of no more than twelve months. No exception applies to statement 4.3 (no silent discard or correction) or statement 4.8 (retention of the original output).

7. Review and maintenance

The Head of Engineering reviews this policy annually, after any processing incident, and when a new service enters the report scope. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Control testing and sampling procedure

How [Organisation] tests its own SOC 2 controls before and during an examination period, with defined populations, sample sizes by frequency, deviation handling and workpapers that an external auditor can re-perform.

Serves: SOC 2 CC4.1; SOC 2 CC4.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.1. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure sets how the controls in SOC-REG-01 are tested by [Organisation] itself, so that a control that has stopped operating is found and repaired months before the external auditor finds it, and so that every test leaves a workpaper the auditor can rely on and re-perform.

2. Scope

Every control listed in SOC-REG-01 Trust Services Criteria control matrix with a status of Operating or Tested, for every system inside the boundary described in SOC-TPL-01. It covers manual controls, controls a system performs on a schedule and controls that run on every transaction. It does not replace the internal audit programme in GOV-PRO-02, which examines the management system as a whole; the two share their findings through GOV-REG-03.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Information Security Manager Owns the testing plan, assigns testers, approves sample sizes, classifies deviations, reports results.
Control owner Operates the control, produces the population on request, responds to deviations and fixes causes.
Tester A person independent of the control's operation who defines the population, selects the sample, performs the test and writes the workpaper.
Internal Auditor Reviews a sample of workpapers each quarter for quality and independence.
Steering committee Receives the quarterly testing summary and decides on unresolved deviations.

4. Procedure

4.1 Testing plan. At the start of each examination period, and at least annually, the Information Security Manager lists every control in SOC-REG-01 with its frequency, owner, the quarter in which it will be tested and the assigned tester. Every control is tested at least once per period. A control with a deviation in the previous period, a linked risk rated High or Critical in GOV-REG-05, or a change during the period is tested twice.

4.2 Population definition. Before selecting anything, the tester writes down the population: what one occurrence of the control looks like (one access review, one change ticket, one backup job, one new starter), the system of record that holds the occurrences, the date range, and the total count. The control owner produces the population as a system export that carries an identifier and a date for every item. A hand-typed list or a filtered screen view is not accepted; the tester records the refusal and requests the export.

4.3 Population completeness. The tester checks the population against an independent source before sampling: the leaver list against the people system, change tickets against the deployment log, new accounts against the identity provider's creation events. A difference above 2 percent of items, or any missing item that should have triggered the control, is a deviation under 4.8 before testing begins.

4.4 Sample sizes. The tester selects at least the number of items in the table below. Where the population is smaller than the sample size, the tester tests every item.

Control frequency Typical items in a twelve month period Minimum sample
Annual 1 1
Semi-annual 2 2
Quarterly 4 2
Monthly 12 3
Weekly 52 5
Daily 250 or more 20
Many times a day, or on every event, performed by a person More than 250 25
Performed by a system on every event Not counted 1 item, plus inspection of the configuration and of the change records for it

For an event-driven control (a joiner, a leaver, an incident, a change) the row is chosen by how many events occurred in the period. For a shorter period the typical counts fall but the minimum samples stay.

4.5 Selection method. The tester selects items at random by a method that can be repeated from the recorded inputs, for example a seeded random number list applied to the exported row numbers. Where the period is long, the tester spreads the sample so that every quarter is represented. The tester records the method, the seed or formula and the selected identifiers. The control owner never chooses the items and does not see the selection until evidence is requested.

4.6 Test methods and attributes. The tester applies at least one of: inspection of a record the control produced, re-performance of the control on the selected item, observation of the control being performed, or inquiry of the operator. Inquiry on its own is never sufficient; it is paired with inspection or re-performance. Each test states the attributes checked, for example: reviewer named, review dated inside the quarter, every account dispositioned, removals actioned within five working days, sign-off by the System Owner.

4.7 Performing the test. For every selected item the tester records the identifier, the date, each attribute checked and a result of Pass or Fail, with a reference to the evidence file named as PB-09 describes. Evidence is taken from the system of record by the tester or in the tester's presence. Evidence forwarded by the control owner without the tester seeing its source is marked To confirm until the source is shown.

4.8 Deviations. Any item that fails an attribute is a deviation. The tester records it the same day with the item, the attribute, the facts observed and the control owner's explanation. The Information Security Manager classifies it within five working days as one of the following.

  • Isolated: one item, a cause that applies only to that item, no effect on others. The tester doubles the sample from the same population; if no further deviation appears, the control is reported as operating with one noted exception.
  • Systemic: more than one item, or a cause that could affect other items (a step nobody owns, a tool change, a person who left). The control is reported as not operating effectively for the period of the cause, and a corrective action is raised in GOV-REG-03 under GOV-PRO-04.
  • Design gap: the control as written cannot meet the criterion even when performed perfectly. SOC-REG-01 is updated with a redesigned control and its start date, and the gap is reported to the steering committee.

4.9 Remediation and retest. The control owner implements the corrective action by the date in GOV-REG-03. The tester retests after at least one full operating cycle of the control has completed following the fix, using a fresh sample drawn from occurrences after the fix date. A control fixed and retested inside the period is reported with both results and both dates.

4.10 Workpaper. Every test produces one workpaper containing: control identifier and text from SOC-REG-01, criteria served, period tested, population definition and count, completeness check, selection method and sample, attributes tested, results per item, deviations and their classification, conclusion, tester name and date, reviewer name and date. Workpapers are stored in the evidence folder area for audit and review, hashed as PB-09 describes and retained with the period's evidence.

4.11 Quality review. Each quarter the Internal Auditor reviews at least [Number] workpapers, checking that the tester was independent, that the population came from a system of record, that the sample was random and recorded, and that the conclusion follows from the results. Findings about testing quality become corrective actions in GOV-REG-03.

4.12 Reporting. The Information Security Manager reports to the steering committee quarterly: controls tested, controls passed, open deviations by classification, retests due, and controls not yet tested in the period. The period-end summary is an input to management review under GOV-PRO-03 and is given to the external auditor on request as evidence for CC4.1 and CC4.2.

5. Records and evidence

  • The testing plan for each period.
  • SOC-REG-01 with Status and Test method completed for every control.
  • One workpaper per test, with the population export, the selection record and the evidence files.
  • Deviation records and their corrective actions in GOV-REG-03.
  • Quarterly testing summaries and the Internal Auditor's quality reviews.

6. Exceptions

A control may be tested by its own operator only where no independent person has the knowledge to test it; the Information Security Manager records the reason and the Internal Auditor re-performs that test in the quarterly quality review. A sample size may be reduced only with the written agreement of the Information Security Manager, recorded in the workpaper with the reason. No exception permits the control owner to choose the sample.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after each external examination (to adopt the auditor's population and sample expectations where they differ), and when the control set in SOC-REG-01 changes materially. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.
