Subservice organisation and vendor assurance report review procedure

How [Organisation] obtains, reviews and acts on the SOC and equivalent assurance reports of its subservice organisations and critical vendors, including bridge letters, exceptions and the complementary user entity controls those reports place on [Organisation].

Serves: SOC 2 CC9.2; SOC 2 CC3.4; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.22. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

A subservice organisation operates controls that [Organisation]'s own service commitments depend on: hosting, identity, payment, email delivery, support tooling. This procedure makes sure those controls have been examined by somebody, that [Organisation] reads the result rather than filing it, and that the user entity controls each report expects of [Organisation] are actually in place.

2. Scope

Every supplier in GOV-REG-07 that is a subservice organisation named in SOC-TPL-01, every Tier 1 supplier, and any other supplier whose failure would cause [Organisation] to miss a service commitment. Assurance reports covered are SOC 1, SOC 2 and SOC 3 reports, ISO/IEC 27001 certificates with their Statement of Applicability, and other independent attestation reports a supplier offers in their place.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Information Security Manager Owns the procedure, performs or assigns the review, keeps the review record, decides on exceptions.
Supplier relationship owner Requests reports and bridge letters, chases overdue items, holds the contract.
System Owner Confirms which supplier services and locations [Organisation] uses, maps complementary user entity controls to [Organisation] controls.
Privacy Officer Reviews reports for suppliers that process personal data, together with PIMS-REG-06.
Steering committee Decides on continued use of a supplier with an unresolved adverse result.

4. Procedure

4.1 Identify. When a supplier is onboarded under GOV-PRO-06, and at each annual review, the Information Security Manager marks in GOV-REG-07 whether it is a subservice organisation (its controls are necessary for [Organisation] to meet a criterion) or a vendor, and records the assurance type expected: SOC 2 Type 2, SOC 1 Type 2, ISO/IEC 27001 certificate, or questionnaire only.

4.2 Request. The supplier relationship owner requests the current report within 30 days of onboarding and then annually, no later than 60 days after the supplier's expected report date. The request names the services and locations [Organisation] uses so that the supplier sends the report that covers them. Reports are stored in the evidence folder area for suppliers, classified Confidential, and used only as the supplier's terms permit.

4.3 Coverage check. Before reading the detail, the reviewer confirms four things and records each: the report type (Type 2 is required for a subservice organisation; a Type 1 is accepted only for a supplier in its first year); the period covered; that the services, systems and locations [Organisation] uses are inside the report's scope; and that the categories match the dependency (a hosting provider must cover Security and Availability, for example). A report that fails any check is treated as absent and step 4.9 applies.

4.4 Bridge letter. Where the report period ended more than three months before the review date, or more than three months before the end of [Organisation]'s own examination period, the supplier relationship owner obtains a bridge letter in which the supplier states whether its controls have changed and whether it knows of any failures since the period end. A gap of more than twelve months without a new report is escalated to the steering committee.

4.5 Opinion and exceptions. The reviewer reads the auditor's opinion first. A qualified, adverse or disclaimed opinion is escalated to the Information Security Manager the same day. The reviewer then lists every exception in the testing section with: the control, the exception, the supplier's management response, and whether the control is one [Organisation] depends on. For each dependent exception the reviewer decides whether [Organisation]'s own controls compensate; if they do not, the reviewer raises a risk in GOV-REG-05 and a corrective action in GOV-REG-03.

4.6 Complementary user entity controls. The reviewer extracts the complementary user entity controls the report lists and, with the System Owner, maps each to a control in SOC-REG-01, recording the mapping in the review record. Each unmapped user entity control is a gap: it is assigned an owner and a due date of no more than 60 days, because the supplier's assurance does not hold without it.

4.7 The supplier's own subservice organisations. The reviewer notes the supplier's carved-out subservice organisations and whether any of them hold [Organisation] data. Those that do are added to GOV-REG-07 as fourth parties with the supplier as relationship owner, and the supplier's monitoring of them is noted in the review record.

4.8 Review record. For every report the reviewer completes a record with: supplier, report type and period, auditor, opinion, scope match, categories, exceptions and their disposition, user entity control mapping, bridge letter status, overall conclusion (Acceptable, Acceptable with actions, Not acceptable), reviewer and date. GOV-REG-07 is updated with the assurance type, last review date, next review date and status.

4.9 No report available. Where a subservice organisation cannot provide an assurance report, the Information Security Manager obtains instead a completed GOV-TPL-04 questionnaire, an independent penetration test summary dated within twelve months, and a contractual right to audit or to receive security information; records the supplier as unattested in GOV-REG-07; and raises a risk in GOV-REG-05 for the steering committee to accept or treat. For [Organisation]'s own report, an unattested subservice organisation is disclosed in SOC-TPL-01 and discussed with the external auditor before the period begins.

4.10 Carve-out or inclusive. For each subservice organisation the Information Security Manager records in SOC-TPL-01 whether [Organisation] uses the carve-out method (the supplier's controls are excluded from [Organisation]'s report and the complementary subservice organisation controls [Organisation] relies on are listed) or the inclusive method (the supplier's controls are examined within [Organisation]'s report, which needs the supplier's written agreement and participation). The carve-out method is the default.

4.11 Actions and follow up. Actions from 4.5 and 4.6 are tracked in GOV-REG-03 and reported at the quarterly supplier review. A supplier whose conclusion is Not acceptable at two consecutive reviews is referred to the steering committee for a decision on exit under GOV-PRO-06.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-07 Supplier register with assurance type, last and next review dates and status.
  • The supplier assurance reports and bridge letters in the evidence folder.
  • One review record per report, including the complementary user entity control mapping.
  • Risks in GOV-REG-05 and corrective actions in GOV-REG-03 arising from exceptions or gaps.
  • Steering committee minutes for escalations.

6. Exceptions

A Tier 1 supplier that is not a subservice organisation may be accepted on an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate and Statement of Applicability without a SOC report where the Information Security Manager records that no [Organisation] criterion depends on the supplier's controls. No exception removes the requirement to map complementary user entity controls where a report lists them.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after any supplier incident, and when a new subservice organisation is added to the system boundary. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Input validation and reconciliation procedure

How inputs to an in-scope service are catalogued, validated, rejected, corrected and reconciled, so that processing starts from complete, accurate and authorised data and every difference between what arrived and what was processed is explained the same day.

Serves: SOC 2 PI1.2; SOC 2 PI1.3. Owner: Head of Engineering.

1. Purpose

This procedure puts SOC-POL-01 statements 4.3 to 4.6 into daily practice. It defines the catalogue of inputs, the validation rules each input must pass, what happens to an input that fails, and the daily reconciliation that proves nothing was lost, duplicated or changed between receipt and processing.

2. Scope

All inputs to services whose processing integrity category is in the report scope: files, interface calls, messages, user forms, manual entries by staff and data fed from other systems. It covers the point of receipt through to confirmation that processing consumed the input.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
System Owner Keeps the input catalogue and validation rules, approves changes to them, reviews monthly measures.
Operations team Monitors validation results, works the quarantine, prepares and reviews reconciliations.
Developer Implements validation and reconciliation checks as specified, with automated tests.
Submitter (customer or internal team) Supplies inputs in the agreed format and corrects rejected items.
Information Security Manager Tests the controls under SOC-PRO-01.

4. Procedure

4.1 Input catalogue. The System Owner keeps, within the processing specification, a catalogue of every input: name, source, channel, format, expected volume and timing, authorisation method, owner, and the validation rules that apply. A new input is added to the catalogue before it goes live and the entry is reviewed at each change under GOV-PRO-09.

4.2 Validation rules. For each input the System Owner defines rules in the following classes and writes the specific values in the catalogue.

  • Format: type, length, encoding, schema version.
  • Range and domain: permitted values, minimum and maximum, dates that cannot be in the future.
  • Referential: identifiers must exist in the master data they refer to.
  • Completeness: mandatory fields present; for a batch, header and trailer present and record count equal to the trailer count.
  • Duplication: an item with the same key as one already accepted inside the deduplication window is rejected or flagged, as the specification states.
  • Authorisation: the submitter is authenticated and permitted to send this input for this account.

4.3 Implementation and testing. The developer implements each rule with an automated test that proves a failing item is rejected and a passing item is accepted. Rules are deployed through GOV-PRO-09 and the change record references the catalogue version.

4.4 Control totals. Every batch input carries a record count and, where values are numeric, a control total generated by the sender. The system compares the received count and total to the batch header before processing. A mismatch rejects the whole batch.

4.5 Rejection and quarantine. A rejected item or batch is written to a quarantine store with the reason code, the time, the submitter and the item identifier. Nothing is deleted and nothing is corrected automatically unless the specification names the correction (trimming surrounding spaces, for example) and the correction is logged. The submitter is notified within [Number] hours with the reason.

4.6 Working the quarantine. The operations team reviews the quarantine at least daily. Each item is dispositioned as Resubmitted (corrected by the submitter and accepted), Corrected internally (only on the submitter's written instruction, recorded against the item, entered by one person and verified by another), or Closed without processing (with the submitter's agreement). An item in quarantine for more than [Number] working days is escalated to the System Owner.

4.7 Daily reconciliation. At the end of each processing day the operations team reconciles, for each input: items received, items accepted, items rejected, items processed and items pending, so that received equals accepted plus rejected, and accepted equals processed plus pending. The figures come from system counts, never from manual tallies.

4.8 Differences. Any difference, or any pending count older than the specification's tolerance, is investigated the same working day. The investigation records the cause, the items involved, the correction and who verified it. A difference caused by a defect raises a change under GOV-PRO-09 and, where a customer commitment was affected, an incident under GOV-PRO-07.

4.9 Reconciliation record. The reconciliation is recorded with date, service, the five figures, differences and their disposition, preparer and reviewer. The reviewer is not the preparer. The record is retained for the examination period plus one further period.

4.10 Interface reconciliation. For inputs received from another system by interface, the sending system's daily count is obtained and compared to items received at least daily. Each interface is listed in GOV-REG-25 with its reconciliation method.

4.11 Monitoring. The System Owner reviews monthly: rejection rate by reason, quarantine ageing, reconciliation differences and time to resolve, and rule changes. A rising rejection rate for one submitter is raised with that submitter; a rising rate across submitters triggers a review of the rules.

5. Records and evidence

  • The input catalogue inside each processing specification, version controlled.
  • Automated test results for validation rules, retained with the release.
  • Quarantine store entries and submitter notifications.
  • Daily reconciliation records with preparer and reviewer.
  • Difference investigations and the changes or incidents they raised.
  • The monthly monitoring report.

6. Exceptions

A reconciliation may be performed weekly instead of daily only for an input with fewer than [Number] items per week, recorded in the catalogue and approved by the Head of Engineering. No exception permits silent correction or deletion of a rejected item.

7. Review and maintenance

The Head of Engineering reviews this procedure annually, after any processing incident, and when an input is added or changed. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Output distribution and storage integrity procedure

How outputs of an in-scope service are checked for completeness and accuracy, delivered on time to authorised recipients only, corrected when wrong, and how inputs, items in processing and outputs are stored so that alteration or loss is prevented or detected.

Serves: SOC 2 PI1.4; SOC 2 PI1.5. Owner: Head of Engineering.

1. Purpose

This procedure puts SOC-POL-01 statements 4.7 to 4.9 into practice. It defines the catalogue of outputs, the checks an output passes before release, the controls on who receives it and how, the handling of corrections, and the integrity controls over every store that holds processing data.

2. Scope

All outputs of services whose processing integrity category is in the report scope: files, reports, interface responses, notifications and data feeds to customers or other systems. It also covers every data store holding inputs, items in processing or outputs for those services, including temporary and queue storage.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
System Owner Keeps the output catalogue and recipient lists, approves recipient changes, reviews monthly measures.
Operations team Monitors delivery schedules, performs completeness and accuracy checks, handles failed deliveries and reissues.
Developer Implements generation checks, checksums and delivery monitoring as specified.
Customer authorised contact Requests recipient changes in writing and acknowledges deliveries where the specification requires.
Information Security Manager Tests the controls under SOC-PRO-01.

4. Procedure

4.1 Output catalogue. The System Owner keeps, within the processing specification, a catalogue of every output: name, content, recipients, channel, format, schedule and deadline, completeness and accuracy checks, retention period and store. A new output is catalogued before it goes live.

4.2 Completeness checks. At generation the system computes the record count and, for numeric values, the control total of each output, and compares them to the items processed for that run. A checksum of each output file is computed at generation and delivered with the file or published where the recipient can verify it. Sequenced outputs carry a sequence number so that a missing delivery is visible to the recipient.

4.3 Accuracy checks. The system applies automated assertions to each output before release: totals balance to inputs, mandatory fields present, no empty values where the specification forbids them, values inside expected ranges. For an output carrying financial values or customer-visible figures, a member of the operations team who did not generate it verifies a sample of [Number] items against source data each run, or each day for continuous outputs, and records the result.

4.4 Timeliness. Every scheduled output is registered in the job monitor with its deadline. The monitor alerts the operations team if the output has not been delivered [Number] minutes before the deadline. A missed deadline is recorded with cause and, where a customer commitment is missed, handled as an incident under GOV-PRO-07.

4.5 Authorised recipients. The System Owner keeps a recipient list for each output, naming the accounts, addresses or endpoints and the customer or team each belongs to. Delivery goes only to listed recipients, only by the catalogued channel, and over encrypted transport under GOV-PRO-23 and GOV-PRO-20. The recipient list is reviewed quarterly with the access reviews in GOV-REG-12 and the review is recorded.

4.6 Recipient changes. A change to a recipient list requires a written request from the customer authorised contact or the internal owner, verification of the requester's identity by a method independent of the request, and approval by the System Owner. The change is recorded with request, approver and date.

4.7 Delivery confirmation. The system records each delivery with time, recipient and result. Where the specification requires acknowledgement, the recipient's acknowledgement or the channel's delivery receipt is captured. A failed delivery is retried as the specification states and then escalated to the operations team within [Number] minutes.

4.8 Corrections and reissue. An output found to be wrong is reissued with a version marker and a note of what changed. The original is retained unaltered. The recipient is told what changed, why, and which version to use. The cause is entered in the processing error log and, where systemic, raised under GOV-PRO-04.

4.9 Storage integrity. Every store holding inputs, items in processing or outputs has access restricted under GOV-PRO-10 to the service identities and roles the specification names. Where the platform offers versioning, write-once retention or object locking, the System Owner enables it for output stores. Each stored object carries a checksum computed on write.

4.10 Integrity verification. The operations team verifies stored checksums on a schedule: monthly for a random sample of at least [Number] objects per store, and in full before any migration and after any restore. A mismatch is an incident under GOV-PRO-07 and the affected objects are restored from backup under GOV-PRO-12.

4.11 Retention and disposal. Stored processing data is kept for the period in PIMS-REG-07 and then deleted by the method PIMS-POL-02 names, with the deletion recorded. A legal hold under GOV-PRO-25 suspends deletion for the objects it names.

4.12 Backup and capacity. Processing stores are backed up under GOV-PRO-12, and the quarterly restore test includes verifying the checksum of at least one restored output. Capacity thresholds for processing stores are monitored under GOV-PRO-19 and a failed write raises an alert.

4.13 Monitoring. The System Owner reviews monthly: outputs delivered late, completeness or accuracy check failures, failed deliveries, reissues, recipient changes, integrity verification results and disposal actions.

5. Records and evidence

  • The output catalogue and recipient lists, with quarterly review records.
  • Generation check results, checksums and sequence records per run.
  • Sample accuracy verification records.
  • Job monitor alerts and delivery logs with acknowledgements.
  • Recipient change requests and approvals.
  • Reissue records and the processing error log.
  • Integrity verification results, disposal records and restore test results.

6. Exceptions

An output may be delivered to an unlisted recipient only in an incident, on the written instruction of the System Owner, with the delivery recorded and the recipient list corrected within one working day. No exception permits alteration of an original output after release.

7. Review and maintenance

The Head of Engineering reviews this procedure annually, after any processing incident or integrity failure, and when an output or store is added or changed. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

1. How to use this template

The system description is written by [Organisation] and included in the SOC 2 report under management's assertion. The auditor tests whether it is fairly presented: complete enough that a reader understands the system, accurate against what the auditor observes, and free of claims the controls do not support. Write in the present tense for the period covered. Every statement about a control must match a row in SOC-REG-01. Remove the italic guidance before issue. Keep names of staff out; use roles. 2. Overview and services provided

Two to four paragraphs. What [Organisation] is, what the service does for its customers, who the customers are in general terms, and the business function the service performs. A reader with no prior knowledge should understand the service after this section.

3. Principal service commitments and system requirements

Service commitments are what [Organisation] promises customers: in contracts, service level agreements, terms of service, privacy notices and public security statements. GDPR-GDE-01 guide Download .docx Markdown

Guide: a GDPR operating model for a product or service team

How GDPR works as a day-to-day operating model for a team that builds or runs a product handling personal data, told through the life of the data and the register each stage updates.

Serves: GDPR Article 5; GDPR Article 24; GDPR Article 25; GDPR Article 30; GDPR Article 32. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Accountability in four things

GDPR is built on accountability: you must not only comply but be able to show it. In practice that means four things kept current. A map of the personal data you process. The operating processes that handle it. The evidence that those processes ran. Consistent statements to the outside world. This guide shows how each stage of the data lifecycle feeds those four things.

2. The roles

A product team usually needs a privacy owner who runs the programme, an approver for external statements, an engineering owner who knows where data actually lives, a support owner who handles requests, and leadership who owns the commitments. One person can hold several of these in a small team, but each must be named.

3. The lifecycle, stage by stage

Each stage below ends with the register it updates. The discipline is simple: when something happens to personal data, a register changes.

3.1 Sign-up or contract. A new customer or user brings personal data into scope. Record the processing, its purpose and its lawful basis, and make sure a privacy notice was shown. Updates: processing inventory (PIMS-REG-01), lawful basis, notice version.

3.2 Data arrives. Documents, uploads and integrations bring data in. Record where it flows and how it is protected in transit, and classify it. Updates: data flow map (GDPR-REG-02), asset register, classification.

3.3 Processing, including any AI feature. The product does something with the data. Where the processing is high risk, or an AI feature makes automated decisions, assess it. Record retention for inputs and outputs. Updates: DPIA register (PIMS-REG-08), AI inventory where relevant, retention schedule.

3.4 Sharing and suppliers. Data goes to a processor or a third party. Confirm the Article 28 terms are in place and that any transfer outside the region has a lawful mechanism. Updates: processor register (PIMS-REG-06), transfer register (PIMS-REG-05).

3.5 A request from a person. Someone asks to see, correct or delete their data. Verify identity, start the one-month clock, act, and respond. Updates: request register (PIMS-REG-02).

3.6 An incident. Data is lost or exposed. Contain it, assess the risk to individuals, and decide within seventy-two hours of awareness whether to notify the authority and the people affected. Record it either way. Updates: breach register (PIMS-REG-03).

3.7 End of the relationship. The customer leaves or the retention period ends. Delete the data across primary storage, derived data, backups and logs, not just the front-end record. Updates: retention schedule (PIMS-REG-07).

4. The cadence

Weekly, work through requests, incidents and supplier changes, and close a few outstanding items. Monthly, export the evidence that controls ran and reconcile the retention and vendor registers. Quarterly, refresh assessments and run an exercise. Annually, review the whole programme. The no-assumption rule holds throughout: every unknown becomes a line with an owner and a due date, and every gap becomes a corrective action.

5. Safe statements

Say what is true and nothing more. You process personal data under recorded lawful bases. You keep a record of processing. You have the processes and evidence to meet your obligations. Avoid "fully compliant" and "GDPR certified"; neither is a thing you can truthfully claim, and both invite a question you do not want.

Data protection policy

The organisation-wide rules for handling personal data lawfully, the responsibilities that make the rules work, and the records that show they are followed.

Serves: GDPR Article 5; GDPR Article 24; GDPR Article 32; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.34. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This policy states how [Organisation] handles personal data about customers, users, staff, applicants, suppliers and anyone else whose data it holds, so that every person who touches personal data knows the rules and so that the organisation can demonstrate that it meets GDPR Article 5 and Article 24.

2. Scope

It applies to every employee, contractor and temporary worker, to every system, service and paper record that holds personal data, and to every processing activity in which [Organisation] acts as a controller, a joint controller or a processor. Where [Organisation] acts as a processor, the customer's documented instructions take precedence over any statement in section 4 that would conflict with them, and PIMS-PRO-01 records which role applies.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Chief Executive Officer Approves this policy, provides the resources it needs, and is accountable for the organisation's compliance.
Privacy Officer Owns the policy, advises on every statement below, keeps PIMS-REG-01, runs the rights and breach processes, and reports to the steering committee under GOV-POL-01.
Data Protection Officer Where one is designated under GDPR Article 37, performs the independent tasks in Article 39 and is the contact point for the supervisory authority. The role may be held by the Privacy Officer only where independence can be shown.
System Owner Applies the statements to the systems they own, supports data subject requests and deletion, and keeps GDPR-REG-02 current for their flows.
Head of each function Confirms once a year that the processing in their function is recorded in PIMS-REG-01 and has a lawful basis.
Information Security Manager Operates the technical and organisational measures required by statement 4.9 under GOV-POL-03.
All staff Follow this policy, complete the training in statement 4.12, and report concerns and suspected breaches at once.

4. Policy statements

4.1 Lawfulness, fairness and transparency. Every processing activity has one lawful basis recorded in PIMS-REG-01 before it starts, and the people concerned are told about it through a notice built from GDPR-TPL-01, GDPR-TPL-02 or GDPR-TPL-03 at the point of collection, or within one month where the data was not collected from them.

4.2 Purpose limitation. Personal data is used only for the purposes stated in the notice and the inventory. A new purpose needs the Privacy Officer's written compatibility assessment, and, where the assessment fails, a new lawful basis and an updated notice before the new use begins.

4.3 Data minimisation. Teams collect only the data fields the recorded purpose needs. Every new form, field, integration and feature is checked against this statement under PIMS-PRO-06 before release.

4.4 Accuracy. Owners of systems that hold personal data provide a way for the people concerned, or staff acting for them, to correct it, and correct or delete inaccurate data within one month of learning that it is wrong.

4.5 Storage limitation. Every category of personal data has a retention period and a trigger recorded in PIMS-REG-07 under PIMS-POL-02. Data past its period is deleted or anonymised across primary storage, derived copies, backups and logs within the windows that schedule sets, and the deletion is recorded.

4.6 Special category and criminal offence data. Data about health, ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetics, biometrics, sex life or sexual orientation, and data about criminal convictions, is processed only where the Privacy Officer has recorded a condition under GDPR Article 9 or Article 10 in PIMS-REG-01, with access limited to named roles.

4.7 Consent. Where consent is the basis, it is collected with a form built from GDPR-TPL-06, recorded in PIMS-REG-04, and withdrawable as easily as it was given. Consent is never bundled with terms of service and is never a condition of a service that does not need the data. Consent from a child is handled under PIMS-PRO-05.

4.8 Legitimate interests. Where legitimate interests is the basis, a completed GDPR-TPL-07 assessment is approved by the Privacy Officer and recorded in GDPR-REG-03 before processing starts, and the people concerned can object.

4.9 Security. Personal data is protected by the controls in GOV-POL-03 and the procedures it mandates, proportionate to the risk recorded in GOV-REG-05 and, where a data protection impact assessment exists, in PIMS-REG-08. Restricted personal data is encrypted at rest and in transit under GOV-PRO-20.

4.10 Data subject rights. Every request to exercise a right under GDPR Articles 15 to 22 is logged in PIMS-REG-02 on the day it arrives and answered under PIMS-PRO-03 within one month, using the letters in GDPR-TPL-05. No request is refused without the Privacy Officer's written reasons.

4.11 Breaches. Anyone who suspects that personal data has been lost, altered, disclosed or made unavailable reports it immediately through the channel in GOV-PRO-07. The Privacy Officer assesses the breach under PIMS-PRO-04, notifies the supervisory authority within 72 hours of awareness where the risk test is met, using GDPR-TPL-10, and records every breach in PIMS-REG-03 whether or not it is notified.

4.12 Training. Every person completes privacy training at induction and annually, and people who handle requests, breaches, HR data or special category data complete role-based training, all recorded in GDPR-REG-05 under GOV-PRO-08.

4.13 Processors and sharing. Personal data is shared with a processor only under a contract that meets GDPR Article 28, built from PIMS-TPL-02 and recorded in PIMS-REG-06, after an assessment using GDPR-TPL-09 under GOV-PRO-06. Sharing with another controller is recorded in PIMS-REG-01 with its basis.

4.14 International transfers. Personal data leaves the region only under a mechanism in PIMS-POL-03, recorded in PIMS-REG-05, and, for transfers relying on contractual safeguards, after a transfer impact assessment using GDPR-TPL-08.

4.15 Privacy by design and impact assessment. Every project, feature and procurement that processes personal data is screened under PIMS-PRO-02 and, where a trigger applies, a data protection impact assessment using PIMS-TPL-01 is completed and approved before go-live, as checked at the gate in PB-07.

4.16 Records. The Privacy Officer keeps PIMS-REG-01 as the record of processing activities required by GDPR Article 30, reviewed under GDPR-PRO-01 at least quarterly.

4.17 Consequences. Breach of this policy is handled under the disciplinary process in GOV-PRO-18. Deliberate misuse of personal data may be gross misconduct and may be reported to the authorities.

5. Records and evidence

  • PIMS-REG-01 Personal data processing inventory, with lawful bases and special category conditions.
  • PIMS-REG-02 Data subject request register, PIMS-REG-03 Personal data breach register, PIMS-REG-04 Consent record register.
  • GDPR-REG-03 Legitimate interests assessment register, PIMS-REG-05 International transfer register, PIMS-REG-06 Processor and sub-processor register.
  • PIMS-REG-07 Retention schedule and the deletion records it requires.
  • PIMS-REG-08 DPIA register.
  • GDPR-REG-05 Privacy training register and GOV-REG-23 Policy acknowledgement register.
  • Minutes of the steering committee showing the Privacy Officer's reports.

6. Exceptions

A legal obligation, a court order or a request from a competent authority may require processing outside a statement above. The Privacy Officer records the obligation, the data disclosed and the date in PIMS-REG-01 and informs the Chief Executive Officer. No other exception applies; a team that cannot meet a statement raises it under GOV-PRO-24.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this policy annually, after a supervisory authority decision or guidance that affects the organisation, after a reportable breach, and after a change in the services offered or the regions served. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01 and are communicated to all staff with a new acknowledgement in GOV-REG-23.

Data mapping and records of processing procedure

How the organisation discovers, records and keeps current every processing activity and every flow of personal data, so that PIMS-REG-01 and GDPR-REG-02 are a true record of processing at any moment.

Serves: GDPR Article 30; GDPR Article 5(2); ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.2.8; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.2.8; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.9. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This procedure produces and maintains the two records that every other privacy process depends on: the processing inventory in PIMS-REG-01, which is the record of processing activities that GDPR Article 30 requires, and the flow and transfer map in GDPR-REG-02, which shows where each item of personal data comes from, where it goes and under what safeguard. Without them a request cannot be answered completely, a breach cannot be scoped, a retention rule cannot be applied and a notice cannot be accurate.

2. Scope

It applies to every function, system, service, supplier relationship and paper process in which [Organisation] processes personal data as a controller, joint controller or processor, including trials, internal tools, analytics, backups, support tooling and features that use machine learning.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Privacy Officer Runs the procedure, facilitates the workshops, owns both registers, decides which activities are distinct, and signs the quarterly review.
Head of each function Names a function representative, confirms the completeness of the function's rows once a year.
Function representative Attends the workshop for their function, supplies the facts for each activity, and reports changes within the triggers in step 4.9.
System Owner Confirms the systems, storage locations, retention settings and integrations for each flow that touches their system, and keeps the GDPR-REG-02 rows for those flows current.
Information Security Manager Supplies the security measures column from the Statement of Applicability and the controls in GOV-REG-25.
Processor customers' contacts Where [Organisation] is a processor, supply the categories and instructions needed for the processor rows.

4. Procedure

4.1 Plan the mapping round. The Privacy Officer schedules one workshop per function (for example product, engineering, sales and marketing, customer support, people, finance) in the first mapping round, and one per changed function in later rounds. Each workshop has a function representative, the owners of the systems that function uses, and the Privacy Officer. The invitation lists the questions in step 4.3 so that representatives arrive with answers.

4.2 Collect the system view first. Before the workshop the Privacy Officer exports the asset list from GOV-REG-10, the supplier list from GOV-REG-07 and the interface list from GOV-REG-25, filters each to items that hold or move personal data, and brings the filtered lists to the workshop as a prompt. A system that holds personal data and appears in no activity is a gap to resolve in the workshop, not a line to delete.

4.3 Identify activities. In the workshop the Privacy Officer walks through what the function does to people, in the people's own terms: who they are (customers, users, staff, applicants, contacts, visitors), what happens to them (sign-up, billing, support, marketing, recruitment, monitoring), and why. Each distinct purpose with its own data set is one activity. Two purposes that use the same data are two activities. The same purpose across several systems is one activity with several systems. The test is whether a reader of the notice would recognise it as a separate thing the organisation does with their data.

4.4 Record each activity. For every activity the representative supplies, and the Privacy Officer records in PIMS-REG-01: the role of [Organisation] (controller, joint controller or processor, decided under PIMS-PRO-01); the purpose; the lawful basis, and the condition where special category or criminal offence data is involved; the categories of data subjects and of data; the source; the recipients, internal and external; whether data leaves the region and the safeguard; the retention period and trigger from PIMS-REG-07; the security measures by reference; the owner; and any DPIA reference from PIMS-REG-08. A row with any of these blank is marked Incomplete in its status and given an owner and a date.

4.5 Trace the flows. For every activity the System Owners trace the data from entry to deletion: the system or party it enters from, each system it is stored in or passed to, each third party it is sent to, and where backups and logs containing it are kept. Each hop is one row in GDPR-REG-02 with the data items that move, the direction, whether the destination is internal or external, the country, the transfer method, the safeguard, the controls on the hop (encryption, authentication, access restriction) and the owner. The team draws the flow as a simple diagram during the workshop and files the diagram against the activity in the evidence folder described in PB-09.

4.6 Resolve the gaps the trace exposes. Three findings are common and each has a fixed response. A flow to a supplier not in PIMS-REG-06 goes to the Privacy Officer, who starts GOV-PRO-06 and marks the flow Under review. A flow out of the region with no safeguard goes to PIMS-POL-03 and a GDPR-TPL-08 assessment, and the flow is suspended if it carries Restricted data. An activity with no lawful basis the representative can state is suspended until the Privacy Officer records one, or records the decision to stop the activity.

4.7 Check against the external statements. The Privacy Officer compares the completed rows with the current privacy notices built from GDPR-TPL-01, GDPR-TPL-02 and GDPR-TPL-03, the cookie inventory in GDPR-REG-04 and the customer-facing processing descriptions. Any activity, recipient, retention period or transfer in the registers that the notices do not describe is raised to PIMS-PRO-05 for a notice change, with the processing recorded as Partial in GDPR-REG-01 until the notice is published.

4.8 Approve the round. The head of each function confirms in writing that the rows for their function are complete and accurate. The Privacy Officer sets the status of each confirmed row to Current, records the round date, and reports the counts (activities, incomplete rows, flows under review, transfers without safeguard) to the steering committee under GOV-POL-01.

4.9 Triggers for an update between rounds. A function representative or System Owner reports to the Privacy Officer within five working days, and the Privacy Officer updates the registers within ten working days, when any of the following happens: a new product feature, form or integration that collects or sends personal data; a new or changed supplier; a new purpose for existing data; a new country of storage, support or processing; a change in retention; a change in the role of [Organisation] for a customer; a merger, acquisition or new entity; a data subject request or breach that reveals an unrecorded activity. The go-live gate in PB-07 and the change procedure in GOV-PRO-09 both ask whether the registers were updated, so a feature cannot ship with an unrecorded flow.

4.10 Quarterly review. Each quarter the Privacy Officer samples at least ten activities, checks each against the live system (a field list, an integration configuration, a supplier console, a retention setting) and records the result. A sample that fails on a material fact (an unrecorded recipient, transfer or data category) triggers a workshop for that function within thirty days.

4.11 Annual round. Once a year the full set of workshops in step 4.1 is repeated. The annual round also retires activities that have stopped, with the stop date recorded and the deletion confirmed under PIMS-POL-02.

4.12 Producing the Article 30 record. When a supervisory authority, an auditor or a customer asks for the record of processing, the Privacy Officer exports PIMS-REG-01 filtered to the role requested (controller rows or processor rows), dated, with the version of the register, and files a copy of what was sent.

5. Records and evidence

  • PIMS-REG-01 Personal data processing inventory, with a status and round date on every row.
  • GDPR-REG-02 Data flow and transfer map, with a diagram per activity in the evidence folder.
  • Workshop attendance notes and the function heads' written confirmations.
  • Quarterly sample records and any workshops they triggered.
  • Copies of every Article 30 export provided to an external party.
  • GDPR-REG-01 rows for Article 30 updated with the evidence reference.

6. Exceptions

An activity may remain Incomplete for no more than sixty days while a supplier or customer supplies a fact only they hold, with the Privacy Officer's agreement noted on the row. No activity runs without a recorded lawful basis.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this procedure annually, after an audit finding or supervisory authority enquiry about the record of processing, and after a change in the organisation's structure. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

HR data handling procedure

How personal data about applicants, employees, contractors and former staff is collected, used, protected, retained and deleted at each stage from recruitment to after departure.

Serves: GDPR Article 5; GDPR Article 6; GDPR Article 9; GDPR Article 88; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.2.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.1. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This procedure gives the people function and line managers a single set of steps for handling the personal data of the workforce, so that recruitment, employment, monitoring, references and leaving are all done on a recorded lawful basis, with the minimum data, for a defined period, and with special category data under tighter control.

2. Scope

It applies to data about job applicants, employees, contractors, temporary workers, interns and former members of any of those groups, in every system and paper file that holds it, including the HR system, payroll, recruitment tools, email, shared drives, access control and monitoring systems, and the files that managers keep.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Head of People Owns the HR processing activities in PIMS-REG-01, approves the retention periods for HR categories, and is the approver for the disclosures in step 4.8.
HR Administrator Performs the day-to-day steps, keeps the HR system current and runs the retention checks in step 4.10.
Line manager Collects only the data the steps allow, keeps no shadow files, and routes requests and concerns to the people function.
Privacy Officer Advises on lawful basis and special category conditions, approves monitoring and new HR tools, handles rights requests from the workforce under PIMS-PRO-03.
Information Security Manager Applies access control, logging and encryption to HR systems and approves any monitoring configuration.
Payroll and benefits providers Act as processors under PIMS-TPL-02 terms recorded in PIMS-REG-06.

4. Procedure

4.1 Recruitment: collection. The HR Administrator publishes the applicant notice built from GDPR-TPL-03 on every application channel before any data is entered. Application forms ask only for the data needed to assess suitability for the advertised role. Equal opportunities monitoring questions are optional, kept separate from the application, and seen only in aggregate. Social media and public sources are searched only where the Head of People has recorded the need for the role, and the applicant is told.

4.2 Recruitment: assessment. Interviewers record their notes in the recruitment system, not in personal files, limit them to evidence against the role criteria, and are told at interview training that the candidate may obtain the notes under a request. Tests and assessments are used only where PIMS-PRO-02 screening shows no automated decision in the sense of GDPR Article 22, or where a human reviews every rejection.

4.3 Pre-employment checks. Checks are proportionate to the role and recorded in GOV-PRO-18. Identity and right to work checks are kept as the law requires. Criminal record checks are run only for roles where the law permits them and the Privacy Officer has recorded the condition in PIMS-REG-01. Reference requests are sent only after the candidate agrees to them, and references received are held on the employee file.

4.4 Unsuccessful applicants. The HR Administrator deletes the data of unsuccessful applicants [Number] months after the decision, no later than twelve, unless the applicant has agreed in writing to be kept in a talent pool for a stated period. The deletion covers the recruitment system, email folders and interviewers' notes.

4.5 Employment records. On joining, the HR Administrator creates one employee record in the HR system, gives the employee the notice built from GDPR-TPL-02 with the contract, and records in GDPR-REG-05 the induction privacy training completed under GOV-PRO-08. Managers hold no local copies of contracts, pay details, absence reasons or performance records; they work in the HR system. Emergency contact details are collected with the contact's name, relationship and number only, and the employee is asked to tell the contact.

4.6 Special category data. Health data (absence reasons, adjustments, occupational health reports), trade union membership, and any other special category data is held in a restricted section of the HR system that only the people function and the Privacy Officer can read. Managers see fitness to work and adjustments needed, not diagnoses. Such data is processed under an employment law condition recorded in PIMS-REG-01, or with explicit consent collected with GDPR-TPL-06 where the law allows and the employee is free to refuse.

4.7 Monitoring. Monitoring of email, internet, devices, access logs or location is introduced only after the Privacy Officer and the Information Security Manager approve a written purpose and scope, the screening in PIMS-PRO-02 is complete, and staff have been told through the notice and GOV-POL-02. Monitoring is targeted at the purpose (security, legal compliance, safety), is not continuous surveillance of individuals, and covert monitoring is used only for a specific suspected serious offence, authorised by the Chief Executive Officer, for a fixed period, and recorded.

4.8 Disclosures. Workforce data is disclosed outside the people function only: to processors in PIMS-REG-06; to tax, social security and other authorities where the law requires; to a prospective employer giving a reference, limited to dates, role and, where the organisation's reference policy allows, factual performance statements; to a customer or client where the contract requires named staff details, limited to name, role and qualifications; to insurers and pension providers for the scheme concerned. Any other disclosure needs the Head of People's written approval and a lawful basis recorded by the Privacy Officer.

4.9 Rights of the workforce. Requests from applicants, employees and former staff follow PIMS-PRO-03. Access requests from employees are common in grievances and disciplinary processes; the HR Administrator searches the HR system, email of the people function and the relevant managers, and shared drives, and applies the exemptions for third party data and confidential references with the Privacy Officer.

4.10 Leavers. On the last day the HR Administrator triggers the offboarding tasks in GOV-CHK-01, moves the employee record to the leaver status, and records the leaving date as the retention trigger. Within thirty days the HR Administrator removes the person from distribution lists, internal directories and any system where their account was not removed by GOV-PRO-10, and confirms to the Privacy Officer.

4.11 Retention and deletion. Each HR category has a period in PIMS-REG-07: the employee file for [Number] years after leaving as employment and tax law require, payroll records for the statutory period, recruitment records under step 4.4, health and safety records for the period the law sets, monitoring records for no more than [Number] months unless part of an investigation. The HR Administrator runs the retention report quarterly, deletes expired records in the HR system, email and shared drives, asks processors in PIMS-REG-06 to confirm their deletion, and records the run.

4.12 New HR tools and changes. A new recruitment, HR, payroll, survey, wellbeing or monitoring tool goes through GOV-PRO-06 and GDPR-TPL-09, PIMS-PRO-02 screening, and the processing inventory update in GDPR-PRO-01 before any workforce data is entered.

5. Records and evidence

  • PIMS-REG-01 rows for recruitment, employment administration, payroll, benefits, performance, absence and health, monitoring and references.
  • GDPR-REG-05 Privacy training register showing induction and HR handler training.
  • Retention report runs and deletion records under PIMS-REG-07.
  • PIMS-REG-02 entries for workforce requests.
  • Monitoring approvals and, where used, covert monitoring authorisations.
  • Disclosure approvals under step 4.8.
  • GOV-CHK-01 completed checklists for joiners and leavers.

6. Exceptions

Records subject to a legal hold, a live grievance, disciplinary case, claim or investigation are kept until the Head of People and the Privacy Officer release the hold in writing, and the hold is recorded on the retention report. No other exception applies.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer and the Head of People review this procedure annually, after a change in employment or data protection law affecting the workforce, after a workforce-related breach or complaint, and after the introduction of a new HR system or monitoring tool. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Privacy notice template (customers and website)

The customer and website privacy notice with every element GDPR Articles 13 and 14 require, as sections with placeholders and guidance notes, maintained under PIMS-PRO-05.

Serves: GDPR Article 12; GDPR Article 13; GDPR Article 14; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.2; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.3. Owner: Privacy Officer.

Guidance notes are in italics and are removed before publication. Every section below corresponds to an element the law requires; do not delete a section, write "not applicable" with a reason instead. Write for the reader, not the regulator: short sentences, no legal citations in the body, a reading age of about twelve. Each fact in this notice must match a row in PIMS-REG-01; the Privacy Officer checks the match before publication and after every change, and records the version in GOV-REG-01. Where data is obtained from someone other than the person, the notice is provided within one month, or at first contact or first disclosure if earlier.

1. Who we are

[Organisation], [registered address], is the controller of the personal data described in this notice. If a representative is appointed under GDPR Article 27, name it here with contact details. If the organisation acts as a processor for business customers, say so and point readers to the customer who decides how their data is used.

You can contact us about anything in this notice at [contact channel]. Where a Data Protection Officer is designated, give the DPO's contact details here; they may be a role mailbox rather than a name.

2. What this notice covers

This notice explains what we do with personal data when you visit [website or application], create an account, use [Product or service], contact us, or receive marketing from us. List every audience the notice covers. Employees and applicants have their own notices built from GDPR-TPL-02 and GDPR-TPL-03. Cookies and similar technologies are covered in the notice built from GDPR-TPL-04 and may be linked from here.

3. The data we collect and where it comes from

One row per category of data. The "source" column satisfies the Article 14 requirement for data not collected from the person; include publicly available sources where used.

Category Examples Source
Account and contact details [Name, email address, telephone number, organisation, role] You, when you register or contact us
Content you provide [Files, messages, settings and other material you upload to the service] You
Usage and device information [Pages viewed, features used, device type, browser, IP address, approximate location derived from it] Collected automatically when you use the service
Transaction and billing data [Plan, invoices, payment status; card details are held by our payment provider, not by us] You and our payment provider
Support and communications [Support tickets, call notes, survey responses] You
Data from other sources [Business contact data from a data provider, information from a partner that referred you, public professional profiles] [Named category of source]

4. Why we use your data and the legal basis

One row per purpose. Each purpose needs exactly one basis from: performance of a contract, legal obligation, legitimate interests (state the interest), consent, vital interests, public task. Where legitimate interests is the basis, the interest named here must match the GDPR-REG-03 entry. Where consent is the basis, say how to withdraw it.

Purpose Data used Legal basis
Providing [Product or service], including creating your account and delivering the features you use Account details, content, usage information Performance of our contract with you
Billing and collecting payment Account details, transaction data Performance of our contract; legal obligation for tax and accounting records
Keeping the service secure, detecting fraud and abuse Usage and device information, account details Our legitimate interest in protecting the service and its users
Improving the service and understanding how it is used Usage information, aggregated where possible Our legitimate interest in improving what we offer; consent for analytics cookies where required
Responding to your questions and support requests Contact details, support communications Performance of our contract, or our legitimate interest in answering enquiries
Sending you marketing about our products Contact details, usage information Consent, or our legitimate interest in marketing to existing customers where the law allows, with an opt-out in every message
Complying with the law and responding to lawful requests Any category, as required Legal obligation
[Features that use machine learning, for example suggestions or classification] [Content and usage data described precisely] [Basis]. Say whether the data is used to train models, and if so on what basis; say whether a human reviews outputs that affect you.

5. Automated decisions

Required where decisions with legal or similarly significant effects are made solely by automated means. If none, keep the first sentence.

We do not make decisions about you based solely on automated processing that have legal or similarly significant effects on you. [If this changes, we will tell you how the decision is made, why it matters and how to ask for a person to review it.]

6. Who we share your data with

List categories of recipients, and name them where the reader would reasonably expect it. Every processor listed here is in PIMS-REG-06. Sharing between group companies counts as sharing.

  • Service providers that act on our instructions: [hosting, email delivery, payment processing, customer support tools, analytics]. They may only use your data to provide their service to us.
  • [Group companies], for [purpose].
  • Professional advisers, insurers and auditors, where needed.
  • Authorities, regulators and courts, where the law requires or allows it.
  • A buyer or successor, if our business or part of it is sold or reorganised, under confidentiality terms.

We do not sell your personal data.

7. Where your data is stored and international transfers

Your data is stored in [country or region]. State every country where data is stored, supported from or processed, including by processors; this must match PIMS-REG-05 and GDPR-REG-02.

Where we transfer your data outside [region], we rely on [an adequacy decision by the relevant authority, standard contractual clauses approved by the relevant authority, binding corporate rules, or a derogation such as your explicit consent or the performance of your contract]. You can ask us for a copy of the safeguards we use at the contact in section 1. Name the mechanism per destination; never write "appropriate safeguards" alone.

8. How long we keep your data

One row per category, matching PIMS-REG-07. Where a fixed period cannot be stated, give the criteria used to decide it.

Category Period
Account and content For as long as your account is open, then deleted within [Number] days of closure, except where we must keep it longer by law
Billing and transaction records [Number] years after the transaction, as tax and accounting law require
Usage and device logs [Number] months
Support communications [Number] years after the ticket is closed
Marketing preferences and consent records Until you withdraw consent or object, and then a record of your choice for [Number] years so that we respect it

9. Your rights

You have the right to ask us for access to your personal data, to correct it, to delete it, to restrict how we use it, to receive it in a portable format, and to object to processing based on our legitimate interests. Where we rely on your consent, you may withdraw it at any time without affecting what was done before. You may object to direct marketing at any time and we will stop.

To exercise a right, contact us at [contact channel]. We will respond within one month and tell you if we need longer. We may ask you to confirm your identity. The response process is PIMS-PRO-03; the letters are in GDPR-TPL-05.

You also have the right to complain to a supervisory authority. Ours is [name of supervisory authority]. We would appreciate the chance to resolve your concern first, but you may contact the authority at any time.

10. Whether you must provide your data

Required where data is collected from the person. State what is needed for the contract or by law and what happens if it is not provided.

To open an account and use [Product or service] you must give us [the data marked as required on the sign-up form]. Without it we cannot provide the service. All other data is optional, and we tell you when it is.

11. Children

[Product or service] is not intended for children under [Number]. We do not knowingly collect data from them. Where the service is offered to children, describe the age check and how parental consent is obtained, under PIMS-PRO-05.

12. Changes to this notice

We will post any change here, with the date, and will tell you by [channel] before a change that affects how we use data we already hold about you. Material changes follow PIMS-PRO-05 and are recorded in GOV-REG-01 with the previous versions kept.

Version [Number], effective [Date].

Employee privacy notice template

The notice given to employees, contractors and temporary workers with their contract, describing how [Organisation] uses workforce data under GDPR-PRO-02.

Serves: GDPR Article 13; GDPR Article 88; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.2. Owner: Privacy Officer.

Guidance notes are in italics and are removed before issue. Give this notice with the employment contract or engagement letter, record the issue in the employee file, and re-issue it after any material change. Each statement must match the HR rows in PIMS-REG-01 and the periods in PIMS-REG-07. Where a works council, staff association or collective agreement exists, consult it before changes to sections 5 and 7.

1. Who we are and who to contact

[Organisation], [registered address], is the controller of the personal data we hold about you as a member of our workforce. Questions about this notice go to [the people function contact channel] or to [the Privacy Officer or Data Protection Officer contact].

2. Who this notice covers

This notice applies to employees, contractors, temporary and agency workers, interns and volunteers, during your engagement and afterwards for as long as we keep your records. Applicants have a separate notice given during recruitment.

3. The data we hold

Category Examples
Identity and contact Name, address, date of birth, personal contact details, emergency contacts, identification documents, right to work evidence
Engagement Contract, role, grade, working pattern, location, start and end dates, manager, notice period
Pay and benefits Bank details, salary, tax and social security references, pension, expenses, benefits elections
Performance and development Objectives, appraisals, training records, qualifications, promotions, disciplinary and grievance records
Absence and health Holiday, sickness absence and reasons, medical certificates, occupational health reports, adjustments (special category data, see section 6)
Security and systems Account identifiers, access rights, building access records, device records, logs generated by using our systems
Monitoring records [Email and internet logs, access logs, CCTV images where installed] as described in section 7
Equality monitoring Ethnic origin, disability, religion, sexual orientation, where you choose to give them (optional, special category)

Most of this data comes from you. Some comes from your manager, from colleagues (for example in appraisals), from referees, from background check providers, and from the systems you use.

4. Why we use your data and on what basis

Purpose Legal basis
Running your contract: paying you, managing holiday, benefits, performance and development Performance of your contract
Meeting legal duties: tax, social security, right to work, health and safety, statutory leave Legal obligation
Managing the workplace: planning, resourcing, communications, internal directories Our legitimate interest in running the organisation
Keeping systems, premises and information secure, including the monitoring in section 7 Our legitimate interest in security and legal compliance
Handling grievances, disciplinary matters, investigations and legal claims Our legitimate interest in managing the workforce and defending claims; legal obligation where it applies
Equality monitoring and reporting Your explicit consent, or a legal obligation where the law requires reporting
Occupational health, adjustments and sickness management Employment and social security law, and the assessment of your working capacity

Where we rely on legitimate interests we have recorded an assessment and you may object; contact us at the channel in section 1.

5. Who we share your data with

  • Payroll, pension, benefits, HR system, training and occupational health providers, who act on our instructions.
  • Tax, social security and other authorities, where the law requires.
  • Customers and clients, where a contract requires your name, role and qualifications.
  • Prospective employers, for references after you leave, limited to [dates, role and factual statements].
  • Professional advisers, insurers and auditors, where needed.
  • [Group companies], for [purpose].

6. Special category data

Health data, trade union membership and the equality monitoring data you choose to give are held in a restricted part of the HR system that only the people function and [Privacy Officer] can read. Your manager sees what they need to support you at work, such as adjustments and fitness to work, not medical detail. We never use this data for any purpose other than the ones in section 4.

7. Monitoring

We monitor the use of our systems for security, to meet legal duties and to protect our information, as set out in the acceptable use policy. Monitoring covers [email and internet logs, system access logs, device management records, building access records, CCTV in the areas marked]. It is not continuous observation of individuals. Covert monitoring is used only to investigate a suspected serious offence, is authorised at the highest level, and is time-limited. The monitoring described here must match the approvals recorded under GDPR-PRO-02 step 4.7 and GOV-POL-02.

8. Where your data is kept

Your data is held in [country or region]. Where a provider processes it outside [region], we rely on [named transfer mechanism] and you may ask for a copy of the safeguards.

9. How long we keep it

Category Period
Employee file [Number] years after you leave
Payroll and tax records [Number] years, as the law requires

Disciplinary and grievance records [Number] years after the matter closes, unless needed for a claim
Monitoring logs [Number] months, unless part of an investigation

You may ask for access to your data, correct it, ask for deletion where we no longer need it, restrict or object to some uses, and withdraw any consent you gave. Contact [channel]. We respond within one month. You may complain to [supervisory authority] at any time.

11. Your obligations

You must keep your personal details current in [HR system], treat colleagues' data in line with GDPR-POL-01, and report any suspected breach at once.

Communicating with you about your application and future vacancies you ask about Our legitimate interest; consent for a talent pool
Equality monitoring and reporting in aggregate Your explicit consent
Defending legal claims about recruitment decisions Our legitimate interest

[Country or region]. Where a provider processes data outside [region] we rely on [named transfer mechanism].

Outcome Period
Unsuccessful application [Number] months after the decision, then deleted, including interview notes

Cookie and tracking technologies notice template

The public notice for cookies, local storage, pixels and software development kits, with the categories table, how consent is collected and withdrawn, and the link to the inventory in GDPR-REG-04 that keeps it true.

Serves: GDPR Article 6; GDPR Article 7; GDPR Article 13; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.2.3. Owner: Privacy Officer.

Guidance notes are in italics and are removed before publication. The ePrivacy rules require consent before any storage or reading on a device that is not strictly necessary for a service the person asked for; GDPR sets the standard of that consent. This notice is generated from GDPR-REG-04: every tracker in the inventory appears in the table below, and nothing appears here that is not in the inventory. The Privacy Officer re-runs the site scan and reconciles the table at least quarterly and before every release that adds a script, tag or SDK.

1. What this notice covers

This notice explains the cookies and similar technologies we use on [website or application], what they do, and how you can control them. "Similar technologies" means anything that stores or reads information on your device: local storage, pixels and web beacons, software development kits in our mobile applications, and scripts that read device characteristics.

2. The categories we use

Category What it does Consent
Strictly necessary Lets the site work: keeping you signed in, remembering your consent choice, protecting against attacks, balancing load Not required; you cannot switch these off
Functional Remembers choices you make, such as language or display settings Required (or "Not required" where the choice was explicitly requested by the user and the storage serves only that choice)
Analytics Measures how the site is used so that we can improve it Required
Advertising Builds a profile of your interests and shows you advertising on our site and elsewhere, including measuring whether advertising worked Required
Social media Lets you share content and lets the social network record that you visited Required

3. The cookies and trackers we use

Reproduce the current GDPR-REG-04 export, one row per tracker. Keep the table under six columns; split by category if long.

Name Set by Category Purpose Duration
[Name] [Organisation or named third party] [Category] [Plain words] [Session, or a period]
[Name] [Organisation or named third party] [Category] [Plain words] [Session, or a period]

Third parties that set cookies through our site act as [controllers in their own right or our processors]. Their own notices are linked in the table where they are controllers. Where a third party receives data outside [region], the transfer relies on [named mechanism], recorded in our transfer register.

4. How we ask for your consent

When you first visit, a banner asks you to choose. Nothing in the Functional, Analytics, Advertising or Social media categories is set until you accept it. The banner offers "Accept all", "Reject all" and "Choose" with equal prominence, and no category is pre-ticked. Closing the banner without choosing, scrolling or continuing to browse is not consent, and only strictly necessary technologies run.

Your choice is recorded, with the date, the version of this notice and the categories you accepted, in a strictly necessary cookie and in our consent record, so that we can show what you agreed to. Record the consent in PIMS-REG-04 or the consent platform's log, keep the log for the period in PIMS-REG-07, and keep the banner wording of each version under GOV-REG-01.

We ask again when we add a new category or a new third party, or after [Number] months, whichever comes first.

5. How to withdraw or change your choice

Open [the "Cookie settings" link in the footer] at any time, change the categories and save. Withdrawing consent stops the technologies in that category from the moment you save; data already collected is handled as described in the privacy notice. Withdrawal is as easy as giving consent: the same number of clicks, no account needed.

You can also delete cookies and block storage in your browser or device settings. If you do, our consent record is deleted too and the banner will appear again.

6. Do Not Track and similar signals

[We honour the Global Privacy Control signal from your browser as a rejection of Advertising and Social media categories.] Delete or adjust to match what the site actually does; never claim to honour a signal that is not implemented.

7. Mobile applications

Our [application name] uses software development kits from [named providers] for [crash reporting, analytics, advertising]. The application asks for the same categories of consent at first launch and in [Settings, Privacy]. Operating system permissions, such as location or advertising identifier access, are requested separately by the device and can be withdrawn in its settings.

8. Contact and complaints

Questions about this notice go to [contact channel]. You may complain to [supervisory authority]. Our full privacy notice explains your other rights.
