Data subject request response letters

Five letters used under PIMS-PRO-03 at the fixed points of a request: acknowledgement, identity verification, extension, response with data, and refusal with reasons and the complaint route.

Serves: GDPR Article 12; GDPR Article 15; GDPR Article 16; GDPR Article 17; GDPR Article 18; GDPR Article 20; GDPR Article 21; GDPR Article 22; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.9. Owner: Privacy Officer.

Guidance notes are in italics. Each letter is sent by the Privacy Officer or the person handling the request, on the day the step in PIMS-PRO-03 is reached, through the channel the requester used unless they asked for another. Record the date sent and the letter used in PIMS-REG-02. Replace every placeholder; delete the guidance; never add legal citations the requester did not ask for. The one month clock runs from the day the request is received, not from the day identity is confirmed, unless the request cannot be acted on without identification and the requester was told without delay.

1. Letter A: acknowledgement

Send within three working days of receipt. Use for every right, changing the second paragraph to name the right.

Dear [Name],

Thank you for your request, which we received on [Date]. Our reference is [PIMS-REG-02 reference]; please quote it in any further message.

We understand that you are asking us to [provide a copy of the personal data we hold about you / correct the following data / delete your personal data / restrict how we use your data / provide your data in a portable format / stop processing your data for the following purpose / review a decision made about you]. If we have misunderstood, please tell us.

We will respond by [Date, one month from receipt]. If your request is complex or you have made several requests, we may need up to two further months, and we will tell you before [Date] if that is the case, with the reason.

We do not charge for handling requests unless a request is clearly unfounded or excessive, in which case we will tell you before doing anything.

If we need to confirm your identity or to ask what data you are looking for, we will write to you separately.

Yours sincerely,

[Name], [Role] [Organisation]

2. Letter B: identity verification request

Send only when the identity of the requester cannot be confirmed from the channel used (for example a request from an authenticated account needs no further check). Ask for the least intrusive evidence that resolves the doubt. Never ask for more than the organisation already holds about the person. Tell the requester that the clock does not run while identification is outstanding only where that is the organisation's documented position.

Dear [Name],

Thank you for your request of [Date], reference [Reference].

Before we act on it we need to be sure that we are dealing with the person the data is about, so that we do not disclose or change someone's data at the request of another person.

Please [sign in to your account and resubmit the request from the request page / reply from the email address registered on your account / provide [one specific item, for example the postcode and the last four digits of the telephone number registered on the account] / provide a copy of one identity document with everything except your name, photograph and date of birth covered].

[If you are acting for someone else, please also provide the written authority of the person the data is about, or evidence of your legal authority to act for them.]

We will delete the identification evidence [Number] days after your request is closed and will not use it for any other purpose.

We will respond within one month of receiving this evidence. If we do not hear from you within [Number] days we will close the request, and you may make a new one at any time.

Yours sincerely,

[Name], [Role]

3. Letter C: extension notice

Send before the one month deadline, never after. The reason must be true and specific: volume, complexity or number of requests. "We are busy" is not a reason. Record the new date in PIMS-REG-02.

Dear [Name],

We are writing about your request of [Date], reference [Reference], which we would normally answer by [original date].

We need more time because [the request covers [Number] years of records across [Number] systems and the search must be completed and reviewed by hand / you have made [Number] separate requests which we are handling together / the request requires us to review material that includes other people's data]. We expect to respond by [new date, no more than two further months after the original date].

We have already [state what has been done]. If it would help, you may narrow the request to [a period, a system or a type of data] and we may be able to respond sooner.

We apologise for the delay.

Yours sincerely,

[Name], [Role]

4. Letter D: response with data (access request)

Attach the data as a structured export where possible, in a commonly used format, through a secure channel; never by unencrypted email. Include the supplementary information below: it is part of the right, not an optional cover note. Where the response also answers another right (correction, deletion, portability, objection), add a paragraph stating what was done and when, and keep the same structure.

Dear [Name],

Thank you for your request of [Date], reference [Reference]. We have completed our search and enclose the personal data we hold about you.

What we searched. [Named systems, email of the named functions, paper files], covering [period]. We searched using [your name, email address, account identifier, customer reference].

What is enclosed. [A file in [format] containing [Number] records, organised by [system or category].] Where a document contains information about other people, we have removed that information or the document, as the law allows; we have noted where this was done.

Why we hold this data and on what basis. [Short list of purposes and bases, matching the privacy notice.]

Where it came from. [You, and the sources named in the enclosed summary.]

Who we have shared it with. [Categories of recipients, and named recipients where known.]

How long we keep it. [The periods, or the criteria used.]

International transfers. [None / The data is processed in [country] under [mechanism], and you may ask for a copy of the safeguards.]

Automated decisions. [We do not make decisions about you by solely automated means. / A description of the logic, significance and consequences of the decision concerned.]

Your other rights. You may ask us to correct or delete this data, to restrict or object to our use of it, or to receive it in a portable format. You may complain to [supervisory authority] if you are unhappy with our response.

[Paragraph for other rights, where applicable: We have corrected [field] on [Date]. / We deleted your personal data from [systems] on [Date]; copies in backups will be removed within [Number] days under our backup cycle and cannot be restored to live use. / We have restricted [data] and will use it only for [purpose]. / We have stopped [processing] on [Date]. / We told the recipients listed above of the correction or deletion on [Date].]

Yours sincerely,

[Name], [Role]

5. Letter E: refusal with reasons and complaint route

A refusal, in whole or in part, needs the Privacy Officer's written approval in PIMS-REG-02 before it is sent. State the specific ground; the common ones are: the request is clearly unfounded or excessive (give the facts); the data is needed for a legal obligation or legal claims; deletion would conflict with a retention duty; the data is a confidential reference or concerns another person who has not agreed; the right does not apply to the lawful basis used (for example portability where the basis is legitimate interests). Where part of the request is granted, combine with Letter D and state what was and was not done.

Dear [Name],

Thank you for your request of [Date], reference [Reference], asking us to [right requested].

We have considered your request carefully, and we are not able to [act on it / act on the following part of it: [part]].

The reason is that [specific ground in plain words, for example: we are required by tax law to keep invoice records for [Number] years, and the data you have asked us to delete forms part of those records. We will delete it when that period ends on [Date]. / the records you asked for contain information about other people who have not agreed to its disclosure, and we cannot separate it from your information. / you have made [Number] requests for the same data since [Date] and we provided it on [Date]; we consider a further copy excessive. If you believe the data has changed since then, please tell us what you expect to find.]

[We have done the following instead: [what was done].]

If you disagree with this decision, you may ask us to review it by writing to [contact], and a person who was not involved in the original decision will review it within [Number] days. You also have the right to complain to [supervisory authority, contact details] and to seek a remedy through the courts.

Yours sincerely,

[Name], [Role]

Consent form templates (customers and employees)

Two consent forms, one for customers and users and one for employees, each containing the elements that make consent valid, with the record that PIMS-REG-04 keeps for every consent given or withdrawn.

Serves: GDPR Article 7; GDPR Article 4; GDPR Article 9(2)(a); ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.2.3; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.2.4. Owner: Privacy Officer.

Guidance notes are in italics and are removed before use. Consent is the right basis only when the person has a real choice and the organisation would accept a refusal; PIMS-PRO-05 records that decision before a form is used. A valid consent is freely given, specific to a stated purpose, informed, and shown by a clear affirmative act. It is never a pre-ticked box, silence, inactivity or a condition buried in terms. The form must be as easy to withdraw as to give, and the organisation must be able to show, for each person, what they consented to, when, how and under which version of the wording.

1. Customer and user consent form

Use one form per purpose, or one form with one separately tickable box per purpose. Each box is unticked by default. The service must work without the box being ticked unless the data is genuinely needed for it, in which case consent is the wrong basis.

[Organisation] would like your permission

We would like to [state the purpose in one sentence, for example: send you a monthly newsletter about new features and offers by email].

To do this we will use [the data concerned, for example: your name and email address]. We will not use it for anything else without asking you.

[Where relevant: We will share it with [named recipient] so that they can [purpose]. / We will keep it for [period] or until you withdraw your permission.]

You do not have to agree. If you do not, [state the consequence, which must be none for the core service, for example: you can still use your account exactly as before].

You can withdraw your permission at any time by [the mechanism, for example: clicking the link at the bottom of any message, or changing the setting at Account, Preferences]. Withdrawing does not affect anything we did before.

[ ] Yes, I agree that [Organisation] may [purpose] using [data]. (one box per purpose; unticked by default)

[ ] Yes, I agree that [Organisation] may share my [data] with [named recipient] for [purpose]. (only where sharing is itself consented to)

Our privacy notice at [location] explains your rights. Questions: [contact].

Where the data is special category data (for example health data in a wellbeing feature), the box must say "explicit" consent in substance: name the type of data, state the purpose and ask the person to confirm. Where the person is a child below the age set by the applicable law, obtain and verify the consent of the holder of parental responsibility under PIMS-PRO-05 and record how it was verified.

2. Employee consent form

Consent from an employee is valid only where refusal carries no detriment and the organisation can show that. Do not use consent for anything the employment contract, a legal duty or a legitimate interest already covers; use it for genuinely optional matters such as a photograph on the public website, participation in a wellbeing programme, equality monitoring, or a reference beyond the standard factual one. Collect it on paper or in the HR system, never by a reply to a group email.

Optional permission request

Name: [Name] Role: [Role] Date: [Date]

[Organisation] would like your permission to [purpose, for example: publish your name, role and photograph on the team page of our public website].

This is optional. Saying no has no effect on your employment, your pay, your development or how you are treated. If you say nothing, we will treat that as no.

The data involved is [data]. It will be seen by [recipients] and kept [for the period, or until you withdraw permission]. It will not be used for any other purpose.

You can withdraw your permission at any time by telling [the people function contact] in writing. We will [action on withdrawal, for example: remove the photograph within five working days]. Withdrawal does not affect anything done before.

[ ] I give my permission for the use described above.

[ ] I do not give my permission.

Signature: [Signature] Date: [Date]

For special category data (for example health data for a wellbeing programme or an occupational health referral beyond the legal duty), add: "I understand that this involves information about my [health / ethnic origin / other] and I explicitly agree to its use for the purpose above and no other."

3. The consent record

For every consent given or withdrawn, create or update one entry in PIMS-REG-04 with the fields below. Where consent is collected in a product, the product must capture the same fields; a boolean flag without the wording version and timestamp is not a record. Keep the wording of every version of each form under GOV-REG-01 so that the record can be read back.

Field Entry
Person identifier [Account identifier, employee number, or email address]
Purpose consented to [The purpose as worded on the form]
Form and version [GDPR-TPL-06 derived form reference and version]
Method [Web form tick, signed paper, HR system tick, verified parental consent]
Date and time given [Date and time]
Evidence [Signed form reference, system event reference]
Withdrawn on [Date and time, or blank]
Withdrawal method [Link, settings change, written notice]
Action taken on withdrawal [What stopped, and when]

4. Checks before a form is used

The Privacy Officer confirms each item and records the check in PIMS-REG-04 or the form's approval record.

  1. The purpose is one the organisation would accept a refusal for.
  2. One box per purpose, none pre-ticked, consent not bundled with terms.
  3. The data, recipients and retention named on the form match PIMS-REG-01.
  4. Withdrawal takes no more effort than giving consent, and the withdrawal action is implemented and tested.
  5. The record in section 3 is captured automatically or by a defined manual step.
  6. For employees, the detriment statement is true and the manager is not the person collecting the form.

Legitimate interests assessment template

The three-part test (purpose, necessity, balancing) completed before any processing relies on legitimate interests, with the outcome, safeguards and review date recorded in GDPR-REG-03.

Serves: GDPR Article 6(1)(f); GDPR Article 21; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.2.2. Owner: Privacy Officer.

Guidance notes are in italics. One assessment per processing activity, completed by the activity owner with the Privacy Officer, approved before the processing starts, and entered in GDPR-REG-03. Legitimate interests is not available for processing by public authorities in the performance of their tasks, and is never a substitute for a condition under Article 9 where special category data is involved. Write for a reader who was not in the room: an auditor or a supervisory authority will read this if the processing is challenged.

1. The processing

Field Entry
Reference [GDPR-REG-03 reference]
Processing activity [PIMS-REG-01 reference and name]
Owner [Name], [Role]
Assessor [Name], [Role]
Date [Date]
Description What is done, with what data, about whom, by which systems, for how long. Two to five sentences.
Data subjects [Customers, users, employees, website visitors, business contacts, other]
Data categories [List]. If any special category or criminal offence data is involved, stop: a separate condition is required and this assessment cannot supply it.
Why consent or contract is not the basis One or two sentences. For example: the processing is not necessary to deliver what the person asked for, and asking for consent would be impractical or would produce an unreliable basis because the processing must continue regardless.

2. Purpose test: is there a legitimate interest?

Question Answer
What interest is being pursued? State it specifically. "Business interests" fails; "detecting accounts created to abuse the free tier" passes.
Whose interest is it? [The organisation, a third party (name the category), both]
Is the interest lawful, clearly articulated and real rather than speculative? [Yes or No], with reasons
What benefit does the processing bring, and to whom? The organisation, the people whose data is used, third parties, the public.
What would happen if the processing did not take place? The loss or harm avoided by the processing.
Is the processing something the people concerned would reasonably expect, given the relationship and the notice they received? [Yes, Partly, No], with reasons

Purpose test outcome: [Passed, Failed]. A failed purpose test ends the assessment; find another basis or do not process.

3. Necessity test: is the processing necessary for that interest?

Question Answer
Does the processing actually help achieve the interest? [Yes or No], with the reasoning
Could the interest be achieved with less data, less intrusive data, or a shorter retention? List the alternatives considered and why each was rejected. "No alternative considered" fails the test.
Could it be achieved without processing personal data at all, for example with aggregated or anonymised data? [Yes or No], with reasons
Is the data limited to what the purpose needs, and is the retention period the shortest that works? [Yes or No], with the fields and the period

Necessity test outcome: [Passed, Failed].

4. Balancing test: do the interests and rights of the people override the interest?

Consider the nature of the data, the reasonable expectations of the people, the likely impact on them, and the safeguards that reduce it. Be honest about impact; an assessment that finds no impact at all is rarely credible.

Factor Assessment
Nature of the data Ordinary business contact data, behavioural data, financial data, data about children, location data, data that reveals something sensitive without being special category.
Relationship with the people Existing customer, former customer, prospect never contacted, employee (note the imbalance of power), member of the public.
Reasonable expectations What the notice told them, what the service implies, what practice in the sector is. Processing that would surprise a reasonable person weighs heavily against.
Possible impact on the people Loss of control, nuisance, financial loss, discrimination, distress, exposure, chilling effect. Rate it Low, Medium or High and say why.
Likelihood of that impact [Low, Medium, High], with reasons
Vulnerable people Children, employees, people in financial difficulty, people with health conditions. State whether any are included and the effect on the balance.
Safeguards applied Pseudonymisation, aggregation, access restriction, short retention, no use for decisions about the person, no sharing, a clear opt-out, human review. Each safeguard must be real and implemented, not planned.
Opt-out Is an objection mechanism offered? For direct marketing it is mandatory and unconditional. Describe it and where it is presented.
Transparency Where the people are told about this processing and the interest, with the notice reference.

Balancing test outcome: [The interest prevails, The interest prevails with the safeguards above, The rights of the people prevail].

5. Decision

Field Entry
Outcome [Approved: legitimate interests may be relied on, Approved with conditions, Not approved]
Conditions Safeguards that must be in place before processing starts, and who confirms them.
Wording of the interest for the privacy notice The sentence that will appear in the notice built from GDPR-TPL-01 or GDPR-TPL-02. It must match section 2.
Objection handling How an objection is received and actioned under PIMS-PRO-03, and the compelling grounds, if any, that the organisation would rely on to continue after an objection. For direct marketing there are none.
Approved by [Name], Privacy Officer, [Date]
Next review [Date]. Twelve months, or earlier on a change to the data, the purpose, the recipients, the technology, or on a complaint or objection trend.

6. Review record

Review date Reviewer Change in processing or context Outcome Next review
[Date] [Name], [Role] [None, or the change] [Confirmed, Revised: new reference, Withdrawn] [Date]

Transfer impact assessment template

The assessment completed under PIMS-POL-03 before personal data is transferred to a country without an adequacy decision on the strength of contractual or corporate safeguards, recording the importer, the destination law, the risk to the data, the supplementary measures and the decision.

Serves: GDPR Article 44; GDPR Article 45; GDPR Article 46; GDPR Article 49; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.5.1; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.5.1. Owner: Privacy Officer.

Guidance notes are in italics. Complete one assessment per transfer or per group of transfers to the same importer under the same safeguard, before the transfer starts, and record the result in PIMS-REG-05. The assessment is needed where the safeguard is standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules or another Article 46 instrument; it is not needed for a destination covered by an adequacy decision, and it does not legitimise a transfer that relies on a derogation under Article 49, which must be occasional and documented separately. Onward transfers by the importer to its own sub-processors are part of this assessment. Revisit the assessment when the law of the destination, the importer, the data or the measures change.

1. The transfer

Field Entry
Reference [PIMS-REG-05 reference]
Exporter [Organisation], acting as [controller, processor]
Importer [Category of organisation and its role: processor, sub-processor, controller, group company]
Processing activity [PIMS-REG-01 reference]
Flows covered [GDPR-REG-02 flow references]
Destination country or countries [List], including the countries from which the importer provides support or holds backups
Onward transfers by the importer [Named sub-processor categories and countries, from the importer's list]
Data categories and subjects [List], with the volume and whether any special category or criminal offence data is included
Purpose and duration of the transfer [Purpose]; [continuous, periodic, one-off]; [period]
Format [Plain, pseudonymised, encrypted in transit only, encrypted at rest with keys held by the exporter]
Transfer mechanism [Standard contractual clauses (module and date signed), binding corporate rules (approval reference), other Article 46 instrument]
Assessor [Name], [Role], [Date]

2. Assessment of the destination law and practice

Answer from public sources: the laws of the destination, published decisions, the importer's transparency reporting, reputable analyses. Record the sources used in section 6. Where an answer is "unknown", treat it as an adverse answer until resolved.

Question Answer and source
Does the destination have a general data protection law, and is it enforced by an independent authority?
Can public authorities compel the importer to disclose personal data, and under what conditions (court order, administrative demand, secret order)?
Is such access limited to what is necessary and proportionate, with independent oversight?
Can the importer challenge a demand, and can it tell the exporter about it?
Do the people whose data is transferred have an effective remedy against the authorities of the destination?
Is there a law requiring the importer to build in access for authorities, to retain data for them, or to hand over encryption keys?
Has the importer received demands of this kind, and what does its transparency reporting say? Ask the importer directly where no reporting exists.
Is the importer, or its sector, a likely target of surveillance given the type of data and the authorities' known practice?
Are there relevant adequacy findings, authority guidance or court rulings about this destination?

Conclusion on the destination: [The law and practice do not impinge on the effectiveness of the mechanism, The law and practice impinge on the mechanism and supplementary measures are required, The law and practice impinge and no measures can address it].

3. Assessment of the risk to the data

Factor Assessment
Sensitivity of the data [Low, Medium, High], with reasons
Volume and number of people
Likelihood that the data is of interest to the destination's authorities [Low, Medium, High], with reasons
Consequence for the people if accessed
Importer's own safeguards Certifications, audit reports, encryption, access controls, internal policy on government demands.

4. Supplementary measures

Required where section 2 found that the law impinges. Technical measures are the ones that can address state access; contractual and organisational measures support them but rarely suffice alone. State for each measure whether it is in place, how it is verified and who verifies it.

Measure Type In place Verified by
Encryption in transit with current protocols and verified configuration Technical [Yes or No] [Role, evidence]
Encryption at rest with keys held only by the exporter or a party outside the destination, so that the importer cannot read the data Technical [Yes or No]
Pseudonymisation before transfer with the key held by the exporter Technical [Yes or No]
Split processing so that no single party in the destination holds identifiable data Technical [Yes or No]
Importer's contractual duty to challenge demands, notify the exporter where lawful, and provide only the minimum Contractual [Yes or No]
Importer's transparency reporting and a warrant canary where lawful Contractual [Yes or No]
Strict access control, logging and least privilege at the importer, with audit rights exercised Organisational [Yes or No]
Internal policy at the importer for handling government demands, reviewed by the exporter Organisational [Yes or No]
Data minimisation: reducing the fields and the retention at the importer Organisational [Yes or No]

Are the measures sufficient to make the mechanism effective in practice? [Yes, No], with reasons.

5. Decision

Field Entry
Outcome [Transfer may proceed under the mechanism, Transfer may proceed with the supplementary measures above, Transfer must not proceed]
Conditions Measures to be implemented before the first transfer, with owner and date; verification method; the PIMS-REG-06 row to update for a processor.
Notice Where the destination is named in the privacy notice built from GDPR-TPL-01 or GDPR-TPL-02 and whether the notice needs a change.
Approved by [Name], Privacy Officer, [Date]
Escalation Where the outcome is "must not proceed" and the business wishes to continue, the matter goes to the Chief Executive Officer under GOV-PRO-24, and a suspension of the transfer is the default until decided.
Next review [Date]. Twelve months, or on a change in destination law, in the importer, in its sub-processors, in the data, or on a demand received.

Source Date consulted What it supported
[Public source description] [Date] [Section 2 question]
[Importer questionnaire response, GDPR-TPL-09 reference] [Date] [Section 3 or 4 item]

Supplier GDPR assessment questionnaire

The questionnaire sent to any supplier that will process personal data for [Organisation], used with GOV-TPL-04 under GOV-PRO-06 to decide whether the supplier can be engaged as a processor, on what terms, and what must be fixed first.

Serves: GDPR Article 28; GDPR Article 44; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.2.6; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.5.6; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.19. Owner: Privacy Officer.

Guidance notes are in italics. Send to every prospective supplier that will store, access or transmit personal data on the organisation's behalf, and to existing suppliers at their annual review. The security questions in GOV-TPL-04 are not repeated here; send both. Each answer needs evidence: a document, a screenshot, a contract clause or a certificate reference. An answer without evidence is scored as "not demonstrated". The Privacy Officer scores the outcome in section 8 and records it in GOV-REG-07 and, where the supplier is engaged, in PIMS-REG-06.

1. Organisation facts

# Question Answer Evidence
1.1 Legal name, registered address and country of incorporation of the entity that will sign the contract.
1.2 The role you will have for this service: processor acting on our instructions, independent controller, or both (explain).
1.3 Do you have a Data Protection Officer or privacy lead? Give the role and contact channel.
1.4 Have you been subject to a supervisory authority investigation, enforcement action or fine in the last five years? Describe.
1.5 Have you had a personal data breach notified to an authority or to customers in the last three years? Describe the cause and the fix.
1.6 Which privacy or security certifications or assurance reports do you hold, with scope and date?

2. Personal data facts

# Question Answer Evidence
2.1 Which categories of our personal data will you process, and for which purposes?
2.2 Will you use any of our personal data for your own purposes, including analytics, product improvement or training models? If yes, on what basis and can it be switched off?
2.3 Will you process any special category data or data about children? What additional controls apply?
2.4 Do you keep a record of processing activities covering the service? Provide the relevant extract.
2.5 How do you apply data minimisation and retention limits within the service? What is retained after we delete a record or close the account?
2.6 Can you return and then delete all our personal data at the end of the contract, within what period, and how do you confirm deletion, including from backups?

3. Security of personal data

# Question Answer Evidence
3.1 Describe the technical and organisational measures that protect our data: encryption at rest and in transit, access control, logging, segregation between customers.
3.2 How is access to our data by your staff restricted, logged and reviewed? Can we see the logs on request?
3.3 Is personal data pseudonymised or encrypted so that your staff cannot read it without a recorded need?
3.4 How do you test the effectiveness of your measures (independent testing, audits), and how often?
3.5 Are all staff with access bound by confidentiality and trained in data protection? Provide the completion rate.

4. Sub-processing

# Question Answer Evidence
4.1 List every sub-processor that will process our data, with its role, location and the data it receives.
4.2 How do you tell us before adding or replacing a sub-processor, how much notice is given, and can we object?
4.3 Do your sub-processor contracts impose the same obligations that our contract imposes on you? Provide a template clause.
4.4 Do you audit your sub-processors, and how often?

5. Location and transfers

# Question Answer Evidence
5.1 In which countries will our data be stored, including replicas and backups?
5.2 From which countries will your staff or sub-processors access our data, including support and operations?
5.3 Can we choose the storage region, and is that choice enforced technically?
5.4 For each transfer outside [region], which mechanism applies, and will you sign the standard contractual clauses in the module we specify?
5.5 Have you assessed the laws of each destination country and can you share that assessment? Have you received government demands for customer data, and do you publish a transparency report?

6. Assistance and rights

# Question Answer Evidence
6.1 How do you help us respond to data subject requests (access, deletion, portability) within our one month deadline? Is there a self-service export and delete?
6.2 Within how many hours of becoming aware will you notify us of a personal data breach affecting our data, and what will the notification contain?
6.3 Will you support our data protection impact assessments and prior consultation with an authority, and on what terms?
6.4 Will you tell us if an instruction we give appears to infringe data protection law?
6.5 What audit rights do you offer: on-site audit, remote audit, third party reports? What notice and cost apply?

7. Contract and exit

# Question Answer Evidence
7.1 Will you sign our data processing agreement, or provide yours for review? Identify any clause you will not accept and why.
7.2 Does your contract require you to act only on our documented instructions, including for transfers?
7.3 What happens to our data at the end of the contract, and in what format is it returned?
7.4 What are your insurance arrangements for data protection liability?
7.5 What is your notice period for changes to the service that affect how personal data is processed?

8. Outcome

Completed by the Privacy Officer. A "Block" on any item means the supplier cannot be engaged until it is resolved; the blocks are: use of our data for the supplier's own purposes without a switch-off (2.2); no deletion at exit (2.6); no breach notification commitment within 48 hours (6.2); undisclosed or unlimited sub-processing (4.1, 4.2); a transfer with no mechanism (5.4); refusal to sign processor terms (7.1).

Field Entry
Supplier and service [Supplier], [service], GOV-REG-07 reference
Tier under GOV-PRO-06 [Tier]
Items not demonstrated [List of question numbers]
Blocks [None, or the list]
Transfer impact assessment required [Yes or No]; GDPR-TPL-08 reference where Yes
Decision [Approve as processor, Approve with conditions, Reject]
Conditions and dates [Each condition, owner and date, for example: signed PIMS-TPL-02 before first data, region lock enabled and verified, sub-processor list added to PIMS-REG-06]
Assessed by [Name], Privacy Officer, [Date]
Next review [Date], annually or on a material change

Personal data breach notification form (to the supervisory authority)

The content the authority needs under GDPR Article 33(3), prepared under PIMS-PRO-04 so that a notification can be made within 72 hours of awareness, in phases where the facts are not yet complete, with the record kept in PIMS-REG-03 whether or not the authority is notified.

Serves: GDPR Article 33; GDPR Article 34; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 6.13.1.5; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex A 7.3.7. Owner: Privacy Officer.

Guidance notes are in italics. Most supervisory authorities provide their own online form; this template collects every fact that form will ask for, so that the Privacy Officer fills it from here rather than from memory under time pressure. The 72 hour clock starts when the organisation becomes aware that a breach has probably occurred, not when the investigation ends. Where the facts are incomplete at 72 hours, notify with what is known and mark the rest as "to follow": a phased notification is permitted; a late one needs reasons. Keep every version of this form against the PIMS-REG-03 entry. Where [Organisation] is a processor, this form is not sent to the authority; the facts are sent to the controller without undue delay and the controller notifies.

1. Notifier and references

Field Entry
Internal reference [PIMS-REG-03 reference], linked incident [GOV-REG-08 reference]
Organisation [Organisation], [registered address], registration or reference number with the authority if any
Role [Controller, Joint controller (name the other), Processor notifying on behalf of a controller with its authority]
Contact point for the authority [Role, for example Data Protection Officer or Privacy Officer], [contact channel]. A role mailbox that is monitored outside office hours.
Notification type [Initial, Phased update number [Number], Final]
Date and time of this notification [Date and time]
Other authorities notified [None, or a list where the breach affects people in several jurisdictions, with the lead authority identified]

2. Timeline

Event Date and time Source
Breach began (or is believed to have begun) Log evidence, report, estimate; say which
Breach ended or was contained
Organisation became aware The moment a person with responsibility had reasonable certainty that personal data was compromised
Processor informed the controller (if applicable)
This notification

Hours from awareness to this notification: [Number]. If more than 72: state the reasons for the delay in section 7; it is mandatory.

3. Nature of the breach

Field Entry
What happened Plain description in three to six sentences: the system or process involved, the cause (for example misdirected message, lost device, compromised credential, misconfiguration, malicious attack, supplier breach), how it was discovered.
Type of breach [Confidentiality (data disclosed or accessed), Integrity (data altered), Availability (data lost or made inaccessible), or a combination]
Categories of people affected [Customers, users, employees, applicants, children, vulnerable people, other], with any that make the risk higher
Approximate number of people affected [Number], or [minimum] to [maximum] with the basis of the estimate; "not yet known" with the date by which it will be
Categories of personal data affected [Identity, contact, financial, authentication credentials, location, health or other special category, criminal offence data, content, other]
Approximate number of records affected [Number], or a range with the basis
Was the data protected [Encrypted with keys not compromised, Pseudonymised, Hashed credentials, Plain]
Is the breach ongoing [Yes, No, Unknown]
Cross-border element [People in other jurisdictions affected: list; main establishment of the organisation]

4. Likely consequences for the people affected

Assess from the point of view of the people, as PIMS-PRO-04 requires. Describe the harm and its likelihood; do not minimise. This section drives the decision in section 6.

Field Entry
Possible harms [Identity theft or fraud, financial loss, loss of confidentiality of professional secrecy, discrimination, reputational damage, physical safety, loss of control over data, distress, other]
Severity for the people [Low, Medium, High], with reasons
Likelihood of harm [Low, Medium, High], with reasons, including whether the data is in the hands of a known malicious party or was recovered
Overall risk to the people [Unlikely to result in a risk, Risk, High risk]

5. Measures taken and proposed

Field Entry
Containment What stopped the breach and when: credentials reset, access revoked, system isolated, message recalled, device wiped remotely, supplier instructed.
Recovery What restored the data or service, and whether data was recovered or confirmed deleted by the recipient.
Mitigation for the people Password resets forced, monitoring offered, accounts frozen, guidance issued.
Root cause and correction What will stop it recurring, with the GOV-REG-03 corrective action reference and dates.
Processor involvement If a processor caused or was involved, its name, what it did, and the contractual steps taken.

6. Communication to the people affected

Field Entry
Decision [Individuals will be informed, Individuals have been informed on [Date], Individuals will not be informed because the risk is not high, Individuals will not be informed because [the data was encrypted and the keys are safe / subsequent measures mean the high risk is no longer likely / individual contact would involve disproportionate effort and a public communication has been made]]
Method and date [Email, letter, in-product message, public notice], [Date]
Content Attach the message. It must describe the breach in plain words, give the contact point, state the likely consequences and the measures taken and recommended.
Number informed [Number]

7. Reasons for delay (where more than 72 hours after awareness)

State the facts: for example, the breach was discovered through a third party report that took time to verify; the scope could not be established until forensic analysis was complete; the responsible person was unavailable and the escalation path failed (and what has been fixed). Do not write "due to internal processes".

[Reasons]

HIPAA

Safeguards and privacy for United States protected health information, mapped to the HIPAA Security, Privacy and Breach Notification Rules

HIPAA-GDE-01 guide Download .docx Markdown

Guide: HIPAA in plain words

What HIPAA covers, who must comply, the rules it sets and the ideas that shape the Security Rule, written for a team new to it. Read the regulation and HHS guidance for the authoritative detail.

Serves: HIPAA 45 CFR 160; HIPAA 45 CFR 164. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. What HIPAA is

HIPAA is United States federal law that protects health information. Its rules are enforced by the Department of Health and Human Services through its Office for Civil Rights. The parts that matter in day-to-day work are the Privacy Rule, the Security Rule, the Breach Notification Rule and the Enforcement Rule, all in 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164. This guide explains them in plain words; the authoritative text is the regulation itself.

2. Who must comply

Two kinds of organisation are bound by HIPAA. A covered entity is a health plan, a health care clearinghouse, or a health care provider that transmits health information electronically for certain transactions. A business associate is an organisation that creates, receives, maintains or transmits protected health information on behalf of a covered entity, for example a cloud host, a billing service or a software vendor. A business associate's own subcontractors that handle the information are also bound. If you build or run software that handles health information for a covered entity, you are almost certainly a business associate.

3. The information it protects

Protected health information, or PHI, is individually identifiable health information held or transmitted in any form. When it is in electronic form it is called ePHI, and the Security Rule applies to it specifically. Information that has been de-identified under the standard in the Privacy Rule is no longer PHI.

4. The four rules

4.1 The Privacy Rule governs how PHI may be used and disclosed. Its central ideas are the minimum necessary principle, the individual's rights over their own information, and the requirement to give a notice of privacy practices. See HIPAA-POL-01.

4.2 The Security Rule requires administrative, physical and technical safeguards for ePHI, to protect its confidentiality, integrity and availability. See HIPAA-POL-02 and the safeguard matrix in HIPAA-REG-01.

4.3 The Breach Notification Rule requires notification to the affected individuals, to HHS, and in larger breaches to the media, when unsecured PHI is breached. See HIPAA-PRO-02.

4.4 The Enforcement Rule sets out how HHS investigates and penalises non-compliance. The practical message is that documented, good-faith safeguards and a real risk analysis matter when something goes wrong.

5. Required and addressable

The Security Rule is deliberately flexible. Each implementation specification is marked either required or addressable. A required specification must be implemented. An addressable specification is not optional in the ordinary sense: you must assess whether it is reasonable and appropriate in your environment, and then either implement it, or document why it is not reasonable and implement an equivalent alternative measure. Addressable never means "ignore"; it means "decide and record".

6. The security risk analysis is the foundation

The one activity that everything else rests on is the security risk analysis required by the Security Rule. It identifies where ePHI lives, the threats and vulnerabilities to it, and the risks that result, and it drives the risk management decisions that follow. An organisation cannot show it meets the Security Rule without it. See HIPAA-PRO-01.

7. How HIPAA sits with the rest of the kit

Most of what the Security Rule asks for is general good security practice that the kit already provides: access control, encryption, logging, incident response, contingency planning, workforce training, risk management and vendor management. The HIPAA set adds the HIPAA-specific pieces, the privacy obligations, the business associate agreement, the breach rule and the safeguard mapping, and points each safeguard at the kit document that implements it. HIPAA-GDE-02 is that map.

Guide: the HIPAA Security Rule mapped to the kit

Each HIPAA Security Rule standard mapped to the kit document that implements it, so a team already running the kit can see what the Security Rule adds. The full matrix, with every implementation specification and its required or addressable flag, is HIPAA-REG-01.

Serves: HIPAA 45 CFR 164.308; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.310; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.312; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.314; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.316. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. How to read this

The Security Rule groups its requirements into administrative, physical and technical safeguards, plus organisational requirements and documentation. This guide maps each standard to the kit document that implements it. The point is simple: most of the Security Rule is good security practice the kit already provides, so a team running the kit is most of the way there. The full matrix, down to each implementation specification and whether it is required or addressable, is the register HIPAA-REG-01.

2. Administrative safeguards (164.308)

Security management process Risk analysis, risk management, sanctions, activity review HIPAA-PRO-01; GOV-PRO-05; GOV-REG-05; GOV-PRO-14
Assigned security responsibility A named security official HIPAA-POL-02; GOV-POL-01
Workforce security Authorisation, clearance, termination GOV-PRO-18; GOV-PRO-10; GOV-CHK-01
Information access management Access authorisation and modification GOV-PRO-10; GOV-TPL-09
Security awareness and training Reminders, malware protection, log-in monitoring, passwords GOV-PRO-08; GOV-PRO-22; GOV-POL-06
Security incident procedures Response and reporting GOV-PRO-07; GOV-REG-08
Contingency plan Backup, disaster recovery, emergency mode, testing, criticality GOV-PRO-12; GOV-PRO-13; GOV-TPL-07
Evaluation Periodic review against the rule GOV-PRO-02; HIPAA-REG-01
Business associate contracts Written assurances HIPAA-TPL-01; HIPAA-REG-02

Standard Theme Kit documents

5. Organisational requirements and documentation (164.314 and 164.316)

Standard Theme Kit documents

Documentation Keep records, make them available, review and update GOV-PRO-01; GOV-REG-01; HIPAA-REG-01

6. What HIPAA adds beyond the kit

Three things are specific to HIPAA rather than general security practice: the business associate agreement and the assurances it carries, the breach notification duties and their time limits, and the required versus addressable judgement recorded for each specification. The HIPAA set provides all three. Everything else is the kit's existing controls, applied to electronic protected health information.

HIPAA privacy policy

How [Organisation] uses and discloses protected health information, applies the minimum necessary principle, and honours the rights of individuals under the HIPAA Privacy Rule.

Serves: HIPAA 45 CFR 164.502; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.514; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.520; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.524; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.526; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.528. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This policy sets out how [Organisation] handles protected health information so that uses and disclosures are permitted, limited to the minimum necessary, and the rights of individuals are honoured, as the HIPAA Privacy Rule requires.

2. Scope

It applies to all protected health information that [Organisation] creates, receives, maintains or transmits, in any form, and to every member of the workforce and every system that handles it. Where [Organisation] acts as a business associate, this policy applies alongside the obligations in its business associate agreements.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Privacy Officer Owns this policy, decides on uses and disclosures that are not routine, and handles individual rights requests and complaints.
Workforce members Use and disclose protected health information only as this policy allows, and report suspected breaches.
System owners Enforce access and minimum necessary controls in the systems they own.
Chief Executive Officer Approves the policy and the notice of privacy practices.

4. Policy statements

4.1 Permitted uses and disclosures. Protected health information is used and disclosed only for treatment, payment and health care operations, for purposes the individual has authorised, or as otherwise permitted or required by the Privacy Rule. Any other use or disclosure requires the individual's written authorisation.

4.2 Minimum necessary. For every use, disclosure and request other than for treatment, the workforce limits protected health information to the minimum necessary to accomplish the purpose. Access rights are set to the minimum each role needs, recorded in the access register.

4.3 Notice of privacy practices. Where [Organisation] is a covered entity, it maintains and provides a notice of privacy practices that describes how it uses and discloses protected health information and the rights of individuals. The notice is kept current and its version is recorded.

4.4 Individual rights. [Organisation] honours the rights of individuals under the Privacy Rule: to access and obtain a copy of their information, to request an amendment, to receive an accounting of certain disclosures, to request restrictions on use and disclosure, and to request confidential communications. Requests are logged, handled within the time limits the rule sets, and answered in writing.

4.5 Authorisations. Where an authorisation is required, it is obtained in the form the rule requires, recorded, and honoured, including any revocation.

4.6 De-identification. Information is treated as protected health information unless it has been de-identified under the standard in the Privacy Rule. De-identification decisions are documented.

4.7 Business associates. [Organisation] discloses protected health information to a business associate only under a written business associate agreement (HIPAA-TPL-01), and obtains equivalent assurances from any subcontractor that will handle the information.

4.8 Workforce training. Workforce members are trained on this policy on joining and periodically, and the training is recorded.

5. Records and evidence

  • The notice of privacy practices and its version history.
  • The individual rights request log, including access, amendment, accounting, restriction and confidential communication requests.
  • Authorisations obtained and revoked.
  • The business associate register (HIPAA-REG-02).
  • Workforce training records.

6. Exceptions

A use or disclosure that this policy does not clearly permit is approved by the Privacy Officer and recorded before it is made, or it is not made.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this policy and the notice of privacy practices annually, and after any change in the law, in the organisation or in the systems that handle protected health information.

  • HIPAA-PRO-02 HIPAA breach notification procedure
  • HIPAA-TPL-01 Business associate agreement
  • GOV-PRO-10 Access management procedure
  • PIMS-PRO-03 Data subject rights handling procedure

HIPAA security policy

How [Organisation] protects the confidentiality, integrity and availability of electronic protected health information through administrative, physical and technical safeguards under the HIPAA Security Rule.

Serves: HIPAA 45 CFR 164.306; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.308; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.310; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.312; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.316. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This policy commits [Organisation] to protecting electronic protected health information through the administrative, physical and technical safeguards the HIPAA Security Rule requires, and points each safeguard at the procedure or control that implements it.

2. Scope

It applies to all electronic protected health information that [Organisation] creates, receives, maintains or transmits, and to the people, systems and facilities that handle it. The detailed mapping of each standard and implementation specification to a kit document is held in the safeguard matrix (HIPAA-REG-01).

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Information Security Manager The assigned security official. Owns the Security Rule programme, the risk analysis and this policy.
Privacy Officer Coordinates privacy and breach obligations with this policy.
System and facility owners Implement the safeguards in the systems and facilities they own.
Workforce members Follow the safeguards and report security incidents.

4. Policy statements

4.1 Security management process. [Organisation] runs a security management process built on a security risk analysis (HIPAA-PRO-01), risk management decisions recorded in the risk register (GOV-REG-05), a sanction policy for violations, and regular review of system activity through logs.

4.2 Assigned security responsibility. A single security official, the Information Security Manager, is responsible for the Security Rule programme.

4.3 Workforce security and access management. Access to electronic protected health information is authorised, granted on the minimum necessary basis, reviewed, and removed promptly when a role ends, under the access management procedure (GOV-PRO-10) and the joiner and leaver checklist (GOV-CHK-01).

4.4 Awareness and training. Workforce members receive security awareness and training, including protection from malicious software, log-in monitoring and password management, under the awareness procedure (GOV-PRO-08).

4.5 Security incident procedures. Security incidents are identified, responded to and documented under the incident management procedure (GOV-PRO-07), and a suspected breach of protected health information is handled under HIPAA-PRO-02.

4.6 Contingency plan. [Organisation] maintains a data backup plan, a disaster recovery plan and an emergency mode operation plan, tests them, and analyses the criticality of its applications and data, under the backup procedure (GOV-PRO-12) and the continuity procedure (GOV-PRO-13).

4.7 Evaluation. [Organisation] periodically evaluates how well its safeguards meet the Security Rule, through internal audit (GOV-PRO-02) and the safeguard matrix.

4.8 Physical safeguards. Facility access, workstation use and security, and the disposal and re-use of devices and media are controlled under the physical security procedure (GOV-PRO-17) and the asset and media procedures (GOV-PRO-16).

4.9 Technical safeguards. Access control with unique user identification and emergency access, audit controls, integrity protection, authentication and transmission security are implemented under the access, logging, cryptography and network procedures (GOV-PRO-10, GOV-PRO-14, GOV-PRO-20, GOV-PRO-21). Encryption of electronic protected health information at rest and in transit is implemented as the reasonable and appropriate measure, and any decision not to encrypt is documented with an equivalent alternative.

4.10 Business associates. [Organisation] obtains satisfactory assurances through a business associate agreement (HIPAA-TPL-01) before disclosing electronic protected health information to a business associate.

4.11 Addressable specifications. For each addressable implementation specification, [Organisation] records in the safeguard matrix whether it is reasonable and appropriate, and implements it or an equivalent alternative, or documents why neither is required.

5. Records and evidence

  • The security risk analysis and risk management decisions.
  • The safeguard matrix (HIPAA-REG-01) with the status and evidence of each standard and specification.
  • Access reviews, training records, incident records and contingency test records.
  • The business associate register (HIPAA-REG-02).

6. Exceptions

An addressable specification that is not implemented is recorded in the safeguard matrix with the reason and the alternative measure. No required specification may be waived.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this policy annually, after the risk analysis is updated, and after any significant change to the systems, facilities or threats that affect electronic protected health information.

Security risk analysis procedure

How [Organisation] performs the security risk analysis the HIPAA Security Rule requires, finding where electronic protected health information lives, the threats and vulnerabilities to it, and the resulting risks, and feeding the risk management decisions that follow.

Serves: HIPAA 45 CFR 164.308; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.306. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure performs the security risk analysis required by the HIPAA Security Rule. It is the foundation of the Security Rule programme: without it, [Organisation] cannot show that its safeguards are reasonable and appropriate. It identifies the risks to electronic protected health information so that they can be managed.

2. Scope

It covers all electronic protected health information that [Organisation] creates, receives, maintains or transmits, wherever it is held, including in systems operated by business associates on [Organisation]'s behalf.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Information Security Manager Runs the analysis, records the results and proposes risk treatment.
System and process owners Describe where electronic protected health information flows and the controls in place.
Chief Executive Officer Accepts residual risk above the appetite.

4. Procedure

4.1 Scope the information. Identify every place electronic protected health information is created, received, maintained or transmitted: applications, databases, file stores, endpoints, backups, logs, email and the systems of business associates. Record them as assets in the asset register (GOV-REG-10) and flag those holding electronic protected health information.

4.2 Identify threats and vulnerabilities. For each place, identify the reasonably anticipated threats, both human and environmental, and the vulnerabilities that a threat could exploit. Use incident history, vulnerability scans, audit findings and known threat sources.

4.3 Assess current controls. Record the safeguards already in place for each place, from the safeguard matrix (HIPAA-REG-01) and the kit procedures.

4.4 Determine likelihood and impact. Using the risk methodology (GOV-PRO-05), judge the likelihood that a threat exploits a vulnerability and the impact on the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the information, and on the individuals it concerns.

4.5 Determine the level of risk. Combine likelihood and impact into a risk level, and record each risk in the risk register (GOV-REG-05), linked to the place and the safeguard it concerns.

4.6 Decide risk management. For each risk above the appetite, decide the treatment: additional safeguards, acceptance with a recorded reason, avoidance or transfer. Record the decision, the owner and the due date. For an addressable implementation specification, record in the safeguard matrix whether it is reasonable and appropriate and what is implemented.

4.7 Record and approve. Produce the risk analysis record, listing the information locations, threats, vulnerabilities, current controls, risk levels and treatment decisions. The Chief Executive Officer accepts any residual risk above the appetite.

4.8 Review. Review and update the analysis at least annually, and after a security incident, a significant change to the systems or facilities that handle electronic protected health information, or a change in the threats.

5. Records and evidence

  • The security risk analysis record and its dated versions.
  • The risk register entries for electronic protected health information (GOV-REG-05).
  • The safeguard matrix status (HIPAA-REG-01).
  • Residual risk acceptances.

6. Exceptions

No part of the analysis is waived. If a place cannot be assessed in time, it is recorded as an open item with an owner and a due date, not omitted.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually and after any change to the risk methodology it relies on.

  • HIPAA-POL-02 HIPAA security policy
  • HIPAA-REG-01 HIPAA Security Rule safeguard matrix
  • GOV-PRO-05 Risk assessment and treatment methodology
  • GOV-REG-05 Information security risk register

HIPAA breach notification procedure

How [Organisation] assesses whether an incident involving unsecured protected health information is a breach, and notifies the affected individuals, HHS and, in larger breaches, the media, within the time limits the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule sets.

Serves: HIPAA 45 CFR 164.400; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.404; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.406; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.408; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.410. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

This procedure handles a suspected breach of unsecured protected health information under the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule. It decides whether a breach has occurred, and makes the notifications the rule requires, within the time limits it sets.

2. Scope

It applies to any incident in which unsecured protected health information held by [Organisation] may have been accessed, acquired, used or disclosed in a way the Privacy Rule does not permit. Where [Organisation] is a business associate, it covers the duty to notify the covered entity. It follows from the incident procedure (GOV-PRO-07), which handles the security side.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Privacy Officer Leads the breach assessment and the notifications.
Information Security Manager Provides the facts from the incident investigation.
Chief Executive Officer Approves notifications and any decision that a breach has not occurred.

4. Procedure

4.1 Identify and contain. When an incident may involve protected health information, the incident team contains it and preserves the facts under GOV-PRO-07, and informs the Privacy Officer without delay. The discovery date is recorded, because it starts the clock.

4.2 Decide whether the information was unsecured. If the information was encrypted or destroyed to the standard the rule recognises, it is secured and the breach notification duties do not arise. Record the basis.

4.3 Assess whether it is a breach. Unless an exception applies, an impermissible use or disclosure is presumed to be a breach. Assess the probability that the information was compromised using at least four factors: the nature and extent of the information, who used it or to whom it was disclosed, whether it was actually acquired or viewed, and the extent to which the risk has been mitigated. Record the assessment and the conclusion.

4.4 Notify affected individuals. Where a breach is found, notify each affected individual without unreasonable delay and no later than sixty days after discovery. The notification describes what happened, the information involved, the steps individuals should take, what [Organisation] is doing, and how to ask questions.

4.5 Notify HHS. Report the breach to the Department of Health and Human Services. A breach affecting five hundred or more individuals is reported without unreasonable delay and no later than sixty days after discovery. A breach affecting fewer than five hundred is logged and reported to HHS within sixty days after the end of the calendar year.

4.6 Notify the media. Where a breach affects more than five hundred residents of a state or jurisdiction, notify prominent media outlets serving that area, within the same sixty-day limit.

4.7 Business associate duty. Where [Organisation] is a business associate, notify the covered entity of a breach without unreasonable delay and no later than sixty days after discovery, with the information the covered entity needs to make its own notifications.

4.8 Record and improve. Record every incident assessed, whether or not it was a breach, in the breach register (HIPAA-REG-03), and open a corrective action (GOV-REG-03) for the lessons.

5. Records and evidence

  • The breach register (HIPAA-REG-03), including incidents assessed and found not to be breaches.
  • The four-factor risk assessment for each incident.
  • Copies of notifications to individuals, HHS and the media.
  • Business associate notifications to covered entities.

6. Exceptions

A decision that an incident is not a breach is recorded with the assessment that supports it and approved by the Chief Executive Officer. The exceptions in the rule, for certain good-faith or inadvertent internal disclosures, are applied only where the facts clearly meet them, and are recorded.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this procedure annually and after any breach, and keeps the notification templates current.

8. Related documents

  • HIPAA-POL-01 HIPAA privacy policy
  • HIPAA-POL-02 HIPAA security policy
  • GOV-PRO-07 Information security incident management procedure
  • HIPAA-REG-03 HIPAA breach register

Business associate agreement template

A plain-English template of the terms a business associate agreement needs under HIPAA, to be completed and reviewed by legal counsel before use.

Serves: HIPAA 45 CFR 164.504; HIPAA 45 CFR 164.314. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. How to use this template

This is a starting point for a business associate agreement between a covered entity and a business associate, or between a business associate and its subcontractor. It states the terms HIPAA requires in plain words. It is not legal advice. Complete every item in square brackets, remove what does not apply, and have it reviewed and signed by the parties' authorised representatives and, where appropriate, legal counsel, before use.

2. Parties and purpose

This agreement is between [Covered entity or business associate], the disclosing party, and [Business associate or subcontractor], the receiving party, in connection with [the services the receiving party provides]. It governs the receiving party's handling of protected health information it creates, receives, maintains or transmits for the disclosing party.

3. Definitions

Terms used here have the meaning given in the HIPAA Rules at 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164. "Protected health information" is limited to the information the receiving party handles for the disclosing party under this agreement.

4. Obligations of the receiving party

4.1 Permitted uses and disclosures. The receiving party uses and discloses protected health information only as this agreement permits, as required by law, or for its proper management and administration, and not in a way that would breach the Privacy Rule if done by the disclosing party.

4.2 Minimum necessary. The receiving party limits its uses, disclosures and requests of protected health information to the minimum necessary for the purpose.

4.3 Safeguards. The receiving party implements administrative, physical and technical safeguards that reasonably and appropriately protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of electronic protected health information, as the Security Rule requires.

4.4 Subcontractors. The receiving party ensures that any subcontractor that handles protected health information agrees in writing to the same restrictions and conditions that apply to the receiving party.

4.5 Reporting. The receiving party reports to the disclosing party any use or disclosure not permitted by this agreement, any security incident, and any breach of unsecured protected health information, without unreasonable delay and no later than [number] days after discovery, with the information the disclosing party needs to make its own notifications.

4.6 Individual rights. The receiving party makes protected health information available so that the disclosing party can meet an individual's rights of access, amendment and accounting of disclosures, within the time the disclosing party requests.

4.7 Access for compliance. The receiving party makes its internal practices, books and records relating to protected health information available to the Department of Health and Human Services for determining compliance.

4.8 Return or destruction. On termination, the receiving party returns or destroys all protected health information it holds for the disclosing party, where feasible, and extends the protections of this agreement to any information it cannot return or destroy.

5. Obligations of the disclosing party

The disclosing party notifies the receiving party of any limitation in its notice of privacy practices, any change in or revocation of an individual's permission, and any restriction the disclosing party has agreed, to the extent these affect the receiving party's use or disclosure.

6. Term and termination

This agreement takes effect on [date] and continues until all protected health information is returned or destroyed. The disclosing party may terminate it if the receiving party breaches a material term and does not cure the breach within [number] days.

7. Signatures

Party Name Title Signature Date
Disclosing party [Name] [Title]
Receiving party [Name] [Title]
