AI governance

Policies and registers for the use and development of AI systems

AI-GDE-01 guide Download .docx Markdown

Guide: AI Governance Frameworks Mapped to the Kit

A short orientation to ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act, in plain words, with a map from each framework's requirements to the kit documents and registers that satisfy them.

Serves: ISO/IEC 42001 clause 4.1; ISO/IEC 42001 clause 6.1; ISO/IEC 42001 clause 8.1; NIST AI RMF GOVERN; NIST AI RMF MAP; NIST AI RMF MEASURE; NIST AI RMF MANAGE; GDPR Article 22. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Why three frameworks

Three public frameworks shape how an organisation is expected to govern AI, and they do different jobs. ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable management system standard: it tells you what a governed AI programme must contain and lets an auditor check it. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary method: it tells you how to think about AI risk and gives a vocabulary that regulators and customers increasingly borrow. The EU AI Act is law: it tells you which systems are banned, which carry heavy obligations and which only need transparency, and it applies to any organisation that places a system on the EU market or whose system's output is used there. An organisation that already runs the kit's security and privacy documents has most of the machinery these three need. This guide shows where each requirement lands.

2. ISO/IEC 42001 in plain words

ISO/IEC 42001 follows the same harmonised structure as ISO/IEC 27001: context (clause 4), leadership (5), planning (6), support (7), operation (8), performance evaluation (9) and improvement (10). The management system is about AI systems specifically, so the standard adds three things the security standard does not demand. First, an AI policy and defined objectives for responsible development and use. Second, an AI system impact assessment: not only risk to the organisation but the consequences for individuals, groups and society of the system's operation. Third, lifecycle controls: requirements for data, for evaluation, for human oversight and for what happens when a system fails, through its entire life. Its Annex A lists reference controls and Annex B explains them; Annex C lists AI-specific objectives and risk sources, and Annex D describes how the standard applies across sectors.

An organisation combining ISO/IEC 42001 with ISO/IEC 27001 runs one management system with two scopes, in the way PB-10 describes. The clauses on document control, internal audit, management review, nonconformity and competence are satisfied once, by the cross documents in the kit. What is new is the AI policy, the AI inventory, the AI impact assessment and the lifecycle procedures.

ISO/IEC 42001 area Kit document or register
Context, interested parties, scope (clauses 4.1 to 4.4) ISMS-PRO-01, ISMS-STM-01 with an AI scope paragraph, ISMS-REG-03
Leadership, AI policy, roles (clause 5) GOV-POL-01, AI-POL-01, AI-POL-02, GOV-STM-01
Risk assessment and treatment, AI system impact assessment (clauses 6.1.2 to 6.1.4) AI-PRO-01, AI-REG-02, PIMS-PRO-02 for the personal data dimension, GOV-PRO-05 for scales
Objectives and planning (clause 6.2) ISMS-PLN-01 with AI objectives, GOV-REG-21
Resources, competence, awareness, communication, documents (clause 7) ISMS-PRO-02, GOV-PRO-08, ISMS-PLN-02, GOV-PRO-01
Operational planning, AI system lifecycle, data, third parties (clause 8) AI-POL-02, AI-REG-01, AI-REG-03, AI-PRO-02, AI-TPL-01, GOV-PRO-15, GOV-PRO-09
Monitoring, internal audit, management review (clause 9) ISMS-PRO-04, GOV-PRO-02, GOV-PRO-03 with AI items on the agenda
Nonconformity, continual improvement, incidents (clause 10) GOV-PRO-04, AI-PRO-03, GOV-REG-03
Annex A controls on policies, roles, resources, impact, lifecycle, data, information for parties, use, third parties Covered across the rows above; record applicability in a Statement of Applicability built the way ISMS-REG-01 is built

3. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework in plain words

The NIST AI RMF is organised around four functions. GOVERN is the culture and structure: policies, accountability, roles, and the decision to treat AI risk as a management matter. MAP is understanding the context: what the system is for, who it affects, what could go wrong, and what the organisation's risk tolerance is. MEASURE is evaluation: choosing metrics, testing the system against them, and tracking how it performs over time, including on fairness, robustness, privacy and security. MANAGE is acting on what was measured: prioritising, treating, monitoring and responding, including planning for incidents and for retirement. The framework describes seven characteristics of trustworthy AI, from validity and safety through explainability and fairness to privacy and accountability, and asks that each be considered rather than prescribing how. A companion playbook, published separately, suggests actions per function.

NIST AI RMF function What it asks Kit document or register
GOVERN Policies, roles, accountability, risk tolerance, workforce competence, supply chain awareness GOV-POL-01, AI-POL-01, AI-POL-02, GOV-PRO-08, AI-PRO-02, AI-REG-04
MAP Context, intended use, affected parties, benefits and harms, categorisation of the system AI-REG-01, AI-POL-02 4.1 to 4.2, AI-PRO-01 4.1 to 4.2 and 4.4, PIMS-PRO-02
MEASURE Metrics, evaluation, testing for trustworthiness characteristics, tracking over time AI-POL-02 4.6 to 4.7, AI-PRO-01 4.6, AI-REG-03, ISMS-PRO-04
MANAGE Prioritise and treat risks, monitor, respond to incidents, plan decommissioning AI-PRO-01 4.5 to 4.8, AI-REG-02, AI-PRO-03, AI-POL-02 4.12, GOV-PRO-24

4. The EU AI Act in plain words

The EU AI Act is a regulation that applies obligations according to the risk a system poses. Four tiers matter in practice. Prohibited practices are banned outright: examples in the Act include manipulative techniques that cause harm, exploitation of vulnerable groups, social scoring by public authorities, and most real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces. High-risk systems are those used as safety components of regulated products, or those in the listed areas such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, access to essential services, law enforcement, migration and justice; these carry obligations on risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency to deployers, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, plus conformity assessment and registration. Limited-risk systems carry transparency duties: people must know they are dealing with an AI system, and synthetic content must be marked. Minimal-risk systems carry no new obligations, and voluntary codes are encouraged. General-purpose AI models carry their own documentation and copyright obligations, with extra duties where a model is classed as posing systemic risk.

The Act distinguishes roles. A provider develops a system or model and places it on the market; a deployer uses a system under its own authority; importers and distributors have narrower duties. Most organisations using this kit are deployers of vendor systems and, for anything they build and sell, providers. A deployer of a high-risk system must use it according to the provider's instructions, keep the logs it generates, assign human oversight to competent people, inform affected workers and individuals, and in some cases complete a fundamental rights impact assessment. Obligations apply in phases over several years from entry into force, with prohibitions first and high-risk duties later; the current timetable is on the public text linked from the resources page.

EU AI Act obligation (deployer and provider) Kit document or register
Identify the risk class of each system; never build or procure a prohibited practice AI-POL-02 4.2, AI-REG-01
Risk management system across the lifecycle (high-risk) AI-PRO-01, AI-REG-02, AI-POL-02 4.3
Data governance for training, validation and test data (high-risk) AI-POL-02 4.4, AI-REG-03
Technical documentation and record keeping, automatic logging (high-risk) AI-POL-02 4.7, AI-REG-03, GOV-PRO-14
Human oversight by competent persons AI-POL-02 4.5, GOV-PRO-08
Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity AI-POL-02 4.6 and 4.8, GOV-PRO-15, GOV-PRO-11
Transparency to users and marking of synthetic content AI-POL-02 4.10, AI-POL-01 4.7
Fundamental rights and data protection impact assessment where required PIMS-PRO-02, PIMS-TPL-01, AI-PRO-01 4.4
Provider instructions followed, logs kept, vendor obligations understood (deployer) AI-PRO-02, AI-TPL-01 question 30, GOV-REG-07
Serious incident reporting AI-PRO-03 4.6, GOV-REG-08
Inform workers and affected individuals; route to contest decisions AI-POL-01 4.6, AI-POL-02 4.5, PIMS-PRO-03

5. Where the frameworks overlap with GDPR

Any AI system that processes personal data is already inside the GDPR and ISO/IEC 27701 documents. Three points carry most of the weight. Article 22 limits decisions based solely on automated processing that have legal or similarly significant effects, which is why AI-POL-01 4.6 and AI-POL-02 4.5 require a human decision maker and a route to contest. Article 35 requires a data protection impact assessment for high-risk processing, which for an AI system is run under PIMS-PRO-02 and recorded in PIMS-REG-08, with AI-PRO-01 supplying the AI-specific risks. Article 28 governs the vendor relationship, which is why AI-PRO-02 and AI-TPL-01 insist on processor terms before personal data reaches a model. Privacy by design under Article 25 is applied to AI systems through PIMS-PRO-06 at the Design gate.

6. A minimum AI governance set

An organisation that wants a defensible position without a full ISO/IEC 42001 programme needs the following, in this order: AI-REG-04 populated with every tool staff use and AI-POL-01 issued and acknowledged; AI-REG-01 populated with every system that uses a model, each with a class and an owner; AI-PRO-01 run on every system that affects people or handles personal or client data, with results in AI-REG-02; AI-PRO-02 run on every vendor whose model receives data; and AI-PRO-03 adopted so that the first failure is handled on a procedure rather than improvised. AI-POL-02 and the full gate model follow when the organisation builds or sells AI systems. Every item above produces a register row or a signed record, which is what any of the three frameworks will ask to see.

Acceptable Use of AI Tools Policy

The rules for staff use of generative and assistive AI tools at work, covering which tools are approved, what may never be entered into them, how output is checked, and how use is recorded and disclosed.

Serves: ISO/IEC 42001 clause 6.1.4; ISO/IEC 42001 clause 7.3; NIST AI RMF GOVERN; GDPR Article 5; GDPR Article 32; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.10; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.12; SOC 2 CC6.7. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This policy lets staff gain the benefit of AI tools without leaking information, breaching a contract or a privacy obligation, or presenting unchecked output as finished work. It sets a short list of approved tools, a shorter list of things that must never be entered, and a single accountability rule: the person who uses the output owns it.

2. Scope

It applies to every employee, contractor and temporary worker of [Organisation], on every device, for every tool that generates, summarises, translates, classifies or transforms text, code, images, audio or data using a trained model. This includes stand-alone assistants, features embedded in office, development, browser and meeting software, and models called through an interface by internal scripts. Development and procurement of AI systems that [Organisation] builds or sells is governed by AI-POL-02; this policy covers the use of tools by people.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Chief Executive Officer Approves this policy and the prohibited uses in 4.8.
Information Security Manager Maintains the approved tool list in AI-REG-04, assesses new tool requests with the Privacy Officer, runs the annual review and investigates reported misuse.
Privacy Officer Confirms the personal data conditions for each approved tool and advises on client disclosure.
Line manager Confirms that staff in their team have completed the training in 4.10 and that client contracts permit the intended use.
Tool owner A named role for each approved tool: configures the tenant settings in 4.2, reviews usage and removes leavers.
All staff Use only approved tools, within the approved uses and prohibited-data limits in AI-REG-04, and review every output before relying on it.

4. Policy statements

4.1 Approved tools only. Staff use an AI tool for work only when it is listed as Approved in AI-REG-04 AI tool approval register, for the uses recorded there. A tool not on the list, or a free personal account for a tool that is on the list, is not approved. Requests for a new tool or a new use go to the Information Security Manager, who records the decision in AI-REG-04 within ten working days.

4.2 Tenant settings. The tool owner configures each approved tool so that prompts and outputs are not used to train the provider's models, retention of prompt history is the shortest the provider offers, access is through single sign-on with multi-factor authentication under GOV-POL-06, and administrative logs are available to the Information Security Manager. The settings are recorded in AI-REG-04 and re-checked at each review.

4.3 Information that must never be entered. Staff do not enter into any AI tool, including an approved one: personal data of customers, employees or any other person unless AI-REG-04 records that the tool is approved for that category and a processor agreement under PIMS-TPL-02 is in place; information classified Confidential or Restricted under GOV-PRO-16 belonging to a client, unless the client has agreed in writing; passwords, keys, tokens, certificates and connection strings; source code of [Organisation] or a client unless the tool is approved for code and the repository owner has agreed; security findings, incident details and vulnerability reports before the affected party has been notified; and information subject to legal privilege or a non-disclosure agreement that forbids third party processing.

4.4 Personal data. Where AI-REG-04 permits personal data in a tool, staff enter the minimum needed for the task, use anonymised or pseudonymised extracts where the task allows, and record the processing in PIMS-REG-01 through the Privacy Officer. Special category data is never entered without a documented assessment under PIMS-PRO-02.

4.5 Output review and accountability. The person who uses an AI output is accountable for it as if they had written it. Before output is sent to a client, published, committed to a repository, or used to make a decision about a person, the user checks it for factual accuracy, for content copied from a third party, for secrets or personal data the model may have reproduced, and for code defects or insecure patterns. Code produced with AI assistance passes the same review and testing steps as any other change under GOV-PRO-15 and GOV-PRO-09.

4.6 Decisions about people. No AI tool makes or materially shapes a decision about recruitment, performance, discipline, pay, credit or access to a service without a named person reviewing the output and recording the decision as their own. Any use of this kind is recorded in AI-REG-01 and assessed under AI-PRO-01 and, where personal data is involved, PIMS-PRO-02.

4.7 Disclosure. Where a client contract, a tender or a professional standard requires it, the engagement lead tells the client in writing which approved tools will be used on their work and for what. A client's written refusal is recorded in AI-REG-04 against the engagement and respected by everyone on it.

4.8 Prohibited uses. Staff do not use any AI tool to: generate content that impersonates a real person or organisation; create or test malicious code outside an authorised engagement with a signed scope; produce material that is discriminatory, harassing or unlawful; circumvent a client's or [Organisation]'s security controls; or process data in a jurisdiction that a contract or PIMS-POL-03 forbids.

4.9 Records of use. Where output forms part of a deliverable, a decision record or a code change, the user keeps the prompt and output, or the tool's conversation link, with the working papers for that item for the retention period in PIMS-POL-02. Tool owners export administrative usage logs quarterly and keep them under GOV-PRO-14.

4.10 Training. Every person completes the AI tool module under GOV-PRO-08 before first use and annually thereafter, and the completion is recorded in GOV-REG-09. The module covers this policy, the prohibited-data list, prompt injection through documents and web pages, and how to report a suspected leak.

4.11 Reporting. Anyone who enters information in breach of 4.3, or sees output that reveals another party's data, reports it the same working day under GOV-PRO-07. The Information Security Manager treats such a report as a potential personal data breach under PIMS-PRO-04 and follows AI-PRO-03.

4.12 Consequences. Breach of this policy is handled under the disciplinary process referenced in GOV-PRO-18. Entering credentials or client confidential material into an unapproved tool is treated as a serious breach.

5. Records and evidence

  • AI-REG-04 AI tool approval register: the approved tools, uses, prohibited data, tenant settings, approver and review dates.
  • AI-REG-01 AI system inventory: entries for tools used in decisions about people.
  • GOV-REG-09 Training and awareness register: completion of the AI tool module.
  • GOV-REG-23 Policy acknowledgement register: annual acknowledgement of this policy.
  • Administrative usage logs exported under 4.9.
  • Incident records under GOV-REG-08 for reports made under 4.11.

6. Exceptions

An exception to 4.1 or 4.3 is granted only under GOV-PRO-24, in writing, for a named person, tool, purpose and period not exceeding ninety days, and is recorded in GOV-REG-06. No exception is available for entering credentials or for the prohibited uses in 4.8.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this policy annually, when a tool is added to or removed from AI-REG-04, after any incident involving an AI tool, and when a client contract or a law introduces a new condition on AI use. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

AI System Development, Procurement and Deployment Policy

The lifecycle rules for any AI system [Organisation] builds, buys or embeds in a product or service, from risk classification through data governance, human oversight, evaluation and logging to incident handling and decommissioning.

Serves: ISO/IEC 42001 clause 6.1; ISO/IEC 42001 clause 8.1; ISO/IEC 42001 clause 8.2; ISO/IEC 42001 clause 8.4; NIST AI RMF MAP; NIST AI RMF MEASURE; NIST AI RMF MANAGE; GDPR Article 22; GDPR Article 25; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.25. Owner: Head of Engineering.

1. Purpose

This policy sets the conditions under which an AI system may be developed, procured, deployed and retired, so that every system has a known risk class, an owner, a tested behaviour, a person who can intervene, and a record of what it did. It applies the same lifecycle gates whether the model is trained in house, fine-tuned, called from a vendor service or bought inside a product.

2. Scope

It applies to every system that uses a trained model to produce predictions, content, recommendations, classifications or decisions, and that [Organisation] operates, sells, embeds in a product, or runs on behalf of a client. It covers internal tools built by staff on a vendor model, product features, autonomous agents that call tools, and vendor services integrated into a workflow. Personal use of assistive tools by staff is governed by AI-POL-01.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Chief Executive Officer Approves deployment of any system classed High in 4.2 and any system that makes decisions about people.
Head of Engineering Owns this policy, the lifecycle gates and the evaluation standard.
System Owner Accountable for one AI system: its entry in AI-REG-01, its risk assessment, its evaluation results, its monitoring and its decommissioning.
Information Security Manager Runs AI-PRO-01 with the System Owner and confirms the security controls at each gate.
Privacy Officer Decides whether a DPIA is required under PIMS-PRO-02 and signs off data governance in 4.4.
Internal Auditor Tests a sample of systems against this policy each year.

4. Policy statements

4.1 Inventory. No AI system is used in production, or exposed to clients or the public, until the System Owner has recorded it in AI-REG-01 AI system inventory with its purpose, model and provider, hosting location, inputs, outputs, personal data flag and risk class.

4.2 Risk classification. The System Owner classifies each system before design starts, using the risk categories of the EU AI Act as the reference scale even where the Act does not apply: Prohibited (practices the Act bans, which [Organisation] never builds or procures), High (systems in the Act's listed high-risk areas, including employment, credit, education, essential services, law enforcement and safety components), Limited (systems that interact with people or generate synthetic content and carry transparency duties), and Minimal (everything else). General-purpose models used as components are recorded with their provider's obligations noted. The class is confirmed by the Information Security Manager and recorded in AI-REG-01.

4.3 Lifecycle gates. Every system passes four gates, each recorded in AI-REG-03: Concept (purpose, class, intended users, owner approved), Design (AI-PRO-01 risk assessment complete, data sources approved under 4.4, oversight design under 4.5 agreed), Pre-release (evaluation under 4.6 passed, logging under 4.7 verified, go-live gate PB-07 passed where a product is involved), and Change (any change to model, prompt template, training data, tools the model can call, or decision threshold re-passes the evaluation before release). High class systems also require Chief Executive Officer approval at Pre-release.

4.4 Data governance. For training, fine-tuning, retrieval and prompt construction, the System Owner records in AI-REG-03 the source of every dataset, its licence or legal basis, whether it contains personal data, how it was cleaned and labelled, and who approved its use. Personal data is used only with a lawful basis confirmed by the Privacy Officer and, for High class or decisions about people, a DPIA under PIMS-PRO-02 recorded in PIMS-REG-08. Client data is never used to train or fine-tune a model without the client's written agreement. Prompts, retrieved documents and outputs are classified and handled under GOV-PRO-16.

4.5 Human oversight. Every system has a named person who can pause it, override an output and roll back a release within the time stated in its AI-REG-01 entry. A system that affects a person's rights, access to a service, employment or finances presents its output as a recommendation to a human decision maker, who records the decision, and the person affected is told that an automated system was involved and how to contest the outcome. Agents that execute actions operate only with the permissions, tool list and spending limits approved at the Design gate.

4.6 Evaluation. Before release and after every Change gate, the System Owner runs the evaluation set agreed at Design: task accuracy against a held-out set, behaviour on the adversarial cases from AI-PRO-01 (prompt injection, data extraction, unsafe output, excessive agency), bias checks across the groups relevant to the use, and performance under load and malformed input. Results, the pass thresholds and the approver are recorded in AI-REG-03. A system that fails a threshold is not released.

4.7 Logging and monitoring. Each system logs, with a timestamp and the calling identity: inputs (or a hash where inputs are sensitive), outputs, model version, tools invoked and overrides by a human. Logs are retained under GOV-PRO-14 for at least the period in PIMS-POL-02. The System Owner reviews drift, error rates, refusal rates and user complaints monthly and records the review in AI-REG-03.

4.8 Security. AI systems follow GOV-PRO-15 for development, GOV-PRO-09 for change, GOV-PRO-11 for vulnerabilities in models, libraries and plugins, and GOV-PRO-26 where hosted in cloud services. Model weights, prompt templates and evaluation sets are assets in GOV-REG-10 with an owner and classification.

4.9 Procurement. A vendor model or AI service is used only after AI-PRO-02 due diligence, recorded in GOV-REG-07 and, where personal data is processed, in PIMS-REG-06.

4.10 Transparency. Users of a Limited or High class system are told they are interacting with an AI system, synthetic content is labelled where a person could mistake it for human-made, and product documentation states the system's intended use and known limitations.

4.11 Incidents. Harmful output, leakage, drift beyond threshold, abuse or a safety event is handled under AI-PRO-03, with GOV-PRO-07 and PIMS-PRO-04 where applicable.

4.12 Decommissioning. When a system is retired, the System Owner removes it from production, deletes or archives training data, logs and model artefacts under PIMS-POL-02, revokes its credentials and tool permissions, informs affected users, and marks the AI-REG-01 entry Retired with the date.

5. Records and evidence

  • AI-REG-01 AI system inventory: one row per system with class, owner, approval and review dates.
  • AI-REG-02 AI risk register: risks and treatments from AI-PRO-01.
  • AI-REG-03 AI change and evaluation log: gate approvals, data approvals, evaluation results, monitoring reviews and rollbacks.
  • PIMS-REG-08 DPIA register: assessments for systems processing personal data.
  • GOV-REG-07 Supplier register and PIMS-REG-06 Processor and sub-processor register: vendor models and services.
  • GOV-REG-29 Go-live gate checklist for product releases.

6. Exceptions

A gate may be bypassed only for a time-limited pilot with no client, public or decision-about-people exposure, approved in writing by the Head of Engineering and recorded in GOV-REG-06 under GOV-PRO-24 for at most ninety days. No exception is available for Prohibited practices, for 4.5 on systems affecting people, or for 4.7.

7. Review and maintenance

The Head of Engineering reviews this policy annually, after any AI incident, when the EU AI Act or a comparable law changes an obligation that applies to [Organisation], and when a new class of system is proposed. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

AI Risk Assessment Procedure

How the risks of an AI system are identified from a standard threat catalogue, scored on the organisation's risk scale with an added impact-on-people rating, treated, tested and recorded in the AI risk register.

Serves: ISO/IEC 42001 clause 6.1.2; ISO/IEC 42001 clause 6.1.3; ISO/IEC 42001 clause 8.2; NIST AI RMF MAP; NIST AI RMF MEASURE; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.2; GDPR Article 35. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure produces, for every AI system in AI-REG-01, a set of scored risks with controls and tests that the System Owner can show at the Design and Pre-release gates of AI-POL-02. It uses the same likelihood and impact scales as GOV-PRO-05 so that AI risks sit in the same appetite and escalation path as every other risk, and adds one rating that the general method lacks: the impact on people.

2. Scope

It applies to every system recorded or proposed for AI-REG-01, at first design, before each release that passes the Change gate, after any AI incident, and at least annually. It covers systems built in house and vendor services integrated into a workflow. It does not replace the information security risk assessment of the hosting platform, which stays in GOV-REG-05.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
System Owner Requests the assessment, supplies the system description, owns the resulting risks and treatments.
Information Security Manager Facilitates the assessment, applies the catalogue, confirms scores, records the register entries.
Privacy Officer Rates impact on people, decides whether a DPIA under PIMS-PRO-02 is needed and links it.
Head of Engineering Approves treatment plans and accepts Medium risks with the System Owner.
Engineering lead for the system Designs and runs the tests in 4.6 and records results in AI-REG-03.

4. Procedure

4.1 Describe the system. The System Owner provides the AI-REG-01 entry plus: the model and version, who can send inputs (staff, clients, the public, other systems), what the model can read (documents, web pages, databases), what it can do (text only, or actions through tools, with the tool list), how output is used (shown to a person, acted on automatically), and the data in prompts, retrieval and training.

4.2 Apply the threat catalogue. The Information Security Manager walks the catalogue below with the System Owner and the engineering lead. Each row that applies becomes one risk scenario in AI-REG-02, written as: a named actor or failure uses a named weakness in the system, with the consequence. Rows that do not apply are recorded as not applicable with a one-line reason. The catalogue draws on the public OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications and MITRE ATLAS; both are consulted for new techniques at each annual review.

Threat What it looks like Controls to consider Test
Data leakage through prompts Staff or users paste confidential or personal data into a tool that retains it, trains on it or shows it to another tenant. AI-POL-01 limits, tenant settings with training opt-out and short retention, data loss prevention under GOV-PRO-23, redaction before send. Submit a marked test string and confirm it cannot be retrieved later or by another account.
Direct prompt injection A user crafts input that overrides the system instructions, extracts them, or unlocks prohibited behaviour. Separate system and user content, constrain output format, limit what the system can reveal, reject instructions in user fields. Run the agreed injection set and record the rate at which instructions are overridden.
Indirect prompt injection Instructions hidden in a document, web page, email or record the model reads cause it to act against the user. Treat retrieved content as untrusted, strip or flag instruction-like text, require confirmation for actions, restrict retrieval sources. Plant instructions in a retrieved item and confirm the model does not follow them.
Insecure output handling Model output is executed, rendered or passed to another system without validation, enabling script injection, command execution or query injection. Encode and validate output as untrusted input, never execute it directly, use allow-lists for generated commands. Prompt the model to emit markup, commands and queries and confirm downstream components neutralise them.
Training data poisoning Manipulated training, fine-tuning or retrieval data introduces backdoors, bias or false facts. Approved data sources under AI-POL-02 4.4, integrity checks, provenance records, held-out evaluation sets. Compare behaviour on canary cases before and after each data change.
Model theft and extraction Weights, prompts or decision boundaries are copied by insiders, through the interface, or by repeated querying. Access control under GOV-PRO-10, rate limits, watermarking where available, weights stored as a Restricted asset. Review access logs for bulk queries; confirm weights are not readable by non-owners.
Supply chain of models and plugins A pre-trained model, library, dataset or plugin contains malicious code, undisclosed data use or a vulnerability. AI-PRO-02 due diligence, pinned versions, signature verification, vulnerability tracking under GOV-PRO-11. Verify provenance and version pins; scan dependencies before release.
Excessive agency An agent has more tools, permissions or autonomy than the task needs and takes a harmful action. Minimum tool list, read-only by default, human confirmation for irreversible actions, spending and rate limits, kill switch. Attempt out-of-scope actions through the agent and confirm they are refused or require approval.
Over-reliance People accept output without review, so errors reach clients, code or decisions. Output review duty in AI-POL-01 4.5, confidence or source display, mandatory human decision for affected people. Sample deliverables for review evidence; test whether reviewers catch planted errors.
Bias and harmful output Output discriminates, defames, misleads or is unsafe for the audience. Evaluation across relevant groups, content filters, refusal rules, user reporting route. Run the bias and safety evaluation set; record failure rate per category.
Denial of service by expensive inputs Very long, recursive or adversarial inputs exhaust tokens, budget or capacity. Input length limits, timeouts, per-user quotas, cost alerts, capacity plan under GOV-PRO-19. Send maximal inputs at rate and confirm limits trigger before cost or availability is affected.
Privacy inference The model reveals or infers personal data about individuals from training data, retrieval or context, including re-identification. Minimisation, pseudonymisation, retrieval scoping by user permission, membership inference testing, DPIA. Query for known individuals in training data; confirm retrieval respects the caller's permissions.

4.3 Score likelihood and impact. The group rates each scenario on the GOV-PRO-05 scales: likelihood within twelve months with current controls, 1 to 5, and impact as the worst credible consequence to [Organisation], 1 to 5. The score is the product and the band follows GOV-PRO-05 4.7: 1 to 4 Low, 5 to 9 Medium, 10 to 15 High, 16 to 25 Critical.

4.4 Rate impact on people. The Privacy Officer rates each scenario's impact on individuals, separately from the organisational impact, on the same 1 to 5 scale: 1 inconvenience, 2 minor distress or cost, 3 significant financial, reputational or access harm, 4 discrimination, loss of a service or right, or harm requiring recovery, 5 physical harm, loss of liberty or irreversible harm. An impact-on-people rating of 4 or 5 raises the band by one step regardless of the score, requires a DPIA under PIMS-PRO-02 where personal data is processed, and makes the system a candidate for High class under AI-POL-02 4.2.

4.5 Treat. The System Owner chooses Modify, Retain, Avoid or Share for each risk under GOV-PRO-05 4.9 and names the controls, the kit documents that implement them and the target band. Acceptance authority follows the GOV-PRO-05 4.8 table, applied to the raised band from 4.4. No High or Critical risk, and no risk with impact on people of 4 or 5, is accepted without GOV-PRO-24.

4.6 Test. For every Modify treatment, the engineering lead runs the test named in the catalogue, or a better one agreed with the Information Security Manager, before the Pre-release gate and after each Change gate. Results with pass thresholds go in AI-REG-03 and the AI-REG-02 row is updated with the residual rating.

4.7 Record and link. The Information Security Manager completes the AI-REG-02 rows, cross-references the AI-REG-01 system ID, the DPIA reference in PIMS-REG-08 where one exists, and any platform risks in GOV-REG-05, and reports High and Critical risks to the steering committee under GOV-POL-01.

4.8 Review. Each risk is reviewed at the frequency its band sets in GOV-REG-05, after any AI incident under AI-PRO-03, when the model, provider, tool list or data sources change, and annually, when the catalogue is also refreshed against the two public sources named in 4.2.

5. Records and evidence

  • AI-REG-02 AI risk register: every scenario with scores, impact on people, treatment, owner, residual rating and review dates.
  • AI-REG-03 AI change and evaluation log: test results against each treatment.
  • PIMS-REG-08 DPIA register: linked assessments.
  • GOV-REG-06 Risk acceptance and exception register: accepted High, Critical and people-impact risks.
  • Steering committee minutes under GOV-TPL-03 showing High and Critical risks reported.

6. Exceptions

A system may be released with an untested treatment only for a pilot approved under AI-POL-02 section 6, with the untested risk recorded as Open in AI-REG-02 and a test date within thirty days. No exception applies to a risk with impact on people of 4 or 5.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure and the catalogue annually, after any AI incident, and when OWASP or MITRE publish a revised version of the sources named in 4.2. Scale or band changes are made only in GOV-PRO-05.

AI Vendor and Model Due Diligence Procedure

How a vendor AI service, hosted model or pre-trained model is assessed before it is approved for staff use or integrated into a system, what the vendor must answer and evidence, and how the decision is recorded.

Serves: ISO/IEC 42001 clause 8.4; ISO/IEC 42001 clause 6.1.2; NIST AI RMF MAP; GDPR Article 28; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.19; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.20; SOC 2 CC9.2. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure answers the questions that matter before a model or AI service touches [Organisation]'s data: whether the vendor trains on customer inputs, how long prompts and outputs are kept and where, who else processes them, how the service is secured, and what evidence exists that the model behaves as claimed. It produces a documented decision that AI-POL-01 and AI-POL-02 require before approval.

2. Scope

It applies to every hosted AI service, interface to a model, embedded AI feature in a product [Organisation] already uses, and pre-trained or open-weight model downloaded for internal use, whether paid or free. It runs alongside GOV-PRO-06, which covers the vendor's general security; this procedure adds the model-specific questions. A new version of an approved model from the same vendor is re-assessed only for the questions whose answers could change (section 4.8).

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Requester Describes the intended use, data involved and users, and names the business owner.
Information Security Manager Runs the assessment, sends AI-TPL-01, reviews answers and evidence, records the decision.
Privacy Officer Reviews personal data, retention, location, sub-processor and contract answers; confirms processor terms under PIMS-TPL-02.
Head of Engineering Reviews evaluation evidence and integration security for systems under AI-POL-02; approves or rejects.
Legal or contracts role Reviews terms of use, licence of model weights, liability and intellectual property clauses.
Tool owner or System Owner Implements the approved configuration and owns the ongoing review.

4. Procedure

4.1 Request. The requester submits the intended use, the categories of data that will be sent to the service (none, internal, client confidential, personal, special category), who will use it, whether output will be acted on automatically, and the expected volume. The Information Security Manager assigns a tier: Tier 1 where no personal or confidential data is sent and output is reviewed by a person; Tier 2 where confidential or personal data is sent or output is acted on automatically; Tier 3 where special category data, decisions about people, or a High class system under AI-POL-02 is involved.

4.2 Gather. The Information Security Manager obtains the vendor's published documentation on data use, retention, security and model behaviour, and sends AI-TPL-01 AI vendor and model questionnaire to the vendor for Tier 2 and Tier 3. For Tier 1, published documentation may answer the questionnaire if the Information Security Manager completes it from those sources and records the source for each answer. GOV-TPL-04 is sent in parallel where the vendor is not already in GOV-REG-07.

4.3 Review the answers. The reviewers named in section 3 each check their questions in AI-TPL-01 and record a verdict per question: Acceptable, Acceptable with condition, or Blocking. The following are Blocking for Tier 2 and Tier 3 unless an exception is approved under section 6: customer inputs used to train the vendor's models without an opt-out that [Organisation] can enforce; prompt or output retention that cannot be set to thirty days or less or that is not stated; processing locations or sub-processors that cannot be named; no processor agreement where personal data is sent; no independent security assurance report or equivalent evidence; no statement of the model's intended use, limitations and known failure modes.

4.4 Verify. For Tier 2 and Tier 3 the Information Security Manager verifies the key answers rather than accepting them: confirms the training opt-out and retention settings in the actual tenant or contract, reads the processor terms, reads the assurance report under SOC-PRO-02, and runs a short technical check that the service refuses a planted secret on retrieval and applies the stated rate and length limits. Results are recorded against the questionnaire.

4.5 Risk assess. For a service that becomes part of a system, the Information Security Manager runs AI-PRO-01 with the questionnaire as input. For a staff tool, the supply chain, data leakage and privacy inference rows of the AI-PRO-01 catalogue are assessed and recorded in AI-REG-02.

4.6 Decide. The Head of Engineering (for systems) or the Information Security Manager with the Privacy Officer (for staff tools) records one decision: Approved, Approved with conditions (listed, with an owner and date), or Rejected. Tier 3 decisions are also approved by the Chief Executive Officer. The decision, tier, approved uses, prohibited data and required configuration are written to AI-REG-04 for a tool, and to AI-REG-01 and GOV-REG-07 for a system component. Where personal data is processed the vendor is also entered in PIMS-REG-06 with the processor agreement reference.

4.7 Configure. The tool owner or System Owner applies the approved configuration (training opt-out, retention, single sign-on, logging, allowed regions, rate limits) before first use and records a screenshot or export of the settings with the AI-REG-04 or AI-REG-01 entry.

4.8 Re-assess. The Information Security Manager repeats 4.2 to 4.6 annually for Tier 2 and Tier 3 and every two years for Tier 1, and sooner when the vendor changes its terms, data use, sub-processors or model version in a way that changes an answer, when an incident involves the vendor, or when a contract or law adds a requirement. A model version change within an approved service is re-assessed on questions 4 to 7 and 24 to 30 of AI-TPL-01 only, unless the answers reveal a wider change.

4.9 Exit. When a service is withdrawn or rejected after use, the Information Security Manager obtains the vendor's confirmation of deletion of retained prompts, outputs and any fine-tuned artefacts, records it in AI-REG-04 or AI-REG-01, and revokes credentials under GOV-PRO-10.

5. Records and evidence

  • Completed AI-TPL-01 questionnaires with per-question verdicts and verification notes.
  • AI-REG-04 AI tool approval register: decision, tier, conditions, configuration evidence, review dates for staff tools.
  • AI-REG-01 AI system inventory and GOV-REG-07 Supplier register: entries for vendor models used in systems.
  • PIMS-REG-06 Processor and sub-processor register: vendors processing personal data, with agreement references.
  • AI-REG-02 AI risk register: supply chain and leakage risks for each approved vendor.
  • Deletion confirmations on exit.

6. Exceptions

A Blocking answer in 4.3 is overridden only by GOV-PRO-24 with a written risk acceptance by the Head of Engineering, limited to ninety days and to a stated use, recorded in GOV-REG-06. The absence of processor terms where personal data is sent cannot be excepted.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure and AI-TPL-01 annually, after any incident involving a vendor AI service, and when a law or client contract introduces a new vendor obligation. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

AI Incident and Model Failure Handling Procedure

How an event involving an AI system or tool, such as harmful output, data leakage, model drift or abuse, is recognised, contained, rolled back, investigated and disclosed, and how it connects to the security incident and personal data breach procedures.

Serves: ISO/IEC 42001 clause 8.3; ISO/IEC 42001 clause 10.1; NIST AI RMF MANAGE; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.24; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.26; GDPR Article 33; GDPR Article 34; SOC 2 CC7.4. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

AI systems fail in ways the general incident procedure does not describe: a model gives a harmful answer to one person, leaks a document to another, drifts quietly until its decisions are wrong, or is manipulated into acting outside its purpose. This procedure names those event types, gives each a first response, and routes the event into GOV-PRO-07 and PIMS-PRO-04 so that one timeline, one register and one set of notifications cover it.

2. Scope

It applies to every system in AI-REG-01 and every tool in AI-REG-04, whether the event is reported by a user, a client, a member of the public, a vendor, monitoring under AI-POL-02 4.7, or an evaluation run. It covers events in production and in pilots with external exposure.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Any person Reports a suspected AI event the same working day through the route in GOV-PRO-07.
Incident lead (role assigned under GOV-PRO-07) Runs the response, keeps the timeline, decides containment with the System Owner.
System Owner or tool owner Executes pause, rollback and configuration changes; supplies logs and the AI-REG-03 history.
Information Security Manager Classifies the event, links it to GOV-REG-08, owns the post-incident review.
Privacy Officer Assesses personal data impact under PIMS-PRO-04 and leads notifications to authorities and individuals.
Head of Engineering Approves re-release after a rollback and any change to evaluation thresholds.
Engagement lead or account role Handles disclosure to the affected client.

4. Procedure

4.1 Recognise and classify. The Information Security Manager classifies the event within four working hours of the report as one or more of the types below, records it in GOV-REG-08 with the type and the AI-REG-01 or AI-REG-04 reference, and assigns the severity under GOV-PRO-07.

Type Examples First response
Harmful or wrong output Discriminatory, defamatory, unsafe or materially false output reached a user, a client or a decision; a decision about a person was shaped by a wrong output. Capture the prompt, output and model version; stop the use case or add a human review step; identify affected people.
Leakage Confidential, client or personal data entered into a tool in breach of AI-POL-01; output revealed another tenant's or person's data; system instructions or retrieval content exposed. Delete the item at the provider where possible and record the request; revoke the affected session; identify data categories and subjects.
Drift or degradation Accuracy, refusal rate, error rate or bias measure crosses the threshold set in AI-REG-03; outputs changed after a provider model update. Pause or roll back to the last evaluated version; re-run the evaluation set; freeze dependent decisions until results are known.
Abuse and manipulation Prompt injection succeeded; an agent took an unauthorised action; the service was used for a prohibited purpose; denial of service through expensive inputs. Disable the affected tool or permission; block the source; preserve logs; check for actions that must be reversed.
Supply chain Vendor incident, terms change, sub-processor breach, or a vulnerable or malicious model, library or plugin. Suspend the integration; obtain the vendor's statement; check AI-REG-04 and AI-REG-01 for every dependent use.

4.2 Contain. The System Owner applies the first response within the time stated for the system in AI-REG-01 and never later than one working day. Where a kill switch, feature flag or version pin exists under AI-POL-02 4.5, it is used before any slower measure. Containment actions and their times go in the GOV-PRO-07 timeline.

4.3 Assess personal data impact. Where personal data may have been entered, exposed, inferred or used in a decision, the Privacy Officer runs PIMS-PRO-04 from the moment of classification. The seventy-two hour clock for a notifiable breach runs from awareness of the event, not from the end of the AI investigation.

4.4 Investigate. The incident lead establishes from the logs required by AI-POL-02 4.7: which inputs produced the event, which model version and prompt template were live, which tools or data sources the model reached, how many users or records were affected, and whether the AI-PRO-01 risk register predicted the scenario. Where a vendor service is involved, the Information Security Manager requests the vendor's incident report through the channel recorded in AI-TPL-01 question 23.

4.5 Roll back and recover. The System Owner restores the last version whose evaluation passed, reverses any actions an agent took that can be reversed, corrects or withdraws decisions about people that were based on the wrong output, and records the rollback in AI-REG-03 with the reason. A system stays paused until the Head of Engineering approves re-release on the basis of a repeated evaluation under AI-POL-02 4.6 that covers the failure case.

4.6 Disclose. The engagement lead tells an affected client in writing within the period the contract sets, or within two working days where it sets none, what happened, what data or output was involved, what has been done and what the client should do. Individuals affected by a wrong decision are told how it was corrected and how to contest it. Public statements are approved by the Chief Executive Officer. Where the system is High class under AI-POL-02 and a law requires a report to an authority, the Privacy Officer or the legal role files it within the statutory period and records it in GOV-REG-08.

4.7 Review and correct. Within ten working days of closure the Information Security Manager completes a post-incident review under GOV-TPL-11, updates AI-REG-02 with the new or re-scored risk, raises corrective actions in GOV-REG-03 under GOV-PRO-04, and adds the failure case to the system's evaluation set in AI-REG-03 so that it is tested before every future release. Where a staff tool caused a leak, AI-REG-04 is updated with any new prohibited data or configuration.

4.8 Learn across systems. Quarterly, the Information Security Manager reviews all AI events in GOV-REG-08 for patterns, reports them to the steering committee under GOV-POL-01, and proposes changes to AI-POL-01, AI-POL-02 or the AI-PRO-01 catalogue.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-08 Incident register: every AI event with type, system reference, severity, personal data flag and status.
  • Incident timelines and GOV-TPL-05 Incident report form entries.
  • PIMS-REG-03 Personal data breach register: AI events that involved personal data.
  • AI-REG-03 AI change and evaluation log: rollbacks, re-evaluations and added test cases.
  • AI-REG-02 AI risk register: re-scored or new risks.
  • GOV-REG-03 Corrective action log: actions from the post-incident review.
  • Client and authority notifications and vendor incident reports.

6. Exceptions

A system that is paused under 4.2 may be re-enabled before the full re-evaluation only for a Minimal class system with no personal data and no client exposure, on the written decision of the Head of Engineering recorded in the timeline. No exception applies to 4.3 or to disclosure obligations under contract or law.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after every Major or Critical AI event, and when GOV-PRO-07 or PIMS-PRO-04 changes. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

AI Vendor and Model Questionnaire

The thirty questions sent to a vendor of an AI service or model under AI-PRO-02, with columns for the vendor's answer, the evidence supplied, and the reviewer's verdict.

Serves: ISO/IEC 42001 clause 8.4; GDPR Article 28; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.19; SOC 2 CC9.2. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. How to use this questionnaire

Send sections 2 to 8 to the vendor with the cover details completed. Ask for an answer to every question and a piece of evidence for each: a contract clause, a documentation page, a configuration screenshot, a report or a signed statement. Do not accept "yes" without evidence for Tier 2 and Tier 3 assessments under AI-PRO-02. The reviewer completes the verdict column (Acceptable, Acceptable with condition, Blocking) and the verification note after the vendor returns the form. File the completed form with the AI-REG-04 or AI-REG-01 entry.

Field Entry
Vendor [Vendor name as recorded in GOV-REG-07]
Service or model [Service name, model name and version]
Requested by [Role]
Intended use [One or two sentences]
Data categories to be sent [None, Internal, Client confidential, Personal, Special category]
Tier under AI-PRO-02 [1, 2 or 3]
Date sent and date returned [Date], [Date]

2. Use of customer data for training

No. Question Answer Evidence
1 Are inputs, prompts, uploaded files or outputs from our account used to train, fine-tune or otherwise improve your models or any third party's models?
2 If such use is possible, is there an opt-out, is it enforceable at the account or contract level rather than per user, and is it on by default for business accounts?
3 Are our inputs or outputs ever reviewed by your staff or contractors, and under what conditions (for example abuse monitoring)? How are reviewers vetted and bound?
4 Which model versions are offered, how are version changes announced, and can we pin a version for a stated period?

3. Retention of prompts, files and outputs

No. Question Answer Evidence
5 How long are prompts, uploaded files, conversation history and outputs retained on your systems by default, and what is the shortest retention we can configure?
6 Can we delete individual items, a user's history or the whole account's data on demand, and how long until deletion is complete across backups?
7 Are any derived artefacts kept after deletion (embeddings, logs, abuse records, fine-tuned weights), for how long, and for what purpose?
8 What is deleted, and confirmed in writing, when the contract ends?

4. Location and transfers

No. Question Answer Evidence
9 In which countries or regions are inputs processed and stored, including inference, logging and backups? Can processing be restricted to a region we choose?
10 Which legal mechanisms cover transfers of personal data outside the region in which we contract (for example standard contractual clauses or an adequacy decision)?
11 Can government or law enforcement access to our data be requested in any processing location, and what is your policy for notifying us?

5. Sub-processors and supply chain

No. Question Answer Evidence
12 List every sub-processor that may receive our inputs or outputs, including the underlying model provider and hosting provider, with location and role.
13 How are we notified of sub-processor changes, with how much notice, and can we object?
14 For the model itself: who trained it, what is its licence, and what is publicly stated about its training data sources and cut-off?
15 For plugins, tools, connectors or extensions available in the service: are they vetted, can we restrict which ones our users may enable, and are third party plugins bound by the same terms as you?

6. Security

No. Question Answer Evidence
16 Which independent assurance do you hold for the service (for example an attestation report or a management system certificate), what is the scope and period, and may we have the report?
17 How is tenant isolation implemented so that one customer's prompts, files, retrieval indexes and fine-tuned models cannot be reached by another?
18 Which authentication options are supported (single sign-on, multi-factor, service credentials), and can administrators enforce them for all users?
19 Which administrative and audit logs are available to us (user activity, data exports, configuration changes), for how long, and in what format?
20 Is data encrypted in transit and at rest, who holds the keys, and can we supply our own?
21 How are vulnerabilities in the service and in the model handled: disclosure route, patch timescales, and how customers are told?
22 What controls exist against prompt injection, retrieval of other customers' data, and extraction of system instructions, and how were they tested?
23 Within what time are customers notified of a security incident or personal data breach affecting their data, and through which channel?

7. Model behaviour and evaluation evidence

No. Question Answer Evidence
24 What is the model's intended use, and which uses do you state as out of scope or unsupported?
25 What documentation describes the model's known limitations, failure modes and the groups or languages on which performance is weaker?
26 Which evaluations have been performed for accuracy, robustness to adversarial input, bias and harmful output, by whom, and may we see the results?
27 Which content safety controls operate on inputs and outputs, can we adjust them, and are refusals and filtered events visible to us?
28 Can we export our prompts, outputs and configuration in a usable format so that we can move to another provider?

8. Contract and compliance

No. Question Answer Evidence
29 Do you offer processor terms that meet the requirements of GDPR Article 28, including instructions, confidentiality, assistance with data subject rights and audit rights, and will you sign ours (PIMS-TPL-02) if yours are not adequate?
30 Which obligations under the EU AI Act or comparable laws do you take on as provider of the model or system, and which do you pass to us as deployer? Where is this stated in the contract?

Completed by [Organisation] after return. One row per question with a verdict; the Blocking conditions are listed in AI-PRO-02 4.3.

Onboarding and offboarding security checklist

The two task lists that Human Resources, the line manager, the IT Manager and the access administrator complete for every person who joins or leaves [Organisation], with the responsible role, due point and evidence for each task.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.5; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.11; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.18; SOC 2 CC6.2; SOC 2 CC6.3. Owner: Human Resources Manager.

1. How to use this checklist

Open one copy per person. Human Resources starts it on the day an offer is accepted or a leaving date is known, enters the person's name, role, start or leave date and line manager at the top, and sends it to the roles named in the tables. Each responsible role marks the task done, writes where the evidence is, and initials it. Human Resources files the completed checklist with the person's record within five working days of the start or leave date and reports any task not done on time to the Information Security Manager. The due points count from the start date for onboarding and from the last working day for offboarding. Where a task does not apply, write "not applicable" and the reason, never leave it blank.

Secure Configuration Baseline Checklist (Server, Workstation, Cloud Account)

Three vendor-neutral checklists that define the minimum secure configuration for a server, a workstation and a cloud account, each check with how to verify it and the evidence to keep.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.9; SOC 2 CC6.8; SOC 2 CC7.1. Owner: Head of Engineering.

1. How to use this checklist

Run the relevant table when a server, workstation image or cloud account is built, after a significant change, and at least annually. Record Pass, Fail or Not applicable per check, with the evidence reference. A Fail on a check marked with an asterisk blocks go-live until fixed or covered by a risk acceptance under GOV-PRO-24; any other Fail becomes a finding in GOV-REG-14. Where a configuration management or posture tool enforces a check continuously, its report is the evidence. Keep the completed checklist with the asset's entry in GOV-REG-24.

2. Server baseline

Ref Check How to verify Evidence to keep
S-01 * Built from an approved, version-controlled image or definition Compare the running build identifier with the approved image list Image identifier and build record
S-02 Only required roles, services and packages are installed List running services and installed packages against the role's allowed list Service and package listing
S-03 * Host firewall denies inbound by default; only required ports are open Export the host firewall rules and scan open ports from another host Rule export and port scan output
S-04 * Vendor default accounts are removed or disabled and default passwords changed List local accounts; attempt sign-in with documented defaults in a test window Account listing and test record
S-05 Local administrative access is limited to named roles; no shared accounts Compare local administrator group members with GOV-REG-13 Group membership export
S-06 * Remote administration uses an encrypted protocol with key or multi-factor authentication; password sign-in is disabled Inspect the remote access daemon configuration and test a password sign-in Configuration excerpt and test record
S-07 * Security updates apply automatically or on the monthly cycle; last update within the GOV-PRO-11 deadline Read the update log and compare with the latest vendor release Update log excerpt

Pre-audit readiness checklist

Forty-nine yes or no checks, grouped by ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 4 to 10, that [Organisation] runs four weeks before an external audit, each naming the evidence to have ready for the auditor.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 4; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 5; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 7; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 8; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 10; SOC 2 CC4.1. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. How to use this checklist

Run it four weeks before a stage 1, stage 2, surveillance, recertification or SOC 2 audit. The Information Security Manager assigns each check to the role that holds the evidence, collects the answers within five working days, and raises a corrective action in GOV-REG-03 for every "No" with an owner and a due date before the audit date. A "No" that cannot be fixed before the audit is disclosed to the auditor at the opening meeting rather than discovered during it. Keep the completed checklist as a record. Evidence should be exported from the system of record, show the date and the account, and be filed under the numbered area used by PB-09.

2. Clause 4: context and scope

Ref Check Evidence to have ready Yes or No
4.1 Internal and external issues have been analysed and the analysis was reviewed in the last twelve months. ISMS-PRO-01 output with review date
4.2 Interested parties and their requirements are recorded and current. ISMS-REG-03
4.3 The scope statement is approved, matches the certificate scope requested, and justifies every exclusion. ISMS-STM-01 with approval record
4.4 Interfaces and dependencies with suppliers and cloud providers are described and match the supplier register. ISMS-STM-01, GOV-REG-07

3. Clause 5: leadership

Ref Check Evidence to have ready Yes or No
5.1 The information security policy is signed by the Chief Executive Officer, is the current version, and is published where staff can find it. GOV-POL-03, GOV-REG-01 entry
5.2 The management commitment statement is signed and current. GOV-STM-01
5.3 Roles, responsibilities and authorities are assigned, communicated and match the organisation chart. GOV-POL-01, organisation chart, role descriptions
5.4 The steering committee has met at the cadence in its charter and the minutes show decisions. Charter, minutes for the last four quarters
5.5 A budget and staffing for the management system were approved for the current year. Budget approval record
5.6 Staff interviewed at random can say where the policy is and how to report an incident. Awareness spot check results

4. Clause 6: planning

Ref Check Evidence to have ready Yes or No
6.1 The risk methodology is approved and its criteria (scales, bands, appetite, authorities) are defined. GOV-PRO-05 with approval
6.2 A full risk assessment was performed in the last twelve months and every risk has an owner. GOV-REG-05 with dates and owners
6.3 Every High or Critical risk has an approved treatment plan or a current acceptance. GOV-REG-05, GOV-REG-06
6.4 Risk owners have approved the treatment plan and residual risks have been accepted by the right authority. Signed treatment plan, GOV-TPL-06 forms
6.5 The Statement of Applicability lists all 93 Annex A controls with justification and implementation status. ISMS-REG-01
6.6 Every control named in a treatment plan is Applicable in the Statement of Applicability, and no Not applicable control is relied on anywhere. Cross-check of GOV-REG-05 against ISMS-REG-01
6.7 Information security objectives are measurable, resourced, owned and have a plan. ISMS-PLN-01, GOV-REG-21
6.8 Changes to the management system in the period were planned and recorded. GOV-REG-01 history, GOV-REG-22

5. Clause 7: support

Ref Check Evidence to have ready Yes or No
7.1 Competence requirements for security and privacy roles are defined and evidence of competence is held. ISMS-PRO-02 matrix, certificates, training records
7.2 Everyone in scope completed induction and the annual refresher; completion rate meets the target. GOV-REG-09 with completion report
7.3 Everyone in scope has acknowledged the policy and the acceptable use policy. GOV-REG-23
7.4 Internal and external communications about security follow the communication plan. ISMS-PLN-02 with examples
7.5 The master list of documents is current, every document is at an approved version, and owners and review dates are set. GOV-REG-01
7.6 Withdrawn documents are removed from the live location and no uncontrolled copies are in use. Sample of document locations
7.7 Records are retained for the required period, protected from alteration and retrievable on request. PIMS-REG-07, sample retrievals

6. Clause 8: operation

Ref Check Evidence to have ready Yes or No
8.1 Operational procedures are followed as written; a sample of the last three months of records shows no unexplained gaps. Samples from access, change and incident records
8.2 The risk treatment plan is on track and implemented controls have evidence. Treatment plan status, control evidence
8.3 Outsourced and cloud processes are controlled: suppliers are tiered, assessed and reviewed on schedule. GOV-REG-07, questionnaires, review records
8.4 Access reviews were completed on schedule and removals were actioned. GOV-REG-12
8.5 Vulnerabilities are remediated within the agreed times or have an approved exception. GOV-REG-14, GOV-REG-06
8.6 Backups run as scheduled and a restore test was performed and recorded in the last quarter. GOV-REG-15
8.7 Incidents are recorded, classified, reviewed and closed with lessons. GOV-REG-08, post-incident reviews
8.8 Changes are recorded with approval, testing and rollback. GOV-REG-11
8.9 Business continuity arrangements were exercised in the period. GOV-REG-16
8.10 The asset inventory is current, owned and classified. GOV-REG-10, GOV-REG-24
8.11 Active exceptions are within their expiry dates and reviewed. GOV-REG-06

7. Clause 9: performance evaluation

Ref Check Evidence to have ready Yes or No
9.1 What is monitored and measured, how, when and by whom is defined, and results are recorded. ISMS-PRO-04, measurement records
9.2 Objectives have been measured and the tracker shows current values and status. GOV-REG-21
9.3 The internal audit programme covers every clause and every applicable control within the cycle. GOV-REG-02, ISMS-PLN-03

9.5 Every internal audit nonconformity has a corrective action with a root cause. GOV-REG-03
9.6 A management review was held in the last twelve months and every mandatory input was covered. GOV-TPL-03 minutes

Ref Check Evidence to have ready Yes or No

Confirm the following before the audit date: the audit plan from the certification body has been received and the auditees in it are available; each evidence area has a named owner who can share screens; a room or call with screen sharing is booked; the previous audit report and certificate are to hand; and the Information Security Manager has walked through this checklist with the executive sponsor.

Information security and privacy governance framework

How [Organisation] governs information security and privacy, naming the steering committee, the roles that carry the management system, who decides what, how results are reported, and how one control set serves several frameworks.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 5.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 5.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 7.4; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.3; SOC 2 CC1.1; SOC 2 CC1.2; SOC 2 CC1.3; SOC 2 CC1.4; SOC 2 CC1.5; SOC 2 CC2.1. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This policy sets out how [Organisation] directs and oversees information security and privacy: the committee, roles, decision rights and recurring mechanisms that keep the management system working between audits.

2. Scope

It applies to the management system defined in ISMS-STM-01, to every framework the organisation has adopted (ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701, SOC 2, GDPR and the AI governance documents in this kit), and to everyone holding a role named below, including contractors.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Executive sponsor (the Chief Executive Officer or a named executive) Chairs the steering committee, signs GOV-POL-03 and GOV-STM-01, approves the risk appetite and the budget.
Information Security Manager Runs the management system day to day: risk register, control set, audits, measures, management review.
Privacy Officer Owns the privacy requirements, processing inventory and rights handling; contact point for supervisory authorities; independent of the teams assessed.
Asset owners and risk owners Protect their assets, own the related risks in GOV-REG-05, decide treatment within their authority, provide evidence.
Internal Auditor Audits under GOV-PRO-02, reports to the executive sponsor, never audits their own work.
All staff Follow the policies, complete training, report incidents and weaknesses, cooperate with audits.

4. Policy statements

4.1 Steering committee. The Information Security and Privacy Steering Committee governs the management system under a charter approved by the Chief Executive Officer. Standing members are the executive sponsor (chair), the Information Security Manager (secretary), the Privacy Officer, the Head of Engineering, the Head of Operations and a Human Resources representative.

4.2 Cadence and quorum. The committee meets at least quarterly. It is quorate when the chair or a deputy named in advance, the Information Security Manager and at least half of the remaining standing members attend. The chair decides after hearing the members; the secretary records the decisions. A decision taken without quorum is provisional until the chair confirms it in writing.

4.3 Decision rights. Each decision is held at the lowest level with the authority below; a decision made higher is recorded with the reason.

Decision Authority
Approve GOV-POL-03, GOV-STM-01, the risk appetite and the scope statement Chief Executive Officer
Approve topic policies and this framework Steering committee
Approve procedures, templates and registers Information Security Manager, or the Privacy Officer for privacy documents
Accept a risk or grant an exception The authority for the risk band in GOV-PRO-05 and GOV-PRO-24
Declare a major incident and approve external communication about it Executive sponsor, advised by the incident lead
Approve the internal audit plan and receive audit reports Executive sponsor

4.4 Reporting lines. The Information Security Manager and the Privacy Officer report on management system matters directly to the executive sponsor, whatever their line management. The Internal Auditor reports to the executive sponsor and the committee, never to the manager of the area audited. The executive sponsor reports to the board or owners at least annually on posture, major risks and incidents.

4.5 One control set, several frameworks. The organisation operates a single set of controls, described in the kit documents and declared applicable in ISMS-REG-01. GOV-REG-27 tags each control with the ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701, SOC 2, GDPR and NIST CSF 2.0 references it serves, so evidence is collected once and reused. A requirement from one framework alone is still met through this control set, never a parallel process.

4.6 Communication. The secretary communicates committee decisions, policy changes and management review outcomes through the channels in ISMS-PLN-02 within ten working days.

4.7 Governance mechanisms. The mechanisms below are mandatory. Each produces a record the Internal Auditor can test.

Mechanism Frequency Purpose Owner
Steering committee meeting Quarterly Direct the programme and decide priorities Executive sponsor
Management review (GOV-PRO-03) At least annually Judge whether the system is suitable, adequate and effective Chief Executive Officer
Internal audit (GOV-PRO-02) Per ISMS-PLN-03 Independent evidence of conformity and effectiveness Internal Auditor
Risk review (GOV-PRO-05) Quarterly and on trigger Keep GOV-REG-05 current and treatment on track Information Security Manager
Objectives and measures report (GOV-REG-21) Quarterly Show progress on objectives Information Security Manager
Compliance obligations review (GOV-PRO-25) Twice a year Detect changes in law, regulation and contract Privacy Officer
Corrective action review (GOV-PRO-04) Monthly Keep GOV-REG-03 moving and spot trends Information Security Manager
Document review (GOV-PRO-01) Annually per document Keep documents accurate and approved Document owners

4.8 Resources and conflicts of interest. The executive sponsor approves a budget and staffing for the management system each financial year; a shortfall that prevents a planned treatment or audit is recorded in GOV-REG-22. No person approves their own risk acceptance, audits their own area or verifies their own corrective action; where a role cannot be separated, the executive sponsor records the conflict and the compensating arrangement in the minutes.

5. Records and evidence

  • Steering committee charter, agendas, attendance lists and minutes.
  • GOV-REG-22 and GOV-REG-21.
  • GOV-REG-27 Framework crosswalk.
  • The executive sponsor's annual report to the board or owners.

6. Exceptions

The Chief Executive Officer may adjust standing membership and quorum for an organisation of fewer than [Number] staff by a written decision, provided the independence rules in 4.4 and 4.8 are preserved. No other exception applies.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this policy annually, and after a change in executive roles, a merger, acquisition or restructuring, or an audit finding about governance. The steering committee approves changes; GOV-PRO-01 governs publication.
