Acceptable use policy

What everyone who uses [Organisation] devices, accounts, email, internet, cloud services, removable media, personal devices and AI tools may and may not do, how use is monitored, how to report a problem, and how the policy is acknowledged.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.10; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.7; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.1; SOC 2 CC1.1; SOC 2 CC6.8. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This policy tells everyone who uses [Organisation] information, devices, accounts and services what they may and may not do with them, so that ordinary daily work does not become the way an attacker gets in or information gets out.

2. Scope

It applies to employees, contractors, temporary staff, interns and supplier personnel who hold an [Organisation] account or device, at any location, and to personal devices used for work under statement 4.9.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
All users Follow this policy, acknowledge it, report incidents and breaches.
Information Security Manager Owns the policy, keeps the approved services list, investigates suspected breaches with Human Resources.
IT Manager Configures devices and services so that the policy can be enforced and evidenced.
Human Resources Records acknowledgements in GOV-REG-23 and runs the disciplinary process.

4. Policy statements

4.1 Permitted use. [Organisation] information, devices, accounts and services are provided for its business. Limited personal use of internet and email is permitted where it does not interfere with work, break a law or this policy, or expose [Organisation] information.

4.2 Devices. Users work on devices issued and managed by [Organisation], keep the GOV-PRO-22 controls switched on, install no software outside the approved catalogue without the IT Manager's approval, and hold no administrative rights on their own device.

4.3 Locking and loss. Users lock their screen whenever they step away and report a lost or stolen device within one hour under GOV-PRO-07.

4.4 Accounts. Each user uses only accounts issued in their own name, never shares a password, one-time code or signed-in session with anyone, including IT staff, and follows GOV-POL-06.

4.5 Email and messaging. Users send Confidential and Restricted information only through the channels permitted in GOV-PRO-16, never forward work email or information to a personal account, and report suspected phishing through the report button rather than replying or clicking.

4.6 Internet. Users do not access or distribute illegal, discriminatory, harassing or sexually explicit material, bypass web filtering or security monitoring, or download software or media from untrusted sources.

4.7 Cloud services. Users store and process [Organisation] information only in services on the approved list kept by the Information Security Manager; a new service is assessed under GOV-PRO-06 before use. Personal cloud storage, note-taking and messaging services are not used for work information above Public.

4.8 Removable media. Removable media is used only with the Information Security Manager's written approval of the specific need; approved media is encrypted, issued by the IT Manager, recorded in GOV-REG-24 and disposed of under GOV-PRO-16.

4.9 Personal devices. A personal phone or computer is used for work only when enrolled in [Organisation]'s device management under GOV-PRO-22, with a passcode, encryption, current updates, [Organisation]'s ability to remove its data, and no Confidential or Restricted information outside the managed applications. Nobody else uses the device while work data is on it.

4.10 AI tools. Users use AI tools only when approved in AI-REG-04, for the uses listed there, under AI-POL-01. Personal data, customer confidential material, credentials, keys and source code are never entered into such a tool unless the register entry permits it. The user checks any output before relying on it and remains responsible for it.

4.11 Information handling. Users classify, label, store, share, print and dispose of information under GOV-PRO-16, keep desks and screens clear under GOV-POL-04, and work away from the office under GOV-POL-05.

4.12 Intellectual property and testing. Users do not copy licensed software or infringe copyright, do not take [Organisation] information, source code or customer data with them when they leave, and do not probe or attempt to defeat any system's security controls unless authorised in writing.

4.13 Monitoring notice. [Organisation] logs the use of its devices, networks, accounts and services and may inspect that activity to protect security and investigate a suspected breach of policy or law. Monitoring is proportionate, follows GOV-PRO-14 and is described in GDPR-TPL-02. Users have no expectation of privacy on [Organisation] systems beyond what the law requires.

4.14 Reporting. Users report a suspected incident, mistaken disclosure or policy breach immediately under GOV-PRO-07. Prompt reporting of a mistake is expected; concealing one is itself a breach.

4.15 Consequences. A breach is handled under the disciplinary process in GOV-PRO-18 and may lead to withdrawal of access, dismissal, contract termination or referral to law enforcement.

4.16 Acknowledgement. Each user acknowledges this policy at induction, after each material change and yearly thereafter, recorded by Human Resources in GOV-REG-23. Access to Confidential or Restricted information depends on a current acknowledgement.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-23 Policy acknowledgement register.
  • The approved services list and AI-REG-04 AI tool approval register.
  • Incident reports in GOV-REG-08 and disciplinary records held by Human Resources.

6. Exceptions

Only the Information Security Manager may grant an exception, in writing, for a named person, a stated reason and a fixed period of at most twelve months, recorded under GOV-PRO-24.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this policy annually, after an incident caused by misuse, and when a new class of service or tool comes into use. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01 and trigger re-acknowledgement under 4.16.

  • GOV-POL-06 Authentication, password and multi-factor policy
  • GOV-PRO-16 Asset management, classification and handling procedure
  • GOV-PRO-18 Human resources security procedure
  • AI-POL-01 Acceptable use of AI tools policy

Information security policy

The top-level policy, signed by the Chief Executive Officer, that states what [Organisation] commits to for information security and privacy, the principles every other document follows, and the topic policies and procedures that are mandatory.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 5.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 5.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.1; SOC 2 CC1.1; GDPR Article 32. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This policy states the intent of [Organisation]'s leadership for information security and privacy. Every other policy, procedure and register in the management system derives from it and may not contradict it.

2. Scope

It applies to all information that [Organisation] owns, processes or is entrusted with, in any form and location; to all systems, networks and services inside the scope defined in ISMS-STM-01; and to every employee, contractor, intern and supplier representative who handles that information.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Chief Executive Officer Signs this policy, sets the risk appetite, provides resources, chairs management review.
Information Security Manager Maintains this policy and the topic documents, runs the risk process, reports performance.
Privacy Officer Applies the policy to personal data, advises on legal duties, decides on rights requests and breach notification.
Line managers Make their staff aware of the policy, check that access matches role, act on breaches.
All staff and suppliers Follow the policy and the topic documents, report incidents and weaknesses.

4. Policy statements

4.1 Commitment. [Organisation] protects the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information, and the rights and freedoms of the people whose personal data it processes, in proportion to risk and in line with the legal, regulatory and contractual obligations recorded in GOV-REG-04.

4.2 Principles. Every control decision follows these principles: risk drives priority; least privilege and need to know govern access; security and privacy are designed in before a system or supplier is used; protection never relies on a single control; everyone is accountable for the information they handle; evidence is kept so that conformity can be shown.

4.3 Objectives. The Chief Executive Officer approves measurable information security objectives at least annually through ISMS-PLN-01. Each objective has a measure, a target, an owner and a reporting frequency recorded in GOV-REG-21. The Information Security Manager reports progress to the steering committee quarterly and to management review.

4.4 Risk management. Risks to information are identified, assessed, treated and reviewed using GOV-PRO-05. A risk above the appetite approved by the Chief Executive Officer is treated or formally accepted under GOV-PRO-24; it is never left unrecorded.

4.5 Legal and contractual compliance. The organisation identifies and meets its obligations under GOV-PRO-25, including the security of processing required by GDPR Article 32 and the security terms it has accepted from customers.

4.6 Mandatory topic policies. The following documents carry the force of this policy and bind everyone within their scope.

Document Topic
GOV-POL-01 Governance framework, roles and decision rights
GOV-POL-02 Acceptable use of devices, accounts and services
GOV-POL-04 Clear desk and clear screen
GOV-POL-05 Remote and mobile working
GOV-POL-06 Authentication, passwords and multi-factor
PIMS-POL-01 Privacy information management
PIMS-POL-02 Data retention and disposal
PIMS-POL-03 International transfer of personal data
GDPR-POL-01 Data protection
AI-POL-01 Acceptable use of AI tools
AI-POL-02 AI system development, procurement and deployment
SOC-POL-01 Processing integrity, where that category is in scope

4.7 Mandatory operating procedures. Access management (GOV-PRO-10), asset classification and handling (GOV-PRO-16), change management (GOV-PRO-09), vulnerability and patch management (GOV-PRO-11), backup (GOV-PRO-12), business continuity (GOV-PRO-13), logging and monitoring (GOV-PRO-14), secure development (GOV-PRO-15), cryptography (GOV-PRO-20), supplier security (GOV-PRO-06) and incident management (GOV-PRO-07) are operated as written. A deviation needs an approved exception under GOV-PRO-24.

4.8 People. Every person receives security and privacy induction within [Number] working days of starting and refresher training at least annually under GOV-PRO-08, and confirms in writing that they have read this policy and GOV-POL-02. Acknowledgements are recorded in GOV-REG-23.

4.9 Incidents. Everyone reports a suspected incident or weakness immediately through the channel in GOV-PRO-07. No one is penalised for a report made in good faith.

4.10 Consequences. A breach of this policy or of a topic document is handled under the disciplinary process in GOV-PRO-18 for staff and under the contract for suppliers. A deliberate or negligent breach may lead to dismissal or termination of contract and, where the law requires it, to referral to the authorities.

4.11 Communication. The Information Security Manager publishes this policy in the approved document location, includes it in induction, and makes it available to interested parties on request. A summary suitable for customers and suppliers is maintained alongside it.

4.12 Continual improvement. Nonconformities, incident lessons, audit results and measurement results feed corrective action under GOV-PRO-04 and management review under GOV-PRO-03.

5. Records and evidence

  • The signed copy of this policy and its revision history in GOV-REG-01.
  • GOV-REG-23 Policy acknowledgement register.
  • GOV-REG-21 Security objectives and measures tracker.
  • Management review minutes (GOV-TPL-03) recording the annual review of this policy.

6. Exceptions

No exception to this policy is permitted. Exceptions to topic policies and procedures follow GOV-PRO-24.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this policy annually, and earlier after a major incident, a change in law or contract that affects it, a change in scope, or an audit finding about leadership. The Chief Executive Officer signs the policy again after every change of meaning.

Approved and signed by the Chief Executive Officer: [Name], version [Number], [Date].

Clear desk and clear screen policy

The rules that keep information off unattended desks, screens, printers, whiteboards and shared spaces, in the office and at home, and how compliance is checked.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.7. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This policy prevents information from being read, photographed or taken by anyone who should not see it, simply because it was left on a desk, a screen, a printer or a whiteboard.

2. Scope

It applies to everyone who works for [Organisation], in every office, shared workspace, meeting room, home workplace and public place where work is done, and to paper, screens, whiteboards, removable media and printed output.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
All staff Apply the statements below every day and leave shared spaces as they found them.
Line manager Provides lockable storage for their team and acts on repeat findings.
Facilities Manager Provides lockable storage, confidential waste bins and pull printing, and carries out the monthly check with the Information Security Manager.
Information Security Manager Owns the policy, records check results and reports trends to the steering committee.

4. Policy statements

4.1 Screen lock. Every device locks automatically after no more than [Number] minutes of inactivity, and in no case more than ten, and the user locks it manually whenever they leave it, however briefly.

4.2 Paper and media. Paper and removable media holding Confidential or Restricted information are locked in a drawer or cabinet whenever the desk is unattended and at the end of every day. Keys and access cards are not left in locks or on desks.

4.3 Credentials. Passwords, PINs, recovery codes and one-time codes are never written on paper, on a whiteboard or in an unprotected file. The approved password manager is the only place they are stored, under GOV-POL-06.

4.4 Printing. Print jobs are collected immediately. Pull printing is used wherever the device supports it. Anyone who finds an uncollected printout places it in confidential waste. Restricted information is printed only under the conditions in GOV-PRO-16.

4.5 Whiteboards and meeting rooms. Whiteboards and flip charts are wiped or removed at the end of every meeting. Meeting rooms are left with no papers, media or connected devices, and any shared screen is disconnected.

4.6 Confidential waste. Paper that holds Internal information or above goes into a locked confidential waste bin or a cross-cut shredder, never into general waste or recycling.

4.7 Shared and hot desks. A shared desk is cleared completely at the end of each use. Work papers are not stored in unlocked pedestals, trays or lockers.

4.8 Screen positioning. Screens are positioned so that they cannot be read from windows, corridors or visitor areas. A privacy filter is used on any screen that shows Confidential or Restricted information in a public place or an open area shared with other organisations.

4.9 Visitors. No Confidential or Restricted material is visible in a room while a visitor is present. A screen shared with a visitor shows only the content the meeting needs, with notifications switched off.

4.10 Post and deliveries. Incoming post marked Confidential or Restricted is handed unopened to the addressee. Outgoing Confidential post is sealed and tracked.

4.11 Home working. The same rules apply at home under GOV-POL-05. Work papers are kept in a lockable container, and devices are locked whenever another member of the household could reach them.

4.12 Checks. The Facilities Manager and the Information Security Manager walk every office area at least monthly outside working hours, record each item found (area, item, classification, action), secure the item and inform its owner. A person with a second finding in twelve months is referred to their line manager, and a third is handled under the disciplinary process in GOV-PRO-18.

4.13 Acknowledgement. Every person acknowledges this policy at induction and after each change, recorded in GOV-REG-23.

5. Records and evidence

  • Monthly clear desk check records with findings and actions.
  • GOV-REG-23 Policy acknowledgement register.
  • Incident reports in GOV-REG-08 where a finding caused an exposure.

6. Exceptions

A team that must keep Confidential paper out during a working session (for example a records review) works in a room that is locked when unattended and clears it at the end of the day. No standing exception applies.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this policy annually, after a move or refit of premises, and after an incident involving exposed paper or screens. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Remote and mobile working policy

The conditions under which [Organisation] staff work from home, while travelling and from other locations, covering devices, networks, physical security, printing, calls, the privacy of household members and incident reporting.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.7; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.1; SOC 2 CC6.6; SOC 2 CC6.7. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This policy sets the conditions for working away from [Organisation] premises, so that information receives the same protection at home, in transit and in public places as it does in the office, and so that the people who share those places are not drawn into [Organisation]'s business.

2. Scope

It applies to everyone who works for [Organisation] and performs any work outside its premises, whether regularly from home, occasionally while travelling, or from a co-working space, customer site or other location, on any device that holds or reaches [Organisation] information.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Remote worker Meets the conditions below before working remotely and keeps meeting them.
Line manager Agrees remote working arrangements and confirms the worker has suitable equipment and storage.
Information Security Manager Owns the policy, confirms home arrangements for Restricted roles, approves working abroad with Human Resources.
IT Manager Provides managed devices, the remote access gateway and remote wipe under GOV-PRO-22 and GOV-PRO-21.

4. Policy statements

4.1 Agreement. Remote working is agreed in writing with the line manager. A role that handles Restricted information from home starts only after the Information Security Manager has confirmed that the home workplace meets statements 4.4 and 4.8.

4.2 Devices. Remote work is done on devices issued and managed by [Organisation] under GOV-PRO-22, or on a personal device enrolled under GOV-POL-02. Nobody other than the assigned user, including family members, uses a device that holds [Organisation] information.

4.3 Connections. Access from outside [Organisation] premises goes through the remote access gateway with multi-factor authentication under GOV-PRO-21. Public or shared wireless networks are used only with the gateway active. A home router has its default administrator password changed, current firmware and current wireless encryption. Shared or public computers are never used for work.

4.4 Physical security at home. The worker chooses a space where the screen cannot be seen through a window or by visitors, locks the device whenever leaving it, and stores devices and papers in a lockable drawer or cabinet when not in use. Devices are never left in a vehicle.

4.5 Travel. Devices travel as hand luggage and are never left unattended. A privacy filter is used in public places. Restricted information is not worked on in public, and Confidential matters are not discussed where they can be overheard. At a border crossing the worker carries only the data the trip needs; if a device is inspected or taken out of sight, the worker reports it on arrival under GOV-PRO-07 so that credentials can be rotated and the device checked.

4.6 Working from another country. Working from outside the country of employment for more than [Number] days in a year needs written approval from Human Resources and the Information Security Manager, because of data transfer rules under PIMS-POL-03, employment and tax law, and systems restricted by country.

4.7 Printing and paper. Printing away from the office is avoided. Where unavoidable, Confidential information is printed only from the managed device, collected immediately, stored locked, and cross-cut shredded or returned to the office confidential waste. Restricted information is never printed away from the office. Work paper never goes into household waste.

4.8 Calls and video. Confidential conversations take place where others cannot overhear, using headphones. Smart speakers and voice assistants are switched off or removed from the room during Confidential calls. The camera background shows no work information. Calls are recorded only with the participants' consent.

4.9 Privacy of household members. [Organisation]'s device management reads device status and work applications only and, on a personal device, no personal content. Monitoring is limited to what GOV-POL-02 describes. The worker does not record household members' personal data in work systems, and cameras are not required in a private space when audio is sufficient.

4.10 Mobile phones. Work accounts are used on a phone only inside the managed profile, with a passcode or biometric lock and automatic locking.

4.11 Incident reporting. A lost or stolen device, a suspected compromise, a mistaken disclosure, an inspection of a device by an authority, or access to work data by a household member is reported within one hour under GOV-PRO-07. [Organisation] may wipe the device remotely and the worker cooperates with the response.

4.12 Equipment. Equipment issued for remote working stays assigned to the worker in GOV-REG-24, is not modified or lent, and is returned on request and on leaving under GOV-PRO-16.

4.13 Acknowledgement. Before first working remotely the worker acknowledges this policy, recorded in GOV-REG-23.

5. Records and evidence

  • Written remote working agreements held by Human Resources.
  • GOV-REG-23 Policy acknowledgement register.
  • GOV-REG-24 entries for equipment assigned to remote workers.
  • Approvals for working from another country.
  • Incident reports in GOV-REG-08.

6. Exceptions

An exception to statements 4.2, 4.3 or 4.7 is granted only by the Information Security Manager in writing, for a named person and a fixed period, and recorded under GOV-PRO-24.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this policy annually, after an incident involving remote or mobile working, and after a change to the remote access technology. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Authentication, password and multi-factor policy

The rules for passwords, password managers, multi-factor authentication, secrets, lockout, initial credentials, recovery and sessions on every [Organisation] system, for people and for services.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.17; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.5; SOC 2 CC6.1. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This policy sets how people and services prove who they are to [Organisation] systems, so that a stolen or guessed password is not enough to get in and secrets do not leak through code, chat or documents.

2. Scope

It applies to every account on every system [Organisation] owns, administers or subscribes to, including user, administrator, service and emergency accounts, and to every password, key, token and certificate used to authenticate to them.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
All users Choose and protect credentials as stated below, enrol in multi-factor authentication, report suspected exposure.
System Owner Configures each system to enforce these statements, or records a risk acceptance.
IT Manager Operates the identity provider, password manager, secrets store and help desk recovery process.
Information Security Manager Owns the policy, reviews configuration evidence quarterly, approves exceptions.

4. Policy statements

4.1 One identity per account. Every account belongs to one person or one named service under GOV-PRO-10, and every system above Public classification requires authentication before access.

4.2 Length. A user password or passphrase is at least 14 characters. Systems accept at least 64 characters and impose no rules on mixing character types. A passphrase of several unrelated words is encouraged.

4.3 Screening. A new password is rejected if it appears on a list of known breached or common passwords, or contains the user's or [Organisation]'s name.

4.4 No scheduled expiry. Passwords change only on suspected compromise, when a person who knew a shared or privileged credential leaves, or where a system cannot meet 4.7 and its risk acceptance requires it. The last [Number] passwords may not be reused.

4.5 Unique passwords. Every account has its own password; a work password is never reused for a personal account or another [Organisation] system.

4.6 Password manager. Every user keeps work credentials in the password manager approved by the IT Manager, protected by a passphrase of at least 20 characters and multi-factor authentication. Credentials are not kept in browser stores, documents, spreadsheets or notes.

4.7 Multi-factor authentication. Multi-factor authentication is required for all remote and privileged access and for every other system that supports it, enrolled before first use. Privileged accounts and identity administrators use phishing-resistant methods (hardware security keys or platform authenticators); other users may use an authenticator application; text message codes are a documented fallback only. Users deny and report any prompt they did not initiate.

4.8 Secrets. Passwords, keys, tokens, certificates and connection strings are never placed in source code, committed configuration, tickets, chat, email, documents or spreadsheets. They live in the secrets store under GOV-PRO-20 with a named owner and an expiry date. A secret found exposed is rotated within 24 hours and reported under GOV-PRO-07.

4.9 Service accounts and keys. Service credentials and API keys are generated at random with at least 32 characters, scoped to the minimum permissions, rotated at least annually and when a person who had access leaves, and recorded in GOV-REG-13.

4.10 Lockout. An account locks after no more than ten consecutive failed attempts, for at least 15 minutes or with a progressive delay. Lockouts are logged and repeated lockouts raise an alert under GOV-PRO-14. A privileged account stays locked until an administrator has confirmed the holder's identity.

4.11 Initial credentials. A first or reset credential is unique, delivered through a channel separate from the account name, valid for no more than 24 hours and changed at first use. Default vendor credentials are changed before a device or application connects to the network.

4.12 Recovery. The help desk resets a credential or re-enrols multi-factor authentication only after verifying identity independently of the request (a call back to a registered number, line manager confirmation or an in-person check), never on a single email or chat request. Self-service resets require multi-factor authentication. Recovery codes are kept in the password manager.

4.13 Sessions. Sessions end after no more than [Number] minutes of inactivity, and sooner for privileged sessions as set by the System Owner. Sensitive actions require re-authentication. Users sign out of shared devices.

4.14 Protection of credentials. Credentials travel only over encrypted channels, are stored only as salted hashes from an algorithm family approved under GOV-PRO-20, and are never written to logs.

4.15 Prohibited behaviour. Users do not share credentials, write them down, enter them on a page reached from a message link without checking the address, or use them on an unmanaged device.

4.16 Configuration evidence. Each System Owner keeps an export of the settings that enforce these statements, refreshed after any change and at least yearly, which the Information Security Manager reviews quarterly.

5. Records and evidence

  • Authentication configuration exports for each system.
  • Multi-factor enrolment, lockout and reset reports from the identity provider and help desk.
  • GOV-REG-13 Privileged account register with rotation dates.
  • Exposure incidents in GOV-REG-08.

6. Exceptions

A system that cannot meet a statement is recorded with compensating controls under GOV-PRO-24, approved by the Information Security Manager and reviewed at least every twelve months. No exception applies to statement 4.8.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this policy annually, after a credential-related incident, and when the identity provider or password manager changes. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Document Control Procedure

How every policy, procedure, plan and record in the management system is created, identified, approved, published, changed, retained and withdrawn.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 7.5; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 6.5; SOC 2 CC2.2; SOC 2 CC5.3. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure keeps the management system's documented information under control, so that staff always work from the approved version, auditors can trace every change, and withdrawn documents cannot be mistaken for current ones.

2. Scope

It applies to every document and record that the information security and privacy management system requires: policies, procedures, plans, statements, registers, forms and the records those forms produce. It applies in every format, including word-processed files, spreadsheets, wiki pages, tickets and exported reports.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Document owner Writes and maintains the document, proposes changes, answers questions about it.
Reviewer Checks the content for accuracy and fit with other documents before approval.
Approver Authorises the document for use. A policy is approved by the role named in its control block.
Information Security Manager Runs this procedure, keeps the master list (GOV-REG-01), publishes approved versions, withdraws superseded ones.
All staff Use only the current version from the approved location and report errors to the owner.

4. Procedure

4.1 Identification. The owner assigns the next free identifier from the master list in the form [Prefix]-[Type]-[Number], for example ISMS-POL-03. The identifier never changes for the life of the document and is never reused.

4.2 Control block. Every document carries a control block with identifier, title, type, owner role, approver role, classification, version, effective date and next review date, and a revision history table. Registers carry the identifier and purpose in rows 2 to 9 of the workbook.

4.3 Drafting. The owner drafts the document in the approved template, writes a version number of 0.x while it is a draft, and marks the status as Draft in the master list.

4.4 Review. At least one reviewer who did not write the document reads it and records comments. The owner resolves every comment or records why it was declined.

4.5 Approval. The approver confirms the document in writing, by signature or by an approval record in the document system. The owner sets the version to 1.0 for a first issue, or increments the major number for a change of meaning and the minor number for a correction that does not change meaning.

4.6 Publication. The Information Security Manager places the approved version in the single approved location, updates GOV-REG-01 with version, date and location, and announces the change through the channel named in the communication plan. Only the approved location is authoritative; copies elsewhere are uncontrolled.

4.7 Change. A change request names the document, the reason, the proposed text and the requester. Changes follow steps 4.3 to 4.6. A change that affects another document triggers a review of that document within thirty days.

4.8 Review cycle. Each document is reviewed on the date in its control block, at least annually, and earlier after an incident, an audit finding, a change in law or contract, or a change in the organisation that affects the document. The outcome of a review is recorded even when nothing changes.

4.9 Withdrawal. When a document is superseded or no longer needed, the Information Security Manager marks it Withdrawn in GOV-REG-01, removes it from the approved location, and keeps one archived copy marked as withdrawn.

4.10 Records. Records produced by following a document (for example a completed access review, a signed acknowledgement, an audit report) are retained for the period in the retention schedule, protected against alteration, and kept legible and retrievable.

4.11 External documents. Standards, laws, contracts and supplier documents that the management system relies on are listed in GOV-REG-01 with their source and version, and are not altered.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-01 Master list of documents and records: the index of every controlled document with status, version, owner, location and review dates.
  • Approval records for every issued version.
  • Review records, including reviews that resulted in no change.
  • The archive of withdrawn versions.

6. Exceptions

A document may be issued without a separate reviewer only when the approver reviews it personally and records that fact in the revision history. No other exception applies.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually and after any audit finding about documented information. Proposed changes follow section 4.

8. Related documents

  • GOV-REG-01 Master list of documents and records
  • GOV-POL-01 Information security and privacy governance framework

Internal audit procedure

How [Organisation] plans, performs, reports and follows up internal audits of the management system so that every requirement and every applicable control is independently checked within the audit cycle.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.2.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.2.2; SOC 2 CC4.1; SOC 2 CC4.2. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure produces independent, evidence-based information about whether the management system conforms to the organisation's own documents and to the frameworks it has adopted, and whether it is effectively implemented and maintained.

2. Scope

It covers every internal audit of the management system: the clause 4 to 10 requirements of ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the applicable Annex A controls in ISMS-REG-01, the ISO/IEC 27701 extensions where adopted, and the SOC 2 criteria in scope. Supplier audits follow GOV-PRO-06. External certification audits are outside this procedure but are prepared for with GOV-CHK-03.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Executive sponsor Approves the audit programme and the annual plan, receives every report, decides on disputed gradings.
Information Security Manager Maintains the programme in GOV-REG-02, schedules audits, tracks corrective actions. May not audit areas they operate.
Internal Auditor Plans and performs the audit, grades findings, writes the report, verifies closure.
Auditee (the manager of the area audited) Provides access, people and evidence, responds to findings, owns corrective actions.
Steering committee Reviews audit results quarterly and trends annually.

4. Procedure

4.1 Programme. The Information Security Manager proposes, and the executive sponsor approves, an audit programme covering a cycle of [Number] years (three years is recommended, matching a certification cycle). The programme schedules audits so that every clause 4 to 10 requirement, every control declared applicable in ISMS-REG-01 and every SOC 2 criterion in scope is audited at least once per cycle. Areas with High or Critical risks in GOV-REG-05, open major nonconformities, recent incidents or significant change are audited at least annually. The programme is recorded in GOV-REG-02 and detailed each year in ISMS-PLN-03.

4.2 Independence. An auditor never audits work they performed, managed or designed. Where the organisation cannot find an independent internal auditor for an area, the Information Security Manager engages a competent person from another department or an external auditor. Independence is recorded for each audit in GOV-REG-02.

4.3 Competence. Before leading an audit alone, an auditor has completed training in audit technique, can explain the requirements being audited, and has taken part in at least [Number] audits under an experienced lead. The competence record is held under ISMS-PRO-02. The Internal Auditor keeps their knowledge current through at least one refresher activity a year.

4.4 Planning. At least ten working days before fieldwork, the Internal Auditor issues an audit plan to the auditee stating the scope, the criteria (documents, clauses, controls), the dates, the people to be interviewed, the records to be made available, and the checklist questions drawn from ISMS-REG-04. The auditee confirms availability within three working days.

4.5 Opening meeting. The Internal Auditor opens the audit with the auditee, confirms scope and timing, explains the grading scale in 4.7, and agrees how evidence will be shared and how confidential material will be handled.

4.6 Evidence gathering. The Internal Auditor collects evidence by document review, interview, observation and sampling of records, and records the source of every piece of evidence. Samples are chosen by the auditor, not the auditee, from the full population for the period under review. The minimum sample is one item for a control operating annually, two for quarterly, three for monthly, five for weekly, and twenty-five for daily or continuous controls, or the whole population where it is smaller. Evidence must show the account, system, date and person involved. A statement without evidence is recorded as unverified, not as conforming.

4.7 Grading. Each finding receives one grade.

Grade Meaning
Major nonconformity A requirement is not implemented, a control has failed systematically, or several minor findings show the same cause.
Minor nonconformity A single lapse against a requirement that does not undermine the control as a whole.
Observation Evidence of a weakness that could become a nonconformity if not addressed.
Opportunity for improvement A way to make a conforming process more effective or efficient.

A nonconformity is written in four parts: the requirement, the evidence seen, the gap between them, and the grade.

4.8 Closing meeting. The Internal Auditor presents every finding to the auditee before leaving, confirms the facts, and records any disagreement. A disputed grading is referred to the executive sponsor, whose decision is final.

4.9 Report. The Internal Auditor issues the report using GOV-TPL-01 within ten working days of the closing meeting to the auditee, the Information Security Manager and the executive sponsor, and records the finding counts by grade and the report reference in GOV-REG-02.

4.10 Corrective action. The auditee raises a corrective action request using GOV-TPL-02 for every major and minor nonconformity, and the Information Security Manager logs it in GOV-REG-03. The auditee proposes a root cause and a plan within ten working days of the report, or within five working days for a major nonconformity. Observations and opportunities are logged with a decision to act or not act. GOV-PRO-04 governs the rest of the process.

4.11 Follow-up. The Internal Auditor verifies the closure evidence for each nonconformity and records the result. A major nonconformity is re-audited within ninety days of the report. An audit is marked Closed in GOV-REG-02 only when every nonconformity it raised is Verified or Closed in GOV-REG-03.

4.12 Reporting to management. The Information Security Manager summarises audit results, open findings and overdue actions for the steering committee each quarter and for management review under GOV-PRO-03.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-02 Audit programme and findings: the programme, each audit's status and finding counts.
  • ISMS-PLN-03 Annual internal audit plan.
  • Audit plans, completed ISMS-REG-04 checklists and evidence files for each audit.
  • Audit reports on GOV-TPL-01.
  • GOV-REG-03 Corrective action log and the GOV-TPL-02 forms behind it.
  • Auditor competence records under ISMS-PRO-02.

6. Exceptions

An audit may be postponed by up to one quarter with the written approval of the executive sponsor, recorded in GOV-REG-02 with the reason. No requirement or applicable control may be left unaudited across a full cycle.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after any external audit finding about internal audit, and when the scope or the adopted frameworks change. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

8. Related documents

  • GOV-REG-02 Audit programme and findings
  • GOV-TPL-01 Internal audit report template
  • GOV-TPL-02 Corrective action request form
  • GOV-REG-03 Corrective action log

Management review procedure

How top management reviews the management system at planned intervals, which inputs must be considered, which outputs must be decided, and how the resulting actions are recorded and tracked to completion.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.3.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.3.3; SOC 2 CC1.2; SOC 2 CC4.1. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

Management review is where leadership judges whether the management system is still suitable, adequate and effective, and decides what to change and what to fund. This procedure makes the review repeatable and its decisions traceable.

2. Scope

It applies to every management review of the information security and privacy management system, including the privacy elements under ISO/IEC 27701 and the SOC 2 criteria in scope. Steering committee meetings under GOV-POL-01 are not management reviews unless they follow this procedure in full.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Chief Executive Officer Chairs the review, takes the decisions, approves the minutes.
Information Security Manager Prepares the input pack, acts as secretary, logs and tracks actions in GOV-REG-22.
Privacy Officer Presents the privacy inputs and the status of data subject rights and breaches.
Heads of function (Engineering, Operations, Human Resources, Finance) Attend, present inputs for their area, own the actions assigned to them.
Internal Auditor Presents audit results and the status of corrective actions.

4. Procedure

4.1 Frequency. The Chief Executive Officer holds a full management review at least once every twelve months. A second review each year is recommended. An additional review is held within thirty days of a major incident, a significant change in scope or organisation, or a major nonconformity from an external audit.

4.2 Attendance. The review is valid when the Chief Executive Officer or a deputy named in writing, the Information Security Manager, the Privacy Officer and at least half of the heads of function attend. The secretary records attendance and apologies on GOV-TPL-03.

4.3 Preparation. Ten working days before the review, the Information Security Manager circulates an input pack with one section per mandatory input in 4.4, each with the data, its source register and a proposed decision where one is needed. Presenters confirm their sections five working days before the review.

4.4 Mandatory inputs. The agenda follows this order and no input may be skipped. Where there is nothing to report, the minutes say so.

Input Source
Status of actions from previous reviews GOV-REG-22
Changes in external and internal issues and in interested parties' needs ISMS-PRO-01, ISMS-REG-03
Nonconformities and corrective actions, with trends GOV-REG-03, GOV-PRO-04
Monitoring and measurement results ISMS-PRO-04, GOV-REG-21
Internal and external audit results GOV-REG-02, GOV-TPL-01
Fulfilment of information security and privacy objectives GOV-REG-21, ISMS-PLN-01
Feedback from interested parties, including complaints and customer questionnaires ISMS-REG-03, GOV-REG-04
Results of risk assessment and status of the risk treatment plan GOV-REG-05, GOV-REG-06
Incidents and personal data breaches, including lessons GOV-REG-08, PIMS-REG-03
Supplier performance and assurance GOV-REG-07
Compliance with legal, regulatory and contractual obligations GOV-REG-04
Opportunities for continual improvement All presenters

4.5 Conduct. For each input the presenter gives a summary, the chair states a decision (accept, act, or investigate), and the secretary records any action with an owner and a due date. The chair confirms or revises the risk appetite, the scope and the objectives for the next period.

4.6 Mandatory outputs. Before closing, the chair records decisions on: opportunities for continual improvement; changes needed to the management system, its policies, scope or objectives; and the resources needed, including budget, people and external support. A decision to provide no additional resource is recorded as a decision, with the reason.

4.7 Minutes. The secretary issues the minutes on GOV-TPL-03 within five working days. The chair approves them within a further five working days. Approved minutes are stored in the approved document location and listed in GOV-REG-01.

4.8 Action tracking. The secretary enters every action in GOV-REG-22 within two working days of the review, with owner, due date and the input it arose from. Owners report progress monthly. An action overdue by more than thirty days is escalated to the chair. An action is marked Completed only when evidence of completion is referenced in the tracker.

4.9 Communication. The Information Security Manager communicates relevant decisions to staff and, where appropriate, to customers and suppliers through ISMS-PLN-02 within ten working days.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-TPL-03 Management review minutes, approved by the chair, for every review.
  • The input pack and the data it drew on.
  • GOV-REG-22 Management review action tracker, showing every action from raising to completion with evidence.
  • Attendance records.

6. Exceptions

The twelve-month interval may be extended by no more than one month on the written decision of the Chief Executive Officer, recorded in GOV-REG-22 with the reason. No mandatory input may be omitted.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually and after any external audit finding about management review. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Nonconformity and corrective action procedure

How [Organisation] records a nonconformity, contains it, finds its root cause, corrects the cause, verifies that the correction worked, and learns from the pattern across many nonconformities.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 10.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 10.2; SOC 2 CC4.2; SOC 2 CC5.3. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

A nonconformity is any failure to meet a requirement of the management system, whether the requirement comes from a kit document, an adopted framework, a law or a contract. This procedure turns each one into a verified improvement rather than a repeated fix.

2. Scope

It applies to every nonconformity, whatever its source, across the information security and privacy management system. Incident response itself follows GOV-PRO-07; this procedure starts when an incident review identifies a failed or missing control.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Anyone Raises a suspected nonconformity.
Information Security Manager Logs every nonconformity in GOV-REG-03, assigns an owner, runs the monthly review, performs trend analysis, closes minor nonconformities.
Action owner Contains the problem, leads the root cause analysis, implements the corrective action, provides evidence.
Verifier A person other than the action owner who checks effectiveness. Usually the Internal Auditor or the Information Security Manager.
Executive sponsor Closes major nonconformities and decides on actions that need resources beyond the owner's authority.
Privacy Officer Co-owns nonconformities involving personal data and decides whether a breach assessment under PIMS-PRO-04 is needed.

4. Procedure

4.1 Sources. Nonconformities arise from internal audits (GOV-PRO-02), external audits, incidents and post-incident reviews (GOV-PRO-07), management review (GOV-PRO-03), monitoring and measurement results (ISMS-PRO-04), complaints from customers or data subjects, supplier reviews, readiness assessments and staff reports. All are handled the same way.

4.2 Raising. The person who finds the problem completes the first part of GOV-TPL-02: what was observed, where, when, and the requirement it appears to breach. The Information Security Manager logs it in GOV-REG-03 within two working days, assigns a reference, a grade (Major, Minor, Observation or Opportunity, as defined in GOV-PRO-02) and an action owner, and sets the status to Open.

4.3 Correction. The action owner first contains the problem: stops the nonconforming activity, restores the control, or limits the consequences. The correction is recorded on GOV-TPL-02 with its date. For a major nonconformity the correction is in place within five working days; for a minor, within twenty.

4.4 Deciding on corrective action. Correction removes the symptom; corrective action removes the cause. The action owner and the Information Security Manager decide whether corrective action is needed by asking whether the problem could recur, whether it has occurred before, whether the same cause could exist elsewhere, and what the impact of recurrence would be. A major nonconformity always needs corrective action. The decision and its reasons are recorded.

4.5 Root cause analysis. The action owner leads the analysis with the people who do the work, using the five whys for a simple failure or a fishbone (cause and effect) diagram where several factors interact. The analysis stops at a cause the organisation can act on, not at "human error". The root cause is written on GOV-TPL-02 and in GOV-REG-03.

4.6 Corrective action plan. The action owner writes the plan on GOV-TPL-02: the actions, the person responsible for each, the resources needed and the due date. The due date is within thirty days of raising for a major nonconformity and within ninety days for a minor, unless the executive sponsor approves a longer period in writing. The Information Security Manager records the plan and sets the status to In progress.

4.7 Extending the check. Before closing the plan, the action owner checks whether the same cause exists in other systems, teams or locations, and raises a linked entry in GOV-REG-03 for each place where it does.

4.8 Implementation. The action owner implements the plan, attaches evidence of each completed action to GOV-TPL-02, and updates any document the change affects through GOV-PRO-01. Where the action changes a risk, the owner updates GOV-REG-05.

4.9 Effectiveness verification. After the corrected process has operated for at least ninety days, or for three operating cycles where the control runs less often, the verifier tests whether the nonconformity has recurred and whether the control now operates as intended. The verifier samples records from the period, interviews the people involved and inspects the configuration or output. The result (Effective or Not effective), the method, the date and the verifier's role are recorded on GOV-TPL-02 and in GOV-REG-03, and the status becomes Verified. A result of Not effective reopens the root cause analysis at 4.5.

4.10 Closure. The Information Security Manager closes a minor nonconformity and the executive sponsor closes a major one, in each case only after the verification is recorded as Effective. The closer signs GOV-TPL-02 and the status becomes Closed. Observations and opportunities are closed when the decision to act or not act is recorded.

4.11 Monthly review. The Information Security Manager reviews GOV-REG-03 monthly, chases overdue actions, and escalates any action more than thirty days overdue to the executive sponsor.

4.12 Trend analysis. Each quarter the Information Security Manager analyses closed and open entries by source, area, requirement and root cause category, identifies repeated causes, and reports the trends with proposed systemic actions to the steering committee and to management review.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-03 Corrective action log: every nonconformity from raising to closure.
  • GOV-TPL-02 Corrective action request forms with evidence attached.
  • Quarterly trend analysis reports.
  • Updated documents and risk entries resulting from corrective actions.

6. Exceptions

A due date may be extended once, by the executive sponsor in writing, with the reason recorded in GOV-REG-03. The verification period in 4.9 may be shortened only where the control runs continuously and the verifier can test at least twenty-five records.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually and after any audit finding about corrective action. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Risk assessment and treatment methodology

The single method [Organisation] uses to value assets, identify and score information security and privacy risks, decide how to treat them, link treatment to the Statement of Applicability, and keep the results current.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 8.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 8.3; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.4.1.2; SOC 2 CC3.1; SOC 2 CC3.2; SOC 2 CC3.3; SOC 2 CC3.4; GDPR Article 32. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This methodology makes risk assessment repeatable, puts treatment decisions at the right level, and lets the Statement of Applicability trace back to the risks that justify it.

2. Scope

It applies to every risk to the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information within the scope in ISMS-STM-01, including risks from suppliers, cloud services and AI systems. Risks to individuals follow PIMS-PRO-02; AI threats use the AI-PRO-01 catalogue with these scales.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Chief Executive Officer Approves the criteria and appetite; accepts Critical risks.
Executive sponsor Accepts High risks; approves the risk treatment plan.
Information Security Manager Owns this methodology and GOV-REG-05, facilitates assessments, consolidates the treatment plan, maintains ISMS-REG-01.
Risk owner Manager with authority over the asset or process; decides treatment, accepts Low risks, keeps entries current.
Asset owner Values the asset; supplies the facts on threats, vulnerabilities and controls.
Privacy Officer Joins every assessment involving personal data; links results to PIMS-REG-08.

4. Procedure

4.1 Criteria and appetite. The Chief Executive Officer approves the scales, bands and authorities below as the risk criteria. The appetite: no risk stays High or Critical without an approved treatment plan or a time-limited acceptance under GOV-PRO-24; Medium risks are treated where the cost is proportionate.

4.2 Asset valuation. The asset owner rates each asset in GOV-REG-10 from 1 to 3 on confidentiality, integrity, availability, legal consequence and reputational consequence. The highest rating is the asset value.

Rating Meaning
1 Inconvenience absorbed within normal operations.
2 Measurable harm: lost working time, a contractual complaint, a correctable legal exposure, local reputational damage.
3 Serious harm: regulatory action, loss of a major customer, harm to individuals, public loss of trust.

4.3 Identifying risks. The Information Security Manager runs a workshop with each area's asset owners at least annually. For each asset or process the group considers seven threat categories (environmental events, technical failure, human error, insider misuse, external attack, supplier failure, legal or contractual change) and six vulnerability categories (technical weakness, missing or weak control, process gap, skill or awareness gap, physical exposure, contractual gap).

4.4 Scenario method. Each risk is a scenario, not a category. The group imagines the incident, asks how it would be detected and by whom, then works back to the causes and the controls that would have prevented it. In GOV-REG-05 the scenario reads: a named threat exploits a named vulnerability on a named asset, with a stated consequence. Each scenario has one owner.

4.5 Likelihood. The group rates the likelihood within twelve months, with the controls operating today.

Level Name Definition
1 Rare No known occurrence in the sector; needs an exceptional combination of events.
2 Unlikely Seen in comparable organisations; not expected here within five years.
3 Possible Could occur within one to five years; precursors seen.
4 Likely Expected within the year; happened here or at a close peer in the last three years.
5 Almost certain Expected more than once a year, or already occurring.

4.6 Impact. The group rates the worst credible consequence, considering the asset value and the five dimensions in 4.2.

Level Name Definition
1 Negligible Absorbed within the day; no external party affected; cost below [Number].
2 Minor Disruption under one day; a few individuals or one customer affected; no notification.
3 Moderate Disruption of one to three days; a notifiable breach or contractual breach possible; cost up to [Number].
4 Major Disruption over three days; regulatory notification; loss of a key customer; significant harm to individuals.
5 Severe Threatens the viability of a service or the organisation; enforcement action; serious harm to many individuals.

4.7 Score, matrix and band. The score is likelihood multiplied by impact: 1 to 4 Low, 5 to 9 Medium, 10 to 15 High, 16 to 25 Critical. GOV-REG-05 calculates both.

Likelihood and impact Impact 1 Impact 2 Impact 3 Impact 4 Impact 5
Likelihood 5 5 Medium 10 High 15 High 20 Critical 25 Critical
Likelihood 4 4 Low 8 Medium 12 High 16 Critical 20 Critical
Likelihood 3 3 Low 6 Medium 9 Medium 12 High 15 High
Likelihood 2 2 Low 4 Low 6 Medium 8 Medium 10 High
Likelihood 1 1 Low 2 Low 3 Low 4 Low 5 Medium

4.8 Acceptance authority. One authority per band accepts the risk or approves its treatment plan.

Band Authority Condition
Low Risk owner Record the decision; review annually.
Medium Information Security Manager with the risk owner Treat where proportionate, else accept with a reason; review twice a year.
High Executive sponsor Treatment plan required; acceptance only under GOV-PRO-24, at most twelve months; review quarterly.
Critical Chief Executive Officer Treatment starts within thirty days; acceptance only under GOV-PRO-24, at most ninety days; review monthly until High or below.

4.9 Treatment options. The risk owner records one option in GOV-REG-05: Modify (add or improve controls), Retain (accept at the current rating under 4.8), Avoid (stop or change the activity), or Share (insurance or contract; accountability stays with the organisation).

4.10 Link to the Statement of Applicability. For every Modify treatment the risk owner names the Annex A controls and implementing kit documents in the treatment plan column. The Information Security Manager marks those controls Applicable in ISMS-REG-01 with the risk IDs as justification. A control marked Not applicable may not appear in any treatment plan. Controls applicable for legal or contractual reasons alone cite GOV-REG-04.

4.11 Raw, treated and target ratings. Raw: likelihood and impact today, with existing controls as they actually operate. Treated: the residual values expected once the treatment is implemented and verified. Target: the band the risk owner intends to reach, within appetite. GOV-REG-05 holds both and calculates both scores; the target band is stated in the treatment plan.

4.12 Risk treatment plan. The Information Security Manager consolidates all Modify treatments into one plan with actions, owners, resources, due dates and residual ratings. The executive sponsor approves the plan, risk owners approve their entries, and the authority in 4.8 accepts each residual risk in writing.

4.13 Review and triggers. The Information Security Manager reviews GOV-REG-05 at the frequency in 4.8 and reassesses everything at least annually. Affected scenarios are reassessed within twenty working days of an incident or breach, an audit finding, a new system, supplier or processing activity, a significant change to architecture, location or organisation, a legal or contractual change, credible threat intelligence, or a DPIA result. Each assessment leaves a dated record of attendees, scenarios, ratings and decisions; superseded ratings are kept.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-05 Information security risk register.
  • GOV-REG-06 Risk acceptance and exception register.
  • ISMS-REG-01 Statement of Applicability.
  • The approved risk treatment plan and workshop records.

6. Exceptions

No alternative scale or band may be used. A unit reporting on a corporate scale maps this scale to it in writing, approved by the Information Security Manager, without changing the ratings here.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this methodology annually, after any audit finding about risk management, and when the appetite, scope or frameworks change. The Chief Executive Officer approves changes to scales, bands or authorities.

  • GOV-REG-05 Information security risk register

Supplier and Third Party Security Procedure

How suppliers and other third parties are tiered, assessed before use, bound by contract, monitored while in use and exited without losing or exposing information.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.19; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.20; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.21; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.22; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.23; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.2.6; ISO/IEC 27701 Annex B 8.5.6; SOC 2 CC9.2; GDPR Article 28. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure controls the risk that a supplier, contractor or cloud service brings to [Organisation]'s information, so that the organisation knows which third parties can reach its information, has assessed each in proportion to that reach, holds the right contract terms, and can leave any of them without losing or exposing data.

2. Scope

It applies to every external party that stores, processes, transmits or can access [Organisation]'s information or systems: cloud and software services, hosting and managed service providers, contractors with accounts, advisers who receive confidential material, and their sub-processors. Where [Organisation] is a processor for its clients, client obligations flow down through this procedure. Suppliers of goods with no information access are recorded at Tier 4 only.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Supplier owner The business role that requested the supplier. Tiers it, collects evidence, holds the reviews, runs the exit.
Information Security Manager Sets tier criteria, assesses due diligence, approves security terms for Tier 1 and Tier 2, keeps GOV-REG-07.
Privacy Officer Decides whether the supplier is a processor, approves processor terms and transfer safeguards, keeps PIMS-REG-06.
Procurement or finance [Role] Releases no purchase order or payment for a supplier not Approved or Conditional in GOV-REG-07.
Legal [Role] Confirms the contract carries the clauses in step 4.5.
Supplier Answers truthfully, provides evidence, notifies incidents within the contracted time, cooperates with reviews and exit.

4. Procedure

4.1 Tiering. Before any contract, trial or free account, the supplier owner assigns the highest tier whose criteria apply and records it in GOV-REG-07.

Tier Criteria Examples
1 Critical Holds Restricted information or personal data of more than [Number] individuals, holds privileged access to production, or its failure stops a critical service within one day Hosting platform, identity provider, payroll processor
2 Important Holds Confidential information or any personal data, or has user-level access to internal systems Collaboration tools, source code hosting, contractor with an account
3 Standard Holds Internal information only and is readily replaceable Training provider, travel booking
4 Low No access to information or systems Office supplies, catering

4.2 Due diligence. The supplier owner collects the evidence for the tier and the Information Security Manager assesses it before approval. Tier 1: the full GOV-TPL-04 questionnaire, a current independent certificate or assurance report covering the service, review of that report under SOC-PRO-02, a penetration test summary from the last twelve months and a financial viability check. Tier 2: the full GOV-TPL-04 questionnaire, or a current certificate whose scope is confirmed to cover the service. Tier 3: the organisation, access control, incident and exit domains of GOV-TPL-04 as a self-attestation. Tier 4: the register entry only. Services with AI features are also assessed under AI-PRO-02. The score and open gaps are recorded in GOV-REG-07.

4.3 Processor determination. The Privacy Officer applies PIMS-PRO-01 to decide whether the supplier processes personal data on [Organisation]'s behalf. Where it does, no personal data is shared until processor terms meeting GDPR Article 28 are signed, using PIMS-TPL-02 or the supplier's own terms reviewed with GDPR-TPL-09. The Privacy Officer records the supplier in PIMS-REG-06, assesses any transfer outside the region under PIMS-POL-03 using GDPR-TPL-08, and records the safeguard in PIMS-REG-05.

4.4 Gaps and risk. Each gap found in due diligence is closed before approval in one of three ways: a remediation commitment with a date written into the contract, a compensating control operated by [Organisation], or an exception accepted under GOV-PRO-24 and recorded in GOV-REG-06. For Tier 1 and Tier 2 the Information Security Manager records the residual supplier risk in GOV-REG-05 using GOV-PRO-05.

4.5 Contract. Before signature the legal [Role] confirms the contract contains, as the tier requires: confidentiality; the security measures the supplier described in its answers; annual assurance evidence, and for Tier 1 a right to audit; notification of incidents affecting [Organisation] within [Number] hours of awareness (24 hours by default for Tier 1, 72 for Tier 2); sub-contracting only with prior notice and the same obligations flowed down; data location and transfer restrictions; return and verified deletion of data at exit within [Number] days; service levels and continuity commitments for Tier 1; and compliance with applicable law. The contract reference is entered in GOV-REG-07.

4.6 Onboarding. The supplier owner requests access under GOV-PRO-10 with named accounts, least privilege, multi-factor authentication and an end date. Contractors sign the confidentiality agreement and policy acknowledgement under GOV-PRO-18. Interfaces are recorded in GOV-REG-25. The Information Security Manager sets the GOV-REG-07 status to Approved, or to Conditional while a contracted remediation is open.

4.7 Monitoring in service. The supplier owner holds a service review quarterly for Tier 1 and annually for Tier 2, covering performance, incidents, service changes and sub-processor notices. The Information Security Manager tracks supplier security notices, records incidents affecting [Organisation] in GOV-REG-08, obtains renewed certificates or reports at expiry, and re-tiers the supplier when its data or access changes. A tier increase repeats step 4.2.

4.8 Annual review. By the next review date in GOV-REG-07 the supplier owner and the Information Security Manager confirm the tier, obtain current assurance, confirm the contract still describes the service, check the supplier's access against GOV-REG-12, review the year's incidents and performance, and record the outcome. The next review is set twelve months ahead, or six months for a Tier 1 supplier with an open finding.

4.9 Supplier incidents. An incident reported by or suspected at a supplier is handled under GOV-PRO-07 with the supplier owner as liaison. Where personal data is involved the Privacy Officer runs PIMS-PRO-04 from the moment [Organisation] becomes aware. A supplier that misses its notification obligation is recorded as a nonconformity in GOV-REG-03 and its tier and status are reviewed.

4.10 Exit. On termination or non-renewal the supplier owner removes access within one working day under GOV-PRO-10, obtains the data in an agreed format, obtains written confirmation of deletion including backups, revokes the keys and interfaces recorded in GOV-REG-18 and GOV-REG-25, and sets the status to Exited with the confirmation reference. Tier 1 suppliers have an exit plan from onboarding, and a data export is tested at least annually under GOV-PRO-26.

4.11 Sub-processors engaged by [Organisation]. Where [Organisation] processes personal data for clients, every supplier that touches that data is approved under this procedure, listed in PIMS-REG-06, and notified to clients as each client contract requires before it starts work.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-07 Supplier register: one row per supplier with tier, assurance, contract, reviews and status.
  • Completed GOV-TPL-04 questionnaires, certificates and assurance reports with assessment notes.
  • Signed contracts and processor terms; entries in PIMS-REG-06 and PIMS-REG-05.
  • Service review, annual review and exit records with deletion confirmations.
  • Supplier risks in GOV-REG-05 and exceptions in GOV-REG-06.

6. Exceptions

A Tier 1 or Tier 2 supplier may start work before due diligence completes only with the Chief Executive Officer's written approval, a completion date within thirty days and an entry in GOV-REG-06. Free, trial and personally registered services that hold Internal or higher information are not exempt. No other exception applies.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after any Severity 1 or Severity 2 supplier incident, after a change in processor obligations or applicable law, and after an audit finding about suppliers. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.
