Information Security Incident Management Procedure

How security events are reported, triaged, graded, contained, investigated, recovered from, communicated and reviewed, and when a personal data breach process is started alongside.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.24; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.25; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.26; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.27; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.28; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.8; SOC 2 CC7.3; SOC 2 CC7.4; SOC 2 CC7.5. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure gets every security event reported quickly, graded consistently and handled by named roles, so that harm is limited, evidence survives, notification duties are met on time and each incident makes the next one less likely.

2. Scope

It covers every event and incident affecting the confidentiality, integrity or availability of [Organisation]'s information, systems, services or people, wherever it occurs, including suspected incidents, near misses and incidents reported by clients or suppliers. Where personal data is involved PIMS-PRO-04 runs alongside this procedure. Where an AI system is involved AI-PRO-03 applies in addition.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
All staff and contractors Report events within one hour of noticing, preserve what they see, do not investigate or discuss outside the response team.
First responder [Role] Logs the report in GOV-REG-08, triages within one hour, escalates to the Incident Lead.
Incident Lead The Information Security Manager or a named delegate. Declares the incident, sets severity, directs the response, keeps the record, decides closure, chairs the review.
Technical lead Contains, collects evidence, eradicates and recovers, with system owners.
Communications lead Drafts internal updates and external statements and holds the single approved version.
Privacy Officer and legal adviser Decide regulatory, contractual and data subject notifications, set evidence preservation requirements, liaise with authorities.
Executive sponsor The Chief Executive Officer or delegate. Approves external communication and decisions that stop a service or involve law enforcement.

4. Procedure

4.1 Reporting. Staff report through [Channel], published in GOV-POL-02 and at induction, within one hour of noticing an event. External parties use the contact published under GOV-PRO-27. Suppliers report within their contracted time. The first responder records every report in GOV-REG-08 with a reference in the form [Prefix]-[Year]-[Number], the reporter, the times detected and reported, and the affected assets.

4.2 Triage. Within one hour the Incident Lead decides whether the report is a false positive (closed with the reason recorded), an event to monitor, or an incident. For an incident the Incident Lead assigns a severity from the matrix, opens a GOV-TPL-05 report and names the response team.

4.3 Severity matrix. Severity is raised as soon as the facts suggest it and lowered only on evidence.

Severity Definition Examples Response targets
1 Critical Confirmed compromise, loss or outage affecting Restricted information or a client-facing production service, a likely regulatory notification, or an attacker still active Ransomware on production, exfiltration of client data, compromised privileged account Lead engaged within 15 minutes, executive sponsor informed within one hour, updates every two hours
2 High Confirmed incident affecting Confidential information or one internal service, limited to few systems or individuals Standard account takeover, malware on one endpoint, personal data sent to the wrong recipient Lead within one hour, sponsor informed within four hours, daily updates
3 Medium Confirmed incident with limited impact and no exposure of personal or confidential information outside [Organisation] Lost encrypted laptop, phishing click with no credentials entered, policy breach without exposure Lead within four hours, working hours response, closed within ten working days
4 Low Event that did not become an incident, or a near miss Blocked phishing campaign, vulnerability found before exploitation Recorded and trended monthly

4.4 Personal data breach trigger. When an incident involves personal data, through loss, destruction, alteration, unauthorised disclosure or unauthorised access, the Incident Lead informs the Privacy Officer immediately and records the time [Organisation] became aware. PIMS-PRO-04 starts at that time, including the 72 hour assessment clock and, where [Organisation] is a processor, notification to the controller without undue delay.

4.5 Containment. The technical lead disables accounts, revokes sessions and tokens, blocks indicators and isolates hosts, keeping them powered where memory evidence is needed. Credentials that may have been exposed are rotated. Actions that affect client service need the Incident Lead's approval. Emergency changes are recorded under GOV-PRO-09 within one working day.

4.6 Evidence preservation. Before any action that would alter evidence, the technical lead copies the relevant logs under GOV-PRO-14, images affected systems for Severity 1 and Severity 2, records a hash value for every collected file, keeps a chain of custody record (who, what, when, where stored) and stores everything in a restricted evidence location. Screenshots show the account, system and time. Evidence is retained until closure plus the retention period, or longer under legal hold.

4.7 Investigation and eradication. The technical lead establishes the entry point, the timeline, the accounts and data affected and the extent of spread, then removes the cause: malware, the unauthorised access path, or the vulnerable component, patched under GOV-PRO-11 or reconfigured. Persistence is checked before recovery: new accounts, keys, scheduled tasks, mail rules and changed permissions.

4.8 Recovery. Systems are restored from clean backups under GOV-PRO-12 or rebuilt, verified before return to service, and monitored more closely for [Number] days. The system owner confirms return to normal service. Where recovery exceeds the recovery time objective, GOV-PRO-13 is invoked.

4.9 Communication. The Incident Lead issues internal updates at the severity cadence on a need to know basis. No statement goes to clients, regulators, data subjects, media, insurers, law enforcement or suppliers without the executive sponsor's approval and review by the Privacy Officer and legal adviser. Regulatory and data subject notifications follow PIMS-PRO-04 and GDPR-TPL-10; contractual notifications follow the timelines recorded in GOV-REG-04. Every notification is logged in GOV-TPL-05 with time, recipient and content.

4.10 Closure. The Incident Lead closes the incident when the cause is removed, service is recovered, notifications are complete, evidence is stored, GOV-TPL-05 is complete and GOV-REG-08 holds the containment and resolution times, root cause and lessons.

4.11 Post-incident review. For every Severity 1 and Severity 2 incident, and any Severity 3 incident the Incident Lead selects, the Incident Lead holds a review within ten working days of closure using GOV-TPL-11. Actions are raised in GOV-REG-03 under GOV-PRO-04, GOV-REG-05 is updated, control changes go through GOV-PRO-09, and human factor findings feed GOV-PRO-08.

4.12 Metrics. The Information Security Manager reports monthly: events and incidents by type and severity, time to detect, report, contain and recover, the share of reviews held within ten working days, and overdue actions. The quarterly trend goes to management review under GOV-PRO-03 and to GOV-REG-21.

4.13 Exercise. The Incident Lead runs a tabletop exercise at least annually on a Severity 1 scenario that includes a personal data breach, records it in GOV-REG-16 and raises findings in GOV-REG-03.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-08 Incident register: every event and incident with times, severity, breach flag, root cause and status.
  • GOV-TPL-05 Incident report form per incident, with timeline and notification log.
  • GOV-TPL-11 Post-incident review per Severity 1 and Severity 2 incident.
  • Evidence files with hash values and chain of custody records.
  • PIMS-REG-03 for personal data breaches, GOV-REG-16 for exercises, GOV-REG-03 for actions.

6. Exceptions

There is no exception to reporting. Where a Severity 1 incident makes the normal approval route unavailable, the Incident Lead acts and records the approvals obtained afterwards within one working day.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after every Severity 1 incident, after each exercise, after an audit finding and after a change in notification law or client contract terms. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Security and privacy awareness and training procedure

How every person who works for [Organisation] receives the security and privacy knowledge their role needs, from induction through annual refreshers, role-based modules and phishing simulation, and how the results are recorded and measured.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 7.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 7.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.3; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 6.4.2.2; SOC 2 CC1.4; SOC 2 CC2.2. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure sets out how [Organisation] plans, delivers, records and measures security and privacy awareness and training, so that every person understands the policies that apply to them, recognises the attacks they are most likely to face, and knows how to report a problem.

2. Scope

It applies to employees, contractors, temporary staff and interns who hold an account on any [Organisation] system or who handle [Organisation] information. Supplier personnel are covered through the supplier's own training obligations under GOV-PRO-06. It covers induction, the annual refresher, role-based training, phishing simulation and awareness messages.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Information Security Manager Owns the programme, approves content, runs the phishing simulation, keeps GOV-REG-09 and reports results to the steering committee.
Privacy Officer Writes and approves the privacy modules and the role-based training for staff who handle personal data.
Line manager Confirms that each new starter completes induction on time, nominates staff for role-based training and follows up overdue training.
Human Resources Notifies the Information Security Manager of every starter, role change and leaver, and holds the signed acknowledgements.
Trainer Delivers a session, completes GOV-TPL-10 and returns it within five working days.
All staff Complete the training assigned to them by the due date and apply it.

4. Procedure

4.1 Annual plan. Each year the Information Security Manager and the Privacy Officer write a training plan that lists every module, its audience, its delivery method, its due dates and its measure of success. The plan takes its topics from the risk register (GOV-REG-05), the incident register (GOV-REG-08), the previous year's phishing results and any audit finding about competence. The steering committee approves the plan.

4.2 Competence matrix. The Information Security Manager keeps a competence matrix listing each role group, the knowledge it needs, the module that provides it and the evidence of achievement, reviewed with the annual plan and when a new role group is created. ISMS-PRO-02 holds the matrix for roles with management system duties. The minimum content is:

Role group Mandatory modules Frequency
All staff Induction, annual refresher, phishing simulation Induction once, refresher yearly, simulation quarterly
Developers Secure coding, secrets handling, dependency hygiene Yearly, and before the first production change
System administrators Privileged access, logging, change and backup duties Yearly, and before privileged access is granted
Personal data handlers Lawful handling, data subject requests, breach recognition Yearly, and before first access to personal data
Managers Approving access, disciplinary handling, incident escalation Yearly
Incident responders Incident procedure walkthrough, evidence handling Yearly, plus one exercise

4.3 Induction. Human Resources tells the Information Security Manager about each starter before the start date. The starter completes the induction module within [Number] working days of starting, and in every case before being granted access to Confidential or Restricted information. Induction covers GOV-POL-03, GOV-POL-02, GOV-POL-06 and GOV-POL-04, classification and handling under GOV-PRO-16, recognising phishing and social engineering, reporting an incident under GOV-PRO-07, and the basics of personal data protection. The starter signs the policy acknowledgement, which Human Resources records in GOV-REG-23.

4.4 Annual refresher. Every person completes the refresher module within the calendar month set in the plan. It updates the induction topics with the past year's incidents, current phishing patterns and policy changes, and ends with an assessment of at least ten questions; the pass mark is [Number] per cent and a person who fails retakes the module within ten working days.

4.5 Role-based training. The line manager nominates staff for the role-based modules in the competence matrix. Role-based training is completed before the related access or duty is granted, and then yearly. The Privacy Officer delivers or approves the personal data modules. The Head of Engineering confirms each year that the developer and administrator modules reflect the current secure development and operational procedures.

4.6 Phishing simulation. The Information Security Manager runs a simulated phishing exercise at least quarterly, with a different scenario each time. Results are recorded by cohort and never used for disciplinary action on a first failure; anyone who clicked receives a short teaching page within one working day. A person who fails two consecutive simulations completes a targeted module within ten working days. The reporting rate is tracked alongside the click rate, because reporting is the behaviour the programme wants to build.

4.7 Awareness messages. Between formal modules the Information Security Manager issues a short awareness message at least monthly through the channel named in the communication plan: a current scam, a reminder of a rule, or a lesson from an incident with identifying details removed.

4.8 Delivery and recording. A trainer who delivers a live session completes GOV-TPL-10 with the content outline, attendance, assessment results and sign-off. For online modules the learning platform's completion report is the record. The Information Security Manager enters every completion, result and due date in GOV-REG-09 within five working days.

4.9 Overdue training. The Information Security Manager sends each line manager a list of overdue training monthly. Training more than thirty days overdue is reported to the steering committee, and the System Owner may suspend the person's access to Restricted information until the module is completed.

4.10 Measuring effectiveness. Each quarter the Information Security Manager reports: completion rate by module and role group, average assessment score, phishing click rate and reporting rate, the number of incidents reported by staff, and the number caused by a human error that training addresses. A measure that misses its target for two consecutive quarters raises a corrective action under GOV-PRO-04.

4.11 Content review. Every module is reviewed yearly, after a significant incident, after a change of law and after a change to a policy it teaches. The review date and reviewer are recorded against the module in the training plan.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-09 Training and awareness register: every module, person, due date, completion date and result.
  • GOV-TPL-10 Awareness session record and acknowledgement: the record of each live session.
  • GOV-REG-23 Policy acknowledgement register: the acknowledgements taken at induction and after policy changes.
  • The approved annual training plan and competence matrix.
  • Phishing simulation reports by quarter.
  • The quarterly effectiveness report to the steering committee.

6. Exceptions

A person who cannot complete induction within the set period because of an absence completes it within [Number] working days of returning and is not granted access to Confidential or Restricted information in the meantime. A request to exempt a role group from a module is handled as a risk acceptance under GOV-PRO-24. No other exception applies.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after any audit finding about competence or awareness, and after an incident whose root cause was a gap in training. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Change Management Procedure

How changes to production systems, infrastructure, configuration and security controls are requested, assessed, approved, tested, implemented, communicated and reviewed.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.32; SOC 2 CC8.1. Owner: Head of Engineering.

1. Purpose

This procedure controls change to [Organisation]'s production environment so that every change is assessed for security and service impact before it happens, approved by someone accountable for the affected system, tested, reversible, and traceable to a record that an auditor can follow from request to review.

2. Scope

It applies to changes to production infrastructure, platforms, applications, databases, network and security configuration, identity and access systems, cloud account settings, monitoring rules, and to the controls listed in the Statement of Applicability (ISMS-REG-01). It covers changes made by staff, contractors and suppliers acting on [Organisation]'s instruction. Source code work before release follows GOV-PRO-15; the release itself is a change under this procedure. Routine data entry and content updates within an application's normal use are not changes.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Change requester Completes GOV-TPL-08, supplies the assessment, test and rollback material, and answers the approver's questions.
System Owner Approves changes to the system they own at Low risk, co-approves at Medium risk, and confirms the post-implementation result.
Head of Engineering Chairs the change advisory group, approves Medium and High risk changes, and authorises emergency changes.
Information Security Manager Reviews every security-relevant change, sits on the change advisory group, and samples GOV-REG-11 quarterly.
Implementer Carries out the change exactly as approved and records the outcome. Never approves their own change.
Tester or reviewer Executes the test plan or reviews the configuration before approval. Is not the implementer.

4. Procedure

4.1 Change types. Every change is one of three types.

Type Definition Approval
Standard A repeatable, low risk change with a documented, tested procedure that the change advisory group has pre-approved and listed in the standard change catalogue. Pre-approved. Each execution is still logged.
Normal Any change that is not standard and is not an emergency. Per the authority table in 4.4, before implementation.
Emergency A change needed within hours to resolve an incident or remove an imminent security risk. Head of Engineering or on-call deputy, recorded. Retrospective record within two working days.

4.2 Request. The requester raises a change record in the change system, or on GOV-TPL-08, with: description, reason, systems and data affected, data classification, risk and impact assessment, test plan and evidence, rollback plan, implementation window, communication plan and the implementer's name. A request without a rollback plan is returned to the requester.

4.3 Risk and impact assessment. The requester rates the change Low, Medium or High using four criteria: the number of users or customers affected, the classification of data touched, whether a security control is changed, and how easily the change can be reversed. The highest criterion sets the rating. A change is security-relevant when it alters authentication, authorisation, network exposure, encryption, logging, backup, or a data flow to an external party. The Information Security Manager reviews every security-relevant change regardless of rating.

4.4 Approval authority.

Rating Approver Lead time
Low System Owner Before implementation
Medium System Owner and Head of Engineering At least two working days before the window
High Change advisory group (Head of Engineering, Information Security Manager, affected System Owners), which meets at least weekly At least five working days before the window

The approver is never the implementer. Approval is recorded with name, date and any conditions.

4.5 Standard change catalogue. The change advisory group admits a procedure to the catalogue only after it has succeeded at least three times as a normal change. The catalogue names the procedure, the systems it applies to, the roles allowed to run it and the checks performed. The group reviews the catalogue annually and removes any entry that has failed in the period.

4.6 Testing. The tester runs the test plan in a non-production environment that matches production configuration, attaches the results to the change record and states whether the change is ready. Configuration and infrastructure definition changes are peer reviewed and approved before they are merged. A change with failed or missing tests is not approved.

4.7 Scheduling and communication. The implementer schedules the change within the published maintenance windows. Affected users are told at least [Number] working days before a Medium or High change. Customer-facing notice follows the contractual commitment for each service.

4.8 Implementation. The implementer follows the approved plan and records start time, end time and result in the change record. If the success criteria are not met within the window, or an unplanned effect appears, the implementer executes the rollback plan and informs the approver. Any deviation from the approved plan stops the change until the approver agrees to the deviation in writing.

4.9 Emergency change. The implementer obtains approval from the Head of Engineering or the on-call deputy through any recorded channel, states the incident or risk that justifies it, implements with a second person present or observing where possible, and completes GOV-TPL-08 within two working days. The change advisory group reviews every emergency change at its next meeting.

4.10 Post-implementation review. The System Owner reviews every High and emergency change within five working days, and a sample of at least [Number] Low and Medium changes each month, confirming that the change achieved its purpose, caused no incidents and left documentation current. A failed change with a process cause raises a corrective action under GOV-PRO-04.

4.11 Related updates. Before the change is closed, the implementer updates the affected entries in GOV-REG-24, GOV-REG-25 and GOV-REG-10, and any network diagram or runbook the change affects. The Information Security Manager samples GOV-REG-11 quarterly to confirm each change has an approval, test evidence and a recorded result.

4.12 Supplier-initiated changes. The System Owner assesses a change notified by a supplier under its contract as a normal change and records the supplier's reference in the change record.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-11 Change log: one row per change with type, rating, approver, dates and result.
  • GOV-TPL-08 Change request form, or the equivalent change record, with test evidence and rollback plan attached.
  • The standard change catalogue and its annual review record.
  • Change advisory group minutes.
  • Post-implementation review records and the quarterly sample review.

6. Exceptions

The emergency path in 4.9 is the only exception to prior approval. A change found in production without a change record is recorded as a nonconformity under GOV-PRO-04 and, where it touched a security control, assessed as an incident under GOV-PRO-07.

7. Review and maintenance

The Head of Engineering reviews this procedure annually, after any change that caused an incident at one of the two highest severity levels in GOV-PRO-07, after an audit finding about change control, and when the deployment platform or change tooling is replaced. Changes to this procedure follow GOV-PRO-01.

Access management procedure (joiners, movers, leavers, privileged access, reviews)

How access to [Organisation] systems and information is requested, approved, granted, changed, reviewed and removed for joiners, movers, leavers, privileged users, break-glass accounts and service accounts.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.15; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.16; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.17; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.18; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.5; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 6.6.2; SOC 2 CC6.1; SOC 2 CC6.2; SOC 2 CC6.3. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure controls who can reach which systems and information at [Organisation], so that every account belongs to an identified person or an approved service, carries only the rights its role needs, is reviewed on a fixed cycle, and is removed as soon as it is no longer needed.

2. Scope

It applies to every account on every system that [Organisation] owns or administers: cloud consoles, applications, databases, network devices, code repositories, collaboration tools and the physical access system. It covers employees, contractors, supplier personnel with access and automated services.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Line manager Requests access for their staff, confirms the business need, reports movers and leavers on the day they are known.
System Owner Defines the access roles for the system, approves requests, runs the periodic access review.
Access administrator Grants, changes and removes access exactly as approved, records the action, holds no approval rights.
Information Security Manager Owns the procedure, keeps GOV-REG-12 and GOV-REG-13, checks that reviews happen, reports the metrics in 4.14.
Human Resources Provides the start, move and leave dates that drive the joiner, mover and leaver steps.
Account holder Uses only their own account, protects credentials under GOV-POL-06, reports access they can reach but should not.

4. Procedure

4.1 Access model. Each System Owner defines the access roles for their system (for example reader, editor, administrator), the permissions each role carries and the job roles entitled to each. Access is granted by role, never by copying another user's rights. The role definitions are the baseline for every review.

4.2 Principles. Every account identifies one person or one named service. Shared accounts are prohibited; where a product offers only one built-in administrator account, its credential is held in the password vault, checked out by name and rotated after each use. Access follows least privilege and need to know.

4.3 Request. The line manager completes GOV-TPL-09 naming the person, the systems, the access role, the business justification and, for temporary access, the end date. A request for Restricted information also records the data owner's agreement.

4.4 Approval. The System Owner approves or declines in writing within two working days. Approval is never given by the person who will hold the access or by the administrator who will grant it. A request for more than the standard role of the job role also needs the Information Security Manager's approval.

4.5 Joiner. Human Resources gives the access administrator the start date at least [Number] working days ahead. Standard access for the job role is provisioned to work on the first day and no earlier than one working day before, and the administrator records the grant on GOV-TPL-09. Access to Confidential or Restricted information is activated only after induction training is recorded in GOV-REG-09.

4.6 Mover. When a person changes role, team or line manager, the new line manager raises a new GOV-TPL-09 within five working days. The access administrator removes the rights of the old role before adding the rights of the new one, so that rights do not accumulate. The old and new System Owners both confirm the change.

4.7 Leaver. Human Resources, or the engaging manager for a contractor, tells the access administrator the last working day as soon as it is known. All access, including remote access, email, cloud consoles, code repositories, physical tokens and any shared secret the person knew, is disabled by the end of the last working day and never later than one working day after it. For a dismissal, or a person on notice who holds privileged access, access is disabled at notification. Disabled accounts are deleted or archived after [Number] days. The remaining tasks follow GOV-CHK-01.

4.8 Privileged access. Administrative rights sit in a separate, identifiable account from the one used for email and daily work. Privileged accounts require multi-factor authentication under GOV-POL-06, are listed in GOV-REG-13 with holder, system, justification, approver and review date, and are reviewed quarterly. Privileged sessions are logged under GOV-PRO-14. Standing privileged access is granted only where time-bound elevation is not possible.

4.9 Break-glass access. Each critical system has at least one emergency account whose credential is stored sealed in the password vault, retrievable only by the System Owner or the Information Security Manager. It is used only when normal privileged access is unavailable during an incident. Every use is logged automatically, reported to the Information Security Manager within one working day, followed by a credential rotation, and recorded in GOV-REG-13.

4.10 Service accounts. Each service account has a named human owner, a documented purpose, the minimum permissions for that purpose, no interactive login where the platform allows it, and a credential kept in the approved secrets store and rotated at least annually and whenever a person who knew it leaves. Service accounts appear in GOV-REG-13 and are reviewed with privileged accounts.

4.11 Supplier access. Supplier personnel receive named accounts for a defined period under GOV-PRO-06, sponsored by a System Owner who raises the leaver step when the engagement ends.

4.12 Access reviews. Each System Owner reviews every account and its rights quarterly for systems holding Confidential or Restricted information and for all privileged accounts, and annually for every other system. The review compares an account export taken on the review date with the current staff list and the role definitions in 4.1, and marks each account keep, change or remove. The access administrator applies the changes within five working days. The Information Security Manager records the review, the counts and the export location in GOV-REG-12. A review without an export is not a review.

4.13 Authentication. Accounts are created with a one-time credential that must be changed at first use, multi-factor authentication is enrolled before first remote or privileged use, and all other rules follow GOV-POL-06.

4.14 Metrics. The Information Security Manager reports quarterly: the percentage of leavers disabled within one working day, reviews completed on time, accounts removed or changed by reviews, and privileged accounts without a current justification.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-TPL-09 Access request and approval form for every grant and change.
  • GOV-REG-12 Access review log with the export reference for each review.
  • GOV-REG-13 Privileged account register, including service and break-glass accounts.
  • Leaver notifications and the administrator's disable confirmations.
  • Break-glass use reports and rotation records.

6. Exceptions

Temporary access outside this procedure is permitted only during an incident declared under GOV-PRO-07, is granted by the System Owner, lasts no longer than the incident, and is recorded in GOV-REG-13 within one working day. Any other departure, including a standing shared account, needs a risk acceptance under GOV-PRO-24.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after any audit finding about access control, after an incident involving misuse of access, and when a new class of system is introduced. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Vulnerability and Patch Management Procedure

How technical vulnerabilities in [Organisation]'s systems are discovered, rated, assigned, fixed within a severity-based deadline, verified and reported.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.8; SOC 2 CC7.1. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure finds technical vulnerabilities in [Organisation]'s systems before an attacker uses them, and fixes them within a deadline set by severity, with evidence that the fix worked.

2. Scope

It applies to every asset in GOV-REG-24 and GOV-REG-10 that runs software: servers, virtual machines, containers and their images, cloud services and their configuration, network devices, workstations and mobile devices, application code and its third party components, and software as a service that [Organisation] administers. Supplier-hosted systems are covered through the supplier's obligations under GOV-PRO-06; this procedure governs how [Organisation] tracks the supplier's remediation.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Information Security Manager Owns the programme, runs or commissions scanning, triages findings, assigns owners, approves severity adjustments and reports the metrics.
System Owner Remediates findings on their systems within the deadline, or requests an exception before the deadline passes.
Head of Engineering Provides patching capacity and approves emergency patch changes.
Platform and endpoint administrators Apply operating system, platform and endpoint updates on the cycle in 4.7.
Developers Fix code and dependency findings through GOV-PRO-15.

4. Procedure

4.1 Coverage. The Information Security Manager assigns every asset class in GOV-REG-24 a discovery method and cadence from the table in 4.3, and confirms quarterly that every production asset appears in at least one scan or inventory report from the period. An asset with no discovery method is itself recorded as a finding.

4.2 Sources. Findings come from authenticated vulnerability scans of hosts and network devices, container image and cloud configuration scans, dependency analysis in build pipelines (GOV-PRO-15), vendor and provider security advisories, threat intelligence and external reports handled under GOV-PRO-27, penetration tests, and incident investigations. Every source feeds the same register, GOV-REG-14.

4.3 Cadence by asset class.

Asset class Method Minimum cadence
Internet-facing hosts and services Authenticated and unauthenticated scan Weekly
Internal servers, virtual machines and cloud workloads Authenticated scan Monthly
Container images Image scan Every build, and weekly for images running in production
Application dependencies Dependency analysis Every build
Cloud account configuration Configuration assessment Continuous, or at least weekly
Workstations and mobile devices Device management compliance report Monthly
Network devices Authenticated scan or configuration review Quarterly
Whole environment Penetration test Annually, and before go-live of a new internet-facing service

4.4 Triage and severity. The Information Security Manager, or a delegate, reviews new findings within two working days, removes confirmed false positives with a written reason, and assigns a severity from the CVSS base score: Critical 9.0 to 10.0, High 7.0 to 8.9, Medium 4.0 to 6.9, Low 0.1 to 3.9. The severity is raised one band when the asset is internet-facing and holds Confidential or Restricted data, or when exploitation in the wild is reported. It is lowered one band only with a written justification approved by the Information Security Manager.

4.5 Deadlines. The found date is the date the source first reported the finding, not the date of triage. GOV-REG-14 calculates the deadline from severity and found date.

Severity Fix deadline
Critical 7 calendar days
High 30 calendar days
Medium 90 calendar days
Low Next scheduled maintenance cycle, and no later than 180 calendar days

A finding under active exploitation on an internet-facing asset is assessed within 24 hours and mitigated within 72 hours by patch, configuration change or removal of exposure, whichever is fastest.

4.6 Remediation. The System Owner fixes the finding by patch, upgrade, configuration change or removal of the vulnerable component, through a change under GOV-PRO-09. Critical and actively exploited findings may use the emergency change path. Where no fix exists, the owner applies a compensating control (network restriction, feature disablement, additional monitoring) and records it against the finding.

4.7 Routine patching cycle. Administrators apply operating system and platform updates at least monthly, and endpoint updates automatically as they are released (GOV-PRO-22). A system that cannot receive updates because it is out of vendor support is recorded in GOV-REG-24 with its end of support date and a replacement plan, and is isolated on the network until replaced (GOV-PRO-21).

4.8 Exceptions. When a deadline cannot be met, the System Owner raises a risk acceptance under GOV-PRO-24 before the deadline passes, naming the compensating controls and an expiry no more than twelve months away. The exception reference is recorded in GOV-REG-14. An overdue finding without an approved exception is reported to the Head of Engineering weekly until fixed.

4.9 Verification. A finding moves to Fixed only when a rescan shows it absent, or when the Information Security Manager confirms the fix by inspection where a rescan is not possible. The verifier and date are recorded. A finding that reappears is reopened with its original found date.

4.10 Metrics. The Information Security Manager reports monthly: open findings by severity, findings past deadline, mean days to fix by severity, assets not scanned in the period, and exceptions in force. The report goes to the Head of Engineering and feeds management review (GOV-PRO-03) and the objectives tracker (GOV-REG-21).

4.11 Retention. Scan and analysis reports are retained for at least twelve months. GOV-REG-14 is retained for the life of the management system.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-14 Vulnerability register: every finding with source, severity, deadline, owner, status and verification.
  • Scan, image and dependency analysis reports.
  • Penetration test reports and retest evidence.
  • Risk acceptances in GOV-REG-06 for findings past deadline.
  • Monthly metrics reports and the quarterly coverage confirmation.

6. Exceptions

Only the risk acceptance route in 4.8 applies. Nobody may close a finding without verification, or defer one without a recorded risk acceptance.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after any incident that exploited a known vulnerability, after an audit finding, and when a customer contract sets different deadlines. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Backup and Restore Testing Procedure

What is backed up, how often and for how long, how backups are protected from the events that threaten the originals, and how restores are tested so that recovery is known to work before it is needed.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.13; SOC 2 A1.2. Owner: Head of Engineering.

1. Purpose

This procedure keeps [Organisation]'s information recoverable. It defines the scope, frequency, retention and protection of backups, and a restore testing cycle whose results are recorded, so that recovery objectives are met in practice.

2. Scope

It applies to all production data and the configuration needed to rebuild production services: databases, file and object storage, application configuration, infrastructure definitions, identity and access configuration, logs held for retention, source code repositories, and the administrative data of software as a service where the provider does not back it up on [Organisation]'s behalf. Personal devices and non-production environments are out of scope unless they hold the only copy of a controlled record.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
System Owner Decides what is backed up for their system, its frequency, retention and recovery objectives, and signs off restore tests.
Backup administrator Configures and monitors backup jobs, performs restores and restore tests, records results in GOV-REG-15.
Information Security Manager Approves the protection design, reviews GOV-REG-15 quarterly, confirms alignment with the retention schedule.
Head of Engineering Owns this procedure, provides capacity and runs the annual recovery exercise.
Privacy Officer Confirms that retention and deletion of personal data in backups meet PIMS-POL-02.

4. Procedure

4.1 Backup requirements. For every system in GOV-REG-10, the System Owner records the data sets to back up, the recovery point objective and recovery time objective from the business impact analysis (GOV-TPL-07), and the retention period from the retention schedule (PIMS-REG-07). The backup administrator designs the schedule to meet them and records the design with the system.

4.2 Default frequency and retention. Unless the System Owner records a stricter requirement:

Data set Frequency Retention
Production databases Continuous or point-in-time capable, with a daily full copy 35 daily copies and 12 monthly copies
File and object storage Daily 90 days, with versioning where the platform supports it
Configuration, infrastructure definitions, identity configuration On every change and daily 12 months
Source code repositories Daily export to a separate account 90 days
Software as a service administrative data Weekly export where the provider offers it 12 months

Retention never exceeds the period the retention schedule allows for the data, except under a recorded legal hold.

4.3 Protection. Backups are encrypted at rest with keys managed under GOV-PRO-20, stored in a separate account, subscription or physical location from the systems they protect, and at least one copy is immutable or offline for its retention period. Credentials that can delete or alter backups are separate from production administration, require multi-factor authentication, and are listed in GOV-REG-13. Backup storage is logged under GOV-PRO-14.

4.4 Monitoring. The backup administrator reviews job results every working day. A failed job is investigated the same day and rerun. Two consecutive failures for a data set with a recovery point objective of 24 hours or less are reported as an incident under GOV-PRO-07.

4.5 Quarterly restore test. Each quarter the backup administrator restores at least one data set from every system rated priority 1 or 2 in the business impact analysis, and a rotating sample of the rest so that every data set is tested at least annually. The test restores to an isolated environment; verifies integrity by record counts, checksums, application start-up and a sample of records read by the System Owner; measures the time taken against the recovery time objective; and confirms the age of the data against the recovery point objective. The result, time, verifier and defects are recorded in GOV-REG-15. A failed test raises a corrective action under GOV-PRO-04 and a retest within 30 days.

4.6 Annual recovery exercise. Once a year the Head of Engineering recovers a complete critical service from backups and infrastructure definitions into a clean environment, as part of the exercise programme in GOV-PRO-13. The exercise is recorded in GOV-REG-16 and GOV-REG-15.

4.7 Operational restores. A restore into production requires the System Owner's written request, is performed as a change under GOV-PRO-09 (emergency path during an incident), and is recorded in GOV-REG-15 with the reason. Restored data is checked for records deleted since the backup was taken; deletions required by the retention schedule or by a data subject request are re-applied within five working days.

4.8 Personal data in backups. Backups are listed in the retention schedule as a storage location. Personal data in a backup is deleted when the backup expires rather than by selective deletion, and privacy notices and request responses say so. The Privacy Officer confirms this annually.

4.9 Decommissioned systems. When a system is retired, its final backup is retained for the retention period of its data, then deleted and recorded in GOV-REG-20. Keys needed to read a retained backup are retained for the same period (GOV-REG-18).

4.10 Supplier-held backups. Where a provider performs backups, the System Owner obtains the provider's backup and restore commitments in the contract (GOV-PRO-06) and tests an export or restore at least annually, recording it in GOV-REG-15.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-15 Backup and restore test log: every restore test and operational restore with time against objective.
  • Backup requirement entries per system, with the recovery objectives.
  • Backup job reports and failure tickets.
  • Restore requests and approvals.
  • Annual recovery exercise record in GOV-REG-16.

6. Exceptions

A data set may be excluded from backup only when the System Owner records in GOV-REG-10 that it can be regenerated from another backed-up source within the recovery time objective. Shortened retention or a missed quarterly test requires a risk acceptance under GOV-PRO-24.

7. Review and maintenance

The Head of Engineering reviews this procedure annually, after a failed restore test, after any incident involving data loss or destructive malware, when the backup platform changes, and when the retention schedule changes. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Business Continuity and ICT Readiness Procedure

How business impact is analysed, how continuity and ICT recovery strategies are chosen and planned, how security is maintained during a disruption, and how plans are exercised and improved.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.29; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.30; SOC 2 A1.2; SOC 2 A1.3. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure prepares [Organisation] to keep delivering its critical services, and to keep information secure, through a disruption. It sets how business impact is analysed, how strategies and plans are built, what the plans contain, how they are exercised and how lessons are applied.

2. Scope

It applies to all processes and systems in the management system scope (ISMS-STM-01), the people and suppliers they depend on, and the offices and remote working arrangements through which they are delivered. It covers disruptions from loss of a site, loss of a cloud provider or region, loss of a key supplier, loss of staff availability, and attacks that take systems offline.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Crisis lead (Chief Executive Officer or named deputy) Activates plans, takes decisions beyond delegated authority, approves external communication.
Business continuity coordinator (Information Security Manager) Runs this procedure, maintains the plans, schedules exercises, keeps GOV-REG-16.
Head of Engineering Owns ICT readiness: recovery designs, runbooks and technical exercises.
Process owners and System Owners Complete the business impact analysis, maintain their recovery runbooks, take part in exercises.
Communications lead Prepares and issues internal and external messages approved by the crisis lead.

4. Procedure

4.1 Business impact analysis. Each process owner completes GOV-TPL-07 for their process annually and when the process changes materially. The worksheet records dependencies (systems, data, people, suppliers, facilities), impact at four hours, one day, three days and one week, the maximum tolerable period of disruption, the recovery time objective, the recovery point objective and the minimum resources needed to operate. The coordinator consolidates the worksheets into a prioritised list of critical processes and systems, which the steering committee approves.

4.2 Strategy selection. For each critical process the coordinator and the process owner identify the options that meet the objectives (redundant infrastructure, alternative provider, manual workaround, reduced service, alternative workplace, cross-trained staff), estimate the cost and recovery time of each, and record the chosen strategy with the reason. The steering committee approves the strategies and the budget they need. A strategy that cannot meet its objective is recorded as a risk in GOV-REG-05.

4.3 ICT readiness. The Head of Engineering designs each critical system so that the approved strategy is achievable: redundancy across failure zones (GOV-PRO-19), backups that meet the recovery point objective (GOV-PRO-12), infrastructure definitions that can rebuild the service, and a documented recovery runbook stating the order of recovery, the people authorised to run it and the credentials they need, held under the break-glass arrangements in GOV-REG-13. Runbooks are reviewed after every change to the system under GOV-PRO-09.

4.4 Plan content. The business continuity plan and each recovery runbook contain: activation criteria and who may activate; roles and deputies; a contact tree held outside the primary systems; the recovery sequence and its dependencies; the minimum service to restore first; message templates for staff, customers and suppliers, and the inputs PIMS-PRO-04 needs where personal data is involved; and the point at which the plan is stood down and normal operation confirmed.

4.5 Security during disruption. Access control, logging, encryption and change control stay in force during recovery. Any relaxation (a shared recovery account, a temporary network opening, a manual process without logging) requires the crisis lead's approval, is recorded in the incident record with an expiry, and is reversed and verified before the incident closes.

4.6 Activation. A disruption is first handled as an incident under GOV-PRO-07. The incident lead recommends activation when the recovery time objective of a critical process is at risk; the crisis lead decides, and the decision and its time are recorded.

4.7 Exercise programme.

Exercise Cadence Minimum content
Tabletop walkthrough of the business continuity plan Annually Scenario, decisions, communication, gaps found
Technical recovery test of each critical system Annually, may be combined with the restore test in GOV-PRO-12 Recovery from backups and definitions into a clean environment, time measured against the objective
Full exercise with relocation or remote operation Every two years End-to-end recovery of at least one critical service
New critical system Within six months of go-live Technical recovery test

The coordinator sets objectives for each exercise in advance and records the outcome, the time achieved against the recovery time objective and the findings in GOV-REG-16.

4.8 Lessons and actions. Within ten working days of an exercise or a real disruption, the coordinator holds a review, records what worked and what did not, and raises each gap as an action in GOV-REG-03 with an owner and due date. Plans are updated within 30 days of the review.

4.9 Maintenance. The coordinator confirms the contact tree quarterly and reviews the plans after a change to a critical system or supplier, after an exercise or disruption, and at least annually.

5. Records and evidence

  • Completed GOV-TPL-07 worksheets and the consolidated priority list with steering committee approval.
  • GOV-REG-16 Business continuity exercise log: every exercise and activation with objectives, time achieved and findings.
  • The business continuity plan and recovery runbooks with version history.
  • Review records and the resulting GOV-REG-03 actions.
  • Records of security relaxations approved during a disruption and their reversal.

6. Exceptions

A critical system may go live without a technical recovery test only under a risk acceptance in GOV-PRO-24 that fixes the test date within six months of go-live.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after any activation, after an exercise that missed its objectives, and when the critical process list changes. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Logging, Monitoring and Alert Handling Procedure

Which events every system must record, how logs are synchronised, protected and retained, how alerts are triaged and reviewed, and the limits that keep monitoring proportionate to staff privacy.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.15; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.16; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.17; SOC 2 CC7.2. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure makes security-relevant activity visible. It defines the minimum events every system records, how logs are protected and kept, how alerts are triaged within set times, how often logs are reviewed, and the privacy limits on monitoring.

2. Scope

It applies to every system in GOV-REG-24 that authenticates users, holds Confidential or Restricted data, provides a network or security function, or forms part of the production environment, including cloud control planes, identity providers, endpoints and software as a service with audit log export. Logs produced by a supplier for [Organisation]'s tenancy are in scope where export is available.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Information Security Manager Owns the logging standard and the alert use cases, runs the review cadence, approves any monitoring that targets an individual.
Security analyst or on-call engineer Triages alerts within the response times in 4.6 and escalates incidents.
System Owner Connects their system's logs, maintains its event list, acts on findings.
Platform team Operates the central log store, time synchronisation and retention.
Privacy Officer Reviews monitoring use cases for proportionality and approves the staff notice.

4. Procedure

4.1 Minimum events. Every in-scope system records at least the following.

Event category Examples
Authentication Success and failure, multi-factor challenge results, password and token changes, account lockout
Privilege use Elevation to administrator, use of break-glass accounts, run-as actions
Account and permission changes Create, modify, disable, delete; group and role membership changes
Configuration changes Security settings, network rules, logging settings, deployments
Access to Restricted data Read, export, download, bulk query and sharing actions
Administrative actions Cloud console and API calls by privileged identities, key management operations
Security tooling Malware detection, scanner findings, loss prevention events, perimeter firewall denials
Operations Backup job results, job failures, service start and stop

4.2 Log content. Each record carries a timestamp in Coordinated Universal Time, the source system, the identity acting, the action, the object acted on, the outcome and the source address where available. Logs never contain passwords, keys, session tokens or payment card numbers, and contain personal data only where needed to identify the actor or the object.

4.3 Clock synchronisation. All systems synchronise to the same trusted time source. The platform team checks drift monthly and corrects any system more than one second adrift.

4.4 Centralisation and protection. Logs are forwarded to the central log store within fifteen minutes of generation. The store is append-only for the retention period, held in an account or tenancy separate from the systems it monitors, and readable only by the security role and auditors. Administrators of a system cannot alter or delete that system's logs in the central store. Loss of a log feed for more than one hour raises an alert.

4.5 Retention. Security logs are kept online and searchable for 90 days and retained for twelve months, or longer where GOV-REG-04 or a contract requires it, then deleted. Retention of logs that contain personal data is listed in PIMS-REG-07.

4.6 Alerting and triage. The Information Security Manager maintains a documented list of alert use cases, each with a priority and an owner. Priority 1 alerts (for example a successful login to a break-glass account, malware on a server, a mass download of Restricted data) are acknowledged within 15 minutes during supported hours and by the on-call engineer outside them; Priority 2 within four hours; Priority 3 by the next working day. The analyst records the triage outcome (true positive, benign, false positive, needs tuning) against the alert. A true positive becomes an incident under GOV-PRO-07.

4.7 Review cadence. The analyst clears the alert queue every working day. The Information Security Manager reviews privileged activity and break-glass use weekly, reviews alert tuning and feed health monthly, confirms quarterly that every in-scope system in GOV-REG-24 is sending logs, and reports alert volumes, triage times and coverage gaps to the Head of Engineering monthly.

4.8 Privacy limits. Monitoring is limited to the purposes of security, service operation and legal compliance. Staff are told what is monitored through GOV-POL-02. No individual is monitored beyond the standard use cases unless the Privacy Officer and the human resources lead approve a written request stating the legal basis, scope and duration. Access to monitoring data for an investigation is granted per case, logged and time-limited. Monitoring data is not used for performance management.

4.9 Onboarding. A new system is connected to the central log store, with its event list and alert use cases confirmed, before it goes live (PB-07, GOV-REG-29).

5. Records and evidence

  • The logging standard with the event list per system.
  • The alert use case list and triage records.
  • Weekly privileged activity reviews, monthly tuning and feed health reviews, quarterly coverage confirmations.
  • Clock drift checks.
  • Approvals for targeted monitoring and investigation access.

6. Exceptions

A system that cannot produce an event in 4.1 is recorded with the gap and a compensating control (for example a daily configuration comparison) under a risk acceptance in GOV-PRO-24.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after any incident where logs were missing or insufficient, after an audit finding, when the log platform changes, and when the law on workplace monitoring changes. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Secure Development Lifecycle Procedure

How security and privacy are built into software from requirements to release, covering threat modelling, the coding standard, peer review, pipeline checks, secrets, test data, environment separation, release approval and open source licences.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.25; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.26; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.27; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.28; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.29; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.30; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.31; SOC 2 CC8.1. Owner: Head of Engineering.

1. Purpose

This procedure builds security and privacy into software that [Organisation] develops or has developed for it, so that vulnerabilities are prevented or found before production and every release is traceable to reviewed, tested code.

2. Scope

It applies to all software developed by or for [Organisation] that runs in production or handles [Organisation] data: applications, interfaces, infrastructure definitions, automation scripts, data pipelines and machine learning components. It binds staff, contractors and outsourced developers. Configuration changes to third party software are covered by GOV-PRO-09.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Head of Engineering Owns this procedure and the secure coding standard, approves exceptions to merge rules.
Product owner Records security and privacy requirements in the backlog and accepts them as done.
Developers Follow the standard, review peers' changes, fix findings.
Security champion (one per team) Runs threat modelling, triages pipeline findings, liaises with the Information Security Manager.
Information Security Manager Sets the analysis tooling requirements, reviews threat models for high risk systems, tracks findings in GOV-REG-14.
Privacy Officer Reviews personal data requirements under PIMS-PRO-06 and approves test data exceptions.

4. Procedure

4.1 Security requirements. At the start of a new service or significant feature, the product owner records as backlog items with acceptance criteria: the classification of data handled, the authentication and authorisation model, logging per GOV-PRO-14, encryption per GOV-PRO-20, input validation, rate limiting, privacy requirements from PIMS-PRO-06, and legal or contractual requirements from GOV-REG-04. The feature is not accepted until these items pass.

4.2 Threat modelling. The security champion runs a threat modelling session for every new service, every new external interface, and every change to authentication, authorisation or data flows. The session draws the data flows and trust boundaries, lists threats per element using a recognised category list, decides a control or an accepted risk for each, and records the result with the design. Threat models for systems holding Restricted data are reviewed by the Information Security Manager and revisited annually.

4.3 Secure coding standard. Developers follow the standard maintained by the Head of Engineering, which covers at least: validate all input on the server; encode output for its context; use parameterised queries; use the platform's authentication and session frameworks rather than custom code; authorise every request on the server for the specific object requested; fail closed; handle errors without exposing internals; pin and verify dependencies; keep secrets out of code; log per GOV-PRO-14. Developers complete secure coding training at induction and annually (GOV-PRO-08).

4.4 Peer review. Every change to a production branch goes through a merge request that at least one developer other than the author approves after reading the change against the standard. Protected branch rules block direct pushes and merges without approval and passing checks. Changes to authentication, cryptography, payment or personal data handling are also reviewed by the security champion.

4.5 Pipeline checks. Every build runs static analysis, dependency vulnerability analysis, secret detection and licence checking. A Critical or High finding blocks the merge unless the Head of Engineering approves a time-limited exception recorded in GOV-REG-14. Findings are triaged within the deadlines in GOV-PRO-11.

4.6 Secrets management. Application secrets are generated and stored in the approved secrets store, injected at runtime, rotated per GOV-PRO-20, and never committed to a repository, placed in a ticket or shared in chat. A secret found in a repository is treated as compromised: it is rotated within one working day and the event is recorded in GOV-REG-14.

4.7 Test data. Non-production environments use synthetic or anonymised data. Production personal data may be used only with the Privacy Officer's written approval for a stated purpose and period, under the same access controls as production, and is deleted at the end of the period with the deletion recorded.

4.8 Separation of environments. Development, test and production run in separate accounts or network segments with separate credentials. Developers hold no standing write access to production. Deployments run through the pipeline under an approved change (GOV-PRO-09). Production data does not flow to lower environments except under 4.7.

4.9 Security testing. Dynamic application testing runs before each major release. A penetration test by a party independent of the development team is performed before go-live of an internet-facing service and at least annually afterwards. Findings go to GOV-REG-14 and are retested after the fix.

4.10 Release approval. A release is a change under GOV-PRO-09 and requires passing pipeline checks, peer approval, test evidence and a rollback plan. A new system also passes the go-live gate in PB-07, with the verdict recorded on GOV-TPL-12. The release record lists the components and versions deployed.

4.11 Open source and third party components. Developers use components only under licences on the approved list maintained by the Head of Engineering; copyleft and unknown licences require review before use. A component inventory is produced for every release and retained with it. Components are kept on supported versions and tracked in GOV-REG-24.

4.12 Outsourced development. Contracts with external developers require this procedure or an equivalent, [Organisation]'s ownership of the code and the right to review and test it, delivery through [Organisation]'s repositories and pipelines, and supplier management under GOV-PRO-06.

5. Records and evidence

  • Backlog items with security and privacy acceptance criteria and their acceptance.
  • Threat models and their reviews.
  • Merge request approvals, protected branch settings and pipeline results.
  • GOV-REG-14 entries for pipeline, test and penetration findings, and merge exceptions.
  • Test data approvals and deletion records.
  • Release records with component inventories and GOV-TPL-12 verdicts.

6. Exceptions

Merge blocking exceptions follow 4.5 and test data exceptions follow 4.7. Any other departure from this procedure requires a risk acceptance under GOV-PRO-24.

7. Review and maintenance

The Head of Engineering reviews this procedure annually, after any incident caused by a software defect, after an audit finding, and when a new language, platform or pipeline is adopted. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Asset management, classification and handling procedure

How [Organisation] keeps an inventory of information and the assets that hold it, assigns owners, classifies information into four levels, labels and handles it by level, recovers assets from leavers, and wipes or destroys media.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.9; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.10; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.11; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.12; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.13; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.14; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.10; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.14; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.10; SOC 2 CC6.1; SOC 2 C1.1; SOC 2 C1.2. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure keeps an accurate record of [Organisation]'s information and of the assets that store, process or transmit it, gives each one an accountable owner, classifies information by the harm its loss would cause, and sets the handling rules that follow from each classification.

2. Scope

It covers information in every form, including data in systems, documents, messages, recordings and printed material, and the assets that hold it: hardware, software, cloud services, storage media and paper. It applies to all staff, contractors and supplier personnel who handle [Organisation] information.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Asset Owner Accountable for an asset, classifies its information, approves access, sets handling, reviews the register entry yearly.
Custodian Operates the asset day to day on the owner's instructions, for example an administrator, a team or a provider.
Information Security Manager Keeps GOV-REG-10, checks completeness, runs the yearly reconciliation.
IT Manager Keeps GOV-REG-24 current for hardware and software, issues and recovers devices, carries out disposal.
All staff Label and handle information by its level, return assets on request and on leaving.

4. Procedure

4.1 Inventory. The Information Security Manager keeps GOV-REG-10 for information assets and the IT Manager keeps GOV-REG-24 for hardware and software. Every entry names an Asset Owner who is a role, a custodian, the location or system, the classification and the date of last review. New assets are registered before use: a new system at design, a new device at issue, a new cloud service at contract signature.

4.2 Valuation. The Asset Owner rates each information asset 1 to 3 for confidentiality, integrity and availability. The asset value is the highest of the three, as in GOV-PRO-05, and drives the classification and the risk assessment in GOV-REG-05.

4.3 Classification levels. Information is classified into one of four levels.

Level Definition Typical examples
Public Approved for release. Disclosure causes no harm. Published website content, marketing material, published policies.
Internal For use inside [Organisation]. Disclosure causes minor inconvenience or embarrassment but no material harm. Internal procedures, organisation charts, general project plans.
Confidential Disclosure causes material harm to [Organisation], a customer or an individual, or breaches a contract or law. Customer data, personal data, contracts, source code, financial records, open security findings.
Restricted Disclosure causes severe harm. Access is limited to named individuals. Credentials and keys, special category personal data, incident details, unremediated test results, strategic plans.

4.4 Classifying. The Asset Owner classifies information when it is created or received. Unlabelled information is treated as Internal. A collection is classified at the level of its most sensitive element. Information received from a customer carries the customer's label, or Confidential if it has none. Only the Asset Owner may lower a classification, and the change is recorded in GOV-REG-10.

4.5 Labelling. Confidential and Restricted documents carry the level in the header or footer, emails carry it at the start of the subject line, and physical media carry it on a label. Systems carry their classification in GOV-REG-10. Public and Internal items need no label on the item itself.

4.6 Handling rules. Each level is handled as follows. Detailed transfer channels are in GOV-PRO-23.

Rule Public Internal Confidential Restricted
Access Anyone All staff Named roles approved by the owner Named individuals approved by the owner, reviewed quarterly
Storage Any Approved systems Approved systems, access controlled, encrypted at rest Approved systems, encrypted at rest, no local or personal copies
Transmission Any channel Organisation email and approved tools Encrypted in transit, approved channels only Encrypted in transit and at rest, approved channels, recipient verified
External sharing Free With a business reason Under contract or confidentiality agreement, owner approval, access-controlled link Owner's written approval per recipient, time-limited link, access logged
Printing Free Allowed, collect immediately Avoid, collect immediately, store locked Only with owner approval, logged, shredded the same day
Disposal Ordinary waste Delete, confidential waste for paper Secure deletion, cross-cut shredding, media logged in GOV-REG-20 Verified secure deletion or destruction with certificate, logged in GOV-REG-20

4.7 Use of assets. Daily rules for devices, accounts, media and services are in GOV-POL-02, remote working in GOV-POL-05 and clear desk in GOV-POL-04.

4.8 Return of assets. A leaver or a contractor at the end of an engagement returns every device, token, key, card and document by the last working day. The line manager checks the return against GOV-REG-24 under GOV-CHK-01 and reports anything unreturned to the Information Security Manager within two working days; the IT Manager wipes an unreturned device remotely under GOV-PRO-22. Information on a personal device is removed and the person confirms this in writing.

4.9 Secure deletion and media disposal. Before reuse or disposal, storage media is wiped by a method suited to it (cryptographic erase for encrypted media, overwrite for other magnetic media) or physically destroyed, and paper is cross-cut shredded. Data in a cloud service is deleted through the provider's documented process and the confirmation kept. Each disposal of a device or medium that held Confidential or Restricted information is recorded in GOV-REG-20 with method, date, person, witness and, for third party destruction, the certificate reference. Equipment leaves the premises for disposal only after wiping or in a locked container under a contract that requires destruction and a certificate.

4.10 Software and hardware lifecycle. GOV-REG-24 records for each product the version, patch cycle, support status and end-of-support date. Software or hardware that will reach end of support within twelve months receives an upgrade or replacement plan recorded against the entry. Unsupported software in use needs a risk acceptance under GOV-PRO-24.

4.11 Reconciliation. Each year the Information Security Manager reconciles GOV-REG-24 against an export from the device management and discovery tools and GOV-REG-10 against the list of systems in scope. Differences are corrected within thirty days and the result is reported at management review.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-10 Information asset register with owner, classification and value.
  • GOV-REG-24 Software and hardware inventory with assignment, patch cycle and end-of-support dates.
  • GOV-REG-20 Media and equipment disposal log and destruction certificates.
  • Signed return confirmations from leavers in GOV-CHK-01.
  • The yearly reconciliation report.

6. Exceptions

A one-off departure from a handling rule needs the Asset Owner's written approval, recorded against the asset. A standing departure needs a risk acceptance under GOV-PRO-24. Classification is never lowered to avoid a handling rule.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after an incident involving mishandled or lost information, and after a change in law or contract that affects classification. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.
