Physical and environmental security procedure

How [Organisation] protects its premises, secure areas, equipment and supporting utilities against unauthorised entry, damage and interference, including what still applies when the organisation runs entirely on cloud services.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.4; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.5; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.6; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.7; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.8; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.9; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.10; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.11; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.12; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 7.13; SOC 2 CC6.4; SOC 2 CC6.5. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure protects [Organisation]'s information and equipment from unauthorised physical access, theft, damage and environmental failure, by defining zones, controlling who enters them, siting and maintaining equipment properly and protecting the utilities it depends on.

2. Scope

It applies to every location where [Organisation] information or equipment is kept: offices, server and network rooms, storage areas, co-working spaces, home workplaces and temporary sites, and to equipment that moves between them. Data centres run by cloud providers are outside [Organisation]'s own physical controls and are assured under GOV-PRO-06 and GOV-PRO-26.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Facilities Manager Operates entry controls, the visitor process and environmental systems, keeps maintenance records, co-runs the yearly inspection.
Information Security Manager Defines zones, approves secure area access lists, reviews GOV-REG-19 monthly, co-runs the yearly inspection.
Zone owner A role accountable for a secure area who keeps its access list current and approves work inside it.
Reception or host Registers visitors, issues badges, escorts, confirms sign-out.
All staff Wear badges visibly, challenge or report unbadged persons, escort their own visitors, follow GOV-POL-04.

4. Procedure

4.1 Zones. The Information Security Manager classifies each area into one of four zones and records them on a floor plan held by the Facilities Manager: Public (reception and meeting rooms open to visitors), Office (general working areas), Secure (server and network rooms, records stores, any room where Restricted information is routinely handled) and Service (power, telecommunications entry and plant rooms). Each Secure and Service zone has a named zone owner.

4.2 Entry controls. Entry to the Office zone requires a personal badge or fob. Doors close and lock automatically and are never propped open. Secure zones require a second factor at the door (a PIN or a second badge read) and carry no external sign describing their contents. The access control system logs every entry and the logs are kept for [Number] months. A lost badge is reported within one hour and disabled on report. Zone owners review their access lists quarterly and record the review in GOV-REG-12 with the physical access system as the system reviewed.

4.3 Visitors. A host pre-registers every visitor. Reception records the visitor's name, organisation, host, purpose, time in, badge number and time out in GOV-REG-19 and checks photographic identity for entry beyond the Public zone. Visitors wear a badge that is visibly different from staff badges and are escorted at all times outside the Public zone. A visitor entering a Secure zone is recorded with the zone and the reason. Contractors with repeated work receive a time-limited badge only after the host confirms the need with the Information Security Manager. Deliveries are received in the Public zone.

4.4 Working in secure areas. Only people on the zone owner's list work unescorted in a Secure zone. Photography and recording need the zone owner's written approval. Third parties are supervised throughout. Food and drink are kept away from equipment. The area is locked whenever it is unattended, and anyone working alone in it tells the Facilities Manager before starting and after finishing.

4.5 Equipment siting. Servers and network equipment are installed in locked racks inside a Secure zone. Screens are positioned so that they cannot be read from windows, corridors or the Public zone. Equipment is kept away from water, heat sources and direct sunlight. Printers used for Confidential output sit in the Office zone with pull printing where the device supports it. Every item carries the asset tag recorded in GOV-REG-24.

4.6 Cabling. Power and data cables run in trunking, under floors or above ceilings, labelled at both ends. Patch panels sit in locked cabinets. Network points in the Public zone are disabled unless in use. Cabling is checked during the yearly inspection.

4.7 Supporting utilities. Equipment in Secure zones runs on an uninterruptible power supply that the Facilities Manager tests quarterly. Fire detection and suppression suitable for electrical equipment, temperature and humidity monitoring with alerts to the Facilities Manager, and water detection where pipework runs nearby are installed and serviced by competent contractors. Test and service dates are recorded.

4.8 Maintenance. Equipment is serviced to the manufacturer's schedule by authorised personnel, who are escorted in Secure zones. Storage media is removed or wiped under GOV-PRO-16 before equipment leaves the premises for repair, unless the repair contract requires confidentiality and the media is encrypted. Maintenance records are kept against the GOV-REG-24 entry.

4.9 Off-site assets. Equipment leaves the premises only when assigned to a named person in GOV-REG-24. Laptops and phones travel as hand luggage, are never left visible in a vehicle and are locked away at home. The rules in GOV-POL-05 apply. Loss or theft is reported within one hour under GOV-PRO-07 and handled under GOV-PRO-22.

4.10 Clear desk and disposal. GOV-POL-04 applies in every zone. Equipment and media awaiting disposal are stored in a Secure zone and disposed of under GOV-PRO-16.

4.11 Inspection. The Information Security Manager and the Facilities Manager inspect every zone yearly against this procedure, record the findings, and raise corrective actions under GOV-PRO-04.

4.12 Cloud-only and small organisations. Where [Organisation] has no server room and runs on cloud services, the following still apply: entry control, visitor registration and clear desk in the office; locked storage for paper and spare devices; encryption, asset registration and loss reporting for laptops and phones; the home working rules in GOV-POL-05; and provider data centre assurance obtained under GOV-PRO-26 and recorded in GOV-REG-07. In a shared co-working space the whole space is treated as a Public zone: [Organisation] relies on device and screen controls, keeps no Restricted paper there, and uses a lockable locker for anything left on site.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-19 Physical access and visitor log.
  • Access control system logs and the quarterly access list reviews in GOV-REG-12.
  • Utility test and maintenance records.
  • The yearly inspection report and resulting corrective actions.
  • Provider assurance records in GOV-REG-07 for cloud data centres.

6. Exceptions

Emergency services enter any zone without registration during an emergency and the Facilities Manager records the event afterwards. Unescorted access for a contractor is granted only in writing by the Information Security Manager for a stated period and is noted in GOV-REG-19. No other exception applies.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after any physical security incident, and before and after a move or change of premises. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Human resources security procedure

How [Organisation] screens people before they join, binds them to security and confidentiality obligations, handles breaches through a fair disciplinary process, and manages security at change of role and departure, with contractors held to the same standard.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.4; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.5; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.6; SOC 2 CC1.1; SOC 2 CC1.4; SOC 2 CC1.5. Owner: Human Resources Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure makes sure that the people who work for [Organisation] are suitable for their roles, understand their security and privacy obligations before they start, are held to them fairly while they work, and leave without taking information or access with them.

2. Scope

It applies to employees, contractors, agency staff, temporary staff and interns, from the point an offer is made until obligations after departure expire. Supplier personnel are covered through the supplier contract under GOV-PRO-06.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Human Resources Manager Owns this procedure, runs screening, issues contracts, keeps GOV-REG-23, runs the disciplinary process.
Hiring manager Sets the screening level with the Information Security Manager, confirms the role's access needs.
Information Security Manager Agrees screening levels, investigates suspected security breaches with Human Resources, confirms leaver access removal.
Privacy Officer Confirms that screening and monitoring are lawful and that candidates and staff receive the right privacy notices.
Line manager Reinforces obligations, reports suspected breaches, completes the mover and leaver steps.
Individual Provides accurate screening information, signs and follows the terms, returns assets and keeps confidentiality after leaving.

4. Procedure

4.1 Screening level. Before recruitment starts, the hiring manager and the Information Security Manager assign the role a screening level, recorded in the job description: Standard, or Enhanced where the role has privileged access, routine access to Restricted information or financial authority.

4.2 Screening. Human Resources completes screening before the start date, in proportion to the level and within what local law permits. Standard screening verifies identity, the right to work, employment history for the past [Number] years, qualifications the role relies on, and two references. Enhanced screening adds a criminal record check and, for roles with financial authority, a credit check, each only where lawful. The candidate receives the applicant privacy notice (GDPR-TPL-03) and gives any consent the law requires. Human Resources keeps the results and shares only the outcome with the hiring manager. If screening cannot finish before the start date, the person is limited to Internal information until it does, and Human Resources records the decision with the Information Security Manager's agreement.

4.3 Terms and conditions. Every contract of employment or engagement includes a confidentiality obligation that survives departure, the duty to follow [Organisation] policies, the acceptable use terms in GOV-POL-02, intellectual property terms, the duty to return assets, notice of monitoring as described in GDPR-TPL-02, and the consequences of a breach. The contract is signed before the first working day.

4.4 Confidentiality agreements. A contractor, agency worker or visitor who will see Confidential or Restricted information signs a confidentiality agreement before access. The agreement names the information covered, its duration, and the duty to return or destroy information at the end. Human Resources, or the engaging manager for a short engagement, records the signed agreement in GOV-REG-23. Agreements are reviewed when the scope of access changes and at least every [Number] years.

4.5 Policy acknowledgement. Each person acknowledges the information security policy (GOV-POL-03), the acceptable use policy (GOV-POL-02) and the other policies that apply to their role at induction, after a material change to any of them, and yearly with the refresher training under GOV-PRO-08. Human Resources records each acknowledgement in GOV-REG-23 and chases any that is overdue after ten working days.

4.6 During employment. Line managers set security duties in objectives for roles that have them, release staff for the training in GOV-PRO-08, and act on the monthly overdue training list. Human Resources tells the Information Security Manager of every change of role or line manager on the day it is agreed.

4.7 Disciplinary process. A suspected breach of a security or privacy policy is reported to Human Resources and the Information Security Manager. Human Resources opens a case, the Information Security Manager preserves evidence under GOV-PRO-07, and the person is told of the allegation and given a chance to respond. Access may be suspended during the investigation where the Information Security Manager judges the risk warrants it. Outcomes are graded: informal guidance, written warning, final warning, dismissal, and referral to law enforcement where a law appears broken. The outcome weighs intent, whether the person had been trained, whether it is a repeat, and the impact. Human Resources records the case and outcome and tells the person in writing. An honest, promptly reported mistake is handled as a learning event unless it is repeated.

4.8 Change of role. When a person moves role, Human Resources notifies the line managers and the access administrator so that the mover step in GOV-PRO-10 runs within five working days. If the new role carries a higher screening level, the additional checks are completed before the new access is granted. Confidentiality obligations from the old role continue.

4.9 Termination. Human Resources notifies the Information Security Manager, the line manager, the IT Manager and the access administrator of the leaving date as soon as it is known, and the line manager runs the offboarding tasks in GOV-CHK-01. At the exit meeting Human Resources reminds the person in writing of the obligations that continue after departure and obtains confirmation that all assets and information have been returned under GOV-PRO-16. For a dismissal, or a leaver with privileged access, access is removed at or before notification under GOV-PRO-10.

4.10 Contractor equivalence. Contractors and agency staff follow every step in this procedure. The engaging manager performs the line manager duties, and the agency or contractor's own company confirms in writing before the start date that screening equivalent to the role's level has been completed. A contractor who cannot show equivalent screening is screened by Human Resources.

4.11 Records. Human Resources keeps screening records, signed contracts, confidentiality agreements, acknowledgements and disciplinary records for the periods in PIMS-POL-02 and handles them under GDPR-PRO-02.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-23 Policy acknowledgement register, including confidentiality agreements.
  • Completed GOV-CHK-01 checklists for each starter and leaver.
  • Screening records and the screening level in each job description.
  • Signed contracts and exit confirmations.
  • Disciplinary case records.

6. Exceptions

A person may start before screening is complete only with the written agreement of the Human Resources Manager and the Information Security Manager, with access limited as in 4.2 and the exception recorded on the person's file. Screening checks that local law does not permit are omitted and the omission is recorded.

7. Review and maintenance

The Human Resources Manager reviews this procedure annually with the Information Security Manager, after an incident caused by an insider, after a disciplinary case that exposed a gap, and after a change in employment or data protection law. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Capacity and Availability Management Procedure

What is monitored, the thresholds that trigger action, how demand is forecast, how redundancy is designed and tested, and how capacity problems link to incident handling.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.6; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.14; SOC 2 A1.1. Owner: Head of Engineering.

1. Purpose

This procedure keeps [Organisation]'s services available and performing within agreed levels, by monitoring capacity against thresholds, forecasting demand before it becomes a problem, and designing and testing redundancy for critical systems.

2. Scope

It applies to production systems and the shared services they depend on: compute, memory, storage, database capacity, network bandwidth, message queues, licence counts, provider quotas and rate limits, certificate validity, and the on-call capacity of the teams that operate them.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Head of Engineering Owns this procedure, approves capacity investment, reviews the quarterly report.
System Owner Sets the availability target and thresholds for their system, owns its forecast and its monthly entry in GOV-REG-17.
Platform team Operates monitoring, responds to threshold alerts, performs scaling changes, calculates monthly availability.
Information Security Manager Confirms that resilience decisions match the risk register and the continuity objectives.

4. Procedure

4.1 Targets. The System Owner records for each production system an availability target (for example 99.9 percent measured monthly), the indicators that define the service as working (latency, error rate, throughput), and the recovery objectives from GOV-TPL-07. Targets promised to customers are taken from the contract.

4.2 Monitoring and thresholds. The platform team monitors every component against a warning and a critical threshold and routes critical alerts through the triage process in GOV-PRO-14. Default thresholds, which the System Owner may tighten, are:

Metric Warning Critical
Processor utilisation, sustained 15 minutes 70 percent 85 percent
Memory utilisation 75 percent 90 percent
Storage used 75 percent 90 percent
Database connections or queue depth 70 percent of limit 90 percent of limit
Error rate against target Half the error budget consumed Error budget exhausted
Provider quota or licence count 80 percent 95 percent
Certificate validity 30 days to expiry 7 days to expiry

4.3 Forecasting. Each month the System Owner reviews utilisation trends and business plans (customer onboarding, feature launches, seasonal peaks) and records in GOV-REG-17 the months of headroom at the current trend. Any component forecast to reach its critical threshold within six months gets an action with an owner and date. The Head of Engineering reviews a consolidated capacity report quarterly and approves procurement or architecture changes.

4.4 Redundancy and resilience. Critical systems, as rated in the business impact analysis, have no single point of failure within the approved strategy (GOV-PRO-13): at least two instances across separate failure zones, load balancing with health checks, replicated storage, and provider services configured for the availability tier the target needs. Failover is tested at least annually and recorded in GOV-REG-16.

4.5 Scaling. Where the platform supports it, automatic scaling rules are configured with upper limits that protect cost and downstream systems. Manual scaling and changes to the limits are changes under GOV-PRO-09.

4.6 Demand management. Public interfaces enforce rate limits and request size limits. Batch and reporting jobs run outside peak hours. Abusive traffic is blocked at the edge and the event is reported under GOV-PRO-14.

4.7 Measurement. The platform team calculates availability and performance against target each month from monitoring data, excluding only maintenance windows announced under GOV-PRO-09, and records the result in GOV-REG-17. A missed target triggers a review by the System Owner within ten working days, with actions recorded.

4.8 Incident link. A critical threshold breach that degrades service is handled as an incident under GOV-PRO-07. The post-incident review states whether capacity or resilience was a cause; resulting actions are recorded in GOV-REG-17 and, where they need investment, as a risk in GOV-REG-05.

4.9 Reclamation. Idle instances, unused capacity and expired licences identified in the monthly review are released through GOV-PRO-09.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-17 Capacity and availability log: monthly results, headroom and actions per system.
  • Monitoring dashboards and alert history.
  • The quarterly capacity report and the Head of Engineering's decisions.
  • Failover test records in GOV-REG-16.
  • Missed target reviews and their actions.

6. Exceptions

A system may run without redundancy only where its business impact rating is below the critical tier and the System Owner records the decision as a risk in GOV-REG-05.

7. Review and maintenance

The Head of Engineering reviews this procedure annually, after any availability incident at one of the two highest severity levels, after a target is missed in two consecutive months, and when the hosting platform changes. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Cryptography and Key Management Procedure

Which cryptographic methods are used for which purpose, and how the keys and certificates behind them are generated, stored, used, rotated, revoked and destroyed.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.24; SOC 2 CC6.1; SOC 2 CC6.7. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure sets the cryptographic methods [Organisation] uses for each purpose and the lifecycle of the keys and certificates behind them, so that encryption protects data in practice and keys are never the weakest point.

2. Scope

It applies to all uses of cryptography in [Organisation]'s systems: encryption of data at rest and in transit, password storage, digital signatures, message authentication, key exchange, application secrets, and public and private certificates, wherever the keys are held: cloud key management services, hardware security modules, secrets stores, certificate stores and devices.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Information Security Manager Owns the approved algorithm list and this procedure, approves exceptions, reconciles GOV-REG-18 quarterly.
Key custodian (named per key store) Generates, rotates, backs up and destroys keys, under dual control where 4.4 requires it.
System Owner Identifies the cryptographic needs of their system and owns its keys and certificates in GOV-REG-18.
Platform team Operates key management services, certificate automation and expiry monitoring.
Developers Use approved libraries and the secrets store; never implement cryptographic primitives.

4. Procedure

4.1 Approved methods by purpose. Only the following families are used. The specific algorithms, modes and parameters are chosen from current public guidance and listed in the approved algorithm list maintained by the Information Security Manager. Custom or modified algorithms are never used.

Purpose Approved family Not permitted
Data at rest Symmetric block cipher with a key of at least 256 bits in an authenticated mode Unauthenticated modes, electronic codebook mode
Data in transit TLS 1.2 or later with forward-secret key exchange and authenticated cipher suites, TLS 1.3 preferred SSL, TLS 1.0 and 1.1, export and null ciphers
Hashing and integrity SHA-2 or SHA-3 family, and keyed hashing built on them MD5, and SHA-1 for any security purpose
Password storage Memory-hard or adaptive password hashing with a unique salt per password Fast general purpose hashes, reversible encryption
Digital signatures RSA of at least 3072 bits, or elliptic curve signatures on approved curves RSA below 2048 bits, DSA
Key exchange Ephemeral elliptic curve or finite field exchange of approved size Static or anonymous key exchange
Random numbers Cryptographically secure generators provided by the platform Application level pseudo-random functions

4.2 Key generation. Production keys are generated inside the key management service or hardware security module, or by an approved library using the platform's secure random source, at the length in the approved list. Keys are never generated on a workstation, typed by hand, or derived from a password, except to protect a single user's device or archive.

4.3 Storage and access. Keys live in the key management service, hardware security module, secrets store or managed certificate store, under access roles granted through GOV-PRO-10. Private keys are not exportable unless the purpose requires it, and an exported copy is wrapped by a key of equal or greater strength. Keys and secrets never appear in source code, repository configuration, tickets, chat, email or documents. Applications receive secrets at runtime from the secrets store.

4.4 Separation of duties. Key administration roles are separate from the data administration roles of the systems the keys protect. Generation, export, destruction and recovery of root, master and key-encryption keys require two custodians acting together, each recorded. No single person holds both parts of a split secret or both factors of a recovery credential.

4.5 Rotation.

Key or certificate Rotation
Data encryption keys Annually, or sooner at the volume limit of the mode
Key-encryption and master keys Every three years, with re-wrapping of dependent keys
Public TLS certificates Before expiry, with validity no longer than the public certificate authority limit, renewed by automation where possible
Internal certificates Validity no longer than one year
Application secrets, API keys and service credentials Every 90 days, and within one working day of a custodian leaving or a suspected exposure
Signing keys Every two years

Any key is rotated at once when compromise is suspected, when a custodian leaves, or when its algorithm is withdrawn from the approved list.

4.6 Certificate lifecycle. The System Owner requests a certificate from the approved internal or public authority with the exact names needed. The platform team validates control of the names, installs the certificate, records it in GOV-REG-18 and enrols it in expiry monitoring, which alerts at 30, 14 and 7 days. A certificate whose private key is exposed is revoked within one working day and replaced. Expired or revoked certificates are removed from every endpoint.

4.7 Inventory. GOV-REG-18 records every key and certificate with purpose, system, algorithm and length, location, owner, custodian, creation date, rotation due, expiry and status. The Information Security Manager reconciles it quarterly against exports from the key management service and certificate store.

4.8 Backup, recovery and destruction. Data encryption keys and key-encryption keys are backed up in a separate protected location so that encrypted backups stay readable for their retention period (GOV-PRO-12). Keys are destroyed under dual control when the data they protect reaches the end of its retention, and the destruction is recorded. Destroying the key is an accepted method of deleting the data (GOV-PRO-16).

4.9 Compromise. A suspected key compromise is an incident under GOV-PRO-07: the key is revoked or rotated, data protected by it is re-encrypted where exposure is possible, and dependent certificates are reissued.

4.10 Legal constraints. Export, import and lawful access requirements for cryptography in the countries where [Organisation] operates are recorded in GOV-REG-04 and respected in product and deployment decisions.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-18 Cryptographic key and certificate inventory, and the quarterly reconciliation.
  • The approved algorithm list and its review record.
  • Dual control records for generation, export, destruction and recovery.
  • Expiry alerts and renewal records.
  • Key compromise incident records in GOV-REG-08.

6. Exceptions

A legacy protocol or algorithm required by an external party is permitted only under a risk acceptance in GOV-PRO-24 with compensating controls (isolation, monitoring) and an end date, recorded against the item in GOV-REG-18.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, when public guidance withdraws an algorithm or parameter in use, after a key compromise, and after any outage caused by an expired certificate. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Network Security and Remote Access Procedure

How networks are segmented, how traffic is allowed by exception rather than by default, how management interfaces and remote access are protected, and how firewall rules are reviewed.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.20; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.21; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.22; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.23; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 6.7; SOC 2 CC6.6; SOC 2 CC6.7. Owner: Head of Engineering.

1. Purpose

This procedure protects [Organisation]'s networks and the services on them by segmenting them into zones, allowing only documented traffic, protecting management interfaces, requiring a multi-factor gateway for remote access, and keeping the rule base current.

2. Scope

It applies to all networks that [Organisation] controls: cloud virtual networks and security groups, office networks, wireless networks, management networks, site-to-site and remote access connections, and the edge services (load balancers, gateways, content delivery and name resolution) that expose [Organisation]'s services. Home and public networks used by staff are governed by GOV-POL-05 and by the device requirements in GOV-PRO-22.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Head of Engineering Owns the network architecture and approves changes to the zone model.
Network or platform administrator Implements and documents rules, operates gateways, runs the quarterly rule review.
Information Security Manager Approves security-relevant rule changes, runs the monthly exposure review, co-signs the quarterly rule review.
System Owner Owns the rules that serve their system and confirms them at review.
All staff and contractors Connect to internal resources only through the approved remote access method.

4. Procedure

4.1 Architecture and zones. The Head of Engineering maintains a network diagram and zone model that separates at least: public edge, application, data, management, corporate user, guest and non-production. Each zone has a written purpose and allowed traffic directions. The diagram is reviewed twice a year and after any change under GOV-PRO-09. Flows that cross zones or organisations are recorded in GOV-REG-25.

4.2 Default deny. Every firewall, security group and network access list denies inbound traffic by default and allows only documented flows. Outbound traffic from the data and management zones is restricted to named destinations. Each rule records its owner, business justification, the change reference and, for a temporary rule, an expiry date. Rules with an unrestricted source or destination on a sensitive zone are not permitted.

4.3 Segmentation. Production is separated from corporate and non-production networks with no shared credentials and no routing beyond the defined flows. Systems holding Restricted data sit in a zone reachable only from the application tier. Systems out of vendor support (GOV-PRO-11) and any operational technology are isolated in a dedicated zone with monitored access.

4.4 Management interfaces. Administrative interfaces (consoles, remote shells, database administration ports, hypervisor and cloud provider APIs) are never exposed to the internet. Administrators reach them through a bastion or privileged access gateway that requires multi-factor authentication, records sessions, and accepts connections only from managed devices. Default credentials are changed before a device is connected, management protocols are encrypted, and management traffic is logged under GOV-PRO-14.

4.5 Remote access. Staff and contractors reach internal resources only through the approved gateway (a virtual private network or an identity-aware proxy) that enforces multi-factor authentication per GOV-POL-06, checks device compliance per GOV-PRO-22, ends idle sessions after [Number] minutes, and logs every session. Access is scoped to the resources the role needs. Third party remote access is granted per engagement, limited in time, supervised or recorded, and removed on completion (GOV-PRO-10).

4.6 Wireless. Corporate wireless uses enterprise authentication with per-user credentials or device certificates and current encryption standards. Guest wireless is isolated from corporate networks and rate limited. The administrator checks offices for unauthorised access points quarterly.

4.7 Filtering. Managed devices and corporate networks resolve names through a filtering resolver that blocks known malicious domains and the categories listed in GOV-POL-02. Blocking events are logged, and staff are told about filtering through GOV-POL-02.

4.8 Edge protection. Internet-facing services sit behind a load balancer or gateway with denial-of-service protection, and behind a web application firewall where the service accepts user input. Only the ports and protocols the service needs are open. Transport encryption follows GOV-PRO-20.

4.9 Exposure review. The Information Security Manager reviews monthly the inventory of public addresses, open ports and public storage against the approved list, and records any unapproved exposure as a High finding in GOV-REG-14.

4.10 Quarterly rule review. The administrator exports every firewall and security group rule each quarter. Each System Owner confirms, removes or re-justifies their rules; expired temporary rules are deleted; the Information Security Manager co-signs the review. The record names the reviewers, the date, and the rules removed and changed.

4.11 Changes. All rule and topology changes are changes under GOV-PRO-09. A change that opens a new inbound flow from the internet, a new zone-crossing flow or a new third party connection is security-relevant and requires the Information Security Manager's approval.

5. Records and evidence

  • The network diagram and zone model with review dates.
  • The rule base with owner, justification and change references.
  • Quarterly rule review records.
  • Monthly exposure reviews and the resulting GOV-REG-14 findings.
  • Remote access and management session logs.
  • GOV-REG-25 Data flow and interface inventory.

6. Exceptions

The Information Security Manager may approve a temporary rule outside the model for at most 30 days, with the expiry set in the rule itself. Anything longer requires a risk acceptance under GOV-PRO-24.

7. Review and maintenance

The Head of Engineering reviews this procedure annually, after any incident that used a network path, after a redesign of the cloud network, and after an audit finding. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Endpoint and Mobile Device Security Procedure

The baseline every laptop, desktop, phone and tablet must meet before it accesses [Organisation] information, how compliance is enforced, the conditions for personal devices, and what happens when a device is lost.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.7; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.9; SOC 2 CC6.8. Owner: Head of Engineering.

1. Purpose

This procedure keeps the devices that access [Organisation]'s information in a known secure state, enforces that state through device management, and defines the response when a device is lost, stolen or leaves the organisation.

2. Scope

It applies to every endpoint that accesses [Organisation] systems or data: devices owned by [Organisation], devices supplied by a contractor, and personal devices used under the conditions in 4.8. Servers and network devices are covered by GOV-CHK-02 and GOV-PRO-21.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Head of Engineering Owns the endpoint baseline and the device management platform.
Endpoint administrator Enrols devices, enforces the baseline, reviews compliance, performs remote lock and wipe.
Information Security Manager Approves the baseline, reviews compliance monthly, leads lost device incidents.
Line manager Approves device issue and personal device use for their staff.
Device user Keeps the device under their control, applies updates when prompted, reports loss immediately.

4. Procedure

4.1 Baseline. Every managed device meets the workstation baseline in GOV-CHK-02 before it accesses data. Minimum settings: full disk encryption with the recovery key escrowed in the management platform; screen lock after at most 10 minutes of inactivity with authentication to resume; host firewall enabled; malware protection active; automatic operating system and application updates; the user works without administrative rights; only software from the approved list; a managed browser; remote lock and wipe enabled; the device recorded in GOV-REG-24 with its user.

4.2 Enrolment. The endpoint administrator enrols each device in the device management platform at issue, applies the baseline profile and records the device in GOV-REG-24. Sign-in to [Organisation] services is permitted only from a device the platform reports as compliant.

4.3 Malware protection. Malware protection runs continuously on every device, updates its detection data at least daily, reports to a central console, and raises alerts into the triage process in GOV-PRO-14. Detected malware is handled under GOV-PRO-07. Removable media are scanned on connection where their use is permitted (GOV-PRO-23).

4.4 Updates. Operating system and application updates install automatically; users may defer for at most [Number] days. Critical updates follow the deadlines in GOV-PRO-11. A device running an operating system version no longer supported by its vendor is blocked until upgraded or replaced.

4.5 Administrative rights. Users hold no standing local administrator rights. Elevation for an approved task is granted just in time through the management platform, expires with the session and is logged. Developers who need elevated rights for their work receive them on a separate account or under a managed exception recorded in GOV-REG-13.

4.6 Phones and tablets. Managed phones and tablets require a passcode of at least six digits or a biometric with passcode fallback, device encryption, automatic updates, and a work profile or application container controlled by the management platform. Devices with vendor restrictions removed are refused.

4.7 Compliance monitoring. The endpoint administrator reviews the compliance report weekly and contacts the user of any non-compliant device. A device that stays non-compliant for seven days is blocked until corrected. The Information Security Manager reviews compliance figures monthly and reconciles the management platform against GOV-REG-24.

4.8 Personal devices. A personal device may access [Organisation] email, calendar and collaboration tools only when the user accepts the conditions in GOV-POL-02, enrols the work profile or container in the management platform, meets the passcode, encryption and supported-version requirements, and consents to remote wipe of the work container. Personal devices do not access systems holding Restricted data, do not store Confidential data outside the container, and are removed from the platform when the person leaves (GOV-CHK-01). [Organisation] wipes only the work container, never personal content.

4.9 Lost or stolen device. The user reports a lost or stolen device immediately, and within one hour at most, through the incident channel in GOV-PRO-07. The endpoint administrator locks the device remotely at once and wipes it if it is not recovered within [Number] hours or if it held Confidential or Restricted data. The Information Security Manager resets the user's credentials and tokens, assesses what data the device held and whether encryption was active, updates GOV-REG-24, and starts the personal data breach assessment under PIMS-PRO-04 where personal data may be affected.

4.10 Return and disposal. At the end of use the device is returned per GOV-CHK-01, wiped through the management platform, and either reissued after a fresh baseline or disposed of under GOV-PRO-16 with the record in GOV-REG-20.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-24 entries per device with user and compliance status, and the monthly reconciliation.
  • Device management compliance reports and weekly follow-up records.
  • GOV-CHK-02 workstation baseline with version history and the Information Security Manager's approval.
  • Lost device incident records, wipe confirmations and breach assessments.
  • Personal device acceptance records.

6. Exceptions

A device that cannot run the management agent (for example a test rig) is recorded in GOV-REG-24 with compensating controls, isolated per GOV-PRO-21, and covered by a risk acceptance under GOV-PRO-24.

7. Review and maintenance

The Head of Engineering reviews this procedure annually, after any incident involving an endpoint, when the management platform changes, and when a major operating system release changes the available controls. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Information Transfer and Data Loss Prevention Procedure

Which channels may carry each classification of information, how external sharing is approved and reviewed, the controls on email, removable media and printing, and how exfiltration channels are monitored within privacy limits.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.14; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.12; SOC 2 C1.1; SOC 2 C1.2. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure controls how information leaves a system or the organisation, so that each classification travels only by a channel that protects it, external sharing is deliberate and time-limited, and loss through everyday channels is detected.

2. Scope

It applies to all transfers of [Organisation] information between people, systems and organisations by email, file sharing, messaging, system interfaces, removable media, printing and physical delivery, by staff, contractors and suppliers. Classification levels are defined in GOV-PRO-16. Transfers of personal data outside the home jurisdiction also follow PIMS-POL-03.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Information owner (System Owner or document owner) Approves transfers of Confidential and Restricted information and sets the sharing conditions.
Information Security Manager Maintains the approved channel list, configures and tunes loss prevention rules, reviews alerts and sharing reports.
Collaboration or platform administrator Implements email, sharing and media controls and produces the quarterly reports.
Privacy Officer Reviews monitoring rules for proportionality and transfers of personal data.
All staff Use only approved channels and report a misdirected or unauthorised transfer within one hour.

4. Procedure

4.1 Approved channels by classification.

Classification Permitted channels Conditions
Public Any channel The owner has approved publication
Internal Corporate email, collaboration platform, corporate file sharing Links limited to the organisation; no personal accounts
Confidential Corporate email with transport encryption, named-recipient sharing links, approved customer or supplier portals Named recipients, link expiry of at most 30 days, download controls where available, owner aware
Restricted Approved secure transfer service, an encrypted file with the key sent by a separate channel, or an authenticated system interface Owner's written approval per transfer or per standing arrangement, recipient under contract, transfer logged

4.2 External sharing. Sharing links default to internal. A link for an external party requires a named recipient, an expiry date and, for Confidential or above, the owner's approval recorded in the sharing platform or a ticket. Guest accounts on collaboration platforms are reviewed quarterly under GOV-PRO-10 and removed when the engagement ends. Standing transfers to a supplier or customer are covered by a contract or data processing terms (GOV-PRO-06) and listed in GOV-REG-25.

4.3 Email controls. The administrator enforces transport encryption for outbound mail, configures sender authentication for [Organisation]'s domains, warns users when a recipient is external, blocks automatic forwarding to external addresses, and blocks attachments matching Restricted data patterns unless they are encrypted. A sender who misdirects mail reports it immediately and it is handled under GOV-PRO-07.

4.4 Removable media. Writing to removable media is disabled on managed devices by default. Where a role needs it, the Information Security Manager approves the exception, the device encrypts the media automatically, and the media is recorded, returned and disposed of under GOV-PRO-16 with the record in GOV-REG-20.

4.5 Printing. Confidential documents are printed only with secure release at the printer and collected at once. Restricted documents are printed only with the owner's approval, numbered where practical, and shredded after use. Printing at home follows GOV-POL-05.

4.6 Messaging and personal services. Staff do not send [Organisation] information to personal email, consumer messaging services or personal cloud storage. Use of external AI tools follows AI-POL-01. Approved messaging platforms are configured for retention and export so that records can be produced.

4.7 Physical transfer. Media and paper carrying Confidential or Restricted information travel encrypted or sealed, by tracked courier or in the personal custody of a staff member, with a chain of custody record signed at each handover.

4.8 System interfaces. Automated transfers between systems or to third parties use authenticated, encrypted interfaces (GOV-PRO-20), are recorded in GOV-REG-25 with owner, data classification and review date, and are reviewed annually by the owner.

4.9 Monitoring of exfiltration channels. The Information Security Manager runs loss prevention rules on email, file sharing and managed endpoints for Restricted data patterns (for example payment card numbers, national identifiers, bulk exports of personal data) and for anomalous volumes. Alerts are triaged under GOV-PRO-14. Each rule is documented with its purpose; the Privacy Officer reviews the rules annually; staff are told these channels are monitored through GOV-POL-02. Content inspection is limited to what the rule needs and is not used for any other purpose.

4.10 Agreements. Before a recurring transfer with another organisation begins, the information owner confirms a signed agreement covering confidentiality, permitted use, security measures, personal data terms where relevant, incident notification, and return or deletion at the end of the relationship.

5. Records and evidence

  • The approved channel list and the loss prevention rule documentation with the Privacy Officer's annual review.
  • External sharing reports and quarterly guest account reviews.
  • Removable media exception approvals and disposal records in GOV-REG-20.
  • GOV-REG-25 Data flow and interface inventory with annual reviews.
  • Chain of custody records.
  • Alert triage records and misdirected transfer incidents in GOV-REG-08.

6. Exceptions

A one-off transfer outside the table in 4.1 requires the Information Security Manager's approval and a record of what was sent, to whom and how. A standing deviation requires a risk acceptance under GOV-PRO-24.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after any data loss incident, when a collaboration or email platform changes, and when a law on data transfer changes. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Exception and risk acceptance procedure

How a deviation from a policy or control, or the acceptance of a risk above appetite, is requested, assessed, limited in time, approved by the right authority, recorded and reviewed before it expires.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 8.3; SOC 2 CC3.2; SOC 2 CC5.1. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

Controls sometimes cannot be applied as written, and some risks cannot be treated at once. This procedure makes every such case visible, time-limited and owned, so that an exception is a recorded decision rather than a quiet gap.

2. Scope

It applies to any request to deviate from a policy, procedure or control in the management system, and to any acceptance of a residual risk in the High or Critical band under GOV-PRO-05. It does not cover changes to the documents themselves, which follow GOV-PRO-01, or changes to systems, which follow GOV-PRO-09.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Requester The manager responsible for the system or process. Completes GOV-TPL-06, implements compensating controls, closes or renews before expiry.
Information Security Manager Assesses the request, rates the risk, records it in GOV-REG-06, runs the expiry review, approves Low and Medium band requests.
Privacy Officer Co-assesses any request involving personal data.
Executive sponsor Approves High band requests.
Chief Executive Officer Approves Critical band requests.
Internal Auditor Samples GOV-REG-06 at each audit for expired or unreviewed entries.

4. Procedure

4.1 When an exception is required. A requester raises an exception before a control is bypassed, a policy statement is not followed, or a High or Critical risk is left untreated. A deviation discovered after the fact is logged as a nonconformity under GOV-PRO-04 and may then be regularised through this procedure.

4.2 Request. The requester completes GOV-TPL-06 with the requirement being deviated from, the systems and data affected, the business reason, the compensating controls proposed, the duration requested and the plan for returning to full conformity. A request without a return plan is accepted only as a risk acceptance, not as an exception.

4.3 Assessment. Within five working days the Information Security Manager, with the Privacy Officer where personal data is involved, rates the risk using the scales in GOV-PRO-05 twice: once as it would stand without the compensating controls and once with them in place. Both bands are recorded on the form. The Information Security Manager also checks whether the deviation breaches an obligation in GOV-REG-04 or a customer commitment, in which case the request is refused unless the customer or regulator has agreed in writing.

4.4 Compensating controls. The requester implements the compensating controls and shows evidence that they operate before approval is given. A compensating control must reduce the band of the risk; a control that merely detects the problem after the fact is recorded as such and does not count as a band reduction unless detection leads to a response within a defined time.

4.5 Time limit. An exception or acceptance is granted for a fixed period of no more than twelve months. A Critical band acceptance is granted for no more than ninety days. There is no automatic renewal.

4.6 Approval. The authority for the band after compensating controls approves or refuses the request in writing on GOV-TPL-06.

Band after compensating controls Approver
Low Information Security Manager
Medium Information Security Manager and the requester's head of function
High Executive sponsor
Critical Chief Executive Officer

4.7 Register entry. On approval the Information Security Manager enters the exception in GOV-REG-06 with its reference, type, linked risk ID, bands before and after, approver, approval date, duration and expiry date, and sets the status to Active. The linked entry in GOV-REG-05 is updated to show the acceptance and the review date. The requester informs the owners of the affected controls.

4.8 Expiry review. Thirty days before expiry the Information Security Manager notifies the requester. The requester then does one of three things: closes the exception because the control is now implemented, with evidence; submits a new request under 4.2 with a fresh assessment; or escalates to the approver with the reason the return plan has slipped. An exception that reaches its expiry date without one of these outcomes is set to Expired, reported to the steering committee at its next meeting, and treated as a nonconformity under GOV-PRO-04.

4.9 Early review. An active exception is reassessed before expiry when the affected system changes materially, an incident touches it, or a related audit finding is raised.

4.10 Quarterly reporting. The Information Security Manager reports the number of active, expiring and expired exceptions by band to the steering committee each quarter and to management review.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-TPL-06 Risk acceptance and exception forms, signed by the approver.
  • GOV-REG-06 Risk acceptance and exception register, showing status and expiry for every entry.
  • Evidence that compensating controls operate.
  • Steering committee minutes recording expired exceptions.

6. Exceptions

This procedure has no exceptions. An urgent operational need is handled as an emergency change under GOV-PRO-09, followed by a request under 4.2 within five working days.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually and after any audit finding about exceptions or risk acceptance. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Legal, regulatory and contractual compliance procedure

How [Organisation] identifies the laws, regulations, contracts and scheme rules that apply to its information, records them, maps each to controls and evidence, watches for change, protects intellectual property and records, and has its compliance independently reviewed.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.31; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.32; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.33; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.34; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.35; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.36; SOC 2 CC1.1; SOC 2 CC2.3; GDPR Article 24. Owner: Privacy Officer.

1. Purpose

An organisation cannot show it is compliant until it can list what it must comply with. This procedure builds and maintains that list, ties every obligation to the control and the evidence that satisfies it, and makes sure someone notices when the obligations change.

2. Scope

It covers obligations that affect information security, privacy and the records of the organisation: data protection law, sector regulation, intellectual property and licensing law, records retention duties, employment law as it touches monitoring and screening, export and sanctions rules as they touch technology, customer and supplier contract terms, and the rules of the certification and attestation schemes the organisation has joined.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Privacy Officer Owns this procedure and GOV-REG-04, leads identification and change monitoring, advises on personal data obligations.
Information Security Manager Maps obligations to controls and evidence, raises gaps as risks or corrective actions.
Legal counsel (internal or external) Confirms the interpretation of each obligation and reviews contract clauses.
Obligation owner A manager named for each row of GOV-REG-04. Operates the controls and keeps the evidence.
Head of Engineering Owns software licensing and open source compliance.
Internal Auditor Performs the independent review in 4.9.

4. Procedure

4.1 Identify by jurisdiction. The Privacy Officer lists every jurisdiction where the organisation is established, employs people, sells, hosts or stores data, or has customers who impose their own law by contract. For each, with legal counsel, the Privacy Officer identifies the obligations in the categories in section 2.

4.2 Identify by role. For each processing activity in PIMS-REG-01 the Privacy Officer records whether the organisation acts as controller, processor or both, because the obligations differ. Obligations that attach only to one role are marked accordingly in GOV-REG-04.

4.3 Record. Each obligation is entered in GOV-REG-04 with a reference, a plain description of what it requires, its source, the jurisdiction, whether it applies as Controller, Processor, Both or not at all, the obligation owner, and the review frequency. One row per distinct requirement, not one row per law.

4.4 Map to controls and evidence. The Information Security Manager names, for each row, the kit documents and the ISMS-REG-01 controls that satisfy it and the evidence that proves it, and sets the status: Compliant, Partial, Gap or Not assessed. A Gap or Partial status creates either a risk in GOV-REG-05 or a corrective action in GOV-REG-03 within ten working days, with the reference recorded in the row.

4.5 Contracts. Before a customer or supplier contract is signed, the Information Security Manager reviews its security, privacy and audit clauses. Commitments the organisation accepts are recorded in GOV-REG-04, and the supplier's obligations to the organisation are recorded in GOV-REG-07. A commitment the organisation cannot meet is refused or negotiated; it is never signed and left unrecorded.

4.6 Monitor change. The Privacy Officer subscribes to the publications of the relevant regulators, professional bodies and legal counsel, reviews GOV-REG-04 twice a year, and assesses any change in law, regulation, guidance or contract within thirty days of learning of it. A change that affects a control triggers a review of the relevant document under GOV-PRO-01 and, where needed, a risk reassessment under GOV-PRO-05.

4.7 Intellectual property. The organisation uses software, content and data only under a valid licence. The Head of Engineering keeps the licence inventory in GOV-REG-24 current, checks open source licences during development under GOV-PRO-15, and removes unlicensed software within ten working days of discovery. The organisation's own intellectual property is classified and handled under GOV-PRO-16, and staff and contractor agreements under GOV-PRO-18 assign rights in work product to the organisation.

4.8 Protection of records. Records that the law, a regulator or a contract requires are listed in the retention schedule PIMS-REG-07 with their period and trigger. The obligation owner protects them against loss, destruction, falsification and unauthorised access for that period, in a format that remains readable, and places them under legal hold when litigation or an investigation is reasonably expected. Disposal follows PIMS-POL-02.

4.9 Independent review. At least once a year, and after any significant change to the business, the law or the systems, the Internal Auditor or an external reviewer who is independent of the areas reviewed examines whether the approach to managing information security and privacy, and its implementation, still meets the obligations in GOV-REG-04 and the organisation's own policies. The result is reported to the executive sponsor and to management review, and findings follow GOV-PRO-04.

4.10 Compliance with policies in each area. Each head of function reviews, at least annually, whether their area follows the policies and procedures that apply to it, using the evidence named in those documents, and records the result. Nonconformities are raised under GOV-PRO-04.

4.11 Personal data. Obligations about personal data are met through PIMS-POL-01 and the procedures it names. The Privacy Officer confirms twice a year that every processing activity in PIMS-REG-01 has a lawful basis, a notice, a retention period and, where required, a DPIA in PIMS-REG-08.

4.12 Reporting. The Privacy Officer reports the status distribution of GOV-REG-04, open gaps and changes assessed since the last report to the steering committee quarterly and to management review.

5. Records and evidence

  • GOV-REG-04 Legal, regulatory and contractual register, with status and evidence for every obligation.
  • Contract review records and the clauses accepted.
  • Change assessments with dates and outcomes.
  • GOV-REG-24 Software and hardware inventory with licence information.
  • Independent review reports and the resulting GOV-REG-03 entries.
  • Area compliance review records from heads of function.

6. Exceptions

An obligation may be marked Not assessed for no more than ninety days after it is identified. A decision not to comply with an obligation is not an exception under this procedure; it is a risk accepted by the Chief Executive Officer under GOV-PRO-24 with legal advice recorded.

7. Review and maintenance

The Privacy Officer reviews this procedure annually, after any regulatory enquiry or contractual dispute about compliance, and when the organisation enters a new jurisdiction or sector. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Cloud Services Security Procedure

How cloud services are used securely, covering shared responsibility, account structure, region and residency decisions, identity federation, the areas that must be proved with evidence, and provider exit.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.23; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 8.9; SOC 2 CC6.1; SOC 2 CC9.2. Owner: Head of Engineering.

1. Purpose

This procedure sets how [Organisation] uses cloud services securely: who is responsible for what, how accounts are structured and administered, where data may be located, how identities are federated, which areas must be proved with evidence before and during use, and how the organisation would leave a provider.

2. Scope

It applies to all infrastructure, platform and software services consumed from cloud providers for [Organisation]'s business, in every account, subscription, project and tenancy that [Organisation] owns or administers, including trials and sandboxes. Assessment of the provider as a supplier follows GOV-PRO-06; this procedure covers configuration and operation of the services.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Head of Engineering Owns the account structure, the guardrails and this procedure.
Cloud platform team Administers the organisation root, the landing zone, identity federation and posture monitoring.
System Owner Owns the accounts and services for their system and the evidence for the must-prove areas.
Information Security Manager Approves region decisions, reviews posture findings monthly, verifies evidence at go-live and annually.
Privacy Officer Confirms residency and processing decisions for personal data.

4. Procedure

4.1 Shared responsibility. For each cloud service in use, the System Owner records which party is responsible for each layer: physical, host and hypervisor, network, operating system, platform, application, identity and access, data, logging and backup. The provider's assurance report (GOV-PRO-06) evidences the provider's side; this procedure and GOV-CHK-02 evidence [Organisation]'s side. The record is kept with the system's entry in GOV-REG-10.

4.2 Account structure. The cloud platform team operates a management or root account used only for organisation settings and billing, with separate accounts, subscriptions or projects for production, non-production, security and logging, and sandbox. Root or global administrator credentials are held under break-glass control: hardware-backed multi-factor authentication, credentials in a sealed store, every use alerting under GOV-PRO-14 and recorded in GOV-REG-13. Organisation-level guardrails prevent disabling audit logging, deploying outside approved regions and creating public storage without an approved exception.

4.3 Region and residency. The System Owner proposes the regions for each system from the residency obligations in GOV-REG-04, the privacy requirements in PIMS-POL-03 and customer contracts; the Information Security Manager and the Privacy Officer approve. Unapproved regions are disabled by guardrail where the provider allows it. Approved regions are recorded per system in GOV-REG-10, and provider services that replicate or process data outside the approved region are listed in GOV-REG-25 as external processing.

4.4 Identity federation. All human access to consoles and APIs comes through [Organisation]'s central identity provider with single sign-on and multi-factor authentication per GOV-POL-06. Local cloud users are limited to break-glass and documented service identities. Roles follow least privilege, privileged roles are time-bound and approved per use, and access is reviewed quarterly under GOV-PRO-10 with results in GOV-REG-12. Workloads use short-lived role credentials; any long-lived key is recorded in GOV-REG-18 and rotated under GOV-PRO-20.

4.5 Must-prove areas. Before a system goes live, and at least annually afterwards, the System Owner produces the evidence below and the Information Security Manager verifies it under the gate in PB-07 using GOV-REG-29. Each item of evidence shows the account, region, date and the identity that captured it (PB-09).

Area What must be true Evidence to capture
Account and region Workloads run only in approved accounts and regions Account list from the organisation; region settings export
Privileged access and multi-factor Every privileged identity is federated with multi-factor enforced; break-glass sealed Identity provider policy export; privileged role membership; last break-glass use record
Exposure No unapproved public storage, addresses, ports or shared snapshots Posture report; public resource inventory against the approved list
Encryption and keys Storage and databases encrypted at rest; customer-managed keys for Restricted data; TLS on every endpoint Encryption settings export; GOV-REG-18 entries; endpoint scan
Logging and retention Audit logging on in every account and region, delivered to the central store, retained per GOV-PRO-14 Logging configuration export; central store retention setting
Backups and restore Backups configured per GOV-PRO-12 in a separate account and restore tested Backup policy export; latest GOV-REG-15 entry
External processing Every provider service and sub-processor that receives data is known and contracted GOV-REG-25 rows; provider sub-processor list; GOV-REG-07 entry

4.6 Baseline and posture. Accounts meet the cloud account checks in GOV-CHK-02. A posture monitoring service evaluates configuration continuously; findings are triaged under GOV-PRO-11 with the same deadlines. Infrastructure is defined in code reviewed under GOV-PRO-15; manual console changes in production are changes under GOV-PRO-09 and are reconciled against the definitions weekly.

4.7 Tagging and ownership. Every account and resource carries tags for owner, system, environment and data classification. Untagged resources are reported weekly and removed after 30 days if unclaimed.

4.8 New services and discovery. A new cloud service or provider requires the System Owner's request, a review against this procedure and GOV-PRO-06, and the Information Security Manager's approval before any data is placed in it. The cloud platform team reviews billing and identity provider sign-in records quarterly to detect unapproved services.

4.9 Provider exit. For each critical provider the System Owner documents the data and configuration to export and in what format, the export procedure and who runs it, the provider's retention and deletion commitments after termination, and the alternative arrangement. The export procedure is tested annually on a sample and recorded in GOV-REG-16.

5. Records and evidence

  • Shared responsibility records per service.
  • Account structure and guardrail configuration exports.
  • Region approvals per system.
  • Must-prove evidence packs per system with the verification record (GOV-TPL-12).
  • Posture findings in GOV-REG-14 and the monthly review.
  • Quarterly discovery reviews and annual provider exit tests.

6. Exceptions

A public resource or a region outside the approved list is permitted only under a time-limited risk acceptance in GOV-PRO-24 approved by the Head of Engineering and the Information Security Manager, with the guardrail exception documented and set to expire.

7. Review and maintenance

The Head of Engineering reviews this procedure annually, after a provider incident affecting [Organisation], when a new provider is adopted, and when a residency obligation changes. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Threat Intelligence and Vulnerability Disclosure Handling Procedure

How threat and vulnerability information is collected, triaged, turned into action and shared, and how vulnerability reports from outside the organisation are received, acknowledged, validated, fixed and credited under a safe harbour.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.7; SOC 2 CC7.1; SOC 2 CC2.3. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. Purpose

This procedure keeps [Organisation] informed about the threats and vulnerabilities that matter to it, turns that information into action within defined times, and gives outside researchers a safe and predictable way to report a vulnerability in [Organisation]'s systems.

2. Scope

It applies to threat and vulnerability information from any source about the technologies, suppliers and sector in which [Organisation] operates, and to reports about [Organisation]'s own systems, products and services received from customers, researchers, suppliers, authorities or the public.

3. Roles and responsibilities

Role Responsibility
Information Security Manager Owns both processes, maintains the sources, triages intelligence and external reports, issues bulletins.
Security analyst Monitors the sources, performs first triage, keeps the reporter informed.
System Owner Confirms relevance to their system and remediates under GOV-PRO-11.
Head of Engineering Receives the monthly summary and allocates remediation effort.
Communications lead and legal adviser Approve the published disclosure policy and any public statement or credit.

4. Procedure

Threat intelligence

4.1 Sources. The Information Security Manager maintains a source list matched to the inventory in GOV-REG-24 and the suppliers in GOV-REG-07: vendor and provider security advisories for every product in use, the national computer emergency response team, a sector information sharing group where one exists, published vulnerability databases, reputable research publications, and [Organisation]'s own incident and monitoring data. The list is reviewed quarterly and when a product or supplier is added.

4.2 Collection. The analyst reviews the sources at least weekly, and advisories marked critical or actively exploited on the day they are published. Each item is recorded with source, date, affected technology and an initial relevance rating.

4.3 Triage. For each item the analyst answers four questions: do we run the affected technology or version; is it exposed to the internet or to untrusted users; does it hold Confidential or Restricted data; is exploitation reported. A relevant item becomes one or more of: a finding in GOV-REG-14 with its severity and deadline under GOV-PRO-11; a detection rule or search under GOV-PRO-14; an update to a risk in GOV-REG-05; a supplier query under GOV-PRO-06; an awareness message to staff under GOV-PRO-08. The decision and the action reference are recorded against the item.

4.4 Dissemination. Urgent items (critical and exploitable in [Organisation]'s environment) go to the Head of Engineering and the affected System Owners within 24 hours of receipt. A monthly summary of relevant threats, actions taken and open items goes to the Head of Engineering and the steering committee. Intelligence received under a sharing agreement is handled according to the sharing marking it carries and is not forwarded beyond the permitted audience.

4.5 Outbound sharing. The Information Security Manager may share indicators and lessons with the sector group or the national team after removing customer and personal data, and records what was shared and when.

Vulnerability disclosure handling

4.6 Published policy. [Organisation] publishes a vulnerability disclosure policy stating: the systems in scope; how to report, through a monitored security contact and a machine-readable security contact file at the recognised location; what to include in a report; what the reporter can expect and when; the safe harbour statement in 4.7; and the testing that is out of bounds (denial of service, social engineering, physical intrusion, and access to other users' data beyond what proves the issue).

4.7 Safe harbour. The policy states, in plain words, that [Organisation] will not pursue legal action against, or report to authorities, a person who finds and reports a vulnerability in good faith, stays within the policy's scope and rules, avoids privacy violations and service disruption, does not exploit the issue beyond what is needed to demonstrate it, and allows [Organisation] a reasonable time to fix it before publishing. The legal adviser approves the wording.

4.8 Receiving a report. The analyst acknowledges every report within three working days, records it in GOV-REG-14 with the source External report and the reporter's reference, and retains all correspondence. A report containing personal data or credentials is handled as Restricted.

4.9 Validation. Within ten working days the analyst reproduces or disproves the issue with the System Owner, assigns severity under GOV-PRO-11 and tells the reporter the outcome. A report revealing an existing compromise becomes an incident under GOV-PRO-07 at once.

4.10 Remediation and updates. The System Owner fixes the issue within the deadline for its severity. The analyst updates the reporter at least every 30 days until closure and confirms the fix to them. Reporters are offered public credit on request. A monetary reward is given only where a formal programme exists.

4.11 Coordinated publication. Where a vulnerability affects customers or other organisations, the Information Security Manager coordinates notification under contractual commitments and GOV-PRO-07, and agrees a publication date with the reporter, by default no later than 90 days after validation unless both parties agree otherwise.

4.12 Measures. Quarterly the Information Security Manager reports: reports received, time to acknowledge, time to validate, time to fix by severity, and intelligence items turned into actions, alongside the vulnerability metrics in GOV-PRO-11.

5. Records and evidence

  • The source list and its quarterly review.
  • The intelligence log with triage decisions and action references.
  • Monthly threat summaries and urgent bulletins.
  • The published disclosure policy with legal approval and version history.
  • GOV-REG-14 entries for external reports and the correspondence archive.
  • Quarterly measures.

6. Exceptions

A report outside the published scope is still acknowledged and triaged; the safe harbour applies only within scope. No other exception applies.

7. Review and maintenance

The Information Security Manager reviews this procedure annually, after any report that was handled late or published before the fix, and when a law on coordinated disclosure or product security changes. Changes follow GOV-PRO-01.

Top management commitment statement

A one-page statement in which the leadership of [Organisation] commits to resourcing, integrating, directing and improving the information security and privacy management system.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 5.1; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.3; SOC 2 CC1.1. Owner: Chief Executive Officer.

1. Statement

The leadership of [Organisation] regards the protection of information, and of the people whose personal data we process, as a condition of doing business, not an addition to it. We have established an information security and privacy management system covering the scope in ISMS-STM-01, and we hold ourselves accountable for its results.

2. What leadership commits to

  1. Direction. We have approved GOV-POL-03 and the objectives in ISMS-PLN-01, and we will keep both consistent with the strategy and risk appetite of the organisation.
  2. Resources. We will fund and staff the management system each financial year, including the people, training, tools and external support needed to treat the risks recorded in GOV-REG-05 within the agreed dates.
  3. Integration. Security and privacy requirements form part of how we plan projects, select suppliers, develop software, hire people and run operations. They are not handled by a separate team after the fact.
  4. Roles. We have appointed an Information Security Manager and a Privacy Officer, given them the authority described in GOV-POL-01, and we expect every manager to carry the responsibilities assigned to them.
  5. Review. We will attend management review under GOV-PRO-03 at least once a year, consider every mandatory input, and record our decisions and the resources we assign.
  6. Improvement. We will act on audit results, incidents, measurement results and nonconformities through GOV-PRO-04, and we will not accept a risk above appetite without recording who accepted it and why.
  7. Compliance. We will identify and meet our legal, regulatory and contractual obligations as recorded in GOV-REG-04.
  8. Culture. We will lead by example, complete the same training as everyone else, and support anyone who reports a weakness or an incident in good faith.

3. How this commitment is demonstrated

Auditors and interested parties may test this statement against the approved budget, steering committee minutes, management review minutes (GOV-TPL-03), the action tracker (GOV-REG-22) and the objectives tracker (GOV-REG-21).

4. Signature

Role Name Signature Date
Chief Executive Officer [Name] [Signature] [Date]
Executive sponsor, if different [Name] [Signature] [Date]

This statement is reviewed annually and re-signed after any change in the signatories.

Supplier Security and Privacy Questionnaire

The questions a supplier answers before it is given information or access, with space for its evidence and a scoring method that produces an approval outcome under GOV-PRO-06.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.19; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.20; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 7.2.6; SOC 2 CC9.2; GDPR Article 28. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. How to use this questionnaire

Send sections 2 and 3 to the supplier. The supplier owner sets the tier under GOV-PRO-06 step 4.1 first: Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers answer every question; Tier 3 suppliers answer domains 3.1, 3.3, 3.6 and 3.11 only. The supplier writes its answer in the Answer column and names the document, export or screenshot it attaches in the Evidence column. An answer without evidence scores lower than an answer with it. The reviewer completes sections 4 and 5. Questions marked with an asterisk are critical: a score of 0 on a critical question blocks approval for Tier 1 and Tier 2 until the gap is remediated or an exception is accepted under GOV-PRO-24.

2. Supplier and service details

Field Entry
Supplier legal name [Supplier]
Service to be provided [Service]
Supplier owner at [Organisation] [Role]
Tier assigned [Tier]

Personal data involved Yes / No. If yes, section 3.10 is mandatory and processor terms are required before any data is shared.
Supplier contact completing this questionnaire [Role]
Date returned [Date]

3. Questions

3.1 Organisation and governance

No. Question Answer Evidence
1* Do you have an approved information security policy, and who in your management is accountable for information security?
