Playbook: Running a Readiness Assessment with the Questionnaire

How to run the 60 question readiness questionnaire in GOV-REG-28, score it, read the result honestly and turn every gap into an owned action.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 4.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.1; SOC 2 CC4.1. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. What the questionnaire is, and what it is not

GOV-REG-28 holds 60 questions in ten domains, six per domain. It measures two things at once: how much of a working security and privacy programme exists, and how much of it can be proved. Each question comes with a sentence on why it matters, so that the person answering understands what the question is for rather than guessing what the asker wants to hear.

It is not an audit. An audit samples records against the clauses of a standard; ISMS-REG-04 does that. It is not a legal gap assessment; GDPR-REG-01 does that for the GDPR. It is not a certification and produces nothing you can show a client as one. It is a structured conversation with evidence attached, and its output is a scored picture of where you stand and a list of actions.

Use it at four moments: at the start, as the baseline before PB-02, PB-03 or PB-04; three months before an external audit, alongside GOV-CHK-03; when a client or a board asks how mature the programme is; and once a year, so that the trend is visible.

2. Before you start

Four decisions, made by the executive sponsor and the Information Security Manager before anyone answers a question.

Scope. The whole organisation, or one business unit, or one service. If a scope statement already exists in ISMS-STM-01, use the same boundary so that the result is comparable with the audit.

Roles. A coordinator, usually the Information Security Manager, who runs the sessions and keeps the register. A reviewer for each domain who did not answer it. An executive sponsor who will receive the result and own the action list. Nobody scores their own domain; that rule is what makes the result worth reading.

Time. Two to three weeks elapsed. Each respondent spends about a day, split across a preparation hour, a ninety minute session and the time to find evidence. The coordinator spends four to five days.

The copy. Take a dated copy of GOV-REG-28 for this assessment. Never answer in the master. The dated copies are the trend.

3. The ten domains and who answers

Domain Typical respondent Typical reviewer
Governance Chief Executive Officer or executive sponsor Internal Auditor
Scope and context Information Security Manager Internal Auditor
Risk Information Security Manager and risk owners Internal Auditor
Policies and documents Information Security Manager and document owners Internal Auditor
People Head of human resources [Role] Information Security Manager
Access Head of Engineering or head of IT [Role] Information Security Manager
Assets and data System owners and the Privacy Officer Information Security Manager
Technology and cloud Head of Engineering Information Security Manager
Suppliers Procurement [Role] and supplier owners Privacy Officer
Incidents and continuity Information Security Manager and operations lead [Role] Internal Auditor

Where the same person holds several roles, which is normal in a small organisation, the reviewer for that person's domains must be someone else, even an external adviser or a board member. The respondent answers; the reviewer sets maturity and status.

4. The three answer types

Every question is prefilled with a suggested answer type. The type says what kind of thing counts as an answer.

Policy. Point to the approved document that states the rule: its identifier, version and approval date. "Yes, we have a policy" is not an answer; "GOV-POL-06 version 1.0, approved [Date], acknowledged by all staff in GOV-REG-23" is. A Policy answer earns maturity 3 only when there is also evidence that the rule is followed, so a Policy question often needs a register or proof reference as well.

Register. Point to the rows of the kit register that hold the record: for example, the access review rows in GOV-REG-12 for the last two quarters. The register must be live, with dated entries and named owners. A register that is still the blank template is a maturity 0 answer with good intentions.

Proof. Attach an artefact that shows the control operating: a system export, a screenshot that meets the rules in PB-09, a signed record, a closed ticket, a test result. One artefact per question is enough if it is the right one.

The respondent may propose a different type where a better form of answer exists; the reviewer decides. Three things are never an answer whatever the type: a sentence with no reference ("we do this"), a plan ("we will do this next quarter"), and the name of a product on its own.

5. Scoring: maturity 0 to 3

The reviewer scores each question after seeing the answer and the evidence.

Maturity Meaning What the reviewer saw
0 Nothing in place, or the respondent does not know No document, no record, no artefact
1 Done informally or occasionally, without a document or record, or with a document nobody follows A verbal account, a draft, a stale record
2 Documented and performed, but the records are incomplete, irregular or not independently checked An approved document and a partly filled register
3 Documented, performed at the stated frequency, records complete, verified by the reviewer Document, live register and proof, all consistent

The Status column carries the reviewer's confidence in the score. Verified means the reviewer saw the evidence and the maturity is final. To confirm means evidence was requested, an owner and due date are set, and the maturity is provisional. Not implemented means the maturity is 0 or 1 and an action is needed. Not applicable means the reviewer agrees the question does not apply, and the row leaves the arithmetic.

The arithmetic is deliberately simple. The Score column in GOV-REG-28 divides maturity by three for every applicable row. A domain percentage is the average Score across the domain's applicable rows, which is the same as the sum of maturity divided by three times the number of applicable questions. The overall percentage is the average of the ten domain percentages, so that every domain weighs the same however many rows were excluded. Report one more number beside the percentages: the count of Verified rows out of 60, the proof ratio. It separates "we have it" from "we can prove it", and auditors live on the second.

6. Running the sessions

Run one session per respondent, sixty to ninety minutes, with the register open on a shared screen.

  1. The coordinator reads the question and the "why it matters" line aloud. The second line stops the conversation turning into a debate about what the question means.
  2. The respondent names the answer. The coordinator records the answer type, the answer and the evidence reference in the row immediately. Nothing is written up afterwards from memory.
  3. Anything without a reference becomes To confirm, with the respondent as owner and a due date inside five working days. This is the no-assumption rule from PB-09 and it applies to every row without exception.
  4. Evidence is filed in the evidence folder under the numbered area that matches the domain, named as PB-09 describes, so that the reference in the register points to something that exists.
  5. Within five working days of the last session the reviewer for each domain opens every reference, sets maturity and status, and writes one sentence in Reviewer notes saying what was seen or what is missing. A reviewer note that says only "OK" is not a review.
  6. The coordinator closes To confirm rows as evidence arrives, and escalates any row still open after its due date to the sponsor. A To confirm row is never quietly extended.

7. Reading the result

Overall percentage Reading What it means for the next step
0 to 39 Foundation The programme does not yet exist in a provable form. Start at the first four steps of PB-02, or the opening phases of PB-03 or PB-04. Do not book an external audit
40 to 69 Developing Rules exist but evidence is patchy. Concentrate on live registers and records. An internal audit now will find major nonconformities, which is useful if the organisation can hear it
70 to 89 Established The programme operates. Close the specific gaps, run the first internal audit cycle under PB-06, and plan the external audit three to six months out
90 to 100 Audit-ready Run GOV-CHK-03 four weeks before the certification audit or the start of the SOC 2 observation period, and keep the evidence habit

Read the shape as well as the number. Any domain below 40 is a priority whatever the overall figure, because a certification audit fails on the weakest clause, not on the average. A high score on Policy questions beside a low proof ratio is a paper programme: the documents exist and the work does not. A domain with many To confirm rows is an ownership problem rather than a control problem, and the fix is a name beside each row, not a new procedure.

Give the sponsor three answers, not a spreadsheet: the lowest domain and why, the largest gap between what is written and what is proved, and how many rows have no owner.

8. Turning gaps into actions

Every row whose status is Not implemented, and every row Verified at maturity 0 or 1, becomes one action in GOV-REG-03 under GOV-PRO-04. The description is the question text plus what is missing. The source is "Readiness assessment, [Date]". The owner is the row owner. The action names the kit document that closes the gap, taken from the table below, and the due date follows priority.

Domain Kit documents that close the common gaps
Governance GOV-POL-01, GOV-POL-03, GOV-PRO-03, GOV-REG-21, GOV-REG-01
Scope and context ISMS-STM-01, ISMS-PRO-01, ISMS-REG-03, GOV-PRO-25, GOV-REG-04
Risk GOV-PRO-05, GOV-REG-05, ISMS-REG-01, GOV-PRO-24, GOV-REG-06
Policies and documents GOV-PRO-01, GOV-REG-01, GOV-REG-23
People GOV-PRO-18, GOV-PRO-08, GOV-REG-09, GOV-CHK-01
Access GOV-PRO-10, GOV-POL-06, GOV-REG-12, GOV-REG-13
Assets and data GOV-PRO-16, GOV-REG-10, PIMS-REG-01, GDPR-REG-02, PIMS-POL-02, PIMS-REG-07, GOV-REG-20
Technology and cloud GOV-CHK-02, GOV-PRO-11, GOV-PRO-09, GOV-PRO-14, GOV-PRO-20, GOV-PRO-12, GOV-REG-15
Suppliers GOV-PRO-06, GOV-REG-07, GOV-TPL-04, PIMS-TPL-02
Incidents and continuity GOV-PRO-07, GOV-REG-08, PIMS-PRO-04, GOV-TPL-11, GOV-PRO-13, GOV-TPL-07, GOV-REG-16

Priority order: first anything that is a legal duty regardless of framework, which in practice means processor terms, the breach process and the processing inventory; then the blockers for the framework you are heading towards; then everything else from the lowest maturity upwards. The sponsor reviews the action list once, approves the dates and resources, and the list goes to the next management review under GOV-PRO-03 with the domain percentages beside it.

9. Repeating the assessment

Repeat annually and before each external audit. Keep every dated copy and compare domain percentages, not individual answers. Do not carry answers forward: a Proof answer older than twelve months is stale and is re-verified, and a Register answer is re-opened to check that entries continued after the last assessment. Put the overall percentage and the proof ratio into GOV-REG-21 as measures, so that the trend reaches management review without anyone having to remember to bring it.

Playbook: Evidence Management That Survives an Audit

How to collect, name, protect and present the evidence that proves controls operate, so that an auditor, a reviewer or an investigator can rely on it without the person who collected it in the room.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 7.5.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.2; SOC 2 CC4.1. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. What evidence is for

Evidence is the proof that a control operated at a point in time. Three audiences depend on it. The auditor, internal or external, who tests a control by sampling its records. The reviewer at a gate or a readiness assessment, who must set a status without taking anyone's word for it. And the organisation itself after an incident, when it has to show what was configured, who had access and when a change was made. To all three, a control without evidence is a control that did not operate. That is not cynicism; it is the only position a person can take who was not there.

Good evidence shares five properties. It is dated by the system that produced it. It shows where it came from: the account, the environment, the tenant or region. It is complete rather than illustrative: a population rather than one example. It is unaltered, and you can show that it is. And it is findable by someone other than the person who filed it.

2. The no-assumption rule

Every unknown becomes To confirm, plus an owner, plus a due date.

Never write "assumed", "should be", "probably", "I believe" or "as far as we know" in a register, a review or a report. If you did not see it, it is To confirm. This applies in GOV-REG-28, in GOV-REG-29, in ISMS-REG-02, in audit preparation and in every incident timeline. The reason is practical. An assumption converts into an audit finding at the worst possible moment; a To confirm row converts into a task today. The two cost the same to write and behave completely differently afterwards.

The rule has a corollary. A To confirm row that passes its due date is escalated to the sponsor or the Information Security Manager, not quietly extended. Extended unknowns are assumptions wearing a different label.

3. The evidence folder structure

One root folder per period: the audit cycle year for the management system, or one per project for a gate. Under the root, numbered areas. The first ten match the ten domains of GOV-REG-28 so that a readiness assessment, an internal audit and an external audit all file in the same place.

Area Holds
01 Governance Steering minutes, management review packs and minutes, objectives reports, policy approvals
02 Scope and context Scope statement, context analysis, interested parties, legal register extracts
03 Risk Risk assessment exports, treatment plans, acceptances and exceptions, Statement of Applicability
04 Policies and documents Approved versions, review records, acknowledgement exports
05 People Screening confirmations, training completion exports, induction records, leaver checklists
06 Access Access request approvals, access review exports, privileged account lists, multi-factor settings
07 Assets and data Asset register exports, classification records, processing inventory, retention checks, disposal records
08 Technology and cloud Configuration exports, vulnerability scan exports, change tickets, backup and restore records, log retention settings
09 Suppliers Questionnaires, certificates, assurance reports, contracts, review notes, exit confirmations
10 Incidents and continuity Incident records, post-incident reviews, breach assessments, exercise records, continuity plans and test results
11 Audit and review Internal audit plans and reports, corrective action records, external audit correspondence
12 Projects and gates One subfolder per gate with its GOV-REG-29 copy, evidence and GOV-TPL-12 note

Inside each area, split by system or by control only when volume demands it. Every area carries two files: an index, which is a simple table of file name, what it proves, which control or question it serves, the date collected and who collected it; and a hash list, described in section 7. The folder is classified Confidential, because evidence routinely contains names, account identifiers and configuration detail. Read access is for reviewers and auditors, write access for collectors, and nobody deletes except the Information Security Manager under the retention schedule.

4. File naming

Name every file as date, system, area, what, joined with underscores and in lower case:

YYYYMMDD_system_area_what.ext
YYYYMMDD_identityprovider_access_mfa-policy-export.csv
YYYYMMDD_backupservice_backups_restore-test-result.pdf
YYYYMMDD_cloudaccount_logging_retention-setting-01.png

The date is the date the evidence was collected, not the date it was filed, and it comes first so that a folder sorts into a timeline. The system is one word that anyone in the organisation would recognise. The area matches the folder. The "what" says what the file proves in two or three words. Add a two digit sequence number when several screenshots make up one proof. Never use "final", "new", "latest", "v2" or a person's name in a file name; the index records who collected it, and the date already says which is latest.

5. What a screenshot must show

A screenshot is admissible only when it answers four questions without the collector present: who was logged in, where, when, and what is being shown.

  • Account. The signed-in user is visible, usually in the top corner of the console. An auditor needs to know the setting was read with an account entitled to see the whole picture.
  • Environment. The tenant, subscription, account identifier or region is visible, or the navigation path makes it unambiguous. Production and staging consoles look identical; the identifier is the only difference.
  • Date and time. The operating system clock or the page's own timestamp is in the frame. A file's modification date is not enough, because files are copied.
  • The whole window. Include the address bar or the navigation path and the page title. A cropped widget proves nothing about where it came from.
  • One fact per image. If a proof needs three settings, take three numbered screenshots, not one scrolled composite.
  • Masking. Mask secrets, keys, passwords and personal data of individuals who are not needed for the proof, with a solid block so that the masking is obvious. Never blur, never crop to hide, never edit anything else.

A screenshot that fails any of these is To confirm until retaken.

6. Exports over screenshots

Where the system can export, export. A system export is complete where a screenshot is a sample; it is dated and attributed by the system; it can be filtered, counted and reconciled; and it is far harder to fabricate. Auditors sample from populations, so give them populations.

Control Prefer this export Not this
Access review The full user and role list for the system as a dated file, with the reviewer's decisions beside each row in GOV-REG-12 A screenshot of the first page of users
Change management The change ticket export for the audit period Three example tickets chosen by the team
Backup The job history export showing every run and result for the period A screenshot of a green status tile
Training The completion export from the training record with names and dates, filed against GOV-REG-09 An email saying everyone finished
Vulnerability management The scan result export with severities and dates, reconciled to GOV-REG-14 A dashboard summary
Logging The retention configuration export and a log query result for a known event A screenshot of a log viewer

Screenshots remain right for settings pages with no export and for events that are visual by nature, such as an alert arriving in the monitored channel.

7. Integrity: hashing and protection

Compute a hash value, using a current algorithm such as SHA-256, for every file at the moment of collection. Record it in the area's hash list with the file name, the collector and the date. Keep a copy of every hash list in a location the collectors cannot modify: the evidence index held by the Information Security Manager, or storage with a write-once setting. Re-verify the hashes before an audit and after any migration of the folder, and record that the verification was done.

This answers two questions before they are asked. From an auditor: how do you know this file was not altered after the fact. From an investigator after an incident: is this the configuration that was in place on that date. In both cases the answer is a hash list in a place the person who filed the evidence could not reach.

8. Retention and access

Keep evidence for at least one full certification cycle, three years for ISO/IEC 27001, or for the SOC 2 examination period plus the following examination, whichever is longer. Where client contracts require longer, GOV-REG-04 holds the period. Evidence that contains personal data follows PIMS-POL-02 and the schedule in PIMS-REG-07 as well: export only the columns the proof needs, and when the retention period ends, delete the evidence and record the deletion in the area index.

Review who has access to the evidence folder quarterly, as part of the access reviews in GOV-REG-12. Auditors receive read access to the period under audit for the duration of the audit, and that access is removed and recorded when the audit closes, exactly as reviewer accounts are removed after a gate under PB-07.

9. What auditors reject

Each of these has cost an organisation a finding. None of them is about the control; all of them are about the evidence.

  1. Undated screenshots, or screenshots whose only date is the file's modification time.
  2. Screenshots that show neither the account nor the environment, so that production cannot be distinguished from staging.
  3. Cropped images with no page context.
  4. A policy document offered as proof that the control operates. A policy proves the rule exists; a record proves it was followed.
  5. Evidence from outside the audit period, however good.
  6. A single example where a population was requested, or examples chosen by the team rather than sampled by the auditor.
  7. Evidence produced during the audit for a control that should have operated months earlier. The evidence may be genuine; the control was not operating.
  8. A file whose creation date contradicts its content.
  9. Exports that have been opened and saved in a spreadsheet application, losing the original format and gaining an edit history.
  10. A ticket closed with no record of what was done or who verified it.
  11. A register that is still the blank template, or has entries that stop three months ago.
  12. A signed acknowledgement that does not say which version of which policy was acknowledged, or when.
  13. An email that says "confirmed" with nothing attached.

If you recognise one of your own files in this list, mark its row To confirm today and collect it properly. It costs an hour now and a finding later.

10. The evidence footer

Every artefact that draws a conclusion ends with three lines. Audit reports, review minutes, risk assessments, gate verdict notes, readiness results, supplier assessments and post-incident reviews all qualify.

Evidence used: [file names or index references the conclusions rest on]
Evidence missing: [items that were To confirm when this was written, each with owner and due date]
Owner: [the role that holds this artefact and will update it]

The footer does two things. It lets a reader separate what the author saw from what the author believed, which is the difference between a finding and an opinion. And it turns every artefact into the to-do list for the next cycle, because the missing evidence is written down where the next person will look. An artefact with an empty "Evidence missing" line is making a strong claim; the author should be sure it is true.

11. Building the habit: evidence by frequency

Evidence collected on the day a control runs costs minutes. Evidence reconstructed before an audit costs days and is often rejected under section 9. Attach the collection to the control's own rhythm.

Frequency Evidence produced at the time Filed against
Daily Alert triage notes under GOV-PRO-14 08 Technology and cloud
Weekly Vulnerability scan export, backup job history export GOV-REG-14, GOV-REG-15
Monthly Incident metrics report, change log export, training completion export GOV-REG-08, GOV-REG-11, GOV-REG-09
Quarterly Access review exports with decisions, restore test record, Tier 1 supplier review notes, steering committee minutes GOV-REG-12, GOV-REG-15, GOV-REG-07, 01 Governance
Annually Risk assessment export, management review minutes, internal audit report, policy acknowledgement export, continuity exercise record, supplier annual reviews GOV-REG-05, GOV-TPL-03, GOV-TPL-01, GOV-REG-23, GOV-REG-16, GOV-REG-07

Organisations heading for SOC 2 keep the same rhythm in SOC-REG-02, which is the calendar form of this table. Whichever form you use, the test is the same: on any given day, could an auditor open the folder and find last month's evidence without asking anyone.

Playbook: one control set, several certifications

How to run one set of controls, one set of registers and one evidence folder so that ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701, SOC 2, the GDPR and NIST CSF 2.0 are served together through the crosswalk GOV-REG-27, with a plain account of where the frameworks genuinely differ and what cannot be shared between them.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 4.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.3; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.4.1.3; SOC 2 CC4.1; GDPR Article 24; GDPR Article 32; NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC. Owner: Information Security Manager.

1. The idea

An organisation that reviews access quarterly does one piece of work. ISO/IEC 27001 calls it an Annex A control, SOC 2 calls it a control activity under two criteria, the GDPR calls it a technical and organisational measure, and NIST CSF 2.0 calls it a subcategory outcome. The work, the record and the evidence are the same. Everything that differs is how each framework asks about them.

So the kit holds one control set, described in its procedures and declared in ISMS-REG-01, and GOV-REG-27 records for each control which criteria, articles and categories it serves. Registers carry framework tags rather than being duplicated. Evidence is collected once, to the strictest standard any framework imposes, and filed once. The audits, attestations and inspections then read from the same system, and the cost of the second and third framework is mostly the parts that cannot be shared, which section 7 lists.

2. What each framework is

Framework What it is Who checks and what you get
ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A management system standard: requirements for how you govern security (clauses 4 to 10) plus a reference list of controls (Annex A) you compare your own choice against An accredited certification body audits and issues a certificate for a three year cycle with annual surveillance
ISO/IEC 27701 An extension to ISO/IEC 27001 that adds privacy requirements and controller and processor controls; it cannot be certified on its own The same certification body extends the certificate scope
SOC 2 An attestation framework: you write a system description and state your controls, and a licensed accountancy firm tests them against the Trust Services Criteria A report with the auditor's opinion, either at a point in time (Type 1) or over a period, usually six to twelve months (Type 2)
GDPR Law: obligations on controllers and processors of personal data about individuals in the European Union, enforced by supervisory authorities and courts No certificate in normal practice; the test is whether you can demonstrate compliance when asked, and the consequence of failure is enforcement
NIST CSF 2.0 A voluntary framework of outcomes in six functions, used to describe current and target posture and to talk to boards and partners Self-assessed, or assessed by a consultant; produces profiles and tiers, not a certificate

3. Where they genuinely differ

Treating the frameworks as interchangeable is the mistake that costs most. They differ on five dimensions, and each difference changes what an assessor will accept.

Dimension Management system (ISO/IEC 27001 and 27701) Attestation (SOC 2) Law (GDPR) Framework (NIST CSF 2.0)
What is assessed The system: scope, risk, objectives, review, audit, improvement, and the controls it chose The controls you stated in your description, and whether they met the criteria Each processing activity: lawful, transparent, limited, secure, demonstrable Outcomes achieved, measured against a target profile
Who decides the controls You, from your risk assessment, checked against Annex A and justified in the Statement of Applicability You, against the criteria; the auditor tests what you claim The law sets the obligations; you choose the measures and must justify them You, through the profile you set
Time dimension A point of certification, then a cycle; records must show the system has operated A defined period; every control must have operated throughout it, and the sample is drawn from the period Always; an obligation applies at the moment it applies, with fixed clocks for notification and rights A snapshot, repeated when you choose
What failure looks like Nonconformities that must be closed before the certificate is issued or kept Exceptions written into the report, which readers see Complaints, investigations, orders and fines A gap between current and target profile
Scope language A scope statement naming locations, services and systems A system description naming services, components, boundaries and subservice organisations The processing activities in your records of processing The organisation or the part you chose to profile

Two consequences follow. First, a SOC 2 auditor cannot accept the ISO certificate as evidence of operation, because the certificate says nothing about the period or the sample; and an ISO auditor cannot accept a SOC 2 report as proof of a management system, because the report never looked for one. Second, the GDPR is not a control set. Security controls satisfy one article; the lawful basis, the notices, the records of processing, the rights process and the breach clock are obligations no security framework will give you.

4. How GOV-REG-27 works

GOV-REG-27 has one row for each of the 93 Annex A controls, carrying the theme in the kit's own words, the SOC 2 criteria the control contributes to, the GDPR articles it helps satisfy, the NIST CSF 2.0 categories whose outcomes it supports, the kit documents that implement it, a note, and a status for your own review of the mapping.

Read a row from left to right as a chain of questions. Take the control for access grant and review. The theme reminds you what the control is. The SOC 2 column says that this one piece of work contributes to the criteria on user registration and removal and on role-based access with periodic review. The GDPR column says it is one of the measures that answer the security obligation. The CSF column points at the identity and access category. The kit column names GOV-PRO-10, GOV-TPL-09 and GOV-REG-12 as the procedure, the form and the record. The same evidence folder entry, a dated access review export with the reviewer's decisions, is what all four assessors will be shown.

Four rules govern the register:

  1. Mapping is partial, and the notes say where. A criterion listed against a control means the control contributes to it, not that it satisfies it alone. Most SOC 2 criteria draw on several controls and on the management system clauses as well.
  2. A mapping is never evidence. The crosswalk tells you which evidence to show to whom. The assessor then tests it to their own rules.
  3. "none" means none. Where a framework has no requirement a control serves, the cell says so. Do not fill the gap with the nearest sounding criterion; an assessor will read it as not understanding their framework.
  4. The register is reviewed annually and when any framework changes edition. Set the Status column to To review for every row at that point and confirm each mapping before resetting it to Confirmed.

The clause 4 to 10 requirements of ISO/IEC 27001 are not in the crosswalk because they have no Annex A number. Their SOC 2 relatives are the CC1 to CC5 criteria and the criteria on monitoring; ISMS-GDE-02 lists the mandatory items and SOC-GDE-03 maps the criteria to the kit.

5. The tag approach: one register, framework tags

Never keep two risk registers, two corrective action logs or two audit programmes. Add a Frameworks column to each shared register and fill it with tags: ISO27001, ISO27701, SOC2, GDPR, CSF. The registers that take tags are GOV-REG-05 for risks, ISMS-REG-02 for controls, GOV-REG-03 for corrective actions, GOV-REG-02 for audits, GOV-REG-04 for obligations and the evidence index in each area of the evidence folder.

Tags come from GOV-REG-27 and from GOV-REG-04, never from memory. A control row in ISMS-REG-02 inherits the tags of its crosswalk row. A risk inherits the tags of the controls that treat it. A corrective action inherits the tags of the control or clause it was raised against. An audit in GOV-REG-02 lists the tags of the criteria it covered.

What the tags buy you:

  • A filter. When the SOC 2 auditor sends the request list, filter every register on SOC2 and you have the population they will sample from. When the certification auditor arrives, filter on ISO27001.
  • One audit programme. ISMS-PLN-03 already covers every applicable control; the SOC 2 criteria ride on the same audits through the tags, and GOV-PRO-02 names them as criteria.
  • One corrective action loop. A SOC 2 exception, an ISO nonconformity and a GDPR gap all become GOV-REG-03 rows and are closed the same way.
  • One steering report. The quarterly report under ISMS-PRO-04 shows measures by tag, so the committee sees the SOC 2 period and the ISO cycle in the same table.

The frequency rule: a control is operated and tested at the strictest frequency any tagged framework needs, and only once. If the SOC 2 period needs quarterly evidence of a control that ISO would accept annually, it is quarterly, and the ISO auditor receives four records instead of one.

6. Evidence reuse

The same artefact answers a different question for each assessor. Collect it so that it answers all of them.

Artefact ISO asks SOC 2 asks GDPR asks CSF asks
Quarterly access review export with decisions, GOV-REG-12 Does the control exist, apply, and operate as the procedure says Did it operate every quarter of the period; sample two and trace the removals Is access to personal data limited to those who need it, and can you show it Is the identity and access outcome achieved and improving
Change ticket export, GOV-REG-11 Are changes controlled per the procedure, including emergency changes For a sample of twenty-five changes across the period, were approval and testing recorded before deployment Were changes to processing assessed for privacy impact where needed Is platform change managed as an outcome
Incident record and post-incident review, GOV-REG-08 and GOV-TPL-11 Was the incident process followed and were lessons fed to improvement Was each incident in the period evaluated, responded to and communicated Was the breach assessed within the notification clock and documented even when not notified Were detection, response and recovery outcomes met
Training completion export, GOV-REG-09 Is competence and awareness evidenced for the roles Did every person in the period complete the training the policy requires Were staff handling personal data made aware of their obligations Is the awareness outcome achieved

The collection rules in PB-09 already meet the strictest reader. Three additions matter when frameworks combine. Date coverage: SOC 2 samples are drawn across the whole period, so evidence that exists only for the month before the ISO audit fails the SOC 2 test; collect on the control's own rhythm, every time. Population exports: SOC 2 auditors sample from populations they choose, so keep the full export, not the items you think are interesting. Retention: keep evidence for the longest of the ISO cycle, the SOC 2 period plus the next period, and any contract term in GOV-REG-04.

7. What cannot be shared

Some artefacts belong to one framework and have no equivalent in another. Budget for them separately and do not try to make one document do two jobs.

  • The SOC 2 system description and the management assertion. Written in the form SOC-TPL-01 sets out, signed by management, and read word for word by the auditor and by every customer who receives the report. ISMS-STM-01 is a source for it, not a substitute.
  • The SOC 2 auditor's own tests. You cannot hand the attestation firm your internal audit and expect it to be relied on. Your internal audit is evidence of monitoring under the criteria; their tests are theirs.
  • The mandatory ISO records. The scope statement, the risk assessment method and results, the Statement of Applicability, the objectives, the management review minutes and the internal audit records are required by clauses 4 to 10. SOC 2 does not ask for a Statement of Applicability and the GDPR does not ask for a management review; neither excuses you from producing them for the certificate.
  • The ISO/IEC 27701 layer. The controller or processor role decision under PIMS-PRO-01, the applicability of the Annex A and Annex B controls, and the privacy extensions to risk and to the Statement of Applicability. PB-05 covers adding them.
  • The GDPR obligations that are not controls. The lawful basis for each processing activity, the records of processing in PIMS-REG-01, impact assessments under PIMS-PRO-02, the notices from GDPR-TPL-01 to GDPR-TPL-04, the rights process under PIMS-PRO-03, the breach clock under PIMS-PRO-04, processor terms from PIMS-TPL-02 and transfer mechanisms under PIMS-POL-03. A certificate and a clean SOC 2 report together leave every one of these untouched.
  • The CSF profile. Current and target profiles and the tier are a separate exercise in describing posture; they reuse the evidence but are not produced by any audit.
  • The assessors and their rules. A certification body works under accreditation rules; an attestation firm under professional standards; a supervisory authority under the law. None of them will adopt another's sampling, period or conclusion.
  • The words you may use. "Certified to ISO/IEC 27001" needs a certificate with the scope wording from ISMS-STM-01. A SOC 2 report is "has obtained a SOC 2 Type 2 report for the period", never "SOC 2 certified". Nothing is "GDPR certified" unless an approved certification scheme says so. ISMS-PLN-02 section 3 holds the safe wording.

8. Adding a framework to a set you already run

Starting point What you already have What you add Kit documents
ISO/IEC 27001 certified, adding SOC 2 Policies, procedures, risk register, controls with evidence, internal audit, corrective actions The system description and assertion; a control matrix stated against the criteria; a period with continuous evidence; a control testing and sampling procedure; the subservice organisation review SOC-TPL-01, SOC-REG-01, SOC-REG-02, SOC-PRO-01, SOC-PRO-02, PB-03
SOC 2 report in hand, adding ISO/IEC 27001 Controls with period evidence, a change and incident history, vendor reviews Scope and context, a risk method and assessment, the Statement of Applicability, objectives and measures, competence records, the internal audit cycle and the management review ISMS-STM-01, ISMS-PRO-01, GOV-PRO-05, ISMS-REG-01, ISMS-PLN-01, ISMS-PRO-02, GOV-PRO-02, GOV-PRO-03, PB-02
Either, adding the GDPR Security measures and evidence, supplier register, incident process The processing inventory, lawful bases, notices, rights process, breach assessment, processor terms, retention schedule, transfer assessments PIMS-REG-01, GDPR-PRO-01, PIMS-PRO-03, PIMS-PRO-04, PIMS-TPL-02, PIMS-POL-02, GDPR-TPL-08, PB-04
ISO/IEC 27001, adding ISO/IEC 27701 The management system Privacy scope and roles, privacy risk, Annex A and Annex B applicability, the privacy registers PIMS-POL-01, PIMS-PRO-01, PIMS-PRO-02, PIMS-GDE-01, PB-05
Any, describing posture with NIST CSF 2.0 Everything above A current and target profile and a tier, drawn from ISMS-REG-02 through the CSF column of GOV-REG-27 GOV-REG-27, ISMS-REG-02

In every case the order is the same: tag what exists, from GOV-REG-27 and GOV-REG-04; list what the new framework needs that nothing serves; create only those items; run one calendar.

9. One calendar

The management system runs on a calendar, and a second framework adds events to it rather than a second calendar. ISMS-PLN-03 fixes the audits, SOC-REG-02 fixes the recurring evidence events for a SOC 2 period, and ISMS-PLN-02 fixes the communications. Put all three in one shared calendar with an owner per event. The quarterly rhythm that satisfies every framework at once is: access reviews, restore tests, Tier 1 supplier reviews, steering committee with the measures report, vulnerability closure review, privacy measures review under PIMS-PRO-07, and the audit for that quarter. The annual rhythm adds the risk assessment, the management review, the policy reviews, the awareness refresher, the continuity exercise, the crosswalk review and the SOC 2 period close.

10. Mistakes to avoid

  1. Treating a mapping as compliance. A row in GOV-REG-27 proves nothing; the evidence behind the control does.
  2. Mapping at the level of titles. Two requirements with similar names often test different things; map requirement to requirement and write the partial cases in the notes.
  3. Answering a SOC 2 request with "covered by our ISO certificate". The auditor needs the period evidence, not the certificate.
  4. Keeping a risk register per framework. One register, tagged, or the two will disagree in front of an auditor.
  5. Keeping an evidence folder per framework. One folder, indexed by control and tagged, as PB-09 describes.
  6. Writing a policy per framework. One policy per topic; the frameworks are listed in its control block.
  7. Treating the GDPR as a control set and forgetting the obligations in section 7.
  8. Forgetting the period. A control switched on the month before the ISO audit is a SOC 2 exception for every earlier month.
  9. Claiming a certification that a crosswalk suggests you deserve. Only a certificate, a report or a scheme supports a claim.
  10. Letting the crosswalk go stale when a framework changes edition.

Master list of documents and records

The index of every controlled document and record in the management system. One row per document, with its current version, owner, approver, location and review dates. Updated whenever a document is issued, changed or withdrawn.

  • Document ID: The permanent identifier

  • Type

  • Approver (role)

  • Status
  • Effective date
  • Next review
  • Location: The single approved location of the current version.

Framework crosswalk

One row per Annex A control of ISO/IEC 27001:2022, recording the SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria the control contributes to, the GDPR articles it helps satisfy, the NIST CSF 2.0 categories whose outcomes it supports and the kit documents that implement it. Used to tag the shared registers and the evidence folder so that one control set serves every framework, as PB-10 describes; a mapping shows which evidence to present to whom, never that a requirement is met.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.3; SOC 2 CC4.1; GDPR Article 24; GDPR Article 32; NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC.

Columns:

  • Annex A control
  • Theme: The same plain words as ISMS-REG-01. Read the standard for the authoritative text.
  • SOC 2 criteria: Criteria the control contributes to
  • GDPR articles: Articles the control helps satisfy. Security controls mostly serve Article 32; none means the regulation has no requirement this control serves.
  • NIST CSF 2.0 category: Category identifiers in the form of function and category
  • Kit documents: Kit IDs separated by semicolons
  • Notes: Where a mapping is partial or conditional.
  • Status: Your own review of the row. Set every row to To review when a framework changes edition.
  • Last reviewed

Audit programme and findings

The internal audit programme for the whole cycle, one row per audit, from planning to closure. It shows what was audited, by whom, when, and how many findings of each grade the report raised, so that coverage of every clause and applicable control can be demonstrated.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 9.2.1; SOC 2 CC4.1.

Columns:

  • Audit ID: One per audit, for example IA followed by year and sequence number.
  • Period: The quarter or month in which the audit is planned.
  • Scope: Areas, processes and systems covered.
  • Criteria: Clauses, Annex A controls, SOC 2 criteria and kit documents audited.
  • Auditor (role): Must be independent of the area audited.
  • Auditee (role)
  • Start date
  • End date
  • Status
  • Major: Count of major nonconformities in the report.
  • Minor
  • Observation
  • Opportunity
  • Total findings
  • Report reference: Reference of the GOV-TPL-01 report and where it is stored.
  • Notes: Postponement approvals, independence arrangements, follow-up dates.
GOV-REG-03 register Download .xlsx

Corrective action log

Every nonconformity, observation and opportunity from any source, followed from raising to verified closure under GOV-PRO-04. One row per GOV-TPL-02 form, so that overdue actions, repeated root causes and the effectiveness of corrections can be reported.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 10.1; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 10.2; SOC 2 CC4.2; SOC 2 CC5.3.

Columns:

  • CAR ID: Assigned by the Information Security Manager; matches the GOV-TPL-02 form.
  • Source
  • Source reference: Audit ID, incident ID, review date or complaint reference.
  • Raised date
  • Raised by (role)
  • Description: The statement of nonconformity: what was observed against which requirement.
  • Grade
  • Root cause: The cause the organisation can act on, from the five whys or fishbone analysis.
  • Corrective action: Summary of the plan on the form.
  • Owner (role)
  • Due date: Within 30 days of raising for a major, 90 for a minor, unless an extension is recorded in Notes.
  • Status
  • Effectiveness check date: At least 90 days after implementation, by someone other than the owner.
  • Effectiveness result
  • Closed by (role): Information Security Manager for a minor; executive sponsor for a major.
  • Closed date
GOV-REG-04 register Download .xlsx

Legal, regulatory and contractual register

The list of obligations that apply to the organisation's information, privacy and records, one row per distinct requirement, maintained under GOV-PRO-25. Each row ties the obligation to the controls and documents that satisfy it, the evidence that proves it, and a status that shows where gaps remain.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.31; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A 5.34; SOC 2 CC2.3; GDPR Article 24.

Columns:

  • Reference: Sequential reference used in ISMS-REG-01 justifications and risk entries.
  • Obligation: What is required, in plain words. One requirement per row.
  • Source: The law, regulation, contract, scheme rule or guidance, with article or clause.
  • Jurisdiction
  • Applies as
  • Owner (role)
  • Controls and documents: Kit document IDs and Annex A controls that satisfy the obligation.
  • Evidence: The record or export that proves compliance and where it is kept.
  • Status
  • Review frequency
  • Last review
  • Next review
  • Linked risk or action: GOV-REG-05 or GOV-REG-03 reference raised for a Gap or Partial status.
  • Notes
GOV-REG-05 register Download .xlsx

Information security risk register

Every information security and privacy risk scenario identified under GOV-PRO-05, with its raw and residual ratings, treatment decision, owner and review dates. The score and band columns calculate from the 1 to 5 scales so that two assessors produce the same result and acceptance goes to the right authority.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 8.2; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 8.3; ISO/IEC 27701 clause 5.4.1.2; SOC 2 CC3.1; SOC 2 CC3.2; GDPR Article 32.

Columns:

  • Risk ID: Permanent reference, never reused.
  • Asset or process: The asset from GOV-REG-10 or the process at risk.
  • Risk scenario: A named threat exploits a named vulnerability on the asset, with the consequence.
  • Threat: Environmental, technical failure, human error, insider misuse, external attack, supplier failure, legal change.
  • Vulnerability: Technical weakness, missing or weak control, process gap, skill gap, physical exposure, contractual gap.
  • Existing controls: Controls in place and operating today.
  • Likelihood (1 to 5): Per the GOV-PRO-05 scale, with existing controls.
  • Impact (1 to 5): Worst credible consequence per the GOV-PRO-05 scale.
  • Score
  • Band
  • Treatment option
  • Treatment plan and SoA references: Actions, the Annex A controls applied and the kit documents that implement them, and the target band.
  • Risk owner (role)
  • Due date: Date by which the treatment is to be implemented.
  • Residual likelihood (1 to 5): Expected once the treatment is implemented and verified.
  • Residual impact (1 to 5)
  • Residual score
  • Status
  • Last review
  • Next review: Monthly for Critical, quarterly for High, twice a year for Medium, annually for Low.
GOV-REG-06 register Download .xlsx

Risk acceptance and exception register

Every approved deviation from a policy or control and every acceptance of a risk above appetite, recorded under GOV-PRO-24 with its approver, duration and expiry. The expiry and days-to-expiry columns calculate from the approval date and duration so that nothing runs past its limit unnoticed.

Serves: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 6.1.3; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 8.3; SOC 2 CC3.2; SOC 2 CC5.1.

Columns:

  • Reference: Matches the GOV-TPL-06 form.
  • Type
  • Linked risk ID: The GOV-REG-05 entry.
  • Description: What is being deviated from or accepted, and why.
  • Requirement deviated from: Document ID and statement, or Annex A control.
  • Compensating controls
  • Band before: Without compensating controls.
  • Band after: With compensating controls; determines the approver.
  • Requested by (role)
  • Approver (role): Low: Information Security Manager. Medium: plus head of function. High: executive sponsor. Critical: Chief Executive Officer.
  • Approval date
  • Duration (months): Maximum 12. Maximum 3 for a Critical band.
  • Expiry date
  • Days to expiry
  • Status
  • Review outcome: Closed with evidence, renewed under a new reference, escalated, or expired.
